SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Arrhythmia is disturbance in heart rate or rhythm

Arrhythmia can be congenital or acquired

ecgpedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Complications

Acute decrease in cardiac output => Heart failure

Degeneration into another arrhythmia such as VF

If continuous may lead to cardiomyopathy

Syncope or sudden death

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Treatment

Medications

Transcatheter ablation

Pacemakers

Defibrillators

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Antiarrhythmic Drugs

Although majority of antiarrhythmic drugs are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in children; but most are still used off label

Arrhythmia mechanism may be different for the pediatric than the adult population.

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Antiarrhythmic Drugs

There may be marked differences in antiarrhythmic drugs pharmacokinetics by age and in comparison, with adults.

Infants may have slower absorption and gastric emptying

Differing sizes of drug tissue compartments affecting the Vd

Hepatic metabolism and renal excretion may vary within the pediatric age-group as well as in comparison to adults

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Antiarrhythmic Drugs

Antiarrhythmic drugs are categorized using the Vaughan-Williams classification

This system comprises 4 classes:

Class I includes agents that primarily block the sodium channel, This is further divided by the strength of the sodium channel blockade (a, b, c)

Class II drugs are the β-blockers

Class III includes agents that prolong repolarization by blocking potassium channels

Class IV drugs are the calcium channel blockers

Sertion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Sinus arrhythmia

Normal physiologic variation in impulse discharges from the sinus node related to respirations

The heart rate slows during expiration and accelerates during inspiration

Occasionally, if the sinus rate becomes slow enough, an escape beat arises from the atrioventricular junction

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Sinus arrhythmia

Sinus arrhythmia characteristics

Variation in P-P interval

No change in P-wave morphology

No change in PR interval

Rocuronium Bromide, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Sinus bradycardia

Slow discharge of impulses from the sinus node,

Rate <90 in neonates and <60 in older children

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Sinus bradycardia

Maybe associated with hypothyroidism, conditions with high vagal tone such as GIT obstruction or elevated intracranial pressure

Frequently associated with junctional escape beats and premature atrial contractions.

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Sinus bradycardia

Sinus bradycardia characteristics:

P wave is present (sinus rhythm)

Rate is below 90 for neonates and 60 for infants and children

James Heilman, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Wandering atrial pacemaker

Intermittent shift in the pacemaker of the heart from the sinus node to another part of the atrium.

It may also be seen in association with sinus bradycardia in which the shift in atrial focus is an escape phenomenon.

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Wandering atrial pacemaker

Wandering atrial pacemaker characteristics:

P wave is present but it differs in shape between beats (depending on its origin if it is sinus or atrial)

There maybe fusion between the sinus P and the ectopic atrial pacemaker

Rocuronium Bromide, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Extrasystole

Produced by the premature discharge of an ectopic focus that may be situated in the atrium, the AV junction, or the ventricle.

Divided into premature atrial contractions (PACs) and premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)

Isolated extrasystoles are of no clinical or prognostic significance, while frequent extrasystoles may be caused by organic heart disease (inflammation, ischemia, fibrosis) or drug toxicity.

SOURCE SLIDE 16

PACs

Common in childhood, in the absence of cardiac disease.

Depending on the degree of prematurity of the beat and preceding R-R interval, PACs may result in a normal, a prolonged (aberrancy), or an absent (blocked PAC) QRS complex.

SOURCE SLIDE 17

PACs

ECG shows either a premature P wave superimposed on and deforming the preceding T wave or a P wave that is premature and has a different contour from that of the other sinus P waves.

PACs may reset the sinus node pacemaker, leading to an incomplete compensatory pause

SOURCE SLIDE 18

PVCs

Arise in any region of the ventricles.

Characterized by premature, widened, bizarre QRS complexes that are not preceded by a premature P wave.

Classified into uniform and multiform

SOURCE SLIDE 19

PVCs

Often, but not always, followed by a full compensatory pause.

Presence of fusion beats proves the ventricular origin of the premature beat.

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Extrasystoles

Extrasystoles produce a smaller stroke and pulse volume than normal

Frequent, extrasystoles may lead to a definite rhythm, e.g., Bigeminy and trigeminy

Daniel Nofftz, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Extrasystoles

Most patients are unaware of single PVCs, while some may be aware of a “skipped beat” over the precordium. This sensation is caused by the increased stroke volume of the normal beat +after a compensatory pause.

Anxiety, a febrile illness, or ingestion of various drugs or stimulants may exacerbate PVCs.

SOURCE SLIDE 22

It is important to distinguish PVCs that are benign from those that are likely to lead to more severe arrhythmias.

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Criteria to furtherly investigate PVCs or not

≥2 PVCs in a row

Multiform PVCs

Increased ventricular ectopic activity with exercise

R-on-T phenomenon

Extreme frequency of beats

Presence of underlying heart disease, a history of heart surgery, or both.

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Treatment

Benign PVCs is reassurance

Malignant PVCs are usually secondary to another medical problem

Treat the underlying cause

Lidocaine, amiodarone …

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Tachycardias

Supraventricular

Ventricular

Madhero88 CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 26

AVRT

Occur in presence of an accessory pathway

in conditions such as WPW syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 27

WPW syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 28

AVNRT

SOURCE SLIDE 29

SVT Treatment

Vagal stimulation Valsalva maneuver, straining, breath holding, or standing on their head

Adenosine, DC

SOURCE SLIDE 30

Refractory SVT

Holter monitoring

EPS studies

SOURCE SLIDE 31

Atrial ectopic tachycardia

Tachycardia originating in a single focus in the atria

SOURCE SLIDE 32

Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Originating from multiple different foci within the atria > 3

Common in infants without cardiac disease

Goal is to slow the ventricular rate

SOURCE SLIDE 33

Accelerated junctional ectopic tachycardia (JET)

Automatic (non reentry) arrhythmia in which junctional rate > sinus node rate

Occur in early postoperative period after cardiac surgery

Reduction of infusion rate of catecholamines and control of fever and pain, amiodarone, sotalol

SOURCE SLIDE 34

Atrial flutter

Supraventricular tachycardia

Intraatrial reentry circuit at a rate of 250-300 in children, 400-600 in neonates

AV node cannot transmit rapid impulses, so some AV block is always present

SOURCE SLIDE 35

Treatment

DC cardioversion

Anticoagulation before conversion

B blockers , CCB

Class I and III antiarrhythmics

Catheter ablation

SOURCE SLIDE 36

Atrial fibillation

Supraventricular tachycardia

Intraatrial reentry circuit that is more chaotic at a rate of 400-700 beats/min

Produces an irregularly irregular ventricular response and pulse

SOURCE SLIDE 37

Ventricular tachycardia

at least 3 consecutive PVCs at >120 beats/min

paroxysmal or incessant

Associated with cardiac disease, prolonged QT interval, WPW syndrome and drug use

SOURCE SLIDE 38

Treatment

DC cardioversion

Amiodarone, lidocaine, procainamide

Temporary or permanent pacemaker

SOURCE SLIDE 39

Ventricular fibrillation

Chaotic intra ventricular reentry rhythm that result in cardiac arrest

CPR and DC defibrillation

Amiodarone or lidocaine

SOURCE SLIDE 40

Long QT syndromes

QTc interval > 480ms

Long QT is associated with torsades de pointes and VF => syncope and sudden death

SOURCE SLIDE 41

Types

Mutations in cardiac potassium and sodium channels

13 variants of long QT syndrome = LQT1, LQT2 …

LQT 1 induced by stress or exertion, LQT3 induced by sleep

Treated by B blockers , pacemaker due to bradycardia

ICD implantation

SOURCE SLIDE 42

Short QT syndromes

Atrial or ventricular fibrillation

Associated with syncope and sudden death

Caused by a gain-of-function mutation in cardiac potassium channels

SOURCE SLIDE 43

Sinus node dysfunction

Sinus arrest

Sinoatrial block

Sick sinus syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 44

Atrioventricular block

First degree

Second degree

Third degree

Definition

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Pneumonia

Pneumonia, is inflammation of the lower respiratory tract (lung parenchyma)

The etiology, clinical presentation, and severity of pneumonia vary greatly based on the age of the child

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Epidemiology

It is the leading infectious cause of death globally among children younger than 5 yr.

Pneumonia mortality is closely linked to poverty, More than 99% of pneumonia deaths are in low- and middle-income countries, with the highest pneumonia mortality rate occurring in poorly developed countries in Africa and South Asia.

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Etiology

Infectious

Pneumonia is mostly caused by viruses, RSV and rhinovirus being the most common, others include influenza virus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and enteroviruses

In neonates (age 0 to 4 weeks), microorganisms in the birth canal such as group B streptococci, Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes are common causes.

S. Pneumonia is the most common bacterial pathogen causing pneumonia in children 4 weeks to 4 years of age while Mycoplasma pneumonia and Chlamydophila pneumonia are most common in children older than 5

S. aureus pneumonia often complicates an illness caused by influenza virus

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Etiology

Infectious

In children with HIV (immunocompromised), pneumonia can be caused by M. tuberculosis, salmonella, E. coli, Pneumocystis jiroveci, pseudomonas and cytomegalovirus

Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, which should be considered when the mother had little or no prenatal care.

Pneumonia can also be caused by aspiration (food, gastric acid, foreign bodies, hydrocarbons or lipoid substances), Hypersensitivity reactions and Drug and radiation induced

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

Viral pneumonia usually results from spread of the virus along the airways, accompanied by direct injury to the respiratory epithelium, which results in airway inflammation then obstruction due to swelling, abnormal secretions, and cellular debris.

The small caliber of airways in young infants (can easily get obstructed) makes such patients particularly susceptible to severe infection.

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

Atelectasis, interstitial edema, and hypoxemia from ventilation–perfusion mismatch often accompany airway obstruction.

Viral infection of the lower respiratory tract lead to disturbance of normal host defense mechanisms (which include mucociliary clearance, macrophages and secretory immunoglobulin A) and also lead to disturbance in respiratory microbiota, this ultimately may lead to secondary bacterial infection

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Pathophysiology

Bacterial pneumonia most often occurs when respiratory tract organisms colonize the trachea and subsequently gain access to the lungs, and pneumonia can also result from direct invasion of lung tissue due to bacteremia.

When bacterial infection is established in the lung parenchyma, the pathologic process varies according to the invading organism.

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Pathophysiology

Mycoplasma pneumoniae attaches to the respiratory epithelium, inhibits ciliary action, and leads to cellular destruction and an inflammatory response in the submucosa. As the infection progresses, sloughed cellular debris, inflammatory cells, and mucus cause airway obstruction, with spread of infection occurring along the bronchial tree, as is seen in viral pneumonia.

S. pneumoniae produces local edema that aids in the proliferation of organisms and their spread into adjacent portions of lung, often resulting in the characteristic focal lobar involvement.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Pathophysiology

Group A streptococcus lower respiratory tract infection typically results in more diffuse lung involvement with interstitial pneumonia. It causes necrosis of tracheobronchial mucosa; formation of large amounts of exudate, edema, and local hemorrhage, with extension into the interalveolar septa; and involvement of lymphatic vessels with frequent pleural involvement.

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Pathophysiology

S. aureus pneumonia manifests as confluent bronchopneumonia, which is often unilateral and characterized by the presence of extensive areas of hemorrhagic necrosis and irregular areas of cavitation of the lung parenchyma, resulting in pneumatoceles, empyema, and, at times, bronchopulmonary fistulas.

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Recurrent pneumonia

Recurrent pneumonia is defined as 2 or more episodes in a single year or 3 or more episodes ever, with radiographic clearing between occurrences.

An underlying disorder should be considered if a child experiences recurrent pneumonia

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Clinical features

The clinical presentation of pneumonia varies with the age of the patient, although most pediatric patients will have some combination of fever, preceding viral illness, tachypnea, respiratory distress, rales, and diminished breath sounds.

Tachypnea is the most sensitive finding in pediatric patients with pneumonia.

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Clinical features

Pneumonia is usually accompanied by respiratory distress which manifest as Increased work of breathing accompanied by intercostal, subcostal, and suprasternal retractions, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles is common.

Severe infection may be accompanied by cyanosis and lethargy, especially in infants.

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Clinical features

Auscultation of the chest may reveal crackles and wheezing, but it is often difficult to localize the source of these sounds in very young children with hyperresonant chests.

In viral pneumonia, fever is usually present but temperatures are generally lower than in bacterial pneumonia.

It is often not possible to distinguish viral pneumonia clinically from disease caused by Mycoplasma and other bacterial pathogens.

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Clinical features

Bacterial pneumonia in older children typically begins suddenly with high fever, cough, and chest pain.

Other symptoms that may be seen include drowsiness with intermittent periods of restlessness, anxiety; and, occasionally, delirium.

In many children, splinting on the affected side to minimize pleuritic pain and improve ventilation is noted; such children may lie on one side with the knees drawn up to the chest.

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Clinical features

Abdominal pain is common in lower-lobe pneumonia due to abdominal distention caused by gastric dilation from swallowed air or ileus.

The liver may seem enlarged because of downward displacement of the diaphragm secondary to hyperinflation of the lungs or superimposed congestive heart failure.

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Clinical features

In infants, there may be a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection and poor feeding, leading to the abrupt onset of fever, restlessness, apprehension, and respiratory distress.

These infants typically appear ill, with respiratory distress manifested as grunting; nasal flaring; retractions of the supraclavicular, intercostal, and subcostal areas; tachypnea; tachycardia; air hunger; and often cyanosis.

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Clinical features

Auscultation may be misleading, particularly in young infants, with findings disproportionate to the degree of tachypnea.

Some infants with bacterial pneumonia may have associated gastrointestinal disturbances characterized by vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, and abdominal distention secondary to a paralytic ileus.

Rapid progression of symptoms is characteristic in the most severe cases of bacterial pneumonia.

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Diagnosis

For most pneumonias, the etiologic agent is never determined.

The diagnosis of pneumonia should primarily be made on clinical grounds; chest radiography is not required and not considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Chest radiography is not 100% sensitive, nor specific for the diagnosis of pneumonia, and does not distinguish between bacterial or viral etiologies. The presence of fever plus tachypnea, decreased breath sounds, or fine crackles predicts pneumonia with 93% to 96% sensitivity. If all four variables are present, the sensitivity is 98%

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Diagnosis

The peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count can be useful in differentiating viral from bacterial pneumonia.

In viral pneumonia, the WBC count can be normal or elevated but is usually not higher than 20,000/mm3 , with a lymphocyte predominance.

Bacterial pneumonia is often associated with an elevated WBC count, in the range of 15,000-40,000/mm3 , and a predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Diagnosis

The definitive diagnosis of a viral infection can be done by detection of viral genome or antigen in respiratory tract secretions using PCR assays

The definitive diagnosis of a typical bacterial infection requires isolation of an organism from the blood, pleural fluid, or lung.

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Diagnosis

Culture of sputum is of little value in the diagnosis of pneumonia in young children, and percutaneous lung aspiration is invasive and not routinely performed.

Blood culture is positive in only 10% of children with pneumococcal pneumonia and only recommended for children who fail to improve or have clinical deterioration, have complicated pneumonia, or require hospitalization. So they are not recommended for nontoxic-appearing children treated as outpatients.

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Diagnosis

Urinary antigen tests should not be used to diagnose pneumonia caused by S. pneumoniae in children because of a high rate of false positives resulting from nasopharyngeal carriage.

Pertussis infection can be diagnosed by PCR or culture of a nasopharyngeal specimen; although culture is considered the gold standard for pertussis diagnosis, it is less sensitive than the available PCR assays

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Diagnosis

Ultrasonography is highly sensitive and specific in diagnosing pneumonia in children by determining lung consolidations and air bronchograms or effusions.

However, the reliability of this imaging modality for pneumonia diagnosis is highly user-dependent, which has limited its widespread use.

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Diagnosis

Routine laboratory testing is not required for well-appearing children with mild community-acquired pneumonia.

For neonates or older patients with significant respiratory distress or toxic appearance, a blood culture, complete blood count, and serum electrolytes should be obtained.

Rapid viral antigen testing (if available) for RSV, influenza, and human metapneumovirus can be valuable if they are quick and specific, as results may negate the need for imaging, invasive testing, and antibiotic therapy.

SOURCE SLIDE 27

Diagnosis

Chest radiography should be reserved for patients in which the differential diagnosis is in question (aspirated foreign body, congestive heart failure, mediastinal mass) or a complication of pneumonia is suspected (failure of outpatient therapy, pleural effusion, cavitary pneumonia, significant patient comorbidities, age <3 months).

SOURCE SLIDE 28

Diagnosis

An infiltrate on chest radiograph (posteroanterior and lateral views) supports the diagnosis of pneumonia; images may show a complication such as a pleural effusion or empyema.

Viral pneumonia is usually characterized by hyperinflation with bilateral interstitial infiltrates and peribronchial cuffing.

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 29

Diagnosis

Repeat chest radiographs are not required for proof of cure for patients with uncomplicated pneumonia.

Diawara Zerouali,Elmdaghri,Abid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 30

Treatment

Treatment of suspected bacterial pneumonia is based on the presumptive cause and the age and clinical appearance of the child.

Neonates and infants younger than 90 days suspected for pneumonia should be hospitalized and given ampicillin + aminoglycoside or third generation cephalosporin (not ceftriaxone)

SOURCE SLIDE 31

Treatment

For mildly ill children over 3 months, with mild symptoms, can be treated outpatient with amoxicillin. With the emergence of penicillin-resistant pneumococci, high doses of amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day orally twice daily) should be prescribed unless local data indicate a low prevalence of resistance. alternatives include cefuroxime and amoxicillin/clavulanate.

SOURCE SLIDE 32

Treatment

For school-aged children and adolescents Azithromycin is preferred, while clarithromycin or doxycycline (for children 8 yr or older) are alternatives. For adolescents, a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) may also be considered if there are contraindications to other agents.

SOURCE SLIDE 33

Treatment

The empiric treatment of suspected bacterial pneumonia in a hospitalized child requires an approach based on local epidemiology, the immunization status of the child, and the clinical manifestations at the time of presentation.

In areas without substantial high-level penicillin resistance among S. pneumoniae , children who are fully immunized against H. influenzae type b and S. pneumoniae and are not severely ill should receive ampicillin or penicillin G.

SOURCE SLIDE 34

Treatment

For children who do not meet these criteria, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime may be used.

If clinical features suggest staphylococcal pneumonia (pneumatoceles, empyema), initial antimicrobial therapy should also include vancomycin or clindamycin.

if infection with M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae is suspected, a macrolide antibiotic should be included in the treatment regimen.

SOURCE SLIDE 35

Treatment

If viral pneumonia is suspected, it is reasonable to withhold antibiotic therapy, especially for preschool-aged patients who are mildly ill, have clinical evidence suggesting viral infection, and are in no respiratory distress.

However, up to 30% of patients with known viral infection, particularly influenza viruses, may have coexisting bacterial pathogens. Therefore, if the decision is made to withhold antibiotic therapy on the basis of presumptive diagnosis of a viral infection, deterioration in clinical status should signal the possibility of superimposed bacterial infection, and antibiotic therapy should be initiated.

SOURCE SLIDE 36

Treatment

Antibiotics should generally be continued until the patient has been afebrile for 72 hr, and the total duration should not be less than 10 days (or 5 days if azithromycin is used).

Shorter courses (5-7 days) may also be effective, particularly for children managed on an outpatient basis.

Studies suggest that a reduction of previously elevated serum procalcitonin levels to an absolute level (0.1-0.25 µg/L) may help determine when to stop treatment.

SOURCE SLIDE 37

Treatment

In addition to antibiotics, oral zinc (10 mg/day for < 12 mo, 20 mg/day for ≥ 12 mo given for 7 days) accelerates healing and reduce mortality among children with clinically defined severe pneumonia.

CPAP improves mortality from pneumonia with hypoxemia compared with standard oxygen therapy in settings without access to ventilator derived CPAP or mechanical ventilation.

SOURCE SLIDE 38

Treatment

Oxygen should be given for respiratory distress or oxygen saturations less than 90% on room air.

Antipyretics should be administered for febrile patients and may resolve tachypnea associated with fever.

outline.heading: Pneumonia in pediatrics
outline.summary: Definition Causes Pathophysiology Clinical features (Signs and Symptoms) Diagnosis Treatment Complications

outline.heading: Pneumonia
outline.summary: Pneumonia, is inflammation of the lower respiratory tract (lung parenchyma) The etiology, clinical presentation, and severity of pneumonia vary greatly based on the age of the child

outline.heading: Epidemiology
outline.summary: It is the leading infectious cause of death globally among children younger than 5 yr. Pneumonia mortality is closely linked to poverty, More than 99% of pneumonia deaths are in low- and middle-income countries, with the highest pneumonia mortality rate occurring in poorly developed countries in Africa and South Asia.

outline.heading: Etiology
outline.summary: Infectious Pneumonia is mostly caused by viruses, RSV and rhinovirus being the most common, others include influenza virus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and enteroviruses In neonates (age 0 to 4 weeks), microorganisms in the birth canal such as group B streptococci, Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes are common causes. S. Pneumonia is the most common bacterial pathogen causing pneumonia in children 4 weeks to 4 years of age while Mycoplasma pneumonia and Chlamydophila pneumonia are most common in children older than 5 S. aureus pneumonia often complicates an illness caused by influenza virus

outline.heading: Etiology
outline.summary: Infectious In children with HIV (immunocompromised), pneumonia can be caused by M. tuberculosis, salmonella, E. coli, Pneumocystis jiroveci, pseudomonas and cytomegalovirus Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, which should be considered when the mother had little or no prenatal care. Pneumonia can also be caused by aspiration (food, gastric acid, foreign bodies, hydrocarbons or lipoid substances), Hypersensitivity reactions and Drug and radiation induced

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: Viral pneumonia usually results from spread of the virus along the airways, accompanied by direct injury to the respiratory epithelium, which results in airway inflammation then obstruction due to swelling, abnormal secretions, and cellular debris. The small caliber of airways in young infants (can easily get obstructed) makes such patients particularly susceptible to severe infection.

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: Atelectasis, interstitial edema, and hypoxemia from ventilation–perfusion mismatch often accompany airway obstruction. Viral infection of the lower respiratory tract lead to disturbance of normal host defense mechanisms (which include mucociliary clearance, macrophages and secretory immunoglobulin A) and also lead to disturbance in respiratory microbiota, this ultimately may lead to secondary bacterial infection

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: Bacterial pneumonia most often occurs when respiratory tract organisms colonize the trachea and subsequently gain access to the lungs, and pneumonia can also result from direct invasion of lung tissue due to bacteremia. When bacterial infection is established in the lung parenchyma, the pathologic process varies according to the invading organism.

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae attaches to the respiratory epithelium, inhibits ciliary action, and leads to cellular destruction and an inflammatory response in the submucosa. As the infection progresses, sloughed cellular debris, inflammatory cells, and mucus cause airway obstruction, with spread of infection occurring along the bronchial tree, as is seen in viral pneumonia. S. pneumoniae produces local edema that aids in the proliferation of organisms and their spread into adjacent portions of lung, often resulting in the characteristic focal lobar involvement.

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: Group A streptococcus lower respiratory tract infection typically results in more diffuse lung involvement with interstitial pneumonia. It causes necrosis of tracheobronchial mucosa; formation of large amounts of exudate, edema, and local hemorrhage, with extension into the interalveolar septa; and involvement of lymphatic vessels with frequent pleural involvement.

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: S. aureus pneumonia  manifests as confluent bronchopneumonia, which is often unilateral and characterized by the presence of extensive areas of hemorrhagic necrosis and irregular areas of cavitation of the lung parenchyma, resulting in pneumatoceles, empyema, and, at times, bronchopulmonary fistulas.

outline.heading: Recurrent pneumonia
outline.summary: Recurrent pneumonia is defined as 2 or more episodes in a single year or 3 or more episodes ever, with radiographic clearing between occurrences. An underlying disorder should be considered if a child experiences recurrent pneumonia

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: The clinical presentation of pneumonia varies with the age of the patient, although most pediatric patients will have some combination of fever, preceding viral illness, tachypnea, respiratory distress, rales, and diminished breath sounds. Tachypnea is the most sensitive finding in pediatric patients with pneumonia.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: Pneumonia is usually accompanied by respiratory distress which manifest as Increased work of breathing accompanied by intercostal, subcostal, and suprasternal retractions, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles is common. Severe infection may be accompanied by cyanosis and lethargy, especially in infants.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: Auscultation of the chest may reveal crackles and wheezing, but it is often difficult to localize the source of these sounds in very young children with hyperresonant chests. In viral pneumonia, fever is usually present but temperatures are generally lower than in bacterial pneumonia. It is often not possible to distinguish viral pneumonia clinically from disease caused by Mycoplasma and other bacterial pathogens.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: Bacterial pneumonia in older children typically begins suddenly with high fever, cough, and chest pain. Other symptoms that may be seen include drowsiness with intermittent periods of restlessness, anxiety; and, occasionally, delirium. In many children, splinting on the affected side to minimize pleuritic pain and improve ventilation is noted; such children may lie on one side with the knees drawn up to the chest.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: Abdominal pain is common in lower-lobe pneumonia due to abdominal distention caused by gastric dilation from swallowed air or ileus. The liver may seem enlarged because of downward displacement of the diaphragm secondary to hyperinflation of the lungs or superimposed congestive heart failure.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: In infants, there may be a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection and poor feeding, leading to the abrupt onset of fever, restlessness, apprehension, and respiratory distress. These infants typically appear ill, with respiratory distress manifested as grunting; nasal flaring; retractions of the supraclavicular, intercostal, and subcostal areas; tachypnea; tachycardia; air hunger; and often cyanosis.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: Auscultation may be misleading, particularly in young infants, with findings disproportionate to the degree of tachypnea. Some infants with bacterial pneumonia may have associated gastrointestinal disturbances characterized by vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, and abdominal distention secondary to a paralytic ileus. Rapid progression of symptoms is characteristic in the most severe cases of bacterial pneumonia.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: For most pneumonias, the etiologic agent is never determined. The diagnosis of pneumonia should primarily be made on clinical grounds; chest radiography is not required and not considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Chest radiography is not 100% sensitive, nor specific for the diagnosis of pneumonia, and does not distinguish between bacterial or viral etiologies. The presence of fever plus tachypnea, decreased breath sounds, or fine crackles predicts pneumonia with 93% to 96% sensitivity. If all four variables are present, the sensitivity is 98%

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: The peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count can be useful in differentiating viral from bacterial pneumonia. In viral pneumonia, the WBC count can be normal or elevated but is usually not higher than 20,000/mm3 , with a lymphocyte predominance. Bacterial pneumonia is often associated with an elevated WBC count, in the range of 15,000-40,000/mm3 , and a predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: The definitive diagnosis of a viral infection can be done by detection of viral genome or antigen in respiratory tract secretions using PCR assays The definitive diagnosis of a typical bacterial infection requires isolation of an organism from the blood, pleural fluid, or lung.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Culture of sputum is of little value in the diagnosis of pneumonia in young children, and percutaneous lung aspiration is invasive and not routinely performed. Blood culture is positive in only 10% of children with pneumococcal pneumonia and only recommended for children who fail to improve or have clinical deterioration, have complicated pneumonia, or require hospitalization. So they are not recommended for nontoxic-appearing children treated as outpatients.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Urinary antigen tests should not be used to diagnose pneumonia caused by S. pneumoniae in children because of a high rate of false positives resulting from nasopharyngeal carriage. Pertussis infection can be diagnosed by PCR or culture of a nasopharyngeal specimen; although culture is considered the gold standard for pertussis diagnosis, it is less sensitive than the available PCR assays

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Ultrasonography is highly sensitive and specific in diagnosing pneumonia in children by determining lung consolidations and air bronchograms or effusions. However, the reliability of this imaging modality for pneumonia diagnosis is highly user-dependent, which has limited its widespread use.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Routine laboratory testing is not required for well-appearing children with mild community-acquired pneumonia. For neonates or older patients with significant respiratory distress or toxic appearance, a blood culture, complete blood count, and serum electrolytes should be obtained. Rapid viral antigen testing (if available) for RSV, influenza, and human metapneumovirus can be valuable if they are quick and specific, as results may negate the need for imaging, invasive testing, and antibiotic therapy.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Chest radiography should be reserved for patients in which the differential diagnosis is in question (aspirated foreign body, congestive heart failure, mediastinal mass) or a complication of pneumonia is suspected (failure of outpatient therapy, pleural effusion, cavitary pneumonia, significant patient comorbidities, age <3 months).

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: An infiltrate on chest radiograph (posteroanterior and lateral views) supports the diagnosis of pneumonia; images may show a complication such as a pleural effusion or empyema. Viral pneumonia is usually characterized by hyperinflation with bilateral interstitial infiltrates and peribronchial cuffing. James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Repeat chest radiographs are not required for proof of cure for patients with uncomplicated pneumonia. Diawara Zerouali,Elmdaghri,Abid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Treatment of suspected bacterial pneumonia is based on the presumptive cause and the age and clinical appearance of the child. Neonates and infants younger than 90 days suspected for pneumonia should be hospitalized and given ampicillin + aminoglycoside or third generation cephalosporin (not ceftriaxone)

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: For mildly ill children over 3 months, with mild symptoms, can be treated outpatient with amoxicillin. With the emergence of penicillin-resistant pneumococci, high doses of amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day orally twice daily) should be prescribed unless local data indicate a low prevalence of resistance. alternatives include cefuroxime and amoxicillin/clavulanate.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: For school-aged children and adolescents Azithromycin is preferred, while clarithromycin or doxycycline (for children 8 yr or older) are alternatives. For adolescents, a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) may also be considered if there are contraindications to other agents.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: The empiric treatment of suspected bacterial pneumonia in a hospitalized child requires an approach based on local epidemiology, the immunization status of the child, and the clinical manifestations at the time of presentation. In areas without substantial high-level penicillin resistance among S. pneumoniae , children who are fully immunized against H. influenzae type b and S. pneumoniae and are not severely ill should receive ampicillin or penicillin G.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: For children who do not meet these criteria, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime may be used. If clinical features suggest staphylococcal pneumonia (pneumatoceles, empyema), initial antimicrobial therapy should also include vancomycin or clindamycin. if infection with M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae is suspected, a macrolide antibiotic should be included in the treatment regimen.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: If viral pneumonia is suspected, it is reasonable to withhold antibiotic therapy, especially for preschool-aged patients who are mildly ill, have clinical evidence suggesting viral infection, and are in no respiratory distress. However, up to 30% of patients with known viral infection, particularly influenza viruses, may have coexisting bacterial pathogens. Therefore, if the decision is made to withhold antibiotic therapy on the basis of presumptive diagnosis of a viral infection, deterioration in clinical status should signal the possibility of superimposed bacterial infection, and antibiotic therapy should be initiated.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Antibiotics should generally be continued until the patient has been afebrile for 72 hr, and the total duration should not be less than 10 days (or 5 days if azithromycin is used). Shorter courses (5-7 days) may also be effective, particularly for children managed on an outpatient basis. Studies suggest that a reduction of previously elevated serum procalcitonin levels to an absolute level (0.1-0.25 µg/L) may help determine when to stop treatment.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: In addition to antibiotics, oral zinc (10 mg/day for < 12 mo, 20 mg/day for ≥ 12 mo given for 7 days) accelerates healing and reduce mortality among children with clinically defined severe pneumonia. CPAP improves mortality from pneumonia with hypoxemia compared with standard oxygen therapy in settings without access to ventilator derived CPAP or mechanical ventilation.

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Bronchioloitis

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis is inflammation of the small airways (Bronchioles) in infants and very young children < 2 years of age leading to fever, cough, rhinorrhea and wheezing, severe cases develop respiratory distress.

There is no agreed on diagnostic criteria for this illness, and it can be easily misdiagnosed as pneumonia or Asthma

It is mild and self limited in most cases

Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Etiology

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases of bronchiolitis. Other agents include human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza, influenza, bocavirus, and adenovirus.

Viral bronchiolitis is rarely followed by bacterial superinfection.

NIAID, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Risk factors

Preterm infants

Low birth weight

Age < 5 months

Low socioeconomic status

Airway anomalies and chronic lung diseases

Immune deficiency disorders

Parental smoking

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathophysiology

Infection causes inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles) leading to edema, small airway epithelial cell necrosis and sloughing, increased mucus production and mucus plugs, and bronchospasm, all of these factors increase resistance in the small airways

Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

So resistance in the small airways is increased during both inspiration and expiration, but because the radius of an airway is smaller during expiration, this result in wheezing, air trapping, and lung hyperinflation. If the airway is obstructed fully, trapped distal air will be resorbed and the child will develop atelectasis. Hypoxemia is a consequence of ventilation-perfusion mismatch. With severe obstructive disease, hypercapnia can develop.

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Epidemiology

Over 100,000 young children are hospitalized annually in the United States with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, making it the most common diagnosis resulting in hospitalization for children younger than 1 yr.

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Epidemiology

Bronchiolitis is more common in males, those exposed to second-hand tobacco smoke, those who have not been breastfed, and those living in crowded conditions. Risk is also higher for infants with mothers who smoked during pregnancy.

Older family members, including older siblings, are a common source of infection; they might experience only minor upper respiratory symptoms (colds) given that bronchiolar edema may be less clinically apparent as airway size increases.

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Clinical features

The infant first develops signs of upper respiratory tract infection with sneezing and clear rhinorrhea and may be accompanied by decrease appetite and fever.

Gradually, respiratory distress occur, with paroxysmal cough, dyspnea, and irritability. The infant is often tachypneic, which can interfere with feeding.

respiratory distress manifest as increased Work of breathing, with nasal flaring and subcostal and intercostal retractions, increased respiratory rate

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Clinical features

wheezing and crackles usually present and Expiratory time may be prolonged.

Complete obstruction to airflow can eliminate the turbulence that causes wheezing; thus the lack of audible wheezing is not reassuring if the infant shows other signs of respiratory distress.

So Poorly audible breath sounds suggest severe disease with nearly complete bronchiolar obstruction.

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Clinical features

Apneic event may precede lower respiratory signs early in the disease, particularly with very young infants. Term infants at a postconceptual age of <44 weeks and preterm infants at postconceptual age <48 weeks are at highest risk for apneic events.

Dehydration can also occur due to poor feeding and tachypnea.

Hypoxemia, cyanosis, altered mental status, are signs of severe disease

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is clinical and does not require laboratory or radiologic studies:

Patients with bronchiolitis are <2 years old (peaking presentation is 6 to12 months of age)

Have an URI (cough and rhinorrhea), and wheezing

Do not have a past history or family history of wheezing or atopic disease

present during an RSV or other respiratory viral pathogen outbreak.

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Chest x rays may show areas of atelectasis in bronchiolitis and may be difficult to distinguish from bacterial pneumonia; so it is quite confusing

And as a result, obtaining chest radiography in a patient whose clinical course and exam are consistent with bronchiolitis may encourage unnecessary antibiotic use.

Matteo Di Nardo, Daniela, Francesca Stoppa, Corrado Cecchetti, Marco Marano and NicolPerrottaa Pirozzi, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Laboratory testing is also not routinely indicated; the white blood cell and differential counts are usually normal and are not predictive of bacterial superinfection.

Viral testing (polymerase chain reaction, or rapid immunofluorescence) is not routinely recommended in the diagnosis of bronchiolitis but may be helpful if such testing prevents more invasive evaluations.

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

Concurrent serious bacterial infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) is unlikely and confirmation of viral bronchiolitis may prevent the need for a sepsis evaluation in the young febrile infant.

For young children with wheezing in whom the presentation does not clinically fit with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, including those without other signs of viral infection, with very severe presentation, or complicated clinical course, further workup should be considered (radiology and laboratory tests)

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Diagnosis

Children with recurrent or refractory episodes of wheezing in infancy, particularly if associated with failure to thrive, may require evaluation for chronic disorders such as cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiency.

Otitis media is a common complication to bronchiolitis

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Differential diagnosis

Asthma: Bronchiolitis and asthma both have wheezing as its most prominent clinical sign.

Most infants with bronchiolitis are unresponsive to both β-agonists and corticosteroids.

Pneumonia: pneumonia can have all the bronchiolitis symptoms but it comes with laboratory findings such as leukocytosis

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Treatment

The treatment of children with viral bronchiolitis is supportive management.

Those who are experiencing respiratory distress (hypoxia, inability to feed, apnea, extreme tachypnea) should be hospitalized.

Risk factors for severe disease include younger age, preterm birth, or underlying comorbidity such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, or immunologic disease.

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment

Hypoxemic children (< 90%)should receive supplemental oxygen. Oxygen can be administered via nasal cannula or Hi-flow nasal cannula in moderate to severe cases or via positive pressure ventilation (CPAP) in severe cases.

Hydration should also be given to children with severe disease. Fluids can be administered intravenously or enterally via nasogastric tube, NG feeding preferred and it is indicated when respiratory rate > 60 breath/min to prevent aspiration

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Frequent suctioning of nasal and oral secretions often provides relief of distress and improves work of breathing and ability to feed, although this should be limited to the nares or oropharynx because deep tracheal suctioning does not provide additional benefit.

Chest physiotherapy provides no benefit to children with bronchiolitis.

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Treatment

Albuterol and corticosteroids are proven ineffective in bronchiolitis; and neither are currently recommended for management.

Nebulized hypertonic saline decreases mucus production and is still used in bronchiolitis although most studies fail to demonstrate it being beneficial

Nasal vasoconstrictors are not indicated and have resulted in tachydysrhythmias.

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Treatment

Racemic epinephrine has not been found to improve length of stay or clinical outcomes among inpatients with bronchiolitis, but there is some evidence suggesting it reducing hospitalization rates if used outpatient.

Ribavirin, the only currently available antiviral medication targeting RSV, is also not currently recommended, because of minimal impact on disease outcomes, and because it is costly, difficulty to administer, and associated with multiple toxicities.

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Prognosis

Infants with acute bronchiolitis are at highest risk for further respiratory compromise in the first 72 hours after onset of cough and dyspnea.

severity increases over the first 3 to 5 days with total duration of illness 7 to 14 days, So, in severe disease, disposition is done when the patient is well after the 5 day mark

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Prognosis

Mortality rate is <1% in developed countries, with death attributable to respiratory arrest and/or failure or severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. A majority of deaths due to bronchiolitis occur in children with complex medical conditions or comorbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, or immunodeficiency.

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Prevention

Meticulous hand hygiene while dealing with these children is the best measure to prevent transmission of the viruses responsible for bronchiolitis.

Palivizumab, an intramuscular monoclonal antibody to the RSV F protein, may be given as a prophylactic agent. Palivizumab has been demonstrated to reduce risk of hospitalization due to RSV bronchiolitis

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Prevention

Palivizumab indications:

In children born at <29 wk completed gestation

In children with significant heart disease or chronic lung disease of prematurity

And it is may be considered in infants with neuromuscular disease and immunocompromised states.

outline.summary: Preterm infants Low birth weight Age < 5 months Low socioeconomic status Airway anomalies and chronic lung diseases Immune deficiency disorders Parental smoking

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: Infection causes inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles) leading to edema, small airway epithelial cell necrosis and sloughing, increased mucus production and mucus plugs, and bronchospasm, all of these factors increase  resistance in the small airways Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: So resistance in the small airways is increased during both inspiration and expiration, but because the radius of an airway is smaller during expiration, this result in wheezing, air trapping, and lung hyperinflation. If the airway is obstructed fully, trapped distal air will be resorbed and the child will develop atelectasis. Hypoxemia is a consequence of ventilation-perfusion mismatch. With severe obstructive disease, hypercapnia can develop.

outline.heading: Epidemiology
outline.summary: Over 100,000 young children are hospitalized annually in the United States with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, making it the most common diagnosis resulting in hospitalization for children younger than 1 yr.

outline.heading: Epidemiology
outline.summary: Bronchiolitis is more common in males, those exposed to second-hand tobacco smoke, those who have not been breastfed, and those living in crowded conditions. Risk is also higher for infants with mothers who smoked during pregnancy. Older family members, including older siblings, are a common source of infection; they might experience only minor upper respiratory symptoms (colds) given that bronchiolar edema may be less clinically apparent as airway size increases.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: The infant first develops signs of upper respiratory tract infection with sneezing and clear rhinorrhea and may be accompanied by decrease appetite and fever. Gradually, respiratory distress occur, with paroxysmal cough, dyspnea, and irritability. The infant is often tachypneic, which can interfere with feeding. respiratory distress manifest as increased Work of breathing, with nasal flaring and subcostal and intercostal retractions, increased respiratory rate

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: wheezing and crackles usually present and Expiratory time may be prolonged. Complete obstruction to airflow can eliminate the turbulence that causes wheezing; thus the lack of audible wheezing is not reassuring if the infant shows other signs of respiratory distress. So Poorly audible breath sounds suggest severe disease with nearly complete bronchiolar obstruction.

outline.heading: Clinical features
outline.summary: Apneic event may precede lower respiratory signs early in the disease, particularly with very young infants. Term infants at a postconceptual age of <44 weeks and preterm infants at postconceptual age <48 weeks are at highest risk for apneic events. Dehydration can also occur due to poor feeding and tachypnea. Hypoxemia, cyanosis, altered mental status, are signs of severe disease

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Diagnosis is clinical and does not require laboratory or radiologic studies: Patients with bronchiolitis are <2 years old (peaking presentation is 6 to12 months of age) Have an URI (cough and rhinorrhea), and wheezing Do not have a past history or family history of wheezing or atopic disease present during an RSV or other respiratory viral pathogen outbreak.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Chest x rays may show areas of atelectasis in bronchiolitis and may be difficult to distinguish from bacterial pneumonia; so it is quite confusing And as a result, obtaining chest radiography in a patient whose clinical course and exam are consistent with bronchiolitis may encourage unnecessary antibiotic use. Matteo Di Nardo, Daniela, Francesca Stoppa, Corrado Cecchetti, Marco Marano and NicolPerrottaa Pirozzi, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Laboratory testing is also not routinely indicated; the white blood cell and differential counts are usually normal and are not predictive of bacterial superinfection. Viral testing (polymerase chain reaction, or rapid immunofluorescence) is not routinely recommended in the diagnosis of bronchiolitis but may be helpful if such testing prevents more invasive evaluations.

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Concurrent serious bacterial infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) is unlikely and confirmation of viral bronchiolitis may prevent the need for a sepsis evaluation in the young febrile infant. For young children with wheezing in whom the presentation does not clinically fit with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, including those without other signs of viral infection, with very severe presentation, or complicated clinical course, further workup should be considered (radiology and laboratory tests)

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Children with recurrent or refractory episodes of wheezing in infancy, particularly if associated with failure to thrive, may require evaluation for chronic disorders such as cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiency. Otitis media is a common complication to bronchiolitis

outline.heading: Differential diagnosis
outline.summary: Asthma: Bronchiolitis and asthma both have wheezing as its most prominent clinical sign. Most infants with bronchiolitis are unresponsive to both β-agonists and corticosteroids. Pneumonia: pneumonia can have all the bronchiolitis symptoms but it comes with laboratory findings such as leukocytosis

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: The treatment of children with viral bronchiolitis is supportive management. Those who are experiencing respiratory distress (hypoxia, inability to feed, apnea, extreme tachypnea) should be hospitalized. Risk factors for severe disease include younger age, preterm birth, or underlying comorbidity such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, or immunologic disease.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Hypoxemic children (< 90%)should receive supplemental oxygen. Oxygen can be administered via nasal cannula or Hi-flow nasal cannula in moderate to severe cases or via positive pressure ventilation (CPAP) in severe cases. Hydration should also be given to children with severe disease. Fluids can be administered intravenously or enterally via nasogastric tube, NG feeding preferred and it is indicated when respiratory rate > 60 breath/min to prevent aspiration

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Frequent suctioning of nasal and oral secretions often provides relief of distress and improves work of breathing and ability to feed, although this should be limited to the nares or oropharynx because deep tracheal suctioning does not provide additional benefit. Chest physiotherapy provides no benefit to children with bronchiolitis.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Albuterol and corticosteroids are proven ineffective in bronchiolitis; and neither are currently recommended for management. Nebulized hypertonic saline decreases mucus production and is still used in bronchiolitis although most studies fail to demonstrate it being beneficial Nasal vasoconstrictors are not indicated and have resulted in tachydysrhythmias.

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Racemic epinephrine has not been found to improve length of stay or clinical outcomes among inpatients with bronchiolitis, but there is some evidence suggesting it reducing hospitalization rates if used outpatient. Ribavirin, the only currently available antiviral medication targeting RSV, is also not currently recommended, because of minimal impact on disease outcomes, and because it is costly, difficulty to administer, and associated with multiple toxicities.

outline.heading: Prognosis
outline.summary: Infants with acute bronchiolitis are at highest risk for further respiratory compromise in the first 72 hours after onset of cough and dyspnea. severity increases over the first 3 to 5 days with total duration of illness 7 to 14 days, So, in severe disease, disposition is done when the patient is well after the 5 day mark

outline.heading: Prognosis
outline.summary: Mortality rate is <1% in developed countries, with death attributable to respiratory arrest and/or failure or severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. A majority of deaths due to bronchiolitis occur in children with complex medical conditions or comorbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, or immunodeficiency.

outline.heading: Prevention
outline.summary: Meticulous hand hygiene while dealing with these children is the best measure to prevent transmission of the viruses responsible for bronchiolitis. Palivizumab, an intramuscular monoclonal antibody to the RSV F protein, may be given as a prophylactic agent. Palivizumab has been demonstrated to reduce risk of hospitalization due to RSV bronchiolitis

outline.heading: Prevention
outline.summary: Palivizumab indications: In children born at <29 wk completed gestation In children with significant heart disease or chronic lung disease of prematurity And it is may be considered in infants with neuromuscular disease and immunocompromised states.

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Peritonsillar abscess

Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is collection of pus behind the tonsil due to infection

It most commonly seen in adolescents and young adults.

It may lead to serious complications such as airway compromise or aspiration pneumronia

James Heilman,MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Etiology

Group A streptococci and mixed oropharyngeal anaerobes are the most common pathogens

More than four bacterial isolates per abscess typically recovered by needle aspiration.

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Epidemiology

It is more common than retropharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal abscesses

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Pathophysiology

It is caused by bacterial invasion through the capsule of the tonsil, leading to cellulitis and subsequently abscess formation in the surrounding tissues.

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Clinical features

The classic presentation is an adolescent with a recent history of acute pharyngotonsillitis who suddenly develops sore throat, fever, trismus, drooling, muffled (hot potato) voice, and dysphagia.

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Clinical features

Physical examination reveals an asymmetric tonsillar bulge with displacement of the uvula away from the affected side. As a rule, the affected tonsil is anteriorly and medially displaced.

An asymmetric tonsillar bulge is diagnostic, but it may be poorly visualized because of trismus.

James Heilman,MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Diagnosis

Diagnosis can be made through careful visualization of the oral cavity, there will be uvular deviation away from the abscess, soft palate displacement and localized fluctuance

In toxic appearing patients, examination is not preferred because it may lead to airway compromise and patient referred for CT with contract or ultrasound

But in typical cases, imaging studies are unnecessary

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Treatment

Treatment includes surgical drainage, pain control, fluids and antibiotics

Antibiotics should cover group A streptococci and anaerobes. (clindamycin IV or ampicillin/sulbactam IV)

Fluids should be given because patient maybe dehydrated due to decrease oral intake and pain control can be given IV or locally

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Treatment

Surgical drainage may be accomplished through needle aspiration, incision and drainage, or tonsillectomy.

Needle aspiration can involve aspiration of the superior, middle, and inferior aspects of the tonsil to locate the abscess.

Intraoral ultrasound can be used to diagnose and guide needle aspiration of a peritonsillar abscess. General anesthesia may be required for the uncooperative patient.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Treatment

Approximately 95% of peritonsillar abscesses resolve after needle aspiration and antibiotic therapy.

The 5% with infections that fail to resolve after needle aspiration require incision and drainage.

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Treatment

Tonsillectomy should be considered if there is failure to improve within 24 hr of antibiotic therapy and needle aspiration, history of recurrent peritonsillar abscess or recurrent tonsillitis, or complications from peritonsillar abscess.

A rare complication is rupture of the abscess, with resultant aspiration pneumonitis.

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Retropharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal abscess

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Retropharyngeal abscess is a collection of pus located in the prevertebral space behind the pharynx (retropharyngeal) while the lateral pharyngeal abscess is located in the lateral part of the pharynx

It can lead to life threatening complications such as airway obstruction or sepsis, so it has to be diagnosed and treated carefully

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Etiology

Retropharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal infections are most often polymicrobial.

The usual pathogens include group A streptococcus, staphylococcus aureus , and oropharyngeal anaerobic bacteria

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Etiology

There is increase incidence with methicillin-resistant strains of staphylococcus aureus.

Other pathogens can include Hemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella, and Mycobacterium avium.

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathophysiology

The retropharyngeal and the lateral pharyngeal lymph nodes that drain the mucosal surfaces of the upper airway and esophagus are located in the neck within the retropharyngeal space and the lateral pharyngeal space

Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

The retropharyngeal space is located between the pharynx and the cervical vertebrae and extending down into the superior mediastinum

The lateral pharyngeal space bounded by the pharynx medially, the carotid sheath posteriorly, and the muscles of the styloid process laterally

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

The lymph nodes in these deep neck spaces communicate with each other, and upper respiratory tract infection will infect the lymph nodes, infection spread from one node to the others leading to suppurative adenitis and lymph abscess

Infection of the nodes usually occurs as a result of extension from a localized infection of the oropharynx.

A retropharyngeal abscess can also result from penetrating trauma to the oropharynx, dental infection, and vertebral osteomyelitis.

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Epidemiology

Retropharyngeal abscess occurs most commonly in children younger than 4 years of age because the retropharyngeal nodes involute after 5 years of age

This means infection in older children and adults is much less common (because there is no lymph nodes to transmit the infection so infection has to come by trauma, dental infection or vertebral osteomyelitis).

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Epidemiology

Abscess formation occurs most commonly in winter and early spring.

Males are affected more than females and approximately two-thirds of patients have a history of recent ear, nose, or throat infection.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Clinical features

Patients with retropharyngeal abscess classically present with fever, irritability, drooling, and dysphagia, and may have inspiratory stridor.

Patients may hold their neck in an unusual position with torticollis, hyperextension, stiffness or the may refuse to move their neck.

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Clinical features

The verbal child might complain of sore throat and neck pain.

Other signs can include muffled voice, respiratory distress, or even obstructive sleep apnea.

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Clinical features

Physical examination can reveal bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall, and this is present in <50% of infants with retropharyngeal abscess.

Cervical lymphadenopathy may also be present.

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Clinical features

Lateral pharyngeal abscess commonly presents as fever, dysphagia, and a prominent bulge of the lateral pharyngeal wall, sometimes with medial displacement of the tonsil.

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Physical examination of the pharynx may show a retropharyngeal mass.

Although palpation commonly will demonstrate fluctuance, this could lead to rupture of the abscess.

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

Lateral neck radiograph performed during inspiration with the neck extended may show increased width or an air–fluid level in the retropharyngeal space.

The diagnosis is suggested when the retropharyngeal space at C2-C3 is more than 1/3 vertebral body width or at C4 downward is more than the full width of the vertebral body

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Diagnosis

Deep neck infections can be accurately identified and localized with CT scans, but CT accurately identifies abscess formation in only 63% of patients.

CT with contrast medium enhancement can reveal central lucency, ring enhancement, or scalloping of the walls of a lymph node and help differentiate abscess from cellulitis.

Syed SS, Aderinboye O, Hanson KE, Spitzer ED, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Diagnosis

Scalloping of the abscess wall is thought to be a late finding and predicts abscess formation.

Incision and drainage and culture of an abscessed node provides the definitive diagnosis

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes acute epiglottitis and foreign body aspiration.

In the young child with limited neck mobility, meningitis must also be considered.

Other possibilities include lymphoma, hematoma, and vertebral osteomyelitis.

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment

Immediate airway stabilization is the first priority, Intubate unstable patients before performing CT.

Treatment include intravenous antibiotics with or without surgical drainage.

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Antibiotic choice is controversial because most retropharyngeal abscesses contain mixed flora, A third-generation cephalosporin combined with ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin to provide anaerobic coverage is effective. The increasing prevalence of methicillin-resistant S. aureus can influence empiric antibiotic therapy.

Studies show that >50% of children with retropharyngeal or lateral pharyngeal abscess as identified by CT can be successfully treated without surgical drainage; the older the child, the more likely it is that antimicrobial treatment alone will be successful.

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Treatment

Drainage is necessary in the patient with respiratory distress or failure to improve with intravenous antibiotic treatment.

Consider adjunctive treatment with parenteral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg IV to a maximum of 10 mg) to reduce inflammation and edema.

The optimal duration of treatment is unknown, and IV antibiotics are given until the patient has begun to improve, followed by a course of oral antibiotics.

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Complications

Complications of retropharyngeal or lateral pharyngeal abscess include significant upper airway obstruction, rupture leading to aspiration pneumonia, and extension to the mediastinum.

Thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and erosion of the carotid artery sheath can also occur.

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Lemierre disease

Another complication is infection of the parapharyngeal space (Lemierre disease), in which infection from the oropharynx extends to cause septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and embolic abscesses in the lungs.

The causative pathogen is Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic bacterial constituent of the oropharyngeal flora.

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Lemierre disease

The typical presentation is that of a previously healthy adolescent or young adult with a history of recent pharyngitis who becomes acutely ill with fever, hypoxia, tachypnea, and respiratory distress.

Chest radiography demonstrates multiple cavitary nodules, often bilateral and often accompanied by pleural effusion. Blood culture may be positive.

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Lemierre disease

Treatment involves prolonged intravenous antibiotic therapy with penicillin or cefoxitin; surgical drainage of extrapulmonary metastatic abscesses may be necessary

SOURCE SLIDE 1

bacterial tracheitis

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Bacterial Tracheitis

Bacterial tracheitis (Aka membranous laryngotracheobronchitis or bacterial croup) is an acute bacterial infection of the trachea that is potentially life threatening

Bacterial tracheitis often follows a viral respiratory infection (especially croup), so it is considered a bacterial complication of a viral disease

By Blausen.com, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Epidemiology

Bacterial tracheitis is uncommon and can present as either a primary or secondary infection.

The mean age of presentation is between 5 and 7 years of age, with slight male predominance.

Bacterial tracheitis is more common than epiglottitis in vaccinated children

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Etiology

It is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, S. pyogenes or β-lactamase–producing gram-negative organisms H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.

Anaerobic organisms can also be the cause

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Clinical Features

Classic presentation is a child with croup (barking cough, low grade fever and non toxic looking), after a few days of improvement then develops high grade fever and toxicity with respiratory distress (tachypnea, retractions and use of accessary muscles) and stridor, sore throat and cough productive of thick sputum

The patient can lie flat, does not drool and doesn’t have dysphagia (symptoms associated with epiglottitis)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Clinical Features

With this disease there is mucosal swelling at the level of cricoid cartilage, complicated by copious, thick , purulent secretions causing pseudo membranes

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Diagnosis and Differential

Diagnosis is clinical: high grade fever, purulent airway secretions and absence of classic findings of epiglottitis

Purulent material is seen below vocal cords during intubation

Blood and purulent material cultures should be taken

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Diagnosis and Differential

Lateral neck x rays may show subglottic narrowing of the trachea with irregular densities and ragged and indistinct borders, it may show pseudo membrane detachment in the trachea.

Bronchoscopy used to confirm the diagnosis if still in doubt

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Treatment

Nebulized epinephrine (which is very effective in croup) is not effective in bacterial tracheitis

Intubation is required in 50% of patients with this disease, younger patients are more likely to need intubation

Suctioning of purulent materials causes temporary relief but doesn’t sufficiently prevent the need for intubation

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Treatment

Provide oxygen

Administer empiric parenteral antibiotics: ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/ kg/dose IV or ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/dose IV plus clindamycin 10 mg/ kg/dose IV. In areas with increasing S. aureus resistance, consider the addition of vancomycin 10 mg/kg/dose IV.

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Prognosis

Prognosis is excellent, patient become afebrile within 2 days of empirical antibiotics therapy

Extubation is done when mucosal edema and purulent secretions are decreased

outline.summary: Bacterial tracheitis (Aka membranous laryngotracheobronchitis or bacterial croup) is an acute bacterial infection of the trachea that is potentially life threatening Bacterial tracheitis often follows a viral respiratory infection (especially croup), so it is considered a bacterial complication of a viral disease By Blausen.com, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Epidemiology
outline.summary: Bacterial tracheitis is uncommon and can present as either a primary or secondary infection. The mean age of presentation is between 5 and 7 years of age, with slight male predominance. Bacterial tracheitis is more common than epiglottitis in vaccinated children

outline.heading: Etiology
outline.summary: It is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, S. pyogenes or β-lactamase–producing gram-negative organisms H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. Anaerobic organisms can also be the cause

outline.heading: Clinical Features
outline.summary: Classic presentation is a child with croup (barking cough, low grade fever and non toxic looking), after a few days of improvement then develops high grade fever and toxicity with respiratory distress (tachypnea, retractions and use of accessary muscles) and stridor, sore throat and cough productive of thick sputum The patient can lie flat, does not drool and doesn’t have dysphagia (symptoms associated with epiglottitis)

outline.heading: Clinical Features
outline.summary: With this disease there is mucosal swelling at the level of cricoid cartilage, complicated by copious, thick , purulent secretions causing pseudo membranes

outline.heading: Diagnosis and Differential
outline.summary: Diagnosis is clinical: high grade fever, purulent airway secretions and absence of classic findings of epiglottitis Purulent material is seen below vocal cords during intubation Blood and purulent material cultures should be taken

outline.heading: Diagnosis and Differential
outline.summary: Lateral neck x rays may show subglottic narrowing of the trachea with irregular densities and ragged and indistinct borders, it may show pseudo membrane detachment in the trachea. Bronchoscopy used to confirm the diagnosis if still in doubt

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Nebulized epinephrine (which is very effective in croup) is not effective in bacterial tracheitis Intubation is required in 50% of patients with this disease, younger patients are more likely to need intubation Suctioning of purulent materials causes temporary relief but doesn’t sufficiently prevent the need for intubation

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Provide oxygen Administer empiric parenteral antibiotics: ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/ kg/dose IV or ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/dose IV plus clindamycin 10 mg/ kg/dose IV. In areas with increasing S. aureus resistance, consider the addition of vancomycin 10 mg/kg/dose IV.

outline.heading: Prognosis
outline.summary: Prognosis is excellent, patient become afebrile within 2 days of empirical antibiotics therapy Extubation is done when mucosal edema and purulent secretions are decreased
