SOURCE SLIDE 1

Epiglottitis

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Epiglottitis

Epiglottitis (Supraglottitis) is acute inflammation of the epiglottis, and it is a medical emergency because there is a risk of sudden airway obstruction and death

Epiglottis is a piece of tissue located at base of the tongue that prevents food from entering the trachea

藤澤孝志, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

סתו כסלו, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Etiology

Epiglottitis is rare nowadays, because it is mainly caused by Hemophilus influenzae type b, and vaccination (Hib vaccine) has decreased its occurrence.

Now it is mostly caused Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species and that occur in immunized children. Candida may be a cause in immunocompromised patients.

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Clinical features

It is characterized by an acute rapidly progressive course of high fever, sore throat, dyspnea and respiratory distress

The degree of respiratory distress at presentation is variable and lack of respiratory distress at presentation is deceiving and it could be the first manifestation

Hariadhi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Clinical features

The classic presentation is usually a healthy child suddenly develops sore throat and fever and within hours, the child appear toxic

Swallowing is difficult, breathing is labored and drooling is present

The child may sit in tripod position, sitting upright and leaning forward with chin up and mouth open while bracing on the arms

Hariadhi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Clinical features

A brief period of air hunger and irritability is followed by rapidly increasing cyanosis and coma

Stridor is a late finding and suggest near complete airway obstruction

The barking cough (typical of croup) is rare in Epiglottitis

Usually no other family members are ill with acute respiratory symptoms

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Diagnosis

The diagnosis is clinical in patients presenting with the classic presentation

If the diagnosis is uncertain, then lateral neck films should be taken at the bedside in extension and during inspiration with a minimum of disturbance. Thumb sign might be seen

If it is not seen then diagnosis require visualization using laryngoscope in the operating room or in the intensive care unit

Med Chaos, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Diagnosis

The epiglottis is large, cherry red and swollen in epiglottitis

Anxiety provoking interventions such as phlebotomy, IV placement, placing the child supine or direct inspection of the oral cavity should be avoided until the airway is secure because they may lead to airway compromise

If patient require to be transported, a physician skilled in airway management and intubation should accompany the child at all times

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Diagnosis

Blood cultures are positive in up to 90% of patients, whereas cultures from the epiglottis are less sensitive.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Treatment

Establish a definitive airway using either endotracheal or nasotracheal intubation or if failed then tracheostomy regardless of the degree of apparent respiratory distress because around 6% of children with epiglottitis without a definitive airway die compared to < 1% of those with a definitive airway

The duration of intubation depends on the clinical course of the patient and duration of epiglottic swelling and extubation is done when swelling subsides, examination is done using direct laryngoscope or flexible fiberoptic laryngoscope

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Treatment

intubation usually last for 2-3 days because response to antibiotics is rapid

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Treatment

During preparation for intubation by gathering the right personnel and equipment

Keep the patient seated and upright. Provide oxygen and administer nebulized racemic or L-epinephrine.

In the event of total airway loss, attempt bag-valve-mask ventilation.

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Steroids are used to decrease mucosal edema of the epiglottis. Use methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg IV or dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg IV.

Administer antibiotics: cefuroxime 50 mg/kg/dose IV, cefotaxime 50 mg/kg/dose IV, or ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/dose IV are appropriate empiric options. In regions with increased cephalosporin resistance, vancomycin 10 mg/kg/dose IV should be added.

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Croup (laryngotrachobronchitis)

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Introduction

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is the most common infection of the middle respiratory tract (larynx, trachea and bronchi) in children and it is responsible for most cases of stridor after the neonatal period.

Croup is most prevalent in the fall and early winter, and children ages 6 months to 3 years are most affected, with a peak at an age of 12 to 24 months. In adolescents, it manifest as laryngitis

Croup could be mild, moderate or severe but most cases are mild, benign, and self-limited

Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Etiology

The most common causse of croup are parainfluenza viruses (types 1,2,3, and 4) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Pathophysiology

It lead to inflammation and swelling of the subglottic area which interferes with normal breathing and produces barking cough, stridor and hoarse voice

It affects children because of small trachea diameter which means that a small decrease in this diameter due to inflammation and swelling increase airway resistance and work of breathing

Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathophysiology

During inspiration, the walls of the subglottic space are drawn together, aggravating the obstruction and producing the stridor

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Stridor

Stridor is a harsh, high pitched respiratory sound produced by turbulent air flow through a narrowed trachea

It is usually inspiratory but could be biphasic

It is a sign of upper airway obstruction

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Severe croup

Severe croups present with signs of upper airway obstruction

Significant Stridor at rest

Labored breathing

Cyanosis

Marked suprasternal, intercostal and subcostal retractions

Wheezing maybe present if there is associated lower airway involvement

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Clinical features

Croup typically begins with a 1-to-3-day prodrome of cough, coryza, inspiratory stridor and low-grade fever, followed by a 3- to 4-day period of classic barking cough, in some cases cough and stridor may be abrupt in onset.

Symptoms peak on days 3 to 4 and are often more severe at night.

Physical examination classically shows stridor, with a greater inspiratory component.

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Diagnosis

The diagnosis of croup is clinical: a barking cough, stridor and low grade fever.

Radiographs are not necessary, unless other causes are being considered and Neck or chest radiographs may demonstrate subglottic narrowing or the “steeple sign,”

Frank Gaillard, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Diagnosis

Laboratory studies are not useful in diagnosis, but used to exclude more serious differentials, leukocytosis suggest epiglottis and bacterial tracheitis

Many PCR tests are available for parainfluenza and RSV viruses

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, parapharyngeal abscess

Non infectious differential include foreign body aspiration, laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, hemangioma, vascular ring and vocal cord paralysis

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Treatment

Patients with significant stridor should be kept in a position of comfort with minimal disturbance; monitor pulse oximetry and provide oxygen as needed.

Dexamethasone reduces symptoms and need for hospitalization in croup and it is administered as one dose orally or IM 0.6- 1 mg/kg (IV formulation can be given orally). Prednisolone can be used as an alternative dosed 2 mg/kg given in two to three divided doses, Nebulized budesonide (2 mg) may also be used.

All patients with croup benefit from corticosteroids Even those with mild symptoms

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Nebulized racemic epinephrine (2.25%), 0.05 mL/kg/dose up to 0.5 mL, or nebulized L-epinephrine (1:1000), 0.5 mL/kg/dose up to 5 mL, should be used to treat moderate to severe cases (which present with significant stridor at rest).

Epinephrine works by reducing subglottic edema by adrenergic vasoconstriction, temporarily producing marked clinical improvement, peak effect within 10- 30 minutes and fades within 60- 90 minutes and a rebound worsening of symptoms may occur so epinephrine need to be repeated every 20 minutes for no more than 2 hours in severe cases

Epinephrine decreases intubation rates

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Treatment

Children with persistent stridor at rest, tachypnea, retractions, or hypoxia, or those who require more than two treatments of epinephrine should be admitted to the hospital.

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Complications

Prognosis is excellent and illness last for 5 days

Most common complication is viral pneumonia which occur in 1% of croup cases

Secondary bacterial tracheitis: very rare complication and occur in immunocompromised patients

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Junctional Rhythm

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Junctional rhythm

In normal heart, the electrical activity originates in the sinoatrial node (default pacemaker) and depolarizes the atria then it passes from the atria through the atrioventricular node and into the bundle of His, from which it travels along Purkinje fibers to reach and depolarize the ventricles (sinus rhythm)

Junctional rhythm (nodal rhythm) is when the electrical activity originates from the atrioventricular node or the His bundle (junction between atria and ventricles) then it travels to the atria and ventricles and depolarizes them

U Bhalraam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

ECG characteristics

Regular rhythms

Normal QRS. Since the impulse still travels down the bundle of His, the QRS will not be wide

Junctional rhythms can present with either bradycardia, a normal heart rate, or tachycardia

Dhaval Desai, MD, MPH, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

ECG characteristics

P wave:

There might be no P wave (this is due to failure of electrical activity to pass through to atria or the p wave is hidden within the QRS complex)

There maybe an inverted P wave before the QRS complex (P wave inverted due retrograde flow of electrical activity to the atria)

The inverted P wave is after the QRS complex means electrical activity flows to the ventricles first then to the atria

Depending on where the rhythm originates in the AV node, the atria can contract before ventricular contraction due to retrograde conduction, during ventricular contraction, or after ventricular contraction. If there is a blockage between the AV node and the SA node, the atria may not contract at all.

U Bhalraam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Dhaval Desai, MD, MPH, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Classification

Depending on the level of the rescue pacemaker within the junction, junctional rhythm rate is different

Junctional bradycardia when the heart beats at a rate less than 40 beats per minute.

Junctional escape rhythm when the heart beats at a rate between 40 and 60 beats per minute.

Accelerated junctional rhythm when the heart beats a rate of between 60 and 100 bpm, common in digoxin toxicity

Junctional tachycardia when the heart beats at a rate above 100 beats per minute.

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Slide 6

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Slide 7

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Slide 8

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Causes

Any disorder that impairs the SA node leading to decreased automaticity or less automaticity than AV node in cases of sinus bradycardia, SA node exit block, or AV block can potentially lead to a junctional rhythm. Some examples include:

Chest trauma

Ischemic heart disease

Sick sinus syndrome

Myocarditis

Hypothyroidism

Hyperkalemia

Muscular dystrophy

Other neuromuscular disorders

U Bhalraam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Causes

Other examples

Radiation therapy

Collagen vascular disease

Medications: clonidine, reserpine, adenosine, cimetidine, antiarrhythmic class I to IV, lithium amitriptyline, beta blockers, ivabradine, opioids and digoxin

Vasovagal stimulation

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity

Inherited channelopathies

Lyme disease

Rheumatic fever

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Notes

If the ventricular rate is too slow, myocardial or cerebral ischemia may develop.

When alternating rhythmically with the SA node, junctional escape beats may cause bigeminal or trigeminal rhythms.

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Presentation

Presentation varies according to underlying cause

If patient is presenting with decompensated heart failure then symptoms include SOB, chest pian and peripheral edema

Patient with rheumatic fever present with heart murmur due to damage of heart valves, fever, joint pain and rash

Some patients present with generalized complains such as dizziness, fatigue, syncope and palpitations

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Isolated, infrequent junctional escape beats usually do not require specific treatment.

If junctional rhythm is producing symptoms, treat the underlying cause.

In unstable patients with junctional rhythm causing bradycardia, give atropine 0.5 mg IV every 5 minutes to a total of 3 mg. This will accelerate the SA node discharge rate and enhance AV nodal conduction.

Use transcutaneous or transvenous pacing in unstable patients not responsive to atropine.

SlETVFSIn8A.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Sinus bradycardia

Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rhythm starting from the SA node but with a reduced rate of electrical discharge, resulting in reduced heart rate (bradycardia) which is lower then 60 beats per min

The ECG characteristics of sinus bradycardia are

normal sinus P waves and PR intervals

Regular rhythm

1:1 AV conduction

Rate: < 60 beats/min

By Ewingdo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

By Ewingdo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Causes

Sinus bradycardia occur in response to three categories of stimuli:

Physiologic: due to vagal tone or in healthy people and athletes due to higher cardiac stroke volume requiring less heart rate to achieve perfusion

Pharmacologic: calcium channel blockers, β-blockers, or digoxin, quinidine, adenosine, class I antiarrhythmic agents, ivabradine, clonidine, reserpine, cimetidine, lithium, amitriptyline

Pathologic: acute inferior myocardial infarction (MI), increased intracranial pressure, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, sick sinus syndrome, eating disorders (such as anorexia nervosa), rhodotoxin poisoning, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, infections (such as diphtheria, acute rheumatic fever, or viral myocarditis), sleep apnea and many more …

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Signs and symptoms

decreased heart rate => decreased cardiac output resulting in symptoms such:

Lightheadedness

dizziness

hypotension

Vertigo

syncope

The slow heart rate may also lead to atrial, junctional, or ventricular ectopic rhythms

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Treatment

Sinus bradycardia does require treatment when the heart rate is slower than 50 beats/min and there is evidence of hypoperfusion.

Lines of treatment include:

Transcutaneous cardiac pacing in unstable cases

Atropine

Epinephrine, dopamine

Transvenous pacing in recurrent cases

Glucagon in beta blocker or CCB toxicity

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Treatment

Transcutaneous cardiac pacing is the first line treatment for unstable patients with bradycardia.

Patient is attached to the monitor using external pacing pads, the first pad is placed over the left lateral precordium and the second pad is placed at the level of the heart in the right infra scapular area.

Slowly increase the pacing output from 0 mA to the lowest point where capture is observed, usually at 50 to 100 mA, but may be up to 200 mA. A widened QRS after each pacing spike denotes electrical capture.

If needed, administer a sedative, such as lorazepam, 1 to 2 mg IV, or an opiate, such as morphine, 2 to 4 mg IV, for pain control.

Rblumel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Treatment

Atropine also can be used

The dose is 0.5 mg IV push, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes as needed up to a total of 3 mg IV.

If given via endotracheal tube, increase the dose by 2 to 2.5 times over the IV dose.

Slow administration or lower doses may cause paradoxical bradycardia.

Atropine may not be effective in cardiac transplant patients since the heart is denervated and has no vagal stimulation.

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Treatment

Epinephrine, 2 to 10 μg/min IV, or dopamine, 3 to 10 μg/kg/min IV, may be used if transcutaneous pacing is not available.

Transvenous pacing is indicated in the patient with symptomatic recurrent or persistent sinus bradycardia due to sick sinus syndrome, second degree Mobitz type II AV block or third degree AV block.

In B blocker or CCB toxicity, Glucagon can be used, dosing is 3 to 10 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes, followed by an infusion of 1 to 5 mg/h

outline.heading: Sinus bradycardia
outline.summary: Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rhythm starting from the SA node but with a reduced rate of electrical discharge, resulting in reduced heart rate (bradycardia) which is lower then 60 beats per min The ECG characteristics of sinus bradycardia are normal sinus P waves and PR intervals Regular rhythm 1:1 AV conduction Rate: < 60 beats/min By Ewingdo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia commons

outline.heading: By Ewingdo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia commons
Causes
outline.summary: Sinus bradycardia occur in response to three categories of stimuli: Physiologic: due to vagal tone or in healthy people and athletes due to higher cardiac stroke volume requiring less heart rate to achieve perfusion Pharmacologic: calcium channel blockers, β-blockers, or digoxin, quinidine, adenosine, class I antiarrhythmic agents, ivabradine, clonidine, reserpine, cimetidine, lithium, amitriptyline Pathologic: acute inferior myocardial infarction (MI), increased intracranial pressure, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, sick sinus syndrome, eating disorders (such as anorexia nervosa), rhodotoxin poisoning, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, infections (such as diphtheria, acute rheumatic fever, or vi

outline.heading: Signs and symptoms
outline.summary: decreased heart rate => decreased cardiac output resulting in symptoms such: Lightheadedness dizziness hypotension Vertigo syncope The slow heart rate may also lead to atrial, junctional, or ventricular ectopic rhythms

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Sinus bradycardia does require treatment when the heart rate is slower than 50 beats/min and there is evidence of hypoperfusion. Lines of treatment include: Transcutaneous cardiac pacing in unstable cases Atropine Epinephrine, dopamine Transvenous pacing in recurrent cases Glucagon in beta blocker or CCB toxicity

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Premature ventricular contractions

SOURCE SLIDE 2

PVCs

Premature ventricular contraction (PVC) are due to impulses originating from single or multiple areas in the ventricles (same as PAC but the impulse originating in the ventricles)

These impulses start beyond the His- Purkinje system and cause direct depolarization to the ventricles leading to wide abnormal QRS complex

AKA ventricular ectopics, ventricular extrasystoles, ventricular premature beats, ventricular premature depolarizations

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

EKG characteristics

The EKG characteristics of PVCs include:

premature and wide QRS complex

no preceding P wave

In most cases, the ST segment and T wave of the PVC are directed opposite the preceding major QRS deflection (Discordant)

many PVCs are conducted into the atrial thus producing an inverted P wave

Kalumet, selbst erstellt, 01.12.2005, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

PVC

PVCs can be unifocal or multifocal

Unifocal: if one focus is producing all the PVCs and they all look the same on the ECG paper

Multifocal: more than one focus is producing PVCs leading to different PVC shapes on the ECG paper

If every other beat is a PVC then it is called bigeminy, and if every third beat is a PVC then it is trigeminy, every fourth beat is a PVC then quadrigeminy

If two consecutive PVCs then called couplet, if three consecutive PVCs then called triplets

SOURCE SLIDE 5

after the PVC comes a fully compensatory pause which means that next normal beat arrives after an interval that is equal to double the preceding RR interval

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Compensatory pause

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Non sustained VT

If three or more PVCs occur in a row, patients are considered to have non sustained ventricular tachycardia

G.steph.rocket, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Ventricular parasystole

Ventricular parasystole occurs when the ectopic ventricular focus fires frequently enough to compete with the SA node and is associated with cardiac ischemia , electrolyte imbalance and hypertensive or ischemia heart disease

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Epidemiology

PVCs are very common, occurring in most patients with IHD and acute MI

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Causes

Myocardial ischemia

Cardiomyopathies

Valvular disease

Myocarditis

Myocardial contusion

Electrolytes imbalances: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia

Hypoxia and/ or hypercapnia (Respiratory failure)

Illicit drug abuse (alcohol, amphetamines, and cocaine)

Medications: digoxin, TCA, sympathomimetics, aminophylline and caffeine

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Pathophysiology

Causes mentioned, especially myocardial ischemia and electrolyte imbalances lead to and ectopic ventricular focus to fire spontaneously by an unclear mechanism

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Presentation

Mostly asymptomatic, but some patients my report fatigue, palpitations, lightheadedness or dizziness

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

ECG

Echocardiography

Electrolyte levels

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Treat the underlying cause

Symptomatic patients are treated with beta blockers (first line), CCB (nondihydropyridine) can be used if beta blockers are contraindicated, if not effective then class 1c antiarrhythmic medications (flecainide or propafane) can be used in patients with out preexisting CAD, but if patient does have CAD then amiodarone can be used

Patient who cannot tolerate pharmacological therapy should be referred for ablation therapy

SOURCE SLIDE 1

tracheal rapid sequence intubation

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Rapid sequence intubation

RSI include simultaneous administration of an induction agent and a neuromuscular blocking agent to facilitate orotracheal intubation

Rapid sequence intubation (RSI) is a technique indicated when rapid control of the airway is required in cases of:

Acute respiratory failure due to inadequate oxygenation or ventilation

Airway protection in a patient with an altered mental status.

Acute upper gastrointestinal bleed with a high risk of aspiration

Pöllö, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Preparation

Airway risk assessment before the intervention

Positioning of the patient

Anatomy

ETT tube size

Blade selection

All necessary supplies must be available at the bedside, including alternative options to secure the airway in case of failure.

A checklist is very helpful

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Assessing Airway Risk

Airway risk assessment is done to determine if an airway will be difficult before the start of the procedure. Multiple mnemonics can be used, a popular one is LEMON

L: Look externally (facial trauma, beard, loose teeth, dentures, large incisors); these factors can indicate a difficult airway.

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Assessing Airway Risk

E: Evaluate the 3-3-2 rule

Can 3 fingers fit between the incisors?

Can 3 fingers fit between the tip of the chin and the hyoid bone?

Can 2 fingers fit from the top of the thyroid notch to the hyoid bone?

A decrease in these distances can be an indication of a difficult airway.

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Assessing Airway Risk

M: Mallampati score; assess how much of the posterior pharynx and uvula can be seen (a higher Mallampati score indicates a more difficult airway).

Mallampati 1 score: Indicates that the entirety of the uvula can be visualized

Mallampati 2 score: Indicates that half of the uvula can be visualized

Mallampati 3 score: Indicates that only the base of the uvula can be visualized

Mallampati 4 score: Indicates that the uvula cannot be visualized

Jmarchn, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Assessing Airway Risk

O: Obstruction or obesity

obesity (body mass index >30) can predict a difficult airway.

Obstruction of the airway, including head and neck cancer and epiglottitis, can indicate a difficult airway.

N: Neck mobility

assess the neck's mobility; a neck that cannot be maneuvered into an ideal position due to trauma, a C-collar, or rigidity can lead to a more difficult airway

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Positioning

The neck should be flexed at the lower cervical spine (C6-C7) and extended at the upper cervical spine (C1-C2) "sniffing position"

This allows for the best visualization of the anatomy, including the epiglottis and vocal cords.

Open Critical Care & World Health Organization, CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

Samir at English Wikipedia., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Anatomy

The epiglottis serves as the primary landmark that will direct successful endotracheal intubation.

The origin of the epiglottis can be found at the base of the tongue.

The valley between the tongue and the epiglottis is called the vallecula.

BruceBlaus, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Anatomy

When intubating with the laryngoscope, the tip of the blade should ideally be placed at the base of the tongue in the vallecula, and a ventral and inferior movement of the blade reveals the vocal cords.

BruceBlaus, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Modified Cormack- Lehane

The modified Cormack and Lehane Grading system allows the physician to evaluate their view of the vocal cord and estimate the chance of successful intubation.

The modified Cormack and lehane grading system consist of 4 grades

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Modified Cormack- Lehane

Tubus, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Table from slide 12
GradeDescriptionApproximate frequencyLikelihood of difficult intubation
1Full view of glottis70%<1%
2aPartial view of glottis20%8%
2bOnly posterior extremity of glottis seen or only arytenoid cartilage5%65%
3Only epiglottis seen, none of glottis seen1%85%
4Neither glottis nor epiglottis seenvery rarevery likely
SOURCE SLIDE 13

Endotracheal Tube Size

For adults:

Female: 7.0- to 7.5-mm internal diameter tube

Male: 7.5- to 8.0-mm tube

For pediatrics:

For uncuffed tubes: (age in years/4) + 4 mm

For cuffed tubes: (age in years/4) + 3.5 mm

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Blade Selection

The most commonly used laryngoscope blades are the Macintosh and Miller blades.

The Macintosh blade has a curved spatula that should be placed inside the vallecula and it is used to approximate the curvature of the tongue and move the epiglottis, mandible, hyoid bone, and other soft tissues out of the view of the glottis

Multiple sizes available

Sasata at English Wikipedia, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Blade Selection

The Miller blade is Flat spatula designed to go over the epiglottis to reveal the vocal cords.

Multiple sizes available

DiverDave, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Induction Agents

Induction agent administred via rapid IV push to induce anesthesia (uncsconsiosness) , options include:

Etomidate: 0.3 mg/kg , it has minimal effect on CVS and RS systems, it decreases ICP

Ketamine: 1-2 mg/kg, it increases heart rate and BP, more suitable in trauma, it lead to bronchodiltation, it increases ICP

Propofol: 0.5- 1.5 mg/kg, it decreases heart rate and BP, it causes the most respiratory depression

Anesthesia is maintained using inhaled volatile liquids, options: sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Paralytic agents

After administration of induction agent, paralytic agent should be administered

Options include:

Succinylcholine: 1 -2 mg/kg of total body weight, ultra rapid onset and offset (ideal for RSI), but very risky in patients with hyperkalemia (in burns, trauma, NMS disease), may cause malignant hyperthermia, bradycardia and increased ICP

Rocuronium: 1- 1.5 mg/kg of total body weight, onset is a little bit delayed (60 seconds) but it has minimal CVS side effects, no risk of malignant hyperthermia and much more safe in general

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Technique

Patient, supplies, and team must be properly prepared

Induction agents can be administered to the patient first, followed by paralytic agents

The bag valve mask should be utilized to pre-oxygenate the patient as much as possible with 100% oxygen and NIPPV.

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Technique

After allowing the paralytic agents to take effect after 60 seconds, place patient in sniffing position and open the mouth with the scissoring technique. The scissoring technique involves placing the right thumb on the right middle finger and inserting the right hand into the patient's mouth. The clinician then "scissors" the patient's mouth open, crossing the thumb and middle finger. This is explained in a video linked in the description

The laryngoscope should then be inserted into the patient's mouth with a sweeping motion from right to left, moving the tongue out of view.

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Technique

The clinician should locate the epiglottis and place the laryngoscope in the vallecula.

A ventral and inferior motion should be performed with a rigid wrist without abduction or "rocking" of the wrist.

Suctioning can be performed to obtain a better view and clear debris, and pressure can be applied to the thyroid cartilage to manipulate the glottis into view.

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Technique

Once the clinician has located the glottis, the endotracheal tube can be passed through the vocal cords.

Once passed, the stilette can be removed from the endotracheal tube.

The tube should be advanced based on the Chula formula: endotracheal tube depth=0.1 (height in cm) + 4.

This equation will give the depth at which the endotracheal tube should be advanced when measured at the patient's teeth.

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Technique

The cuff should be inflated after the tube is advanced to the proper distance.

End-tidal capnography, and bilateral lung sounds should all be used to verify placement initially.

A chest X-ray should be performed to assure adequate placement.

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Contraindications

Absolute contraindications include: complete upper airway obstruction and the loss of facial or oropharyngeal landmarks, which will require a surgical airway to be placed

Relative contraindications include:

Injuries to the airway

Anatomic abnormalities

The proficiency of the clinician

These relative contraindications can be evaluated using the L.E.M.O.N. mnemonic and Cormack and Lehane Grading system discussed already.

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Premature atrial contract inside (PAC)

SOURCE SLIDE 2

PACs

Premature atrial contractions occur when another region in the atria (other than the SA node) depolarizes before the SA node triggering a premature heartbeat

Premature atrial contractions (PACs), AKA Supraventricular ectopic beats (SVE), Supraventricular extrasystole (SVES), atrial premature complexes (APC) or atrial premature beats (APB)

Maxim Masiutin, CC BY-SA 4.0,via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

PACs

PACs have the following ECG characteristics:

The ectopic P waves appears sooner (premature) than the next expected sinus beats

The ectopic P waves may have a different shape and direction (because it is originating in a region other than the SA node)

The ectopic P waves maybe conducted through the AV node resulting in a NARROW QRS complex but if the PAC is premature enough, it would reach the AV node during its refractory period => not conducted

Maxim Masiutin, CC BY-SA 4.0,via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

PACs

Most PACs are conducted with typical QRS complexes but some may be conducted aberrantly through the infranodal system typically with a RBBB pattern

When the PAC occurs during the absolute refractory period it is not conducted

SOURCE SLIDE 5

PACs

If two PACs occur in a row, they are called doublets and three PACs triplets and the rhythm is called atrial bigeminy, trigeminy, or quadrigeminy

If two PACs occur in a row and at a frequency of 100 or more beats/ min, it is called atrial tachycardia

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Slide 6

Since the sinus node is often depolarized and reset, the interval between normal P waves before and after the PAC will not be twice the existing P to P interval , creating a shortest pause than a fully compensatory pause (unlike that seen after most premature ventricular contractions)

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

PACs

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Etiology

Idiopathic: diagnosed if other etiologies are excluded

Structural causes of PACs include coronary artery disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, left atrial appendage aneurysm, left ventricular hypertrophy, valvular heart disease, septal defects and Congenital heart malformation

Biochemical causes include sodium channel malformations and BMP2 mutations

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Etiology

Chemical causes incdeudde berta agonists, digoxin, chemotherapeutic drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and even beta blockers

Medical pathologies associated with increased incidence of PACs include MI, CHF, hypertension , DM, COPD, Coxasckie virus and higher CHA2DS2-VASC score

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Etiology

Also there is some states that predispose PACs such as anxiety , pregnancy, fatigue, alcohol and tobacco

Caffeine has not been associated with increased incidence of PACs (opposite to popular belief)

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Diagnosis

Patients are often completely asymptomatic or sometimes they will describe a skipped beat or sudden fluttering or movement in the chest

PACs can be diagnosed using ECGs but mostly caught on Holter studies

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Epidemiolgy

PACs are common the general population and increase with age

Over 99% of the general population will have at least one PAC in a 24 hour period

Many PACs can indicate increased risk of A fib and/or ischemic stroke

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Treatment

Asymptomatic patients require no treatment

Symptomatic patients are treated by treating the underlying disorder or discontinuation of precipitating drug and reassurance

A beta blocker or Type 1A, type 1C or type III antiarrhythmic medication can suppress PAC, but given accordingly after careful consideration to their pro arrhythmic nature; attempts should be made to control PACs non pharmacologically first

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

In patients with refractory symptoms despite medical therapy or those with cardiomyopathy or heart failure linked to PACs, and those patients whom PACs trigger atrial arrhythmias like A Fib; further interventional therapy is indicated such as atrial pacing, catheter ablation of the PAC origin

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Complications

PACs may lead to A Fib and ischemic stroke

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Extra glottic devices

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Extraglottic airway

It refers to a diverse collection of devices that are blindly inserted into the pharynx to provide an airway for ventilation and delivery of anesthetic gases without the need for tracheal intubation (they create patent airway without entering the trachea)

Extraglottic airway is less invasive than tracheal intubation, it also provides more reliable airway than a face mask for spontaneous ventilation and for PPV

ICUnurses, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Extraglottic airway

Extraglottic devices are most commonly used in the ED after a failed ETT tube, but may also be used primarily during cardiac arrest, for difficult mask ventilation or as part of rapid sequence airway procedures

It is critical to always have an appropriately seized EGD available during airway management to place the device in case difficulties are encountered but don’t rely on an EGD to the exclusion of surgical airway when critical hypoxemia is encountered

EGDs don’t protect trachea from obstruction or aspiration , they maybe used for several hours until a definitive airway can be secured

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Advantages

Advantages of EGDs include:

Faster and easier to apply than an ETT tube

Reduced anesthetic requirements

Reduced need for muscle relaxation

Avoidance to other risks that comes with tracheal intubation (trauma to teeth, sore throat, and bronchospasm)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Disadvantages

Disadvantages include smaller seal pressures than ETT tubes which means ineffective ventilation when higher airway pressures are required , also they provide no protection from laryngospasm, and older EGDs models provide less protection from gastric regurgitation and aspiration than newer models

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Classification

Supraglottic airways: that include a mask that sits internally over the glottic opening

Retroglottic airways: dual balloon devices that sit within the proximal esophagus and include distal and proximal balloons to direct the ventilation that occurs through holes between the two balloons into the airway

ICUnurses, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Classification

Many of these devices include a channel for gastric decompression (theoretically lessens the risk of aspiration) and some facilitate blind or endoscopic intubation

All EGDs can be placed without directly seeing the glottis (also called "blind" placement)

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Supraglottic airways

Supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) create a seal over the glottic opening to create an airway for ventilation

Examples of SGAs include: ambu auragain, LMA supreme, LMA Protector, LMA fastrach, inter surgical IGEL , AND Cook Gas AirQ.

The most commonly used SGA and extraglottic device in general is the laryngeal mask airway (LMA).

SOURCE SLIDE 9

SGAs

SGAs can be placed in under 30 seconds, making them advantageous for emergency use and has a success rate of 98%

Serious complications are rare and usually result from nerve and soft tissue trauma in the pharynx during placement.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Retroglottic airways

Retroglottic airway devices (RGAs) dual balloon device that pass behind the glottis and into the esophagus to create a seal allowing oxygen to be delivered directly to the trachea.

Examples include: the King laryngeal tube, esophageal trachea combitube, and the rusch easyTube

Like SGAs, most complications from RGAs result from trauma to the pharynx during placement.

Ochiwar, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

Vavoor, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Spine motion restriction

Previously it was called cervical spine immobilization and since true immobilization of the spine is unattainable, that is why spine motion restriction term was used instead

Spine motion restriction (SMR) is the maneuver done to reduce movement in a patient’s spine in trauma victims, thereby preventing spinal cord injury in a potentially unstable spine => preventing disability

Sgt. David Bedard, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Spine motion restriction

Spine motion restriction is achieved by applying a rigid cervical collar, rigid extrication device (for extrication), long back board (also for extrication) and a gurney with appropriate straps and sandbags for stabilization

Alexisrael, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Spine motion restriction

Spine motion restriction can be done manually by an emergency provider by applying hands to the both sides of the head into the neck to stabilize the c spine of the patient

If the patient on cervical collar need airway management, then the collar is removed and head is stabilized manually and airway management is done and then the collar put back again

SOURCE SLIDE 4

SMR indications

Any altered mental status (GCS < 15) => patient is confused or AMS then needs SMR, Pediatric patients may demonstrate altered mental status with agitation , apnea , hypopnea or somnolescence

Focal neurological signs and/or symptoms (e.g. weakness , tingling or numbness)

Midline neck or back pain and/ or tenderness, painful rotation/tilt of the neck

SOURCE SLIDE 5

SMR indications

Anatomic deformity of the spine

Unreliable patient interaction including distraction with a painful injury or distressing circumstances

Communication/ language barrier that prevent accurate assessment

SOURCE SLIDE 6

SMR indications

Lack of cooperation or contribution during exam

High energy trauma mechanisms: Axial load injuries (diving injuries , spearing tackles) , sudden acceleration/ deceleration injuries, lateral bending forces to neck/ torso

65 years of age or older

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Equipment

Adjustable rigid cervical collar

Short, rigid extrication device

X-ray translucent long back board for extrication

Soft padding placed where there is contact between skin and devices mentioned

Gurney with appropriate straps for stabilization of the patient

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Procedure

1- Assess airway and manage the airway if it need to be managed while maintaining manual SMR

2- Do a pre SMR assessment of the motor, sensory and circulatory examination and document it

3- Place the rigid cervical collar and adjust size

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Procedure

4- If patient can self extricate then assist them in getting into the gurney but if not then extrication is required, extrication device is used as needed to move the patient to gurney Then, it is removed by log roll

5- Secure the patient to the gurney with straps in a supine position, if supine position can’t be tolerated then position of comfort is done, if patient is obviously pregnant then left lateral position is preferred

6- Do a post SMR assessment of the motor, sensory and circulatory examination and document it

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Contraindications

Bleeding that is can’t be controlled with the SMR in place

Uncontrolled vomiting because SMR risk airway patency

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Notes

Effort should be made to diagnose or exclude the spine injury and remove the patient from this form of rigid device as soon as possible (because it is not comfortable for the patient)

Rigid backboards use is limited to extrication and transfer of patients to a gurney, because their prolonged use may induce pain, agitation, respiratory compromise and lead to pressure ulcers

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Notes

SMR is performed with the patient supine, it cannot be safely performed with a patient in a sitting position

If elevation of the head is required, maintain alignment of the neck and torso while elevating the head consider reverse Trendelenburg, if stretcher allows

Saltanat ebli, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Notes

Children may require additional padding under the shoulders to avoid excessive cervical spine flexion with SMR

flB-sPYNJ34.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Sinus arrhythmia

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Sinus arrhythmia

Some variation in sinoatrial node discharge rate is common, normally it should be less than 120 ms (3 small squares in ECG paper) between the longest and shortest P-P interval

Sinus arrhythmia is when the variation exceeds 120 ms

Rocuronium Bromide, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Sinus arrhythmia

ECG characteristics of sinus arrhythmia include:

Normal sinus P waves (P wave is monoform and in pattern consistent it originating from the sinus node) and PR interval

1:1 atrioventricular conduction (AV conduction)

Variation of at least 120 ms between the shortest and longest P – P interval

Ewingdo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Sinus arrhythmia

Occasional junctional escape beats maybe present during very long P-P interval

No treatment is required

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Sinus arrhythmia

Sinus arrhythmias are affected primarily by respiration (because during respiration, intermittent vagus nerve activation occurs, which result in beat-to-beat variation in the resting heart rate)

Sinus arrhythmia commonly found in children and young adults, disappearing with advancing age

It indicates good cardiovascular health

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Presentation

Sinus arrhythmia is an incidental finding on ECGs

Rarely it may lead to symptoms like SOB and palpitation

SOURCE SLIDE 7

DDx

If two or more different P waves morphologies are present then atrial ectopy, wandering atrial pacemaker or another competing non sinus focus maybe present

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Mask Ventilation

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mask ventilation

Indications

Apnea or impending respiratory arrest (gasping)

Prior to intubation

Mask ventilation can be achieved with:

One provider: using BVM, one hand pressing the bag, the other one making a seal with the face

Two providers: using BVM, one dedicated to maintaining a tight seal while the second one is responsible provides just enough volume to raise the chest or

One provider and mechanical ventilator

vintagelove67, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Bag valve mask

BVM contain a self inflating bag, attached to a nonrebreathing valve and then to a face mask and an oxygen source which is attached to a reservoir bag

Mike6271, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mask ventilation

Step 1: Patients should be placed in a sniffing or ramped position (head tilt/chin lift and/or jaw thrust), in trauma patients suspected for C spine injury, only jaw thrust is done

Step 2: Airway adjuncts should be placed (NPA and OPA if the patient doesn’t have gag reflex)

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Staff Sgt. Haley Zimmerman, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Mask ventilation

Step 3: Apply a properly fitted mask (covers mouth and nostrils without any gaps between the mask and face), there is adult and pediatric masks

Step 4: make a good seal between the mask and the face. A CE (anesthetist grip) grip can be used, if it is done by one hand and gripped from the side then the mask will tilt to one side allowing the air to leak under the opposite side

vintagelove67, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

“A good seal”

If the mask gripped around the lower half of the face then it allows the air to escape through the nasal bridge

If the mask gripped with a rotated grip (rotated hold) then it provides better seal than both of the techniques mentioned already

SOURCE SLIDE 7

“A good seal”

If two providers are involved then mask ventilation will be more effective, one provider (the operator) can concentrate on their BVM technique while the second provider (the assistant) can use both hands to provide an effective mask seal one the patient face

For the assistant, two grips can be used:

CE grip

Thenar eminence grip (TE): it is achieved by using thenar muscles to place downward pressure one the mask while the four finger of each hand pullin the jaw upward

SOURCE SLIDE 8

“A good seal”

If you are unable to achieve a mask seal consider placing an extraglottic device if there is no gag reflex or other contraindications or endotracheal intubation

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Mask ventilation

Step 5: Volume, Rate and pressure

Volume: previously volume per ventilation for adults was 800 ml but recent guidelines suggest a more conservative 6- 8 ml/kg per ventilation (same as the normal tidal volume) ( for an adult weighing 80kg approx. 480- 640 ml per ventilation) and even less for patients with known respiratory illness

Higher volume than 8 ml/kg would risk gastric insufflation and aspiration, also it leads to hypocapnia and barotrauma to lungs

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Mask ventilation

In reality, metrics are not that useful because they will vary with each patient weight and lung capacity. So it is best to look for adequate chest rise and fall with each ventilation

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Rate

For patients in cardiac arrest, current UK and European guidelines recommend inflation duration of one second every 5 seconds resulting in a rate of one complete ventilation every 6 seconds or 10 ventilation in a minute

For patients breathing spontaneously then the normal resting minute ventilation in humans is around 70- 100 ml/kg/min and it achieved by delivering the normal tidal volume (6-8 ml/kg/ventilation) in a rate of 12- 16 breaths /min (same as normal respiratory rate)

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Pressure

In BVM ventilation it is possible to over inflate the patient by squeezing the bag too hard or too fast or too much

Inspiratory pressure if exceeds 20 mmHg, this would increase the risk of forcing the air in the stomach (gastric insufflation) and spiration

Inspiratory pressures should be around 15 mmHg

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Pressure

BVM that are equipped with a pressure responsive, and flow limiting valves, reduces mean airway pressure thus reducing the risk for gastric insufflation compared to standard bags

SOURCE SLIDE 14

PEEP

Positive end expiratory pressure may be used during BVM to improve oxygenation, PEEP keeps more alveoli open and prevents atelectasis thus improving oxygentation and it also prevent lung injury

PEEP should be used cautiously in hypotensive or heart failure patients

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Difficult BVM

Characteristic of difficult BVM are collected in mnemonic MOANS

M Mask seal: facial hair or facial trauma can interfere in achieving adequate seal

O obesity/ obstruction: obesity means increased soft tissue in the airway and may cause further occlusion when the patient is AMS

A age: extremes of age can be difficult to ventilate due to anatomic changes

N no teeth: BVM in no teeth patient is ineffective

S snoring: snoring means that soft tissues (e.g. tongue) is occluding the airway and airway maneuvers and adjuncts are required

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Difficult BVM

In difficult BVM , supraglottic airway or intubation is preferred

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Complications

Mask ventilation may:

Accelerate hypoxia if not enough oxygen is provided

Accelerate hypercapnia if not enough CO2 is removed, leading to brain damage

Over ventilation can exacerbate existing lung injuries and lead to gastric insufflation and subsequently aspiration

outline.heading: Mask ventilation
outline.summary: Step 3: Apply a properly fitted mask (covers mouth and nostrils without any gaps between the mask and face), there is adult and pediatric masks Step 4: make a good seal between the mask and the face. A CE (anesthetist grip) grip can be used, if it is done by one hand and gripped from the side then the mask will tilt to one side allowing the air to leak under the opposite side vintagelove67, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: “A good seal”
outline.summary: If the mask gripped around the lower half of the face then it allows the air to escape through the nasal bridge If the mask gripped with a rotated grip (rotated hold) then it provides better seal than both of the techniques mentioned already

outline.heading: “A good seal”
outline.summary: If two providers are involved then mask ventilation will be more effective, one provider (the operator) can concentrate on their BVM technique while the second provider (the assistant) can use both  hands to provide an effective mask seal one the patient face For the assistant, two grips can be used: CE grip Thenar eminence grip (TE): it is achieved by using thenar muscles to place downward pressure one the mask while the four finger of each hand pullin the jaw upward

outline.heading: “A good seal”
outline.summary: If you are unable to achieve a mask seal consider placing an extraglottic device if there is no gag reflex or other contraindications or endotracheal intubation

outline.heading: Mask ventilation
outline.summary: Step 5: Volume, Rate and pressure Volume: previously volume per ventilation for adults was 800 ml but recent guidelines suggest a more conservative 6- 8 ml/kg per ventilation (same as the normal tidal volume) ( for an adult weighing 80kg approx. 480- 640 ml per ventilation) and even less for patients with known respiratory illness Higher volume than 8 ml/kg would risk gastric insufflation and aspiration, also it leads to hypocapnia and barotrauma to lungs

outline.heading: Mask ventilation
outline.summary: In reality, metrics are not that useful because they will vary with each patient weight and lung capacity. So it is best to look for adequate chest rise and fall with each ventilation

outline.heading: Rate
outline.summary: For patients in cardiac arrest, current UK and European guidelines recommend inflation duration of one second every 5 seconds resulting in a rate of one complete ventilation every 6 seconds or 10 ventilation in a minute For patients breathing spontaneously then the normal resting minute ventilation in humans is around 70- 100 ml/kg/min and it achieved by delivering the normal tidal volume (6-8 ml/kg/ventilation) in a rate of 12- 16 breaths /min (same as normal respiratory rate)

outline.heading: Pressure
outline.summary: In BVM ventilation it is possible to over inflate the patient by squeezing the bag too hard or too fast or too much Inspiratory pressure if exceeds 20 mmHg, this would increase the risk of forcing the air in the stomach (gastric insufflation) and spiration Inspiratory pressures should be around 15 mmHg

outline.heading: Pressure
outline.summary: BVM that are equipped with a pressure responsive, and flow limiting valves, reduces mean airway pressure thus reducing the risk for gastric insufflation compared to standard bags

outline.heading: PEEP
outline.summary: Positive end expiratory pressure may be used during BVM to improve oxygenation, PEEP keeps more alveoli open and prevents atelectasis thus improving oxygentation and it also prevent lung injury PEEP should be used cautiously in hypotensive or heart failure patients

outline.heading: Difficult BVM
outline.summary: Characteristic of difficult BVM are collected in mnemonic MOANS M Mask seal: facial hair or facial trauma can interfere in achieving adequate seal O obesity/ obstruction: obesity means increased soft tissue in the airway and may cause further occlusion when the patient is AMS A age: extremes of age can be difficult to ventilate due to anatomic changes N no teeth: BVM in no teeth patient is ineffective S snoring: snoring means that soft tissues (e.g. tongue) is occluding the airway and airway maneuvers and adjuncts are required

outline.heading: Difficult BVM
outline.summary: In difficult BVM , supraglottic airway or intubation is preferred

outline.heading: Complications
outline.summary: Mask ventilation may: Accelerate hypoxia if not enough oxygen is provided Accelerate hypercapnia if not enough CO2 is removed, leading to brain damage Over ventilation can exacerbate existing lung injuries and lead to gastric insufflation and subsequently aspiration

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation involves the delivery of oxygen into the lungs via positive pressure through a face mask without the need for endotracheal intubation.

Non-invasive means using face masks and invasive means ETT tube insertion or surgical airway.

James Heilman, MD, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

CPAP & BPAP

NIPPV is delivered via a full-face mask using either continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BPAP) using a ventilator or stand-alone reusable device.

CPAP provides the same amount of pressure support during inspiration and expiration (5 to 20 mmHg)

PruebasBMA, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

CPAP & BPAP

BPAP provides different values for inspiration and expiration (IPAP and EPAP) so it allows for increasing inspiratory pressures up to 15 mm Hg without overwhelming the patient with expiratory resistance, which may remain at 5 to 10 mm Hg.

There are no studies showing a significant advantage to one system over another.

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Normal physiology of respiration

Breathing is negative pressure process, negative pressure comes from expansion of the chest (increase in volume) due to elevation of the ribs and relaxation of diaphragm (negative pressure ventilation)

In expiration ribs depresses and diaphragm contract to get the air out leading to positive pressure

Henry Vandyke Carter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

NPPV

NPPV works by increasing the outside pressure, air enters the lungs easier

In COPD, there is air trapping inside the lungs due to emphysema and bronchitis, leading to increased pressures inside them, so by increasing the outside pressures, breathing will be easier

Same applies when the alveoli are filled with water in pulmonary edema

Henry Vandyke Carter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Indications

NPPV is indicated in respiratory failure (hypoxia and/or hypercapnia), that is when the lungs are not working well and they need help

According to American thoracic society and European respiratory journal guidelines, NPPV is strongly recommended in the setting of respiratory failure due to:

Acute exacerbation of COPD where PH < 7.35

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Indications

NPPV is also effective but to lesser degree in:

Post operative acute respiratory failure

Early NPPV Immunocompromised patients with ARF

Palliation to dyspneic patients in terminal cancer and other terminal conditions

Chest trauma patients with ARF

Chronic stable COPD with hypercapnia

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

Obstructive sleep apnea

Respiratory failure due to neuromuscular disease and restrictive thoracic disorders

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Indications

NPPV also used for pre oxygenation prior to intubation in any medical condition, or as an alternative to invasive airway management in some cases, such as in patients with DNR or DNI status.

NPPV is not that effective for pneumonia, it may even delay mechanical ventilation leading to worse outcome; it is used only in case of shortages of invasive ventilation equipment and facilities (e.g.during covid 19)

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Device setting

CPAP: one pressure setting, start with 5 mmHg and titrate up according to response (clinical improvement and vitals) (max is 20 mmHg)

BPAP: two pressure settings, IPAP start with 10 and EPAP start with 5, the sum of both should be less than 20

Pressures above 20 mmHg for both would lead to abdominal distension

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Device parts

Mask: on several types including nose masks, nose-mouth masks and helmets

Tubing

Oxygen supply

Power supply

Humidifier

Zboralski, via Wikimedia Commons

Michael Symonds, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Complications

Mask discomfort

Skin rash secondary to infection or hypersensitivity reactions

nasal bridge ulcers (rare)

Aerophagia and hypersalivation

Ear and sinus pain and gastric insufflation due to the pressure

Serious side effects include pneumothorax, pneumocephalus, pneumomediastinum and aspiration

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Complications

In patient with heart failure, who are hypotensive, NPPV might aggravate hypotension due to increased intrathoracic pressure, increased right ventricular afterload and decreased preload

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Complications

Patient ventilator dyssynchrony in BPAP: failure to trigger the breathing cycle leading to IPAP applied during expiration and EPAP applied during inspiration which lead to inadequate gas exchange and unnecessary expiratory muscle use , e.g. in COPD where rapid inhalations may not give the BPAP adequate time to cycle from inspiration to expiration thus patient is expiring against ventilator effort to deliver inspiratory pressure leading to respiratory distress

Also failure to trigger can be seen in Neuromuscular disease such as ALS where patient cannot generate enough negative pressure during inspiration to trigger assisted breath

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Contraindications

Patient with a lot of secretions requiring frequent suckers

Vomiting

Agitation

Comatose patient

Sedated patient

Hypotensive patient

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Prognosis

NPPV has been shown to reduce intubation in COPD and cardiogenic pulmonary edema

It is also shown to reduce the need for reintubation in hypercapnic respiratory failure following extubation.

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Airway management

Patients with GCS of 8 or less may have lost pharyngeal muscle tone, cough reflex and swallow reflex (can’t protect their airway) so they need airway management

We have several different modalities of airway management

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Modalities of airway management

Basic airway management:

Maneuvers: head tilt/chin lift and jaw thrust

Airway adjuncts: OPA and NPA

Advanced airway management:

EGD and ETT tube

Surgical airway: cricothyrotomy and tracheostomy

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Maneuvers

Head tilt/ chin lift: it is achieved by tilting the head back while keeping the mouth closed (teeth approximated) (sniffing position)

Extension of the head lead to posterior oropharynx get further away from the base of the tongue and opens the airway; chin lift will lift the mandible which is attached to the tongue (so lifting the tongue) and opening the airway

Original: Vassia Atanassova Vector: Offnfopt, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Maneuvers

Head tilt/chin lift is used in non trauma patients (patients with no suspected c spine injury) because this maneuver manipulate the c spine into injuring the spinal cord so jaw thrust is done instead

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Maneuvers

To perform jaw thrust in trauma patients, two emergency providers have to be involved, one to perform the jaw thrust , the other one is to stabilize the head and neck area

Jaw thrust is done by both hands on the face, palms are on the zygomatic bone and fingers lift the jaw, thumbs open the mouth

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Spine motion restriction

Spine motion restriction is the maneuver done to stabilize the head and neck area in case of a suspected c spine injury

Spine motion restriction can be done by applying a rigid cervical collar (it is not enough) and furtherly stabilizing the spine using sandbags and several straps on a stretcher

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Spine motion restriction

Spine motion restriction can be done manually by an emergency provider by applying hands to the both sides of the head into the neck to stabilize the c spine of the patient

if the patient on cervical collar need airway management, then the collar is removed and head is stabilized manually and airway management is done and then the collar put back again

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Airway adjuncts

Oropharyngeal airway (OPA)

Nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)

SOURCE SLIDE 9

OPA

OPA is put to bypass the tongue (thus preventing tongue prolapse)

It will provide airway patency but not protection so it is a temporary measure

Indication of OPA is coma , when patient doesn’t have gag reflex

Hospital, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

OPA

OPA comes in different sizes and it has to be measured from the first incisors to the angle of the jaw

if OPA size is less or more than ideal size for the patient, it might lead to airway obstruction instead of opening,

Too small might push the tongue into closing the airway

Too big might go into the esophagus and block the airway

SOURCE SLIDE 11

OPA

Placement is by entering it upside down until it touch the hard palate then it is flipped and entered (to bypass the dome of the tongue)

It can also be inserted by depressing the tongue by a tongue depressor and inserting the piece

Open Critical Care & World Health Organization, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

NPA

if patient does have gag reflex then OPA is contraindicated and NPA can be used instead because anything introduced nasally is less gag stimulating

NPA is longer than OPA for the same patient

Pflegewiki-User Würfel, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 13

NPA

Contraindications to NPA:

Basal skull fractures: patient present with symptoms such as otorrhea, raccoon eyes and battle sign. Cribriform plate could be fractured in these patients and NPA can enter the brain through the cribriform and cause brain injury

Severe midface fracture and those are commonly associated with basal skull fractures

Marion County Sheriff's Office, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

NPA

NPA is measured from Infront of the nose and should reach the angle of the jaw or tragus of the ear

NPA is used with water soluble lubricant to prevent injury and then introduced into the nose

Device is inserted until the flared end rest against the nostril

Staff Sgt. Haley Zimmerman, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Basic airway management

Always remember that airway maneuvers and adjuncts are just a bridge to the creation of a definitive airway

If both adjuncts are contraindicated then continue to do maneuvers until definitive airway can be done

In pediatrics maneuvers and adjuncts have to be done together to keep airway open because tongue size is big

SpjIi-cbawo.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Advanced airway support

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Bedside assessment of the airway

Bedside assessment of the airway is done to decide if patient need airway management or not

In bedside assessment of the airway => we follow the Steps of Look, listen and feel

Same steps are applied in the breathing and circulation assessment and they all done at the same time but here we will focus on the airway only

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Look

In looking you assess:

Consciousness

Color of the patient

Mouth

Neck

Chest

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Consciousness

Brain is responsible of keeping the consciousness and the brain does have other functions including keeping the pharyngeal muscle tone which keeps the airway open

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pharyngeal muscle tone

one of the important muscles in keeping the airway open is the pharyngeal muscles

when we lie supine, gravity pulls down the tongue posteriorly but the pharyngeal muscles tone keep the tongue up and prevent tongue prolapse

LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pharyngeal muscle tone

One of the brain functions is to keep the pharyngeal muscle tone active, some brain neurons always firing to keep these muscles active

When there is a pathology that causes disturbance in brain function and patient become unconscious, other brain function maybe also get affected including the muscle tone leading to loss of tone and posterior tongue prolapse and blocked airway

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Consciousness

If patient consciousness is impaired (coma or AMS) then the other brain functions might be also impaired (such as pharyngeal muscle tone) and this means that the airway is compromised and requires management

General guidelines suggest that at GCS of 8 or lower, airway management with a definitive airway is required

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Glasgow Coma Scale

Table from slide 8
ScoreEye openingVerbal response Motor response
1None None None
2Open to pain Incomprehensible sounds (like moaning)Extensor posturing
3Open to voice Inappropriate words (random)Flexor posturing
4Open spontaneously Confused or disoriented Withdrawal in response to pain
5Oriented Localize pain
6Follows commands
SOURCE SLIDE 9

Conscioussness

Also airway reflexes such as the cough reflex and swallow reflex are most likely impaired when GCS is 8 or below

So if the patient GCS is 8 or below, this patient requires airway management

if patient has altered mental status such as agitation or somnolescence (drowsy), this might be caused by hypoxemia which might be caused by airway obstruction so always look for that

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Conscioussness

CO2 retention is also might be caused by airway obstruction in rare cases, because it is mostly caused by breathing problems

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Color of the patient

if patient color is blue (cyanosis), this is due to increased deoxygenated hemoglobin above 5 g/dl (for the average HB of 15 g/dl), this is also termed severe hypoxemia when O2 saturation is in the 60s

This could be due to airway obstruction so look for that

Eva-Leonne Göttgens, Kristian Baks, Cornelis L. Harteveld, Kristel Goossens & Adriaan J. van Gammeren, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Mouth

In looking at the mouth, you look for secretions coming out (drooling)

Drooling could be due to airway related problem especially in pediatrics, that is because to swallow secretions, there has to be a period where glottis closes (respiration stops) to allow secretions to cross, but if the child is dyspnic, they can't stop breathing so they let secretions out and focus on breathing, (e.g. epiglottitis)

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Mouth

When there is increased secretions such as in organophosphorus poisoning , this may lead to aspiration of secretions and pneumonia because there is a certain limit to amount of secretions that can be swallowed, if secretions exceeded that limit, aspiration occurs

If the patient is unconscious then you also look inside the mouth if there is foreign body or if there is secretions, (secretions inside the mouth indicate swallow reflex is lost and patient need airway management)

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Mouth

Foreign bodies like fractured teeth or blood clots should be removed and all secretions should be suctioned out of unconscious patient mouth

You also look at the face, if there is severe fascial trauma this means patient might need airway management

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Neck

In trauma cases, Look for expanding mass (hematoma), this might compress the airway and lead to obstruction

Also look if patient is using accessory muscles such as scalenus or sternocleidomastoid , this means labored breathing ,

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Chest

You also look at the chest if there is recessions , this also indicates labored breathing

Labored breathing is mostly due to breathing problem but it could be due to airway problem too

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Chest

Also look at the chest if it is moving or not and calculate the respiratory rate

look at the pattern of breathing

in complete airway obstruction , look for paradoxical breathing (diaphragm and ribs move in opposite directions during inspiration and expiration)

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Listen

List for

Abnormal upper airway breath sounds: Stridor, Gurgling and Snoring

Speech

Stridor: it is mainly an inspiratory sound but could be inspiratory-expiratory, for stridor to develop, trachea has to be blocked by 90 % or more (severe obstruction) => airway management is necessary

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Listen

Gurgling: this is due to air passing through secretions, and normally secretions have to be swallowed so if gurgling is heard then secretions are not being swallowed (swallow reflex lost) and airway have to be managed

Snoring: it is made due to loss of the muscle tone in the soft palate leading to redundant soft palate which blocks the airway when the patient is supine, so for the air to pass, it has to push the redundant soft palate and flow leading to the snoring sound => this requires putting the patient in left lateral position and airway management is required

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Listen

Noisy breathing: it is a mix between snoring and gurgling and this definitely requires airway management

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Listen

Also, listen to patient’s speech, if patient can speak this means that it is unlikely problem in the airway; if patient can't complete a sentence and tachypneic then this is mostly a breathing problem but could be due to airway

if patient has muffled sound after trauma to larynx , then this patient has a direct laryngeal trauma and may need airway management

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Listen

Hot potato speech: This maybe due to airway problem In peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) which has to be drained , it also might be due to bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy but that is not related to the airway

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Feel

Feel the larynx, if it is clicking When pressed on, this means it is fractured, in this case airway may get obstructed so airway management might be needed

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Feel

Feel the neck, if there is crackling sensation felt, same as when you press on wet sponge, this is due to surgical emphysema , mostly coming from pleura when there is lung injury or it could be coming from the airway if there is airway injury, this has to be excluded

Surgical emphysema is not life threatening because it will spread to all body subcutaneous tissue because there is no septa between subcutaneous tissue; but airway injury or lung injury has to be looked for and treated

outline.heading: Bedside assessment of the airway
outline.summary: Bedside assessment of the airway is done  to decide if patient need airway management or not In bedside assessment of the airway => we follow the Steps of Look, listen and feel Same steps are applied in the breathing and circulation assessment and they all done at the same time but here we will focus on the airway only

outline.heading: Look
outline.summary: In looking you assess: Consciousness Color of the patient Mouth Neck Chest

outline.heading: Consciousness
outline.summary: Brain is responsible of keeping the consciousness and the brain does have other functions including keeping the pharyngeal muscle tone which keeps the airway open

outline.heading: Pharyngeal muscle tone
outline.summary: one of the important muscles in keeping the airway open is the pharyngeal muscles when we lie supine, gravity pulls down the tongue posteriorly but the pharyngeal muscles tone keep the tongue up and prevent tongue prolapse LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Pharyngeal muscle tone
outline.summary: One of the brain functions is to keep the pharyngeal muscle tone active, some brain neurons always firing to keep these muscles active When there is a pathology that causes disturbance in brain function and patient become unconscious, other brain function maybe also get affected including the muscle tone leading to loss of tone and posterior tongue prolapse and blocked airway

outline.heading: Consciousness
outline.summary: If patient consciousness is impaired (coma or AMS) then the other brain functions might be also impaired (such as pharyngeal muscle tone) and this means that the airway is compromised and requires management General guidelines suggest that at GCS of 8 or lower, airway management with a definitive airway is required

outline.heading: Conscioussness
outline.summary: Also airway reflexes such as the cough reflex and swallow reflex are most likely impaired when GCS is 8 or below So if the patient GCS is 8 or below, this patient requires airway management if patient has altered mental status such as agitation or somnolescence (drowsy), this might be caused by hypoxemia which might be caused by airway obstruction so always look for that

outline.heading: Conscioussness
outline.summary: CO2 retention is also might be caused by airway obstruction in rare cases, because it is mostly caused by breathing problems

outline.heading: Color of the patient
outline.summary: if patient color is blue (cyanosis), this is due to increased deoxygenated hemoglobin above 5 g/dl (for the average HB of 15 g/dl), this is also termed severe hypoxemia when O2 saturation is in the 60s This could be due to airway obstruction so look for that Eva-Leonne Göttgens, Kristian Baks, Cornelis L. Harteveld, Kristel Goossens & Adriaan J. van Gammeren, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Mouth
outline.summary: In looking at the mouth, you look for secretions coming out (drooling) Drooling could be due to airway related problem especially in pediatrics, that is because to swallow secretions, there has to be a period where glottis closes (respiration stops) to allow secretions to cross, but if the child is dyspnic, they can't stop breathing so they let secretions out and focus on breathing, (e.g. epiglottitis)

outline.heading: Mouth
outline.summary: When there is increased secretions such as in organophosphorus poisoning , this may lead to aspiration of secretions and pneumonia because there is a certain limit to amount of secretions that can be swallowed, if secretions exceeded that limit, aspiration occurs If the patient is unconscious then you also look inside the mouth if there is foreign body or if there is secretions, (secretions inside the mouth indicate swallow reflex is lost and patient need airway management)

outline.heading: Mouth
outline.summary: Foreign bodies like fractured teeth or blood clots should be removed and all secretions should be suctioned out of unconscious patient mouth You also look at the face, if there is severe fascial trauma this means patient might need airway management

outline.heading: Neck
outline.summary: In trauma cases, Look for expanding mass (hematoma), this might compress the airway and lead to obstruction Also look if patient is using accessory muscles such as scalenus or sternocleidomastoid , this means labored breathing ,

outline.heading: Chest
outline.summary: You also look at the chest if there is recessions , this also indicates labored breathing Labored breathing is mostly due to breathing problem but it could be due to airway problem too

outline.heading: Chest
outline.summary: Also look at the chest if it is moving or not and calculate the respiratory rate look at the pattern of breathing in complete airway obstruction , look for paradoxical breathing (diaphragm and ribs move in opposite directions during inspiration and expiration)

outline.heading: Listen
outline.summary: List for Abnormal upper airway breath sounds: Stridor, Gurgling and Snoring Speech Stridor: it is mainly an inspiratory sound but could be inspiratory-expiratory, for stridor to develop, trachea has to be blocked by 90 % or more (severe obstruction) => airway management is necessary

outline.heading: Listen
outline.summary: Gurgling: this is due to air passing through secretions, and normally secretions have to be swallowed so if gurgling is heard then secretions are not being swallowed (swallow reflex lost) and airway have to be managed Snoring: it is made due to loss of the muscle tone in the soft palate leading to redundant soft palate which blocks the airway when the patient is supine, so for the air to pass, it has to push the redundant soft palate and flow leading to the snoring sound => this requires putting the patient in left lateral position and airway management is required

outline.heading: Listen
outline.summary: Noisy breathing: it is a mix between snoring and gurgling and this definitely requires airway management

outline.heading: Listen
outline.summary: Also, listen to patient’s speech, if patient can speak this means that it is unlikely problem in the airway; if patient can't complete a sentence and tachypneic then this is mostly a breathing problem but could be due to airway if patient has muffled sound after trauma to larynx , then this patient has a direct laryngeal trauma and may need airway management

outline.heading: Listen
outline.summary: Hot potato speech: This maybe due to airway problem In peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) which has to be drained , it also might be due to bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy but that is not related to the airway
