outline.summary: Feel the larynx, if it is clicking When pressed on, this means it is fractured, in this case airway may get obstructed so airway management might be needed

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Advanced airway support: Introduction

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Airway management

Airway management is not well covered in textbooks

Airway comes first (ABC) in resuscitation, whatever you do in resuscitation is useless if the airway is blocked

LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Anatomy of the airway

Airway starts from nasal orifices and ends in alveoli, but we manage the upper airway in resuscitation which is supraglottic , (everything above glottis) also everything in neck and above , not thoracic (extra thoracic)

Now let’s talk a little bit about anatomy, so we have nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, laryngeal opening, epiglottis , vallecula (groove)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Characteristics of the normal airway

Patent: open

Protected: by neurological reflexes like cough reflex and swallow reflex

Maintained: airway stays open if patient position changed or if time passed

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Maintained airway

In case patient GCS is less than 8 =severe depression in consciousness, This means that other brain functions also severely depressed

One of these functions is pharyngeal muscles tone (certain brain neurons is continuously discharging to keep pharyngeal muscle tone) , if depressed then tongue will prolapse posteriorly and airway get blocked (airway is not maintained)

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Maintained airway

In case of angioedema to lips and tongue , this also means airway is not maintained because airway might get blocked in the future when angioedema reaches the pharynx and larynx

Adebayo PB, Alebiosu OC, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

When to manage the airway

Any problem in patency, protection or maintenance , this will require airway management by creating an artificial airway that has all characteristic of normal airway (patent, protected and maintained), this is called definitive airway

Definitive airway is a tube that connect the external environment with the trachea and has a cuff inflated below vocal cords (to prevent secretions from entering the trachea)

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Examples of definitive airways

ETT tube: tube inserted nasally or through the mouth and enters the trachea and it has a cuff inflated below the vocal cords

ETT tube is patent (made of relatively hard material resistant to kinking) , protected by the cuff that prevents secretions from entering the trachea and frequent suctioning and it is maintained because it is open regardless of time and position of the patient

bigomar2, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Examples of definitive airways

Cricothyroidotomy: you open cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage) you go in trachea , it also has a cuff inflated below vocal cords

Olek Remesz (wiki-pl: Orem, commons: Orem), CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Examples of definitive airways

Tracheostomy: in suprasternal notch we open into the trachea, also has a cuff

In emergency department, first choice is ETT tube and if failed you can put a cric or a tracheostomy

National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (NIH), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Examples of definitive airways

Cric is more preferred to tracheostomy in emergency settings, because it is faster to make , in tracheostomy you have to dissect through muscles you might hit a bleeder while in cric you go through a thin membrane into the airway

Tracheostomy can be permanent while cric can’t be left for more than 72 hours because of risk cartilage necrosis due to pressure from the tube

SOURCE SLIDE 13

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Hepatic encephalopathy

Hepatic encephalopathy is a syndrome of disordered consciousness and neuromuscular abnormalities resulting from the buildup of neurotoxic substances in the bloodstream (e.g. ammonia) which affect the brain function

It commonly affects patients with chronic liver disease, but sometimes it may develop in patients without prior liver conditions who develop acute liver failure

Because liver function is to detoxify the blood coming from intestine, and once the liver is ill, toxins pass into the systemic circulation

SOURCE SLIDE 2

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

In This Video

Hepatic encephalopathy

Causes

Pathophysiology

Clinical features

Diagnosis

Treatment

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Causes

Chronic liver disease or acute fulminant liver failure => liver cannot detoxify toxins coming from intestine into systemic circulation => toxins reaching the brain => hepatic encephalopathy

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Causes

Redirection of blood flow away from the liver (portosystemic shunting) e.g. TIPS and spontaneous shunts=> toxins are bypassing the liver into the systemic circulation => toxins reaching the brain => hepatic encephalopathy ; Hepatic encephalopathy occur in up to 50% of patients undergone TIPS procedure

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Causes

Spontaneous portosystemic shunts occur when fetal shunt pathways between the portal and systemic circulation open due to high blood pressure inside the portal veins in diseases such as cirrhosis, eventually the systemic shunt increases in volume and poral circulation declines

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

Intestinal bacteria and digestive enzymes breakdown dietary proteins, releasing ammonia within the GI tract. The produced ammonia get absorbed into the venous circulation and to the portal vein into the liver

In the normal liver, ammonia is converted to urea via the urea cycle and excreted through the kidneys

In cases of liver failure or systemic shunts, ammonia can accumulate and get diverted to the systemic circulation leading to hyperammonemia

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Pathophysiology

Ammonia is neurotoxic substance and it can cross the BBB

Ammonia impairs excitatory neurotransmission leading to disruption of neuronal function and encephalopathy

Also ammonia will be converted to glutamine in the brain which act as osmolyte causing increase in cerebral volume and brain edema; risk of cerebral edema is really high when arterial ammonia levels surpass 200 micromole/ L; those levels are reached in fulminant acute liver failure more than chronic liver failure

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Important note

If hepatic encephalopathy occur in patients with chronic liver disease, then it is potentially reversible and treatable while if it occurs in patients with acute liver failure then this lead to rapid increase in blood ammonia levels which is difficult to control and result in widespread brain edema and structural brain injuries and those might be irreversible

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Clinical features

Hepatic encephalopathy is characterized by appearance of neurocognitive and neuromuscular manifestations

Neurocognitive manifestations include reduced awareness of one’s surrounding and stimuli, accompanied by behaviors such as yawning sleeping for short period of times, insomnia or hypersomnia, as the condition progresses, patients develop increased levels of confusion, lethargy, and personality changes

neurocognitive manifestations are variable and precede neuromuscular manifestations

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Clinical features

Neuromuscular manifestations include bradykinesia, asterixis, slurred speech, ataxia, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes and nystagmus; in later stages, patient may experience jactitation (twitching of a limb or muscle) , and positive Babinski sign

Less frequently patient may develop areflexia, transient decerebrate posturing and coma

Some patients develop focal neurological deficit despite negative CT or MRI brain scan

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Clinical features

If hepatic encephalopathy developed in patient with chronic liver disease, then other clinical features related to chronic liver disease might be present: muscle wasting, jaundice, ascites, palmar erythema, edema, spider telangiectasias and fetor hepaticus

But if hepatic encephalopathy developed in patient with fulminant hepatitis without a history of chronic liver disease then some of these findings such as muscle wasting, spider telangiectasias and palmar erythema are absent

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

To diagnose hepatic encephalopathy, liver disease should be confirmed through LFTs, radiologic imaging or liver biopsy and there should be clinical features of hepatic encephalopathy present

It is also important to exclude etiologies that mimic hepatic encephalopathy including intracranial lesions, stroke, post seizure encephalopathy, CNS infections or toxic encephalopathy from other toxins such as lead and pesticides

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Ammonia level: elevated ammonia levels in arterial or venous blood is not sufficient for diagnosing hepatic encephalopathy, clinical features are more important

LFTs: abnormal due to acute or chronic liver disease, manifest as elevated bilirubin, elevated ALT, AST, elevated INR and decreased albumin

Electrolytes disturbances: such as hyponatremia or hypokalemia due to hepatic dysfunction or use of diuretics

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

EEG: abnormal findings would be present but not specific to hepatic encephalopathy

Imaging tests: such as CT or MRI and utilized to exclude differential diagnoses such as intracranial lesions, stroke or hemorrhage; CT scan may show generalized or localized cerebral edema in hepatic encephalopathy (MRI is superior in showing this change)

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Treatment

Treatment includes supportive therapy and ammonia lowering therapy

Supportive therapy includes:

Supporting nutrition

Avoiding dehydration

Avoiding electrolyte abnormalities

Providing safe environment and preventing accidents and falls

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Treatment

Ammonia lowering therapy includes:

Lactulose/ lactitol

Rifaximin

Initiating ammonia lowering therapy is based on clinical signs of hepatic encephalopathy and it is not related to ammonia levels because ammonia levels are not elevated all the time in hepatic encephalopathy patients

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Nutritional support

Proteins should not be restricted for these patients and it should be maintained at around 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/ day

Caloric intake should be around 35 to 40 kcal/kg/day

Consumption of small meals throughout the day and prevent fasting because fasting lead to increased ammonia production

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Safe environment

Hepatic encephalopathy patients maybe agitated and pose risk to themselves and to caregivers

It is crucial not to use sedative medications such as benzodiazepines in treatment of agitation because they exacerbate encephalopathy

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Hepatic encephalopathy triggers in chronic liver disease patients, those include

Renal failure

GI bleeding (e.g. from esophageal varices)

Constipation

Infections (e.g. spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or UTI)

Medications noncompliance

Excessive dietary protein intake

Dehydration (due to factors like fluid restriction, diuretics, diarrhea, vomiting or excessive paracentesis

Electrolyte imbalances (e.g. hypokalemia or hypoglycemia)

Alcohol consumption

The use of sedatives or analgesics

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Lactulose

Lactulose breakdown in the GIT lead to acidic PH which facilitates conversion of ammonia NH3 into ammonium NH4+

Ammonium NH4+ would not diffuse to bloodstream as much as ammonia NH3 diffuses due to its charge; also it can’t cross BBB for the same reason

By this mechanism, it work to lower blood ammonia

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Rifaximin

It is an antibiotic that is poorly absorbed in the GIT

It work by eliminating bacteria that produce ammonia in the GIT => lower ammonia levels

It is considered for patient not responding to lactulose

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Liver transplantation

Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease patients

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Complications

Seizures

Residual cognitive impairment in patients who improve

Cerebral edema, seizures and brain herniation in patients with acute fulminant liver failure

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

GERD is a GI disorder characterized by regurgitation of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus or beyond into the mouth, larynx or lungs; leading to irritation and inflammation in these areas

It is the most commonly diagnosed GI disorder in the US, affecting 20% of population

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Causes

There is no specific cause for GERD but there is risk factors, those include:

Esophageal problem: Esophageal dysmotility => impaired esophageal acid clearance

LES problem: Impairment in the tone of lower esophageal sphincter (LES)

LES problem: Transient LES relaxation

Stomach problem: Delayed gastric emptying

Anatomical problem: presence of hiatal hernia

Increased intra abdominal pressure in obesity and pregnancy

Psychosocial stress

Impaired saliva production: saliva neutralize acid

Olek Remesz (wiki-pl: Orem, commons: Orem), CC BY-SA 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Causes

There is no specific cause for GERD but there is risk factors, those include:

Esophageal problem: Esophageal dysmotility => impaired esophageal acid clearance

LES problem: Impairment in the tone of lower esophageal sphincter (LES)

LES problem: Transient LES relaxation

Stomach problem: Delayed gastric emptying

Anatomical problem: presence of hiatal hernia

Increased intra abdominal pressure in obesity and pregnancy

Psychosocial stress

Impaired saliva production: saliva neutralize acid

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Other risk factors

Age > 50 years

Low socioeconomic status

Tobacco use

Consumption of alcohol

Connective tissue disorders

Postprandial supination

Use of medications including anticholinergic drugs, benzodiazepines, NSAIDs or aspirin, nitroglycerin, albuterol, CCB, antidepressants and glucagon

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Clinical features

GERD most commonly present as heartburn and regurgitation

heart burn is retrosternal burning sensation that may radiate to the neck that occur after meals

Regurgitation is food regurgitation into mouth or hypopharynx that occur after meals

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Clinical features

GERD can also may present as:

Chest pain: it is hard to be differentiated from ACS

Belching

Nausea

Dental erosions: due to acid damaging teeth

Chronic cough: due to irritation of the throat

Asthma: acid act as asthma trigger

Dysphonia and hoarseness

Globus sensation

Alarm symptoms: dysphagia, odynophagia, anemia, hematemesis and weight loss

Dr. A. Dickson, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Classification

According to endoscopic and histopathologic appearance, GERD is classified into:

Non erosive reflux disease (NERD) also known as reflex esophagitis: most common type 60% of all cases

Erosive esophagitis (EE)

Barret esophagus (BE): least common

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Histopathology

In all of these types, there is some histopathological changes affecting esophageal lining including inflammation, basal cell hyperplasia, papilla elongation and dilation of intercellular spaces, those are caused by gastric acid, pepsin and bile salts come into contact with esophageal lining

Erosive esophagitis is characterized by erosions and ulcer formation in the esophageal mucosa in addition to the changes above

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Histopathology

In Barret esophagus there is also metaplastic change of the esophageal lining from stratified squamous epithelium into simple columnar epithelium in addition to the previously mentioned changes

Samir धर्म, Copyrighted free use, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Diagnosis

The diagnosis is made clinically (based on patient history) and response to PPI

If patient present with alarm symptoms then they are sent to be evaluated by EGD to rule out GERD complications or PUD

GERD complications: erosive esophagitis, Barret’s esophagus, esophageal stricture and esophageal adenocarcinoma

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

ACG guidelines recommend screening for H pylori infection in patients with GERD

Radiographic studies such as contract studies are not required for diagnosis and they are ordered only if there is suspicion of severe esophagitis, esophageal stricture, hiatal hernia and tumors

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Ambulatory esophageal reflux monitoring: indicated in refractory GERD and in patients with normal endoscopy evaluation but they have GERD symptoms; it utilizes a telemetry PH capsule or a trans nasal Cath and it help in detecting acid reflex, frequency of reflux and correlation of symptoms with reflux episodes

Important Note: if there is suspicion for Acute coronary syndrome then ECG, cardiac enzymes and other tests should be done to exclude ACS because antisecretory meds might relieve pain in ACS too which make it really hard to differentiate the two diseases

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Treatment

Lifestyle modifications: cornerstone of GERD therapy

Weight loss in obese patients

Avoiding meals at least 3 hours before bedtime

Maintaining good sleep hygiene as shown that minimal sleep disturbances resulted in suppression of LES relaxation => decreased acid reflux

Elevation of the head end of the whole bed by 8 inches improves GERD symptoms

Diet modification: elimination of spicy foods, carbonated beverages, caffeine, high fat foods and chocolate

Avoid bending or stooping

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Treatment

Medical therapy: it is indicated in patients who don’t respond to lifestyle modifications

Antacids

Antisecretory meds: H2 receptor antagonists or PPI; PPI therapy is the most effective for all types of GERD; ACG guidelines recommend PPI therapy once a day dosing before first meal of the day, if this fails then twice daily dosing is done

Prokinetic agents: e.g. metoclopramide and domperidone; prokinetic agents use in GERD is limited due to lack of data on their efficacy and also due to their profound adverse effects profile, especially their effects on CNS and CVS

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Surgical therapy

Surgical therapy indications:

Patients with medically refractory GERD

Patients not compliant to lifestyle modifications or pharmacological treatment

Patients with large hiatal hernia

Patients who desire to discontinue long term pharmacological treatment

Surgical options:

Laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication

Laparoscopic anterior 180 degree fundoplication

Bariatric surgery in obese patients

Magnetic sphincter augmentation and transoral incision-less fundoplication

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Complications

Erosive esophagitis: characterized by erosions or ulcers of esophageal mucosa

Esophageal strictures: chronic acid irritation of distal esophagus lead to scarring and strictures => patients present with dysphagia or food impaction ; treatment with esophageal dilation and PPI therapy

Barret esophagus: metaplastic changes; risk factors include Caucasian males older than 50, obesity, history of smoking ; with Barret esophagus there is high risk of development of esophageal adenocarcinoma

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Complications

Laryngitis

Sinusitis

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Esophageal adenocarcinoma

SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

H. Pylori Treatment

Treatment regimens and dosing

How to choose a treatment regimen

What to do if treatment regimen fails

Who should receive H. pylori treatment

Doc James, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Treatment Regimens

According to the American college of gastroenterology (ACG), we have multiple treatment regimens for H. pylori infection that will be explained in the next slides:

Clarithromycin triple therapy

Bismuth quadruple therapy

Concomitant therapy

Sequential therapy

Hybrid therapy

Levofloxacin triple therapy

Fluoroquinolone sequential therapy

Rifabutin triple therapy

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Clarithromycin Triple Therapy

This is a 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI: standard or double the standard dose BID

Clarithromycin: 500 mg BID

Amoxicillin 1g BID or metronidazole 500 mg TID

This is the treatment of choice if the strain is susceptible to clarithromycin and metronidazole; and the patient should have no previous history of macrolide exposure for any reason

SOURCE SLIDE 4

PPI standard dose

Table from slide 4
PPI Standard dose
Omeprazole 20 mg
Esomeprazole 20 mg
Lansoprazole 30 mg
Rabeprazole 20 mg
SOURCE SLIDE 5

Bismuth Quadruple therapy

This is a 10- 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI: standard dose BID

Bismuth Subsalicylate: 300 mg BID

Amoxicillin (in children < 8) 1 g BID or tetracycline (in children > 8 and adults) 500 mg QID

Nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole) 500mg BID

bismuth quadruple therapy is used when resistance to both clarithromycin or metronidazole is not known; and it is used in patients with any previous macrolide exposure or who are allergic to penicillin (older than 8)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Concomitant therapy

This is a 10- 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI: standard dose BID

Clarithromycin: 500 mg BID

Amoxicillin: 1 g BID

Nitroimidazole: 500 mg BID

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Sequential therapy

This is a 10- 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI (standard dose BID) with amoxicillin (1 g BID) for 5-7 days followed by PPI with nitroimidazole 500 mg BID and clarithromycin 500 mg BID for 5-7 days

Sequential therapy should not be given if the strain is resistant to metronidazole or clarithromycin

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Hybrid therapy

This is a 10- 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI (standard dose BID) and amoxicillin 1g BID for 7 days followed by a PPI, amoxicillin, clarithromycin 500mg BID and a nitroimidazole 500mg BID for 7 days

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Levofloxacin triple therapy

This is a 10- 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI: standard dose BID

Levofloxacin: 500 mg QD

Amoxicillin : 1 g BID

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Fluoroquinolone sequential therapy

This is a 10- 14 day regiment and it consist of:

PPI standard or double the standard BID and amoxicillin 1 g BID for 5-7 days followed by PPI, fluoroquinolone 500 mg QD and nitroimidazole 500mg BID for 5-7 days

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Rifabutin triple therapy

This is a 10 day regiment suggested as a salvage treatment if first line treatment fails and it consist of:

PPI: standard dose BID

Amoxicillin: 1 g BID

Rifabutin: 300 mg QD

SOURCE SLIDE 12

LOAD regimen

Levofloxacin: 350 mg QD

PPI: double standard dose

Nitazoxanide: 500 mg BID

Doxycycline: 100 mg QD

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Choosing a first line regimen

Choosing a regimen depends on patient previous antibiotic exposures and if patient has penicillin allergy or no

The best regiment for a specific patient is the regiment that the patient had minimal exposure to its antibiotics

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Slide 14

SOURCE SLIDE 15

If treatment fails

Testing to prove eradication should be performed using urea breath test, fecal antigen test or biopsy based testing at least 4 weeks after completion of therapy, if positive result then treatment is failed

Bismuth quadruple therapy or levofloxacin therapy is preferred treatment options for patient received clarithromycin containing treatment first; while clarithromycin or levofloxacin containing treatments are preferred if patient received bismuth quadruple therapy first

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Slide 16

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Slide 17

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Who should receive H. pylori treatment

All patients tested positive for H. pylori active infection should receive H. pylori treatment

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Indications for H. Pylori testing

All active PUD patients and patients with history PUD

MALT lymphoma patients

History of endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer

Patients with uninvestigated dyspepsia

GERD patients

Patients taking long term low dosse aspirin

Patients on NSAIDs

Patients with unexplained IDA

Adults with ITP

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Important notes

Esomeprazole and rabeprazole are preferred to be used in Asian and Caucasian population because the other options are rapidly metabolized in these patients due to CYP2C19 polymorphism

SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Bismuth Subsalicylate

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Contraindications

Doc James, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of action

Bismuth Subsalicylate when it reaches the stomach after administration, it is hydrolyzed into bismuth and salicylic acid

Salicylate is completely absorbed into the blood while the bismuth remains unabsorbed in the GI tract

The salicylates part that is absorbed fully work to inhibit the COX enzyme thus inhibiting PG synthesis => inhibition of inflammation and hypermotility (this is helpful in treatment of diarrhea)

User:Chemicalinterest, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Bismuth in the GI tract forms bismuth salts which contain bactericidal and antimicrobial activity and prevent bacteria from binding and growing on the lining of the stomach and rest of GI; by this mechanism Bismuth helps in H. pylori and other GI infections treatment

Bismuth also work to inhibit H. Pylori enzyme activities including phospholipase, protease and urease (helpful in H. pylori treatment)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

By preventing bacterial binding to the GI lining, Bismuth also lead to a lot of other benefits, those include:

Preventing intestinal secretion (helpful in diarrhea treatment)

Promoting absorption of fluid, sodium and chloride (helpful in diarrhea treatment)

Reducing inflammation (helpful in diarrhea treatment)

Promoting of ulcer healing (helpful in peptic ulcer disease treatment)

Bismuth subsalicylate although it has antimicrobial and bactericidal effects; interestingly enough it does NOT affect the normal flora of the stomach

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic Uses

Bismuth subsalicylate is over the counter med and it is FDA approved indications include:

Diarrhea

Heartburn

Nausea

Gastrointestinal discomfort

It is the preferred self treatment for mild diarrhea over antimicrobials ( mild diarrhea means < 4 stools passed a day without dehydration)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Therapeutic Uses

Off label uses:

H. Pylori infection treatment: American gastroenterological association recommends using Bismuth subsalicylate in quadruple therapy for H. pylori infection treatment (with PPI, tetracycline and metronidazole) and this is recommended for patients with previous macrolide exposure or who are allergic to penicillin (because if the patient doesn’t have previous macrolide exposure and is not allergic for penicillin then treated with H. pylori triple drug therapy)

In treatment or prophylaxis against traveler’s diarrhea: antibiotics are superior

Treatment of cholera in children: antibiotics are superior

Treatment of symptomatic microscopic colitis in patients unable to undergo budesonide therapy

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Adverse effects

Common adverse effects: bitter taste, nausea, diarrhea, black tongue and black stools

Black tongue and stool in some patients occur due to sulfur in saliva and color binding to bismuth and forming bismuth sulfide which insoluble black salt and this discoloration is temporary and harmless

Uncommonly, this medication might lead to toxicity (if used for more than 6 weeks); toxicity present as fatigue and deterioration of mental status

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Rarely, this medication might lead to fatal neurotoxicity

Other reported ADR: hearing loss, tinnitus, muscle spasm, anxiety, confusion, depression, headaches and slurred speech

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Contraindications

Patient allergic to salicylates (e.g. aspirin)

Children or adolescents with flue like symptoms : salicylates may lead to Reye’s syndrome in these patients

Patients with bleeding problems (salicylate aggravate bleeding)

Patients on medications increasing risk of bleeding like anticoagulants, sulfinpyrazone, probenecid, methotrexate and any medication with high salicylate concentrations

SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Peptic Ulcer Disease

Definition

Causes

Clinical features

Diagnosis

Regulation of HCl secretion and treatment of PUD

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Peptic ulcer literally means ulcer caused by digestive enzymes

Peptic ulcer disease is characterized by discontinuation in the inner lining of the gastrointestinal tract (usually occur in the stomach or proximal duodenum, it may involve lower esophagus, distal duodenum or jejunum)

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Causes

Peptic ulcer occur due to imbalance between local invasive factor (amount of HCl acid produced) and the protective mechanisms (mucus production and bicarbonate secretion by the gastric mucosa)

The most common causes being H. Pylori associated PUD and NSAID associated PUD

SOURCE SLIDE 4

H. Pylori associated PUD

Most common cause of PUD

H. pylori is a gram negative bacilli that is found within the gastric epithelial cells

This bacteria is responsible for 90% of duodenal ulcers and 70-90 % of gastric ulcer, it is commonly acquired in childhood

SOURCE SLIDE 5

H. Pylori associated PUD

H. Pylori has multiple different virulence factors allowing it to adhere and inflame gastric mucosa and impairs bicarbonate secretion (it destroys the defensive mechanisms)

Virulence factors include:

Urease: H. pylori secretes urease to break down urea into ammonia which protect the organism by neutralizing the gastric acid

Toxins: H. pylori also secretes toxins that lead to mucosal inflammation and tissue damage

Flagella: H. pylori has flagella that provide motility and allow movement towards the gastric epithelium through the mucus layer

SOURCE SLIDE 6

NSAID associated PUD

Second most common cause of PUD

Prostaglandin secretion work to decrease amount of HCl produced by the parietal cells and it work to thickens the mucus layer protecting the mucosa

NSAIDs work to block the prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting COX 1 enzyme leading to high HCl secretion and less mucus production and it also lead to decrease gastric mucosal blood flow resulting in PUD

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Other medications causing PUD

Corticosteroids

Bisphosphonates

Potassium chloride

Fluorouracil

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Smoking and Alcohol may lead to PUD

Smoking may lead to duodenal ulcers

Alcohol can irritate gastric mucosa and increase acidity

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Other causes of PUD

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: gastrinoma

Malignancy (gastric/lung cancer, lymphomas)

Stress (Acute illness, burns, head injury): increase acid secretion

Vascular insufficiency: less blood = less mucus production

Radiation therapy: direct injury

Crohn disease

Chemotherapy

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Clinical features

Epigastric pain usually occurs within 15-30 min following a meal in patients with gastric ulcer, while in patients with duodenal ulcer the pain tend to occur 2-3 hours after a meal

Patient also may experience bloating, abdominal fullness, nausea and vomiting, weight loss/gain, hematemesis and melena

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Clinical features

Warning (Alarm) symptoms that require urgent referral and EGD testing include:

Unintentional weight loss

Progressive dysphagia

Overt gastrointestinal bleeding

Iron deficiency anemia

Recurrent emesis

Family history of upper GI malignancy

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

History and physical examination

EGD: gold standard and most accurate test to diagnose gastric and duodenal ulcer; American society of GI endoscopy recommends EGD evaluation for patients over 50 years of age and new onset of dyspeptic symptoms; also recommends EGD evaluation for all patients present with alarm symptoms

Contrast swallow (indicated when EGD is contraindicated)

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

CBC: to look for infections

LFT: to check for liver disease

Amylase and lipase: pancreatic disease

Serum gastrin level: if Zollinger Ellison syndrome is suspected

H. Pylori testing

SOURCE SLIDE 14

H. Pylori testing

Serologic testing

Urea breath test: high sensitivity and specificity

Antibodies to H. pylori levels

Stool antigen test and urine ELISA and rapid urine test

Endoscopic biopsy

SOURCE SLIDE 15

PUD Treatment

Treatment of PUD is done through returning the balance between local invasive factor (amount of HCl acid produced) and the protective mechanisms (mucus production and bicarbonate secretion by the gastric mucosa)

So this is done by either decreasing the local invasive factor (decreasing HCl acid secretion) or by strengthening the defensive mechanisms

To understand how the local invasive factors are reduced, first we have to understand how the HCl acid secretion is regulated

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Regulation of HCl secretion

Stomach contain gastric glands which contain multiple types of cells including parietal cells (secretes HCl), chief cells (secreting pepsin), G cells (secreting gastrin), enterochromaffin cells (secreting histamine)

Histamine is the main activator of the parietal cells to secrete HCl

Boumphreyfr, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Regulation of HCl secretion

Parietal cell has many receptors, including M1 receptor, G receptor, H2 receptor and prostaglandin receptor

Any stimulation to the M1, G, H2 receptor lead to increase HCl secretion from the parietal cell

While stimulating the prostaglandin receptor would lead to decrease HCl secretion

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Regulation of HCl secretion

Stimulating M1, G receptors would give a weak stimulation to HCl secretion from the parietal cell compared to H2 stimulation which gives powerful stimulation leading to a lot of acid secretion

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Regulation of HCl secretion

Vagal stimulation from the myenteric plexus would increase acetylcholine levels leading to simulation of M1 receptors on parietal cells, but not just that; it also stimulate the g cells to produce more gastrin which work on the enterochromaffin cells to secrete histamine which go back to bind to the parietal cells giving powerful stimulation to acid secretion

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Regulation of HCl secretion

Now stimulating the H2 receptors on the parietal cells lead to increase cAMP levels => activation of many protein kinases inside the cell => break down of H2CO3 into hydrogen and bicarb

Hydrogen exit into the stomach lumen by the H/K ATPase (proton pump)

Hydrogen bind to Cl in the lumen to form HCl

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Regulation of HCl secretion

Prostaglandin antagonizes this cycle by decreasing cAMP and decreasing HCl secretion

Prostaglandin also responsible for protective mucus production and bicarbonate secretion

Prostaglandin also responsible for vasodilatation to increase blood flow to the stomach => ulcer heals faster

SOURCE SLIDE 22

PUD Treatment

Drugs that neutralize HCl: antacids

Drugs that decrease HCl secretion (Antisecretory drugs)

H2 blockers: cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine

Proton pump inhibitors: omeprazole, lansoprazole …

PPI have largely replaced H2 receptor blockers due to their superior efficacy

SOURCE SLIDE 23

PUD Treatment

Drugs that increase mucosal defense mechanisms:

PGE1 analogues: misoprostol

Sucralfate

Colloid bismuth compounds: e.g. bismuth subcitrate

Carbenoxolone

SOURCE SLIDE 24

PUD Treatment

Treatment for H. Pylori infection: PPI + Antibiotics

Refractory cases require surgery

SOURCE SLIDE 25

PUD Treatment

Life style modifications

Stop smoking, spicy food, alcohol, coffee and tea : because they increase HCl

Avoid stress: because it elevates HCl

Avoid medication that promote ulcer formation: e.g. NSAIDs

SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Oxygen Therapy

Oxygen Storage

Oxygen delivery devices

Indications of oxygen therapy

Monitoring of oxygen therapy

Adverse effects

CO2 retention

Hazards and risks

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Oxygen therapy means the use of supplemental oxygen for medical treatment

Nenad Stojkovic, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Oxygen storage

Oxygen can be stored as a compressed gas in a high pressure oxygen storage cylinders

Oxygen also stored as a liquid in dewar, cryogenic liquid cylinder

Pawar0365, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Oxygen storage

Oxygen concentrators are also available for long term home use

They work by concentrating the oxygen from the room air by selectively removing nitrogen using electricity

i_am_jim, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen is commonly delivered to the patient through nasal cannula

Nasal cannula can provide oxygen at low flow rates from 1-6 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 24-40%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen is commonly delivered to the patient through simple face mask

Simple face mask can provide oxygen at 5- 10 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 35-55%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen also can be delivered through venturi mask

Venturi mask can accurately deliver a predetermined oxygen concentration of 24-50%

Open Critical Care & World Health Organization, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen also can be delivered through a partial rebreather mask which based on a simple mask but with a reservoir bag

Partial rebreather mask can provide oxygen at 5- 15 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 40-70%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen also can be delivered through a non rebreather mask (reservoir mask) which draws oxygen from attached reservoir bag with on way valves that direct exhaled air out of the mask

Partial rebreather mask can provide oxygen at > 10 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 60-80%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen also can be delivered through the bag valve mask, endotracheal tube, laryngeal mask airway, it can be given through bypassing the airway in ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) therapy

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Indications of oxygen therapy

Acute hypoxic conditions: acute MI, acute pulmonary edema, carbon monoxide poisoning, cardiac and respiratory arrest, major trauma, anaphylaxis, major bleeding, shock, active convulsions, hypothermia, metabolic acidosis ( bicarbonate < 18 mmol/l) and decompression sickness

Chronic hypoxic conditions (long-term oxygen therapy): COPD, cystic fibrosis, chronic bronchitis, emphysema and heart failure

It is also used in treatment of cluster headache and in induction of anesthesia

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Indications of oxygen therapy

British medical journal recommends that oxygen therapy is stopped for saturations > 96%; and it should not be started for saturations > 90% (there is association between excessive oxygenation and mortality)

Exceptions for this rule is carbon monoxide poisoning, cluster headaches, sickle cell crisis and pneumothorax

In cases of carbon monoxide toxicity or cardiac arrest, saturations should be as high as possible

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Oxygen therapy monitoring

Pulse oximetry or ABG analysis is what is used for monitory of oxygen therapy

Oxygen should be titrated to a target level based on pulse oximetry of 94-96% in most patients or 88-92% in patients with COPD to avoid CO2 retention

Rcp.basheer, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Arterial blood gas normal values and interpretation

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis

Table from slide 15
Parameter Normal range
pH 7.35- 7.45
Arterial O2 saturation (SaO2)
94-100%
Arterial O2 partial pressure (PaO2) 80- 100 mmHg
10.6- 13 kPa
Arterial CO2 partial pressure (PaCO2) 35- 45 mmHg
4.5-6 kPa
HCO3 22-26 mmol/L
SOURCE SLIDE 16

Important notes

Hypoxia means low oxygen level at the tissues while hypoxemia means low oxygen level in the arterial blood

Dyspnea does not necessarily indicate hypoxemia. Severe hypoxemia can be present without dyspnea and vice versa

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Oxygen therapy adverse effects

Oxygen should not be used routinely unless there is evidence of hypoxia because when used in excessively high concentrations, it can result in oxygen toxicity (lung damage, CNS damage and eyes damage) leading to respiratory failure and death

Oxygen can also dry out the airways if used without humidification leading to Irritation of nose, pharynx and trachea => mucus hypersecretion

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Oxygen therapy adverse effects

In infants with respiratory failure, administration of high levels of oxygen may promote overgrowth of new blood vessels in the retina of the eye leading to blindness; this condition is known as retinopathy of prematurity

Oxygen therapy may also lead to CO2 retention; in those at risk (COPD patients), saturations of 88-92% are preferred

SOURCE SLIDE 19

CO2 retention

In patients with COPD who receive supplementary O2, CO2 retention can occur through 2 mechanisms:

Increase O2 saturation of blood reduces deoxygenated Hb which carries CO2 in blood (in the forms of bicarbonate) => higher CO2 levels => more retention

In patients with COPD, hypoxia is the main drive of respiration, so If 100% O2 was administered, hypoxia is corrected and the hypoxic drive is lost leading to CO2 retention

Co2 retention can lead to headache, drowsiness (narcosis) or death

in people with COPD, CO2 toxicity can be prevented by maintaining oxygen saturation between 88-92%

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Hazards and risks

Oxygen itself is not flammable but the addition of concentrated oxygen to a fire greatly increases its intensity; and concentrated oxygen can aid the combustion of material that are relatively inert under normal conditions

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Intro

Ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic

Here we will talk about what ibuprofen does to your body

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Administration

Ibuprofen when taken orally, it would go through the mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach and it would get absorbed in the intestine , in the intestine it would get absorbed into the blood, once it is in the blood, then it would get distributed everywhere in the body

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

Ibuprofen work as a COX enzyme inhibitor

To simplify the COX

COX enzyme help produce prostaglandins, prostaglandins mediate pain sensation, inflammation and fever

So by inhibiting COX , ibuprofen suppress prostaglandins and achieves its analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory properties

SOURCE SLIDE 5

After that the ibuprofen is metabolized by the liver and excreted through the kidney in urine

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Side effects

Now what could go wrong during all of this? (side effects)

It may lead to GIT bleeding

To really understand this we have to go back to the prostaglandins, we mentioned that prostaglandins mediate pain inflammation and fever, they also mediate the production of gastroprotective mucous (help protect the staomach against gastric acid)

Since ibuprofen inhibit COX => inhibit prostaglandins => inhibit production of gastric mucus => gastric bleeding

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Renal side effects

Ibuprofen express nephrotoxic properties

Prostaglandins has vasodilatory effects on the kidney , they increase renal blood flow

This effect is worse during dehydration especially in dehydration

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Skin rash (allergic)

Headache

High blood pressure (prostaglandins also control blood pressure)

Bronchospasm (prostaglandisn help in respiratotion )

Hepatotoxicity

Increase risk of heart attack

outline.heading: Intro
outline.summary: Ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic Here we will talk about what ibuprofen does to your body

outline.heading: Administration
outline.summary: Ibuprofen when taken orally, it would go through the mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach and it would get absorbed in the intestine , in the intestine it would get absorbed into the blood, once it is in the blood, then it would get distributed everywhere in the body

outline.heading: Mechanism of action
outline.summary: Ibuprofen work as a COX enzyme inhibitor To simplify the COX COX enzyme help produce prostaglandins, prostaglandins mediate pain sensation, inflammation and fever So by inhibiting COX , ibuprofen suppress prostaglandins and achieves its analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory properties

outline.heading: After that the ibuprofen is metabolized by the liver and excreted through the kidney in urine
Side effects
outline.summary: Now what could go wrong during all of this? (side effects) It may lead to GIT bleeding To really understand this we have to go back to the prostaglandins, we mentioned that prostaglandins mediate pain inflammation and fever, they also mediate the production of gastroprotective mucous (help protect the staomach against gastric acid) Since ibuprofen inhibit COX => inhibit prostaglandins => inhibit production of gastric mucus => gastric bleeding

outline.heading: Renal side effects
outline.summary: Ibuprofen express nephrotoxic properties Prostaglandins has vasodilatory effects on the kidney , they increase renal blood flow This effect is worse during dehydration especially in dehydration

outline.heading: Skin rash (allergic)
outline.summary: Headache High blood pressure (prostaglandins also control blood pressure) Bronchospasm (prostaglandisn help in respiratotion ) Hepatotoxicity Increase risk of heart attack

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Introduction

Sternoclavicular joint connects the sternal end of the clavicle with the clavicular notch of the sternum and it is stabilized by many ligaments

SC injuries are uncommon, and mostly caused by trauma (e.g. lateral compression of the shoulder during RTA and crush injuries) or it can also be atraumatic due to ligamentous laxity

DrJanaOfficial, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Introduction

Some of these injures are dangerous, there might be damage done to mediastinal structures lying behind the clavicle

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

SC injuries are classified into

Sprains and subluxations

dislocations (anterior or posterior)

Physeal fracture in patients younger than 25 years old (Salter-Harris type 2)

Anterior dislocations of SC joint is more common than posterior dislocation

Anatomography, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Clinical features

Sprains and subluxations

Patient complain of pain at the joint area

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Clinical features

SC Anterior dislocation

the dislocated clavicle forms a prominent swelling on the SC joint

Patient complain from pain at the joint

There are usually no damage to mediastinal structures with anterior dislocation

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Clinical features

SC Posterior dislocation

Posterior dislocation is dangerous, dislocated medial clavicle might pressure trachea causing dyspnea or might pressure large vessels causing venous congestion of the neck and arm or it may pressure esophagus causing dysphagia (look for these findings)

Patient also complain from pain at the joint area

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Imaging

Plain x rays are difficult to detect SC dislocation on

CT scan is the ideal method for diagnosis

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Treatment

Sprains and subluxations do not require specific treatment other than sling for comfort and return to unrestricted activity by 3 months

Anterior dislocation can be reduced by putting pressure on the clavicle while pulling on the arm with the shoulder abducted, full function might take several months to return

Re dislocation is common

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Treatment

Internal fixation is usually unnecessary and potentially dangerous (large vessels are lying close behind the sternum and might be injured)

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Treatment

Posterior dislocation should be reduced, reduction is done closed (GA might be used), patient in supine position with sandbag between scapulae and then arm is pulled with shoulder abduction and extended, joint reduce with a snap and stay reduced

If this fails => medial end of the clavicle is grasped by bone forceps and pulled but if failed => open reduction is done (care taken not to damage mediastinal structures)

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Treatment

After reduction in both types (anterior and posterior dislocations) shoulders are braced with a figure of eight bandage for 3 weeks

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Complications

Arterial or venous compression

Tracheal and laryngeal edema

Esophageal injury

Pneumothorax

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Overview

AC injuries are common in athletes and workers who use heavy equipment and they occur in any age, specially 20-40 years age group, they represent more than 40% of all shoulder injuries

Mild injuries are not associated with any significant morbidity while severe injuries are associated with chronic pain and significant loss of shoulder function

BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of injury

A fall on the shoulder with arm adducted => AC ligaments are torn first => CC ligaments are torn with higher forces leading to complete dislocation of the joint

Fall onto an outstretched hand or elbow may also result in AC joint injures

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Injury is graded according to the Rockwood classification of AC joint injuries

Rockwood classification is a 6 grade system and it is a modification of Allman and Tossy’s 3 grade system, the first and second grades are same in both systems, while grade three in Allman and Tossy classification is subdivided into four grades in Rockwood classification

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Classification

Rockwood classification classify AC joint injures based on:

Acromioclavicular joint alignment

Coracoclavicular ligament status

Deltoid and trapezius muscles status (both attach to the lateral part of the clavicle)

Frederick Henry Gerrish (1845-1920), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

AC Joint Normal Anatomy

The inferior edge of the clavicle bone and inferior edge of the acromion should be leveled (on the same line) on clavicle AP view with 20 degree cephalic tilt

It is okay if the superior edges don’t match up

The joint space should be uniform and joint distance less than 8 mm (normal 5-8 mm)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

AC Joint Normal Anatomy

Normal Coracoclavicular distance is between 11- 13mm and there should be no greater than 5mm difference between right and left

No soft tissue swelling

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Rockwood Grade I

AC joint sprain

The clavicle is not elevated in respect to acromion (X ray appears normal)

Acromioclavicular ligament: sprained

Coracoclavicular ligament: normal

AC Joint capsule: normal

Trapezius muscle: attached

Deltoid muscle: attached

Yosi I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Rockwood Grade II

AC joint subluxation

Clavicle elevated but not above superior border of acromion

Acromioclavicular ligament: torn

Coracoclavicular ligament: sprained

Joint capsule: torn

Trapezius muscle: minimal detachment

Deltoid muscle: minimal detachment

Yosi I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Rockwood Grade III

AC joint dislocation

Clavicle elevated above the superior border of acromion, the coracoclavicular distance is less than 25mm

Acromioclavicular ligament: torn

Coracoclavicular ligament: torn

Joint capsule: torn and joint is dislocated

Trapezius muscle: complete detachment

Deltoid muscle: complete detachment

Yosi I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Rockwood Grade IV

Result from posteriorly directed forces that make the clavicle penetrates the trapezius muscle, sometimes completely.

Acromioclavicular ligament: torn

Coracoclavicular ligament: torn

Joint capsule: torn

Trapezius muscle: complete detachment

Deltoid muscle: complete detachment

Yosi I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Rockwood Grade V

Clavicle is markedly elevated and coracoclavicular distance is more than 25mm

Acromioclavicular ligament: torn

Coracoclavicular ligament: torn

Joint capsule: torn

Trapezius muscle: complete detachment

Deltoid muscle: complete detachment

Yosi I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Rockwood Grade VI

Inferior displacement of clavicle beneath the coracoid process

Acromioclavicular ligament: torn

Coracoclavicular ligament: torn

Joint capsule: torn

Trapezius muscle: detached

Deltoid muscle: detached

Yosi I, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Clinical features

Patient complain of shoulder pain and swelling; and they can locate where the pain exactly is (AC joint)

On examination, there is tenderness while palpating the shoulder, if there is no deformity seen then the injury is either Grade I or II, but if there is deformity then it is Grade III,IV,V,VI

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Clinical features

Shoulder movements are limited due to pain but active abduction to 45 degrees would exclude rotator cuff tear

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Imaging

AP clavicle with 20 degrees cephalic tilt: this view show inferior edge of the clavicle at the same line as the inferior edge of acromion

axillary views: confirm whether there is posterior displacement of the clavicle (Rockwood type IV)

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Emergency management

ATLS trauma protocol

closed reduction is not helpful in these injures

Provide a sling and pain relief

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Definitive management

Grade 1 and 2 (sprains and subluxations) are treated with sling immobilization for around 1 week until pain subsides and patient encouraged to exercise shoulder, elbow and fingers

Grade 3 (dislocations) is treated non operatively unless there is extreme prominence of the clavicle, or in patients who want to resume their strenuous overarm or overhead activities then treated operatively

Grade 4,5,6 are treated operatively

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Definitive management

Operative treatment include accurate reduction, and fixation of the clavicle with the acromion is done using a hook plate

There is also the modified Weaver- Dunn procedure

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Modified Weaver-Dunn procedure

Modified Weaver- Dunn include excision of the lateral end of the clavicle and coracoacromial ligaments are transferred to the outer end of the clavicle and attached by trans osseous sutures

Clavicle is anchored to the coracoid with anchors or slings to reduce the tension on the repair during the healing phase

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Modified Weaver-Dunn procedure

Elbow and forearm exercises begun one day after operation and assisted shoulder exercises are started 2 weeks later, active movements are started 4-6 weeks after and strenuous lifting is avoided for 6 months

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Complications

Supraspinatus tendonitis: is sometimes associated with AC joint injures and supraspinatus tendinitis may occur directly due to the primary injury or may result from edema or inflammation occurring after the initial injury

Unreduced dislocation: affects function, treated with reconstruction of CC ligaments, if failed then Modified Weaver- Dunn procedure is done

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Complications

Ossification of ligaments: especially in severe injures, ossification of ligaments lead to late rotator cuff dysfunction

Osteoarthritis is a late complication that might occur with these injures

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Omphalocele

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Omphalocele is a congenital abdominal wall defect, in which the abdominal viscera is herniating through the umbilical cord outside meaning the viscera will be covered by a sac (umbilical cord lining)

The location of the omphalocele defect could be mid abdominal, hypogastric or epigastric

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Definition

Omphalocele sac is comprised of an inner peritoneal layer and an outer amnion layer with Wharton’s jelly in between

Most commonly organs herniating are intestine, stomach and liver

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Epidemiology

Omphalocele incidence is around 1 in 1500 in 14-18 weeks of gestation and 1 in 5000 at birth (most of omphalocele cases discovered early will be spontaneously lost or the pregnancy is terminated)

Incidence of omphalocele remained stable in comparison with gastroschisis incidence which is increasing

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Epidemiology

Omphalocele has relatively high incidence of other congenital anomalies by 50-70% of the cases, these include:

Cardiac anomalies

GIT anomalies

Exstrophy of the bladder

Neural tube defects

Lung hypoplasia

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Omphalocele can be associated with several syndromes including:

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

Pentalogy of Cantrell

Trisomies 13, 18 and 21

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Beckwith- Weideman Syndrome

Omphalocele

Macroglossia

Organomegaly

Hypoglycemia

increased risk of Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma and neuroblastoma in the future

Sydney S. Gellis and Murray Feingold, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Pentalogy of Cantrell

Omphalocele

Diaphragmatic hernia

Cardiac anomalies

Pericardial defect

Sternal cleft

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology of omphalocele is related to embryonic folding

Embryonic folding is the process by which the fetus converts from flat sheet of cells, into a tube like structure and it start at 4 weeks

Embryonic folding has to be complete for the abdominal wall to close , if not then omphalocele develops

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Pathophysiology

If the deficit in the embryonic folding process was related to the cranial fold then the omphalocele would be associated with other cranial fold defects like diaphragmatic hernia, cardiac anomalies, pericardial defect and sternal cleft

if the deficit is related to caudal fold then omphalocele might be associated with bladder exstrophy

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Causes

Cause unknown

But there is risk factors

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Risk factors

Genetic predisposition and chromosomal abnormalities

Maternal age of 35 years and older

Maternal use of salicylates like aspirin

Maternal diabetes

Maternal cigarette smoking or alcohol or illicit drug use

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Omphalocele can be diagnosed by routine two dimensional US evaluation by 18 weeks of gestation, first trimester detection is possible only with three dimensional US

Elevation of maternal serum AFP present in most cases same with gastroschisis

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Gastroschisis can be differentiated from omphalocele by US too, in gastroschisis there is lack of membranous covering of the bowel

In Omphalocele there is high probability of CVS, CNS and genitourinary anomalies, 70% of these anomalies can be detected by US thus knowing the survival rate (survival rate is highly hindered by cardiac anomalies), in comparison to Gastroschisis there is low probability for GIT, CNS, CVS, MSK and genitourinary anomalies

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Delivery of Omphalocele baby

The goal is to deliver omphalocele patient as close to term as possible to maximize fetal growth and lung development

Spontaneous vaginal delivery is the preferred since C section has not shown any advantage

BUT many neonates with giant omphaloceles continue to be delivered by C section in many centers worldwide

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Resuscitation

After delivery of omphalocele newborn, ventilation or intubation might be needed

Blood glucose is checked immediately and Dextrose might be given if it was low (Beckwith Wiedemann syndrome)

NG decompression tube should be inserted and IV access obtained

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Resuscitation

Thorough search for associated anomalies is important, chest x ray looking for elongated thorax (pulmonary hypoplasia) and echocardiography looking for cardiac anomalies

The sac should be covered with saline soaked gauze and dressed to minimize fluid losses

Bolus IV normal saline 20 ml/kg after delivery might be needed to substitute the third space fluid loss and insensible fluid losses, fluid and temperature losses are much less than with gastroschisis

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Resuscitation

Initial dose of ampicillin and gentamicin shortly after delivery to prevent GIT infections

Parenteral nutrition is very important in omphalocele and should be used until bowel function goes back to normal

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Risk assessment

Risk assessed based on presence of associated anomalies

Isolated omphalocele (no associated anomalies) has the best survival of 90%, presence of associated anomalies decreases survival

Omphalocele can be classified into hypogastric, central and epigastric

Epigastric has the worst survival rate because of the presence of cardiac anomalies

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Treatment is with surgery goal is to return the intestine back to the abdominal cavity and slowly introduce feeding to the baby

Treatment options depend on the size of the omphalocele, baby’s gestational age and presence of associated comorbidities like respiratory insufficiency and associated anomalies

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Treatment options

Primary closure of the defect: used in small omphaloceles (< 3 cm)

Delayed closure: used when the patient has giant omphalocele or has small omphalocele with associated comorbidities

Staged closure: used in patients with large defects and no associated comorbidities

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Primary closure

Immediate primary closure consist of excision of the omphalocele sac, reduction of its content, umbilical cord is dissected and ligated and closure of the fascia and skin over the abdominal contents

Primary closure used in small defects < 3 cm in diameter

Larger defects that are easy to close (in case of minimal loss in abdominal domain) also can be treated by primary closure in the first month of life

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Delayed closure

Used when the patient has giant omphalocele or has small omphalocele with associated comorbidities

This method include:

Umbilical cord is ligated and excised

the defect is then dressed daily with topical sulfasalazine non adherent dressing

with time the amnion become epithelized and the defect size decreases

In around 1 year when comorbidities have improved and the defect size decreased then definitive closure can be performed

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Staged closure

Used in patients with large defects and no associated comorbidities

When there is significant loss of domain in the abdominal cavity, primary closure is not possible (lead to abdominal compartment syndrome), and that is when the staged closure comes in context

Staged closure is done using amniotic sac inversion technique

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Staged closure

All of the amnion inversion procedure is done extraperitoneal and there is less risk of future adhesions and intestinal obstruction with this method

The amnion is inverted by attaching a silastic silo to the amnion-skin junction using sutures

The bowel and liver are progressively reduced into the abdomen, the intraabdominal pressure is monitored using NG tube (should not exceed 20 mmHg) to prevent abdominal compartment syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Staged closure

Reduction progresses on a daily basis until the contents lays flat and that is when the silo is removed

then the amnion is pulled and detachment of intestine is done from the amnion then it is inverted back and the edges are approximated and this process is repeated multiple times until simulated totoal closure of the abdominal wall is possible

Finally, The amnion is everted and dissected and abdomen is closed

SOURCE SLIDE 27

Complications

Early complications include

Pulmonary hypoplasia and chronic lung disease and those are due to omphalocele disease process,

Cholestasis, sepsis, developmental delay, hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency, renal failure and abdominal compartment syndrome and those come as a result from the treatment

Late complications include hernia and GERD due to increase abdominal pressure

outline.summary: Pathophysiology of omphalocele is related to embryonic folding Embryonic folding is the process by which the fetus converts from flat sheet of cells, into a tube like structure and it start at 4 weeks Embryonic folding has to be complete for the abdominal wall to close , if not then omphalocele develops OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Pathophysiology
outline.summary: If the deficit in the embryonic folding process was related to the cranial fold then the omphalocele would be associated with other cranial fold defects like diaphragmatic hernia, cardiac anomalies, pericardial defect and sternal cleft if the deficit is related to caudal fold then omphalocele might be associated with bladder exstrophy

outline.heading: Causes
outline.summary: Cause unknown But there is risk factors

outline.heading: Risk factors
outline.summary: Genetic predisposition and chromosomal abnormalities Maternal age of 35 years and older Maternal use of salicylates like aspirin Maternal diabetes Maternal cigarette smoking or alcohol or illicit drug use

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Omphalocele can be diagnosed by routine two dimensional US evaluation by 18 weeks of gestation, first trimester detection is possible only with three dimensional US Elevation of maternal serum AFP present in most cases same with gastroschisis

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Gastroschisis can be differentiated from omphalocele by US too, in gastroschisis there is lack of membranous covering of the bowel In Omphalocele there is high probability of CVS, CNS and genitourinary anomalies, 70% of these anomalies can be detected by US thus knowing the survival rate (survival rate is highly hindered by cardiac anomalies), in comparison to Gastroschisis there is low probability for GIT, CNS, CVS, MSK and genitourinary anomalies

outline.heading: Delivery of Omphalocele baby
outline.summary: The goal is to deliver omphalocele patient as close to term as possible to maximize fetal growth and lung development Spontaneous vaginal delivery is the preferred since C section has not shown any advantage BUT many neonates with giant omphaloceles continue to be delivered by C section in many centers worldwide

outline.heading: Resuscitation
outline.summary: After delivery of omphalocele newborn, ventilation or intubation might be needed Blood glucose is checked immediately and Dextrose might be given if it was low (Beckwith Wiedemann syndrome) NG decompression tube should be inserted and IV access obtained

outline.heading: Resuscitation
outline.summary: Thorough search for associated anomalies is important, chest x ray looking for elongated thorax (pulmonary hypoplasia) and echocardiography looking for cardiac anomalies The sac should be covered with saline soaked gauze and dressed to minimize fluid losses Bolus IV normal saline 20 ml/kg after delivery might be needed to substitute the third space fluid loss and insensible fluid losses, fluid and temperature losses are much less than with gastroschisis

outline.heading: Resuscitation
outline.summary: Initial dose of ampicillin and gentamicin shortly after delivery to prevent GIT infections Parenteral nutrition is very important in omphalocele and should be used until bowel function goes back to normal

outline.heading: Risk assessment
outline.summary: Risk assessed based on presence of associated anomalies Isolated omphalocele (no associated anomalies) has the best survival of 90%, presence of associated anomalies decreases survival Omphalocele can be classified into hypogastric, central and epigastric Epigastric has the worst survival rate because of the presence of cardiac anomalies

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Treatment is with surgery goal is to return the intestine back to the abdominal cavity and slowly introduce feeding to the baby Treatment options depend on the size of the omphalocele, baby’s gestational age and presence of associated comorbidities like respiratory insufficiency and associated anomalies

outline.heading: Treatment options
outline.summary: Primary closure of the defect: used in small omphaloceles (< 3 cm) Delayed closure: used when the patient has giant omphalocele or has small omphalocele with associated comorbidities Staged closure: used in patients with large defects and no associated comorbidities

outline.heading: Primary closure
outline.summary: Immediate primary closure consist of excision of the omphalocele sac, reduction of its content, umbilical cord is dissected and ligated and closure of the fascia and skin over the abdominal contents Primary closure used in small defects < 3 cm in diameter Larger defects that are easy to close (in case of minimal loss in abdominal domain) also can be treated by primary closure in the first month of life

outline.heading: Delayed closure
outline.summary: Used when the patient has giant omphalocele or has small omphalocele with associated comorbidities This method include: Umbilical cord is ligated and excised the defect is then dressed daily with topical sulfasalazine non adherent dressing with time the amnion become epithelized and the defect size decreases In around 1 year when comorbidities have improved and the defect size decreased then definitive closure can be performed

outline.heading: Staged closure
outline.summary: Used in patients with large defects and no associated comorbidities When there is significant loss of domain in the abdominal cavity, primary closure is not possible (lead to abdominal compartment syndrome), and that is when the staged closure comes in context Staged closure is done using amniotic sac inversion technique

outline.heading: Staged closure
outline.summary: All of the amnion inversion procedure is done extraperitoneal and there is less risk of future adhesions and intestinal obstruction with this method The amnion is inverted by attaching a silastic silo to the amnion-skin junction using sutures The bowel and liver are progressively reduced  into the abdomen, the intraabdominal pressure is monitored using NG tube (should not exceed 20 mmHg) to prevent abdominal compartment syndrome

outline.heading: Staged closure
outline.summary: Reduction progresses on a daily basis until the contents lays flat and that is when the silo is removed then the amnion is pulled and detachment of intestine is done from the amnion then it is inverted back and the edges are approximated and this process is repeated multiple times until simulated totoal closure of the abdominal wall is possible Finally, The amnion is everted and dissected and abdomen is closed

outline.heading: Complications
outline.summary: Early complications include Pulmonary hypoplasia and chronic lung disease and those are due to omphalocele disease process, Cholestasis, sepsis, developmental delay, hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency, renal failure and abdominal compartment syndrome and those come as a result from the treatment Late complications include hernia and GERD due to increase abdominal pressure

Abdominal Wall Anatomy

DarthVader0706, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Abdominal wall

Abdominal wall connects the rib cage superiorly with the pelvis inferiorly

Abdominal wall is composed of muscle, bone and fascia

it functions as a protective barrier enclosing the GIT and urogenital organs but it also has a role in mobility (flexion, extension, rotation)

Sklmsta, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Anterolaterally from superficial to deep

Skin

Subcutaneous tissue

Fascia

Fatty superficial fascia (Camper’s fascia)

Deep fibrous fascia (Scarpa’s fascia)

Muscles

External oblique

Internal oblique

Rectus abdominis

Transversus abdominus

Transversalis fascia

Fat

Parietal peritoneum

Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Anterolaterally

Anterolateral muscles extend from ribs to pelvis and they are supplied by thoracoabdominal nerves T7-T11, subcostal nerve T12, iliohypogastric, lateral cutaneous and ilioinguinal nerve

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Posteriorly

Skin

Subcutaneous tissue

Spine

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Posteriorly

Muscles

Quadratus lumborum (most superficial) originates from iliac crest and insert into transverse processes of L1-L4 and inferior border of 12th rib and it is supplied by anterior rami of T12- L4 nerves, it work as extensor and lateral flexor of the spinal column

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Posteriorly

Psoas major (deeper to quadratus lumborum): originates from the transverse process of T12-L5 and attaches to lesser trochanter of the femur, it is supplied by anterior rami of L1-L3 nerves , it work as a thigh flexor and a lateral flexor of spinal column

Anatomography, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Posteriorly

Psoas minor (deeper to psoas major): originates from vertebral bodies T12- L1 and attaches to superior ramus of pubic bone, supplied by anterior rami of the L1 nerve and work as flexor for the vertebral column

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Posteriorly

Iliacus: originates from surface of iliac fossa and anterior inferior iliac spine, and insert to lesser trochanter of the femur, supplied by femoral nerve L2-L4 and work as a flexor and lateral rotator for the femur bone

Posterior aspect of the diaphragm

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Posteriorly

Fascia

Thoracolumbar fascia: most superficial (more superficial than quadratus lumborum)

Psoas fascia: covers psoas and it is deeper than psoas muscles

So the two fascias enclose the posterior abdominal muscles

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Abdominal pressure

Roof of the abdomen is formed by the diaphragm which separates thoracic cavity above from the abdominal cavity below

Thoracic cavity has negative pressure while abdominal cavity has positive pressure

Weakness of diaphragm can lead to bowel herniating to thoracic cavity
