SOURCE SLIDE 1

Gastroschisis

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Gastro means GIT tract, schisis means splitting or separating

Gastroschisis is a congenital abdominal wall defect, there is a full thickness hole in the abdominal wall at which the infant’s abdominal organs herniate

the hole mostly located on the right of the umbilicus

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Definition

herniated organs has no cover, they have direct contact with external environment

Most commonly organs herniating through this hole are intestine, stomach and liver

Must be differentiated from omphalocele (this is explained a little bit later in the gastroschisis vs omphalocele chapter of this video)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Epidemiology

Gastroschisis incidence is 1 in 2500 live births and it is increasing every decade

10% of cases are associated with anomalies outside GI tract

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Epidemiology

Gastroschisis infants have high risk of intrauterine growth restriction 60% thus greater risk for preterm labor too

Risk of preterm delivery in gastroschisis 25% in comparison with normal babies 5%

Gastroschises survival rate is 90% with treatment, 0% without treatment

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology of gastroschisis is related to embryonic folding

Embryonic folding is the process by which the fetus converts from flat sheet of cells, into a tube like structure and it start at 4 weeks

Embryonic folding has to be complete for the abdominal wall to close , if not then gastroschisis occurs

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

This is caused by inadequate blood supply due to right umbilical artery premature regression (normally right umbilical artery stays longer until it regress while in gastroschisis it regress prematurely)

So there is not enough blood going to the abdominal wall and this lead to Gastroschisis which is hole in the right side of the abdominal wall that allows intestine to protrude through it

Intestine get irritated and inflamed when exposed to amniotic fluid

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Pathophysiology

This lead to reduced bowel motility and absorption because of the irritation

Herniated bowel may have compromised vascular supply which lead to impaired bowel development

Complications: Intestinal stenosis, short bowel, intestinal atresia, perforation, necrosis, volvulus or GIT infections can occur

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Causes

Cause unknown

But there is risk factors

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Risk factors

Young maternal age < 20 years

Maternal low body mass index

Maternal use of salicylates like aspirin

Maternal genitourinary infection during first trimester

Maternal cigarette smoking or alcohol or illicit drug use

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Gross appearance

Defect to the right of the umbilical cord insertion site, smooth edges and it is usually less than 4 cm in diameter

The defect is separated from the base of umbilical cord by small bridge of skin

Intestine are thickened with no overlying membrane

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Gastroschisis vs omphalocele

Omphalocele is when the intestine protrudes into the umbilical cord and it stay sealed by the umbilical cord which protect it from the amniotic fluid while in gastroschisis there is no cover

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Variants of gastroschisis

Closed or vanishing gastroschisis: abdominal wall defect has closed before birth => blood supply to the herniated bowel is impaired now => herniated bowel is now ischemic and necrosis occur

Left sided gastroschisis (rare): the only difference is that the defect is to the left of the umbilicus

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Gastroschisis can be diagnosed at the end of the first trimester by ultrasound, because the physiological return of intestine should be complete by 11 weeks of gestation if not then it is gastroschisis

US shows multiple loops of bowel floating freely in the amniotic fluid, bowel herniation is seen on the right of the umbilical cord insertion

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

Gastroschisis can be differentiated from omphalocele by US too, in gastroschisis there is lack of membranous covering of the bowel

In Omphalocele there is high probability of CVS, and genitourinary anomalies while in Gastroschisis there is low probability for GIT, CNS, CVS, MSK and genitourinary anomalies

Some of those anomalies can be identified by US too

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Diagnosis

Injury to the herniated bowel from exposure to the amniotic fluid or contracture of the umbilical ring is common

The injury also can be identified by US, features include: dilatation of the bowel, loss of peristaltic activity, changes in bowel wall echogenicity, alterations in mesenteric blood flow and changes in stomach position

Maternal alpha fetoprotein levels are elevated too

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Delivery of gastroschisis baby

Vaginal delivery is possible with all gastroschisis cases unless the liver is herniated then C section delivery has to be done

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Resuscitation

After delivery of gastroschisis newborn, ventilation or intubation might be needed

NG decompression tube should be inserted and IV access obtained

If there is bowel congestion, try to look for any kinking and relieve by repositioning of the bowel

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Resuscitation

Bolus IV normal saline 20 ml/kg after delivery is obligatory to substitute the third space fluid loss and insensible fluid losses, sometimes 80 ml/kg is needed initially

Initial dose of ampicillin and gentamicin shortly after delivery to prevent GIT infections

Parenteral nutrition is very important in gastroschisis and should be used until bowel function goes back to normal

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

The goal is to return the intestine back to the abdominal cavity and slowly introduce feeding to the baby

The two main options of treatment are

primary closure

staged closure with the use of a temporary silo and progressive reduction

Silo is a clear, sterile plastic or silicone bag that is placed over the exposed organs for putting pressure for gradual reduction and also the silo is effective in protection and preventing fluid loss

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Primary closure

this procedure include reduction of the bowel back to the abdominal cavity and closing the defect

This procedure done quickly after birth as an attempt to return the herniated organs back to their place, if failed then silo method is done

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Primary closure

Failure of primary closure is when

Intestine can’t be placed back into the abdominal cavity (not enough space)

Intestine can be placed but the intraabdominal pressure is higher than 10mmHg

Central venous pressure is greater than 4 mmHg when bowel placed back

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Staged closure using silo

This method developed in the 1990s

This method start by applying silo (plastic or silicon bag) in the delivery room, after application the bowel is reduced gradually back into the abdominal cavity

Silo positioned around the opening without the need for sutures or anesthesia

Adewale O. Oyinloye1*, Auwal M. Abubakar1, Samuel Wabada2 and Lateef O. Oyebanji1, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Staged closure using silo

Bowel viability is assessed continuously while in silo to ensure no impairment in the blood supply

This process takes between 1 and 14 days until bowel is reduced, and then definitive closure is done which is similar to the primary closure

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Intestinal atresia

Sometimes gastroschisis is associated with intestinal atresia

Intestinal atresia has to be anastomosed again

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Post operative care

Ensure there are no effects from increased abdominal pressure (e.g. abnormal ventilation, decreased renal function, GIT ischemia), if abdominal compartment syndrome is suspected then laparotomy and silo placement should be performed

In Gastroschisis bowel function is decreased (motility and absorption are affected), and it gradually improves in most patients

SOURCE SLIDE 27

Post operative care

No enteral feeding in gastroschisis until bowel function returns, during that time NG decompression, parenteral nutrition are required

When bowel activity returns, enteral feeding started gradually until enteral feeding is enough and that is when the patient can be discharged, this can take from 1 to 2 months

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Meconium Aspiration Syndrome

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

MAS is neonatal respiratory distress that occurs when neonate pass meconium in utero leading to meconium stained amniotic fluid and aspirate it during labor resulting in respiratory distress

MAS is diagnosed only if the respiratory distress can not be attributed to another cause like pneumonia, sepsis, TTN, RDS, CHD

MAS symptoms can range from mild RS distress to severe RS distress with respiratory failure

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Epidemiology

Meconium stained amniotic fluid is seen in 10-20% of all deliveries

5% of those infants have meconium stained amniotic fluid develop MAS

Mortality is about 2% of MAS infants

MAS is common in infants with breech presentation

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Causes

Fetal distress and hypoxia: hypoxic stress on the fetus => enhance intestinal peristalsis and relax anal sphincter => passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid

Fetal maturity: intestinal parasympathetic innervation and myelination increases in later pregnancy => parasympathetic increase intestinal peristalsis => passing of meconium into amniotic fluid

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathophysiology

Baby passes meconium in utero due to the causes mentioned before

During the delivery process, hypoxia cause the fetus to start breathing and gasping which lead to aspiration of the meconium stained amniotic fluid into the lungs

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

Meconium is thick material (contains cellular debris of skin, GI tract and hair, also contains GI secretions, blood, and mucus) when aspirated, it blocks the respiratory airways (same with foreign bodies), so meconium can cause lung atelectasis when it completely obstruct the right or left bronchi, or it can cause partial obstruction

Meconium triggers inflammation, in 24-48 hours after birth the airways get inflamed in form of chemical pneumonitis and respiratory distress occurs

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

Inflammation lead to inactivation of surfactant => surfactant deficiency lead to increase surface tension of the alveoli => alveoli collapsing => which furtherly aggravate the respiratory distress

Blood supply to the Obstructed airways and collapsed alveoli would be decreased due to vasoconstriction, as an attempt from the lungs to shunt more blood towards the open airways to maintain oxygenation

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Pathophysiology

If the previous process occurs extensively in the lungs, this will lead to substantial increase vascular resistance in the lungs which lead to a condition called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), PPHN may cause right heart failure

All of these factors lead to ventilation- perfusion mismatch => hypoxemia

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Pathophysiology

Meconium obstruct airways leading to air trapping, overdistension of the lungs, extra alveolar air leaks and subsequently pneumothorax

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Risk factors of MAS

Fetal distress during labor

Post term pregnancy: the greater infant’s gestational age, the greater the risk of passing meconium in utero

Prolonged labor: increase chance of fetal hypoxia

maternal related risk factors: diabetes, hypertension => Placenta problems => increase resistance to blood flow through the placenta => fetal hypoxia

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Risk factors of MAS

IUGR

Maternal substance abuse: tobacco, amphetamines or cocaine

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Clinical features

A term or post term infant present with respiratory distress and meconium stained amniotic fluid

Respiratory distress present as tachypnea (> 60/m), intercostal and subcostal retraction, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles

On physical exam, there might be signs of post maturity like peeling skin, long fingernails and vernix

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Chest x ray shows:

Multiple patchy densities bilaterally

Hyperinflation

Flattening of diaphragm

Atelectasis

Collapsed lung due to pneumothorax

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Cerevisae, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

Oxygen saturation

Arterial blood gas analysis: to evaluate for respiratory failure and acid-base balance

Echocardiography to look for right ventricular dysfunction due to PPHN

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Diagnosis

Blood cultures looking for sepsis, empirical antibiotic should be considered

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Treatment

Infant born to meconium stained amniotic fluid should have routine postnatal care with monitoring for signs of respiratory distress, endotracheal suctioning is no longer recommended

If infant developed respiratory distress then management is supportive

Oxygen supplementation is needed if oxygen saturation drops below 95%

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Treatment

Assisted ventilation techniques are used if the hypoxemia is refractory to oxygen therapy

Blood glucose

Surfactant maybe needed

Nitric oxide is pulmonary vasodilator that can be used in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment

Glucocorticoids can be used to suppress inflammation

Antibiotics are used if cultures positive

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Complications

PPHN

Pneumothorax

Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Prevention

If meconium stained amniotic fluid is seen by obstetrician then obstetrician should suction the infant oropharynx before delivering the rest of their body

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Neonatal Sepsis

meg and rahul, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Staff Sgt. Matthew Rosine, CC BY 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Neonatal sepsis is infection involving blood stream with some type of pathogen in newborn infant less than 4 weeks of age.

Neonatal sepsis is a serious illness and it may lead to multi organ failure and death

Neonatal sepsis is classified into

Early onset sepsis (EOS): up to 72 hours after birth

Late onset sepsis (LOS): 72 hours to 28 days

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Causes

EOS is caused by transmission of microorganisms from female genitourinary tract to the neonate, this could be:

Either an ascending infection (microorganisms ascend through the birth tract to the uterus and to amniotic fluid and then to baby)

Or neonate could get infected during delivery as they pass through the colonized birth tract

EOS is typically caused by group B streptococci, E. coli, coagulase negative staphylococci, H. influenza, Klebsiella, salmonella and listeria

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Causes

LOS is caused by transmission of microorganisms from surrounding environment after delivery, e.g. contact with healthcare workers and caregivers, equipment used early in life like needles, bag masks …

LOS could be a manifestation of an infection transmitted from the mother (vertical transmission)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Causes

LOS is caused by many microorganisms, most commonly by coagulase negative staph (accounts for 50% of LOS cases), could be also caused by bacteria like (H. influenza, S. Pneumonia and Meningococcus) and viruses like (HSV, CMV, enteroviruses)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

Infants have immature immune system, they have slow inflammatory response, reduced complement activation pathways and show deficit in phagocytic migration to sites of infection, their white blood cells are less effective

Preterm infants also have immature immune system but not just that, they also have deficiency in the amount of immunoglobulins transferred from mother compared to mature infants, this make immature infants at higher risk for sepsis

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

After pathogens infect the blood stream, they might travel to the CNS where they lead to meningitis and encephalitis

5% of neonatal sepsis cases are associated with meningitis

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Risk factors for sepsis

Related to the neonate

Preterm infant: weak immune system, immature epithelial barrier, increase need for vascular access => preterm infants are six times more susceptible to sepsis more than term infants

Low birth weight

Poor feeding

Poor cord care

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Risk factors for sepsis

Related to the mother

Maternal chorioamnionitis or GBS colonized birth tract

Maternal PPROM

Foul smelling liquor

Maternal fever

Difficult and prolonged labor

SOURCE SLIDE 10

EOS signs and symptoms

Initially non specific symptoms

Infant with EOS present in the first 3 days of life with grunting, poor feeding and pallor

Then infant develops lethargy, hypothermia, cyanosis and neutropenia

Respiratory failure, hypotension and meningitis are common in EOS

SOURCE SLIDE 11

EOS signs and symptoms

Infant with EOS may also develop DIC, acute tubular necrosis and peripheral gangrene as a complications

Initially it is difficult to differentiate sepsis from RDS because both present with grunting and no lethargy in septic infant initially (a lot of similarities with RDS) => all grunting infants should receive empirical antibiotics until blood cultures arrive

SOURCE SLIDE 12

LOS signs and symptoms

Infant with LOS is healthy after birth but then they would comeback after in the period 3- 28 days after birth with non specific symptoms

Then they would develop lethargy and poor feeding

Infants also develop hypotonia, fever, bulging fontanelles and seizures

There is also conjugated hyperbilirubinemia

SOURCE SLIDE 13

LOS signs and symptoms

Meningitis occur in 75% of cases

Other complications include osteomyelitis (occur if the cause was group B strep or staph aureus), arthritis (occur if the pathogen was gonococci, staph aureus, candida, many other gram negative bacteria)

When examining LOS infants, focus on examination of bones looking for pseudo paralysis (limitation of movement) of a certain limb

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Septic infants are asymptomatic initially, that is why labs are important for diagnosis

In neonate with risk factors, blood cultures should be drawn

If blood cultures are positive then CSF analysis is indicated looking for meningitis

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

CBC, CRP for excluding sepsis

Neutropenia (absolute neutrophils < 1750/ml) is more specific than neutrophilia for sepsis in CBC

Chest x ray to look for pneumonia

If pneumonia is confirmed, ABG is important to monitor for hypoxemia and metabolic acidosis

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Diagnosis

Blood pressure and urine output, peripheral pulses and skin color should be monitored to look for septic shock

If septic shock occurs then treatment with fluids and vasopressors

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Treatment

Empirical antibiotic therapy should be started if sepsis is suspected (don’t wait for blood cultures to arrive, but at the same time don’t start unless blood cultures are withdrawn)

Typical empirical antibiotic regimens for EOS include IV ampicillin + aminoglycoside (e.g. gentamicin) for 2 weeks, this regimen covers most bacteria in EOS esp. GBS, E.coli and Listeria, alternative option would be ampicillin + cefotaxime

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Treatment

For LOS, vancomycin + aminoglycoside should be enough to cover for coagulase negative staphylococci, staph aureus and pseudomonas

If meningitis is expected in EOS or LOS, then most of the previously mentioned antibiotics have poor penetration to CNS, that is why adding a third gen cephalosporin to the regimen is important (e.g. cefotaxime) and treatment period should be extended to 3 weeks

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment

Avoid ceftriaxone because it lead to hyperbilirubinemia and cause calcium deposition

If CSF cultures are negative after a while then you can stop the antibiotic treatment at 2 weeks

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Oral feeding should be withheld, nasogastric tube inserted to relieve distension and aspirate stomach contents

Maintenance fluid therapy and electrolytes replacements are important, parenteral nutrition maybe administered

Assisted ventilation and cardiovascular support maybe needed for the infant to survive

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Treatment

If peripheral pulses are weak and capillary refill time is prolonged (normal less than 3 seconds), skin color is pale and urine output is poor then give NS or RL 10 ml/kg over 10 minutes (bolus dose) and repeat 2 times over 45 minutes if needed

If those parameters still poor then dobutamine or dopamine is needed to maintain perfusion

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Treatment

Intratracheal surfactant maybe beneficial for the respiratory distress

If the mother birth tract is colonized with group B strep then empirical penicillin prophylaxis is beneficial, also penicillin prophylaxis is beneficial if the mother has other risk factors (fever, preterm labor, previous infant with EOS and chorioamnionitis)

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Neonatal Cyanosis

Author: Jules Atkins, RMSupplied by: Brandi Catt, Attribution, via Wikimedia Commons

Cornelia Csuk, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Cyanosis Definition & Types

Bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes

It is on two types: peripheral and central

Peripheral cyanosis is bluish discoloration of distal extremities (hands and feet of the neonate) while the rest of the body is normal in color (pink to white)

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Cyanosis Definition & Types

Peripheral cyanosis in newborn for the first 2 days is normal and it is called acrocyanosis and it occurs due to immature control of vascular tone in newborns (vessels in extremities stay dilated, which lead to vascular congestion and bluish discoloration)

The second type of cyanosis is the central cyanosis, it is bluish discoloration of the entire body, especially tongue, mucous membranes and trunk

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Cyanosis Definition & Types

Central cyanosis is caused by increase the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the newborn blood

Central cyanosis in newborn is normal for the first 5-10 minutes after birth, if it persist then it requires immediate evaluation because it reflects serious underlying condition that has to be managed fast

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology

Cyanosis occurs due to increase the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the blood due to many causes (will be explained a little later)

Cyanosis become evident at ≥ 3 g/dl of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the neonate blood

If you ask at which oxygen saturation this occurs? It is variable

meg and rahul, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology

There is no specific oxygen saturation you would see cyanosis at, because cyanosis depends on amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin

E.g. if the infant has hemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dl, their oxygen saturation has to reach to less than 70% to develop clinical cyanosis (30% of 10 g/dl is 3 g/dl which is the concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin needed for clinical cyanosis to develop), if the infant hemoglobin conc is 20 g/dl, their oxygen saturation has to reach below 85% for them to develop clinical cyanosis (15% of 20g/dl 3 g/dl)

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology

There is 5 possible scenarios for deoxygenated hemoglobin to increase (thus leading to cyanosis)

Hypoventilation: Asphyxia

V/Q mismatch: PPHN

Diffusion abnormalities: MAS

Oxygen transport: Methemoglobinemia

Heart problems: TGA

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis

Wide differential diagnosis including:

Hypoglycemia

Sepsis: second most common cause

CVS (third most common cause)

Cyanotic congenital heart diseases: TGA, TOF, truncus arteriosus … => should be identified quickly

Heart failure due to sepsis, myocarditis, SVT, heart block…

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis

RS

RDS: surfactant deficiency (first most common cause)

Transient tachypnea of newborn: self limiting

Meconium aspiration: impairs oxygen diffusion

Diaphragmatic hernia

Pneumothorax

Pneumonia

Persistent pulmonary hypertension

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis

Nervous system

Asphyxia

Intracranial hemorrhage

Neuromuscular disease

Maternal sedative drugs

Meningitis

Blood

Blood loss

Polycythemia

Methemoglobinemia

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Peripheral Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis

There is specific differential diagnosis for peripheral cyanosis if it persists for more than 24 hours:

Sepsis

Cardiogenic shock

Hypovolemia

Exposure to cold air or water

SOURCE SLIDE 12

What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination

Check ABCs and check vitals

If oxygen saturation is less than 95% then administer supplemental oxygen

Assess for signs of respiratory distress: nasal flaring, chest retractions, tachypnea (more than 60 breaths/min), stridor and grunting, if those are seen on the baby then think of differentials related to respiratory system

SOURCE SLIDE 13

What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination

If neonate has weak, irregular or absent respirations then think of differential diagnoses related to heart and nervous system

Hyperoxia test differentiate between cardiac and non cardiac causes of cyanosis (100% oxygen is supplied for neonate for 10 minutes, and their oxygen saturation is checked after, if their saturation increases substantially then the cause pulmonary or CNS related, if their saturation still same then cardiac)

SOURCE SLIDE 14

What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination

Take full history from mother (pregnancy history, birth history, medical history)

Do complete physical examination of the neonate

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Management

After checking ABCs, Neonate may need respiratory support in form of bag mask ventilation or intubation

Send for CBC (check for anemia and lymphocytosis), blood cultures looking for sepsis, blood glucose looking for hypoglycemia

Send for chest x ray looking for pneumothorax, heart failure

ECG and echocardiogram looking for congenital heart diseases

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Management

Manage accordingly

outline.heading: Peripheral Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis
outline.summary: There is specific differential diagnosis for peripheral cyanosis if it persists for more than 24 hours: Sepsis Cardiogenic shock Hypovolemia Exposure to cold air or water

outline.heading: What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination
outline.summary: Check ABCs and check vitals If oxygen saturation is less than 95% then administer supplemental oxygen Assess for signs of respiratory distress: nasal flaring, chest retractions, tachypnea (more than 60 breaths/min), stridor and grunting, if those are seen on the baby then think of differentials related to respiratory system

outline.heading: What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination
outline.summary: If neonate has weak, irregular or absent respirations then think of differential diagnoses related to heart and nervous system Hyperoxia test differentiate between cardiac and non cardiac causes of cyanosis (100% oxygen is supplied for neonate for 10 minutes, and their oxygen saturation is checked after, if their saturation increases substantially then the cause pulmonary or CNS related, if their saturation still same then cardiac)

outline.heading: What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination
outline.summary: Take full history from mother (pregnancy history, birth history, medical history) Do complete physical examination of the neonate

outline.heading: Management
outline.summary: After checking ABCs, Neonate may need respiratory support in form of bag mask ventilation or intubation Send for CBC (check for anemia and lymphocytosis), blood cultures looking for sepsis, blood glucose looking for hypoglycemia Send for chest x ray looking for pneumothorax, heart failure ECG and echocardiogram looking for congenital heart diseases

outline.heading: Management
outline.summary: Manage accordingly

Hernia Treatment

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

U.S. Navy photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Principles of hernia treatment

Hernia is treated with surgical repair (there is no conservative therapy for hernia)

Reducible abdominal wall hernia doesn’t necessarily require repair, unless the patient request the repair for symptomatic relief, or for cosmetic reasons

Surgeon might request the repair to establish diagnosis if in doubt

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Principles of hernia treatment

Irreducible abdominal wall hernia always require repair, because if not repaired then complications are likely to occur (e.g. bowel obstruction, strangulation and infarction), if patient tolerance for surgery or anesthesia is in doubt (due to morbidity) then irreducible hernia surgery is done only if benefits outweigh risks

All cases of femoral hernia should be repaired because of high risk of strangulation associated with this type of hernia

SOURCE SLIDE 4

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Principles of hernia treatment

Reducible hernia with increasing difficulty in reduction and increasing size are also indications of surgery

Smaller hernias can be more dangerous than larger ones due to higher risk for strangulation

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Surgical approach to hernia

All hernias are treated through following these steps

Reduction of the hernia content into the abdominal cavity with debridement and bowel repair if necessary

Excision and closure of a peritoneal sac if present and reducing it back deep to the muscles

If peritoneal sac is left without it being reduced, there is a risk of fluid formation within the sac (seroma)

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Surgical approach to hernia

All hernias are treated through following these steps

Closure of the abdominal wall defect is ideal, but it might be impossible if the defect is large, Muscle flap can be used to close large defects

The defect can be closed with sutures alone but this method is associated with high recurrence rates, additional reinforcement of the defect with a non absorbable mesh is better and lowers the recurrence rates

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Mesh used in hernia repair

It is a prosthetic material, it can be a net or a flat sheet

It is used to strengthen the abdominal wall defect, so the abdominal organs and fatty tissues can not protrude through the defect again (it lowers hernia recurrence)

Anpol42, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Mesh types

Synthetic mesh

the most commonly used type

Synthesized from polypropylene, polyester or PTFE

Most of them are non absorbable but there is some that are absorbable but rarely used

Biological mesh

Derived from human or animal dermis, bovine pericardium or porcine intestinal mucosa

Quite expensive

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Positioning of the mesh

Mesh should be placed on a firm and well vascularized bed with good overlap with the defect

Mesh could be placed

Onlay: just outside the muscle in the subcut space

Inlay: within the muscle (muscle that has the defect in it)

Extraperitoneal sublay: immediately under the muscle

Intraperitoneal sublay: inside peritoneal cavity

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Anpol42, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Hernia Symptoms Progression

Herecomesdoc, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

1. First symptom of hernia

Hernia start as a visible bulge that can be seen only when coughing or straining and it goes back to normal afterwards

AfroBrazilian, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Hernia contents

Intestine

Omentum

Fallopian tube or uterus in women

Stomach

Saltanat ebli, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

2. First progression of hernia

Bulge become more visible and it has to be pushed back to get reduced (reducible)

Pressure at the affected area

Strenerkou, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

3. Second progression of hernia

The visible bulge can’t be reduced back anymore (irreducible or incarcerated)

Pain or discomfort at the area

It might be associated with bowel obstruction (gives symptoms like nausea and vomiting)

Treatment with surgery is urgent

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Svenscar69, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

4. Third progression of hernia

irreducible hernia become strangulated (blood supply to the hernia content become compromised)

Onset of burning or sharp pain

Swelling

Nausea and vomiting, constipation

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

4. Fourth progression of hernia

Fever

Treatment with surgery is emergent (it has to be done right now)

If not treated then the content of the hernia become infarcted and die and this lead to peritonitis

Milliways, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

U.S. Navy photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Alcoholic Hepatitis

CDC / Dr. Thomas F. Sellers / Emory University, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Polygon data is generated by Database Center for Life Science(DBCLS)[2], CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Alcoholic liver disease stages

Alcoholic fatty liver disease: accumulation of fatty acids in the liver in heavy drinkers

Alcoholic hepatitis: inflammation after binge drinking

Liver cirrhosis: recurrent injuries to the liver caused by alcohol end up with fibrosis

Ashley Pomeroy, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Alcoholic hepatitis

It is hepatitis (inflammation of the liver), it is a severe disease that occur after heavy drinking

Patients mostly have a history of at least 10 years of heavy alcohol drinking

Alcoholic hepatitis can range from mild to severe, mortality in untreated cases is 50% in 30 days

The condition comes suddenly and progress rapidly

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Pathophysiology

There is direct hepatocyte damage by alcohol and its metabolites like acetaldehyde

Alcohol damages enterocytes and disrupt the tight junctions between them, this increase intestinal permeability and allows bacteria and fungi to enter portal circulation and travel to liver and cause damage to it too

These two mechanisms acutely lead to alcoholic hepatitis and with time lead to liver fibrosis (cirrhosis)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Signs and symptoms

Fever

Fatigue

CDC, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Signs and symptoms

Jaundice (yellowish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes)

CDC / Dr. Thomas F. Sellers / Emory University, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Signs and symptoms

Abdominal pain, especially right upper quadrant with tenderness

CDC, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Signs and symptoms

Ascites: fluid accumulation in the abdominal cavity

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Signs and symptoms

Hepatic encephalopathy: brain dysfunction due to liver disease, present with

DLOC

Asterixis

Change in behavior

FelipeIbazeta, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Diagnosis

History of heavy alcohol intake

For men, consuming 5 or more drinks on any day or 15 or more per week.

For women, consuming 4 or more on any day or 8 or more drinks per week.

Physical examination reveals tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, hepatomegaly and RUQ pain and tenderness, there might be also spider naevi, muscle wasting, gynecomastia..

LFTs: AST/ ALT ratio is more than 1.5

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Diagnosis

AST in most cases between is less than 500 U/L and ALT is normal

Bilirubin > 3 mg/dL

Liver biopsy not required

US is used to exclude differential diagnosis

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Treatment

Abstain from alcohol

Glucocorticoids can be used to suppress inflammation for patients with severe disease (elevated PT/PTT or very high bilirubin)

Nutrition supplementation with proteins and calories

N acetylcysteine

Liver transplantation maybe needed

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Alcoholic hepatis vs alcoholic steatohepatitis

ASH is diagnosis based on liver histology while AH is a clinical diagnosis

ASH liver biopsy shows steatosis, infiltration of neutrophils (inflammation) and fibrosis

AH is characterized by history of heavy alcohol consumption until at least 4 weeks before onset of symptoms (jaundice, fever hepatomegaly…)

HU4JW4Pq8Ro.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Acute Liver Failure

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Liver functions

Liver is responsible for

Detoxification

Support metabolism

Immunity

Digestion

Synthesis of protein such as albumin, coagulation factors…

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Definition

Acute liver failure should have all of these elements to be considered acute liver failure :

Severe acute liver injury (hepatocyte necrosis)

Duration is less than 26 weeks

Evidence of encephalopathy: DLOC, change in behavior

Impaired Synthetic function of the liver: abnormal coagulation profile (INR ≥ 1.5)

The patient should not have liver cirrhosis or pre existing liver disease

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Causes

When patient present with acute liver failure, think of liver diseases that cause a lot of damage in short period of time

Drug induced hepatitis due to paracetamol ingestion (first most common)

Viral hepatitis (second most common)

Shocked liver (ischemia or hypoxia)

Budd Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis)

Veno occlusive disease

Mushroom ingestion

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Causes

Wilsons disease

Sepsis

Autoimmune hepatitis

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

HELLP syndrome

Heat stroke

Malignant infiltration

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Causes

Slow progressive liver diseases don’t cause acute liver failure, but rather cause chronic liver failure

NAFLD

Hemochromatosis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Primary biliary cirrhosis

Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pathophysiology

Most causes lead to hepatocyte ATP depletion and cellular swelling => cell membrane disruption

Massive hepatocyte necrosis and apoptosis => liver failure

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Signs and Symptoms

Fatigue, weakness

Confusion because of hepatic encephalopathy

Jaundice due to hyperbilirubinemia

Hepatomegaly (liver congestion)

Abdominal pain especially right upper quadrant

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Signs and Symptoms

Abnormal LFTs

Abnormal coagulation profile, elevated PT/PTT

Thrombocytopenia due to loss of TPO

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Medical history

Comprehensive history helps to exclude DDX, ask for:

Timeline of symptoms and progression

Any history of hepatic disease

Drug history looking for acetaminophen toxicity

Family history looking for Wilson disease and thrombotic disorders

Any recent surgeries looking for possible toxic medications used like some anesthetic agents

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Examination

Check vitals looking for hypotension (sepsis)

Abdominal palpation looking for pain and tenderness

Special tests looking for ascites

Altered mental status

Fever (infection)

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

Requirements to diagnose Acute liver failure

Evidence of liver injury: Elevated AST/ALT

Evidence of hepatic encephalopathy: change in behavior, decreased level of consciousness, coma

INR more or equal to 1.5

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Follow up investigations

Look for hypoglycemia

Look for hyperbilirubinemia

Low PLT

US to look for Budd Chiari syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Look for acute kidney injury (elevated urea and creatinine)

Electrolyte abnormalities

Abdominal imaging looking for cirrhosis, features of portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, vascular problems

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Histopathology

Done only if the cause didn’t get identified through history, examination, investigations

Trans jugular liver biopsy taken and examined

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Management - Definitive management

Admit to ICU

If you already know the cause then treat the cause

If you don’t know the cause then give N acetylcysteine (paracetamol antidote) and then you can look for the cause

Treat the identified cause

Liver transplantation if treatment not succeeded

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Management - Supportive management

IV fluid with controlling acid base balance and electrolytes

Monitor for any bleeding (patient have coagulopathy) and treat with blood products

Blood and urine cultures and start empirical antibiotics if patient have fever

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Management - Supportive management

Monitor hepatic encephalopathy and protect airway

Provide nutrition

Monitor for hypoglycemia and maintain blood glucose between 160- 200

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Complication

Renal failure

Sepsis

Hypoglycemia

Cerebral edema (most common cause of death in ALF) : edema lead to intracranial hypertension, ischemic brain injury and herniation, triggers include hypoxia, hypotension, decreased cerebral perfusion and increased ammonia levels

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Complications

Encephalopathy

Coagulopathy

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Liver Panel Tests Interpretation

Richardelainechambers, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Zorn, A.M., Liver development (October 31, 2008), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.25.1, http://www.stembook.org., CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Standard liver panel tests

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT or SGPT)

Aspartate aminotransferase (AST or SGOT)

Alkaline phosphatases (ALP)

Gamma glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)

Bilirubin

Albumin

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)

found in hepatocytes cytoplasm, also found in kidneys, heart and muscles (catalyzes transamination reactions)

ALT is elevated more than AST in most types of hepatitis due to cellular damage

Normal ALT < 50 U/L

SOURCE SLIDE 4

ALT elevation

Rise of ALT up to 300 IU/ L is not specific to the liver (it can be due to damage of other organs containing this enzyme)

When ALT rises more than 500 IU/L it becomes specific to the liver

In pregnancy ALT elevate during second trimester but to < 100

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)

Found inside the hepatocellular mitochondria and the cytoplasm too, also found in high concentration in heart, muscle, kidney, brain, pancreas and lungs and that make it less specific indicator of liver injury

Alcohol is a mitochondrial toxin, that’s why in alcoholic liver disease and alcoholic hepatitis AST is much more elevated than ALT

Normal AST < 40 IU/L

SOURCE SLIDE 6

AST & ALT elevation ranges and interpretation

If AST & ALT both elevated higher than normal limit and up to < 500 then think of

Cirrhosis

Chronic viral hepatitis

Fatty liver disease

Alcoholic hepatitis

If elevated 500- 1000 then think of

Acute viral hepatitis

Autoimmune hepatitis

SOURCE SLIDE 7

AST & ALT elevation

If AST & ALT elevated > 1000 then think of

Shocked liver (ischemia)

Acetaminophen toxicity

SOURCE SLIDE 8

AST/ALT ratio

AST/ALT ratio increases in liver function impairment

AST/ALT ratio is around 1.45 in alcoholic liver disease, 2 in alcoholic hepatitis, 0.9 in non alcoholic hepatitis,

AST/ALT ratio is 4.5 in Wilson disease and hyperthyroidism

AST/ALT ratio is around 1.33 in post necrotic liver cirrhosis

AST/ALT ratio is around 1.17 in viral cirrhosis

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

enzyme in the cells lining the biliary tract of the liver, it is also found in the small intestine, kidney, bones and placenta, it is important in calcification of bones and lipid transposition in small intestine

ALP elevates in cholestasis (significant elevation) and most of other liver conditions (mild elevation)

Serum ALP also increase in pregnancy (placenta secrete the enzyme), thyroid disease and bone disease

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

Normal range 40- 140

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Gamma glutamyl (GGT)

Microsomal enzyme found in hepatocytes, cells lining biliary tract, kidney, pancreas and intestine (almost similar to ALP)

No GGT in the bone so it is not elevated in bone disease (beneficial in differentiating the cause of ALP increase)

If GGT and ALP both elevated then hepatobiliary cause of elevated ALP

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Gamma glutamyl (GGT)

Also elevated in cholestasis (significant elevation) and other liver conditions (mild elevation)

Also elevated in heavy alcohol consumption

Elevated in other conditions like DM, acute pancreatitis, MI, Guillian barre syndrome, hyperthyroidism …

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Bilirubin

Bilirubin is a waste product from heme breakdown (RBC die and give heme => bilirubin)

Unconjugated bilirubin get conjugated by the liver and gets excreted through bile

Bilirubin gets elevated when there is a problem in the liver because it can’t be excreted anymore

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Bilirubin

Normal total bilirubin is 0.1- 1 mg/dL

Normal unconjugated bilirubin is 0.2- 0.7 mg/dl

Normal conjugated bilirubin is 0.1- 0.4

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Albumin

Protein made by liver, it is the main protein of plasma proteins

Albumin levels decrease in chronic liver disease (e.g. cirrhosis)

Albumin is a measurement of the synthetic function of the liver, glucose and coagulation factors also measure the synthetic function and all of these decrease in chronic liver disease

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Liver test abnormal patterns

Hepatocellular pattern due to problems in hepatocytes, examples are hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease

Cholestatic pattern due to problems in the biliary tract, examples are biliary obstruction and primary biliary cirrhosis

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Slide 17

Table from slide 17
Test Normal range Hepatocellular pattern Cholestasis pattern
ALP40- 140 < 280 > 420
AST < 40 > 400 Around 80
ALT < 50> 500 Around 100
SOURCE SLIDE 18

Follow up testing

Cholestatic pattern on liver function test:

Best initial test: ultrasound to evaluate biliary ducts

Dilated: extrahepatic cause of obstruction (stone, mass)

Normal: intrahepatic cause of obstruction (primary biliary cirrhosis, pregnancy)

Hepatocellular pattern on liver function test:

Followed by blood tests looking for viral hepatitis and autoimmune hepatitis

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Burn Assessment

User:Westchaser, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Burn & Trauma Research Center, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Burn assessment

Burn is assessed by calculating the total body surface area affected by the partial thickness (second degree) and full thickness (third degree) burns using one of these methods:

Rule of nine

Rule of palms

Lund and Browder chart

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Burn assessment

Superficial (first degree) burns are not included in the calculation of TBSA

Cleaning of debris and soot is mandatory to avoid confusing debris with burns

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Calculating TBSA affected by burns benefits

Calculating TBSA affected by burns is helpful in:

Understanding the severity of the burn

Determining the amount of fluid needed for resuscitation using Parkland formula

Nutritional support

Pain management

Infection control

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Rule of nine

Originally called Wallace rule of nine relative to the British plastic surgeon alexander Wallace who first developed this method

Mainly used as initial assessment tool in pre hospital and emergency department to estimate the TBSA affected by burn, in burn units the Lund Broader chart is used to re calculate the TBSA again because it is more precise

Quick and easy methods that is used for large surface area burns

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Rule of nine

Jmarchn, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Table from slide 6
Body part Estimated body surface area
Adults Children < 10
Left arm 9%9%
Right arm 9%9%
Head & neck 9% 18%
Entire back 18%18%
Chest & abdomen18%18%
Genitals 1%0%
Left leg 18%14%
Right leg 18%14%
SOURCE SLIDE 7

Rule of nine

Example: if patient right arm and right leg both entirely burned with their chest also burned then

Right arm = 9%

Right leg = 18%

Chest only = 9%

TBSA affected by burn is 36%

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Rule of nine

Rule of nine is best accurate in underweight to normal BMI adults

The accuracy is less for children and obese patients

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Rule of palm

Best used for burns < 10% TBSA

The size of the patient’s palm (including fingers) equals approx. 1% of patient’s TBSA

Estimation is made by visual assessment

More practical in infants and young children because body surface area is small and easily calculated

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Rule of palm

It is also used as initial assessment tool for TBSA in pre hospital and emergency department, Lund Browder chart is then used again to re calculate TBSA in burn units once patient reaches there

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Lund and Browder chart

Developed by the American surgeons Charles Lund and newton Browder in 1942

Takes into account the age of the patient (unlike the other methods)

In children, decreasing percentage of TBSA for the head and increasing percentage of TBSA for the legs as the child ages

Best method and most accurate

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Slide 12

Giftrapped, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Third degree burn

Full thickness injury through epidermis and dermis into subcutaneous fat

Loss of sensation (painless)

All dermis is involved

Always require surgery (excision and grafting)

Takes months to heal and sometimes it doesn’t

Scarring, contractures will form

Amputation could be required

xRK6YWTL7C8.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Second Degree Burns

The original uploader was Snickerdo at English Wikipedia., CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

User:Westchaser, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Second degree burns

The second degree burn involve the epidermis and the dermis and it is on two types:

Superficial partial thickness: extends into papillary dermis (superficial layer of dermis)

Deep partial thickness: extends into reticular dermis (deep layer of dermis)

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Superficial second degree burn presentation

Extends into papillary dermis but the reticular dermis is spared

Redness of the burned skin because blood vessels still intact in the reticular dermis

Intense pain because nerve fibers are located in the reticular dermis and it is still intact

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Superficial second degree burn presentation

Formation of clear blister (pockets of skin containing fluid)

Themidget17, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Superficial second degree burn presentation

Erythematous and blanch to touch

Moist

Spares hair follicles and sweat glands (both are in the reticular layer of the dermis)

Local infection (cellulitis) is common

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Superficial second degree burn healing

Heals without scarring/ minimal scarring

Heals within 7- 14 days

Treatment with cooling the burn with running water for 10-20 min and applying antibiotic ointment and dressing

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Deep second degree burn presentation

Injury to epidermis and both layers of the dermis (all the dermis involved)

Appears pale because the blood vessels are in the reticular layer and once injured skin would be pale

Don’t blanch to touch

Less painful, remain painful to pinprick (nerve endings are in reticular layer, once injured pain would be much less)

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Dr. med. Peter Illing, Kassel, Germany, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/de/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Deep second degree burn presentation

Blisters sometimes present

Dry

Hair follicles and sweat glands might be damaged or destroyed

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Deep second degree burn healing

Heals within 2-6 weeks

Severe scarring and contractures

May require excision and skin grafting

SOURCE SLIDE 1

First Degree Burns

QuinnHK at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Bejinhan, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

First degree burn

Injury localized to the epidermis

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Presentation

Reddened skin means that the dermis is intact

Skin is dry

QuinnHK at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Presentation

Pain at burn site means that the nerve endings in the reticular dermis are intact

Burned skin is blanch to touch meaning when press with your finger against the burned skin it turns to white color and then when release finger it is back to red color meaning the blood vessels in the dermis are intact

First degree burns are NOT associated with blisters

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Healing

First degree burns heals perfectly without scarring

Examples: sun burn, minor scald from kitchen accident

Treatment is to relieve pain with topical soothing agents like cool water for 10- 20 min, aloe vera gel, silver sulfadiazine cream, Vaseline +/- NSAIDs

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Frazzmatazz, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Healing

First degree burns heals in 4 days to a week

Repeated sunburns increase the risk of skin cancer

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Intravenous Fluids

K, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Michaelberry at English Wikipedia, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

IV fluid types

Crystalloids

Solutions that contain small molecules that can pass through semipermeable membrane (blood vessel wall). They are typically composed of water, electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride ...) and small molecules like glucose ….

E.g.: saline, half saline, D5W

أمين, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

IV fluid types

Colloids

Solutions that contain larger molecules like proteins which don’t cross the semipermeable membrane like blood vessels wall, they are expensive

E.g.: albumin, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate

DiverDave, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Crystalloids

Normal saline

Ringer’s lactate

Half saline

D5W

Hypertonic saline

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Normal saline

0.9% normal saline

أمين, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Normal saline

Saline means fluid containing salt

Normal saline is 9 grams of NaCl dissolved in 1 L of water

Approximately same osmolarity as plasma (isotonic) and that is why it is called normal

308 mOsm/L vs. 275-295 mOsm/L plasma

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Normal saline

Uses

Used for volume replacement in hypovolemic and septic shocks

Wound care: clean and irrigate wounds to help prevent infection and promote healing

It is used for diluting medications and administration of IV medications

Laboratory and diagnostic procedures

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Normal saline

If normal saline supplied in high quantity:

Results in influx of chloride ions (Cl-) because it contain chloride and this causes the bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) to shift into cells which causes acidosis

Because of the acidosis, the potassium shifts out of the cell into the circulation which lead to hyperkalemia

And that is why the lactated ringers are superior in supplying large quantities

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Ringer’s lactate

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Membranous Nephropathy

Dr. Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

Membranous nephropathy is the second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, FSGS being the most common

Most common in men older than 40 years, usually people of European origins

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Etiology

Primary: Idiopathic (70% of cases)

Secondary

Systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus could lead to membranous or to lupus nephritis which is nephritic

Solid tumors: colon cancer, lung cancer, melanoma

Infectious: hep B, hep C, syphilis

Drugs: penicillamine, gold, NSAIDs

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Pathogenesis

Primary is an autoimmune disease mediated by IgG antibody (autoantibodies) directed to the phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) on the podocytes, this attack lead to thickening of glomerular basement membrane which will be obvious on light microscopy

Secondary due to direct injury to the glomerular basement membrane

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Renal_corpuscle.svg: M•Komorniczak -talk- (polish Wikipedist)derivative work: Huckfinne, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Renal biopsy

Light microscopy: Shows thickened glomerular basement membrane and that is why it is called membranous

Immunofluorescence shows deposition of granular IgG/ C3

Electron microscopy: subepithelial deposits (spike and dome appearance

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Slide 7

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Presentation

Frothy urine

Pitting edema, worse in lower extremities,

Periorbital edema

Nephrotic syndrome, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Presentation

Abdominal pain due to ascites, severe hypovolemia, peritonitis, pancreatitis, thrombosis, or steroid induced gastritis

Hypertension

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Presentation

Patients may develop white nails sometimes in bands (Muehrcke's lines) during relapses

Lyrl, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Presentation

Patients may develop xanthomas and xanthelasma because of hyperlipidemia

Bobtheowl2 at the English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

Nephrotic range proteinuria, urine dipstick test 3+, 4+

24 hours urine protein is > 3.5g

Urine protein creatinine ratio of more than 3

Comprehensive metabolic panel looking for Hypoalbuminemia: serum albumin < 3

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Renal function test: BUN and creatinine looking for renal dysfunction

Serum electrolytes looking for calcium and other electrolytes changes because Total serum calcium and vitamin D decreased due to decrease protein bound calcium and decrease vitamin D binding proteins lost in urine respectively, ionized calcium is usually normal

Mild hyponatremia during relapses

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Normal serum completements

PLA2R antibodies positive in 70- 80% of primary MN cases and these antibodies with the nephrotic syndrome presentation are enough for MN diagnosis (no need of biopsy

Hepatitis serology testing

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

Elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels and thrombocytosis are usually found during relapse as result of plasma volume contraction

Confirmatory test is renal biopsy

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Prognosis

One third of the patients with idiopathic MN undergo spontaneous remission, one third remain in nephrotic state and one third develop progressive CKD

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Progression to ESRD

15% of patients with MN progress to ESRD in 5 years if untreated, 40% at 15 years

Risk factors for progression

Elderly patients

Male gender

> 8 g of proteinuria at presentation

Tubulointerstitial fibrosis on biopsy

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Treatment

Supportive therapy

Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs

Hyperlipidemia treated with statins

Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics

Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation

Infections treated with antibiotics

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment

Primary MN: Patient treated if they have risk factor for progression or nephrotic syndrome that can’t be controlled by ACEs or other supportive therapies

Cyclophosphamide + prednisolone

Cyclosporine + low dose prednisolone for those who cannot tolerate the first option

Rituximab (superior to other options)

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Secondary MN treated by treating the secondary cause

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis

Pixabay, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Terminology

Focal means when doing a biopsy there is less than 50% of glomeruli involved

Segmental means portion of the glomerulus is involved, others are normal

Glomerulosclerosis: sclerosis means scar

So it means less than 50% of glomeruli are scarred

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Overview

FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults (in children most common cause of nephrotic syndrome is the MCD)

FSGS is second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children

FSGS is common in people of west African descent (the primary genetic type)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Overview

FSGS famous for causing damage to transplanted kidney in less than 24 hours

Minimal change disease and FSGS on the same spectrum of podocyte injury (both affect foot processes): MCD is mild injury, FSGS is severe

Poor prognosis

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Etiology

Primary FSGS:

idiopathic

Genetic/ familial

Secondary FSGS

HIV

Sickle cell anemia

Drugs (pamidronate, heroin)

Massive obesity

Renal injury (e.g. renal injury from HUS)

Systemic disease

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathogenesis

In primary FSGS there is injury to the podocyte due to a circulating toxin

Secondary FSGS

Reduced renal mass, sickle cell and obesity lead to increased glomerular capillary blood pressure lead to hyperfiltration through the glomerulus and subsequent podocyte injury

In HIV, drugs (heroin, pamidronate) there is a direct injury to the podocyte either by the virus or the drug

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Renal biopsy

Light microscopy shows segmental sclerosis

Immunofluorescence shows deposition of C3 complement and IgM in area of the scar

Electron microscopy shows effacement of foot processes

Since FSGS is focal, the abnormality may not show on renal biopsy and it would be normal leading to initial diagnosis of MCD

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Serum electrolytes looking for calcium and other electrolytes changes because Total serum calcium and vitamin D decreased due to decrease protein bound calcium and decrease vitamin D binding proteins lost in urine respectively, ionized calcium is usually normal

Mild hyponatremia during relapses

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Diagnosis

Elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels and thrombocytosis are usually found during relapse as result of plasma volume contraction

Confirmatory test is renal biopsy

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Treatment of primary FSGS

Primary FSGS may respond to high dose glucocorticoids therapy (0.5-2 mg/kg/day) but the response is not as fast as in MCD

Calcineurin inhibitors, cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate mofetil sometimes used but their efficacy is variable

Progression to CKD is common patients who don’t respond to glucocorticoids and disease recurs after renal transplantation

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment of secondary FSGS

Treat secondary causes

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Supportive therapy

Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs

Hyperlipidemia treated with statins

Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics

Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation

Infections treated with antibiotics

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Complications

Kidney failure is a common long term complication among the FSGS patients

Untreated cases all progress to end stage kidney disease except for less than 10% of them

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Minimal Change Disease

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Polarlys, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

One of the primary glomerular diseases that lead to nephrotic syndrome

MCD is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, it accounts for 90% of nephrotic syndrome cases in children younger than 5y and 50% of nephrotic syndrome cases in children older than 10y

MCD accounts for 10-15% of nephrotic syndrome cases in adults

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Overview

Minimal change disease has good prognosis

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Causes

Primary: Idiopathic

Secondary

Drugs: NSAIDs, antimicrobials, lithium

Neoplasms: Hodgkin’s and NHL, leukemia, thymoma

Allergy: atopy, vaccinations, insect stings, foods

Viral infections (URTI)

Primary disease might relapse after exposure to the secondary causes

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathogenesis

Immune attack initiated by T cells against the podocytes for unknown reason

T cells injuries the podocyte foot processes leading to effacement of these foot processes and subsequently nephrotic syndrome

Children younger than 10 presenting with features does not go with minimal change disease like gross hematuria, renal dysfunction then renal biopsy is indicated

Children older than 10 and Adults: renal biopsy is indicated to establish diagnosis

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Treatment

Curative therapy

MCD responds very well to corticosteroids

Corticosteroids are used in high doses for 12-16 weeks then tapered over 6 months

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Treatment

Curative therapy

Cyclosporine for steroid resistant patients

Cyclophosphamide, Mycophenolate mofetil or rituximab for steroid dependent patients (relapse if steroids are stopped)

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Treatment

Supportive therapy

Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs

Hyperlipidemia treated with statins

Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics

Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation

Infections treated with antibiotics

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Nephrotic Syndrome

CharlesPicavet, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Polarlys, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

Normally, protein molecules shouldn’t be lost in urine in concentrations higher than 150 mg per day

If the urine protein excretion exceeds 150 mg per day then this is called proteinuria and it is caused by many diseases including UTI, nephrotic syndrome, CKD…

When the urine protein become > 3.5 g per day then it is called nephrotic range proteinuria and it is caused by nephrotic syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Cause

In nephrotic syndrome the kidney glomerulus would have some kind of problem that make it pass protein molecules into the urine, the problem exactly in the podocyte (NephrOtic = POdocyte)

Artwork by Holly Fischer, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Slide 5

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

Due to the albumin lost in urine, liver tries to compensate by increasing albumin synthesis but it fails to reach the normal albumin levels

As a result of the protein lost in urine, the oncotic pressure decreases which stimulate the hepatic lipoprotein synthesis which lead to hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia

Lipid become entrapped in casts and enclosed by the plasma membrane of a degenerative renal tubular cells which lead to oval fat body in urine

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Presentation

Frothy urine

Polarlys, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

Presentation

Edema

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Presentation

Swelling around the eye (periorbital edema)

CharlesPicavet, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Presentation

Ascites

Dyspnea due to pleural effusion or due to diaphragmatic compression with ascites

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Presentation

Hypertension

Steven Fruitsmaak, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Presentation

Hyperlipidemia (serum cholesterol > 300)

Proteinuria (3.5 g/day)

Hypoalbuminemia

Mark-shea at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Presentation

Anemia because transferrin is also lost in urine

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Presentation

Increase risk of infection

Increased risk of thrombosis

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Diagnosis

Best initial test is urinalysis which detect protein lost in urine, and any urinary casts

24 hour urine protein test

Normal protein excretion < 150 mg/day

Nephrotic range > 3.5 g/day

Urine protein to creatinine ratio

Easier to obtain than 24 hours urine collection

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Diagnosis

Comprehensive metabolic panel looking for hypoalbuminemia (normal albumin= 3.5-5 g/dl)

Renal function test: blood urea nitrogen and creatinine

Serum electrolytes and lipid profile looking for any changes

Confirmatory test is renal biopsy looking for the exact pathology

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Treatment

Curative treatment

Treat the cause usually with immunosuppressive therapy

Supportive treatment

Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs

Hyperlipidemia treated with statins

Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics

Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation

Infections treated with antibiotics

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Complications

Thrombosis

Thrombosis typically seen in > 10g of proteinuria

Coagulation and anti coagulation factors are lost into the urine including anti thrombin III factor

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Complications

Thrombosis

Liver tries to compensate for that by making more pro coagulation factors which make the problem worse

Volume depletion from diuretic therapy and reduced oncotic pressure lead to hemoconcentration and increased PLT aggregation which lead to thrombus formation and thrombosis

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Complications

Infection

Immunoglobulins lost in urine

Patient become more susceptible to infections mostly with staphylococci and streptococci bacteria

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Complications

Acute renal failure Due to hypovolemia (fluid shifted from intravascular into tissues = edema)

Pulmonary edema

Growth retardation

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Etiology

Primary glomerular diseases include immune mediated injury to the podocytes

Minimal change disease

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

Membranous nephropathy

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Etiology

Secondary glomerular diseases includes systemic diseases that also affect the glomerulus

Amyloidosis

Diabetic nephropathy

Systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus nephritis)

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Skin Graft and Flap

Giftrapped, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Raymund E. Horch, G. Bjoern Stark, Justus P. Beier: Unusual explosive growth of a squamous cell carcinoma of the scalp after electrical burn injury and subsequent coverage by sequential free flap vascular connection – a case report In: BMC Cancer 2005, 5:150 doi:10.1186/1471-2407-5-150, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

Skin grafting or flapping is a type of surgery involves transplantation of skin from the donor site to the recipient site.

Grafting or flapping used in

Extensive wound or trauma

Burns

Areas of extensive skin loss due to infection

Surgeries require skin replacement like removal of skin cancers

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Skin graft

Skin graft consist of epidermis and some portion of the dermis that is removed from its blood supply and transferred to another location

Humberto Guerra, Juan Carlos Palomino, Eduardo Falconí, Francisco Bravo, Ninoska Donaires, Eric Van Marck, and Françoise Portaels., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Skin graft uses

Close any wound with good blood supply

Temporary closure (in case of allografts given to patient that keep them covered for 2 weeks and then they automatically shed because of rejection)

Control infection

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Skin graft uses

Close donor site (in case taken flap from a donor and site was large it closed with graft)

Mucosal replacement (urethra, oral cavity)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Skin graft types

Autograft => same person

Allograft (homograft) => from different human

Xenograft (heterograft) => from different species

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Graft types according to thickness

Full thickness skin grafts contain epidermis and entire dermis with its elastic fibers => full thickness skin graft have elastic properties and primary contracture which make it good for replacing the sites that need elasticity like anterior elbow joint skin

Partial thickness skin grafts contain epidermis and varying thickness of the dermis and it is associated with secondary contracture

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Primary contracture vs secondary contracture of skin graft

Primary contracture is the immediate recoil of freshly harvested grafts as a result of the elastin in the dermis, the more the thickness the more the dermis the more the primary contracture, primary contracture is the good types of contracture making graft more elastic

Secondary contracture involve the contracture of the healed graft due to myofibroblast activity and it is more in the split thickness grafts. Secondary contracture is bad making the graft more prone to hypertrophic scarring

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Survival of skin graft

Survival of skin graft depends on the ability of the graft to receive nutrients through revascularization. Revascularization of skin graft occurs in three phases:

Serum imbibition phase which last for the first 24 hours after grafting. when graft placed into the recipient bed binding the graft to the bed, absorption of nutrients into the graft occurs by capillary action from the recipient bed

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Survival of skin graft

Inosculation phase for the second 24 hours after grafting. In which vascular network is established between the cut vessels on the underside of the skin graft and the capillary beds in the wound bed

Revascularization phase: in the third 24 hours after grafting. the graft is revascularized through kissing of the capillaries that are already formed in phase 2

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Graft failure causes

hematoma under graft => elevation of graft and no kissing of blood vessels

infection

inadequate immobilization => like in anterior elbow you want to put back slap to immobilize elbow for success of graft

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Graft failure causes

Misevaluation of the wound => in bed with poor blood supply or infection

Dependent position

Graft upside down => in thin graft you can't differentiate between up and down

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Mesh graft

Graft taken and made into mesh

Used in big defect and limited donor area, also used in high exudate wound, and irregular bed of graft

Bezbozhnik, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Flap

Transplantation of tissue with its blood supply

Doctor roach, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Flap uses

Covering recipient beds that have poor vascularity

Reconstructing the full thickness of the eyelids, lips, ears, nose, and cheeks

Padding body prominences like heel

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Flap uses

When it is necessary to operate through the wound at a later date to repair underlying structures

Flaps provide functional motor unit

Flaps used in controlling infection to increase blood supply

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Flaps types according to location taken from

Local flaps from same site as the defect, and there are many types of them

advancement flaps => moved forward

rotational flaps => rotated circularly

Transpositional flap

Regional flaps from same region as the defect like in arm or hand

Distant flaps is from another region

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Taylornate, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Flaps types according to pattern of blood supply

Flaps are classified according to blood supply into axial flaps and random flaps:

Random flap: random blood supply

Axial flap: there is a well named artery in the pedicle of the flap

island flap

Peninsular flap

free flap

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Types of flap according to content

Skin

Muscle

Omentum

Fascial

Chondral

Periosteal

Mixed

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Flap causes of failure

Intrinsic factors

Inadequate blood supply

Arteriovenous shunts

Extrinsic factors

Infection

Hypotension

Compression

Hematoma

Smoking

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Monitoring viability of the flap

Monitor by clinical tests, chemical and instrumental methods

Clinical tests

Color and temperature of the flap and area around it

Capillary refiling

Dermal bleeding

Atropine absorption

Histamine test

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Monitoring viability of the flap

Chemical method: fluorescein dye injection

Instrumental

Doppler US

Photoplethysmography

Tissue PH, PO2, PCO2

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Hypertrophic Scar vs Keloid

Htirgan, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

User:Cgomez447, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

Both of these scars form due to excess collagen deposition during wound healing

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Hypertrophic scar

Raised scar that don’t grow beyond the boundaries of the original wound

Maybe associated with itchiness and pain

Develops due to trauma, wounds …

Kauczuk, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Hypertrophic scar

Hypertrophic scar ranges in color from red to brown

Develop 4 weeks after injury and continues to thicken for up to six months

Often regresses in one or two years

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Hypertrophic scar

Tension and flexor areas and restrict movement if they are located near a joint

Treatment using cryosurgery and silicon sheeting maybe helpful

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Keloid scar

Firm, rubbery lesions or shiny, fibrous nodules that can be sometimes itchy and painful

Form because of injury or a wound and usually after 3 months to years of the initial insult, but sometimes arise spontaneously

Autosomal dominant predisposition

Htirgan, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Keloid scar

They Extend beyond original wound

Color vary from pink to dark brown

Rarely regress spontaneously

Keloid scar is benign
