SOURCE SLIDE 1

Infectious Mononucleosis

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Ed Uthman, MD., CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

it is called infectious mononucleosis because infectious means the disease can spread to other people, mononucleosis because there is increase in mononuclear cells count (reactive lymphocytes

It is also called glandular fever and kissing disease

Glandular because it is associated with swollen lymph nodes

Kissing because it spread through saliva

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Overview

It is primarily spread through saliva but can rarely be spread through semen or blood. Incubation period is about 4 weeks and infected people spread the disease during this period before symptoms develop

IM not highly contagious thus isolation of cases is not necessary

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Presentation

Fever which resolves after 2 weeks

Pharyngitis: with tonsillar exudates

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Presentation

lymphadenopathy: non tender cervical anterior and posterior, inguinal and axillary lymphadenopathy

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Presentation

Splenomegaly

Palatal petechiae

Periorbital edema

Fatigue

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Presentation

Death is rare but can occur due to respiratory obstruction, hemorrhage from splenic rupture, thrombopenia and encephalitis

In children under 10 years disease is mild, in adults over 30 disease is severe and prlonoged

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Causes

Epstein Barr virus: about 90% of cases of IM are caused by that

Cytomegalovirus: 5-7% of cases

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Pathophysiology

Virus replicates in epithelial cells in the pharynx leading to pharyngitis

Virus infect B cells through CD21 => the body respond to this by activating the cytotoxic T cells which attack the infected B cells resulting in enlarged atypical lymphocytes (downey cells)

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Diagnosis

Medical history: Highest risk in ages 10-30, close contact with other infected people, fever and sore throat

Physical examination by lymph node examination looking for enlargement , and abdominal examination looking for enlarged spleen

Heterophile antibody test (AKA mononuclear spot test is positive in IM

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Differential diagnosis

Acute cytomegalovirus infection and toxoplasmosis present with similar symptoms as IM but differentiated using Heterophile antibody test which will be negative in both of these conditions and positive in IM

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Treatment

Self limiting

Symptomatic treatment

Avoid contact sports and weight training to decrease the risk of splenic rupture (because some cases of IM there would be splenic enlargement)

If pharyngeal edema is severe, short course of glucocorticoids is indicated

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Almost all people given amoxicillin or ampicillin antibiotic eventually develop generalized, itchy maculopapular rash because of the immune response triggered by the interaction of the antibiotic with the virus

So avoid these antibiotics

Sgamer1770, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

RainbowKatie, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Complications

Splenic rupture

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

Lymphoma

A lot more, but rare

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Portal hypertension

Schistosomiasis in a child (Philippines), CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Contents

Overview

Pathophysiology

Causes

Clinical features

Diagnosis

Treatment

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Overview

Portal hypertension is increased pressure within the portal venous system

Pressure difference of 6 mmHg or more between the portal vein and the inferior vena cava confirms portal hypertension diagnosis

Liver cirrhosis is the most common cause for portal hypertension

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Pathophysiology

Portal vein collects blood from bowel and go through the liver and into the hepatic vein and then to inferior vena cava

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathophysiology

Portal hypertension develops when the resistance to the portal blood flow increases leading to increase the pressure difference between portal and inferior vena cava

Resistance could be in the liver in form of cirrhosis, or it could be prehepatic in the portal vein in form of portal vein thrombosis, or it could be post hepatic like Budd Chiari syndrome (occlusion of the hepatic vein)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

When the portal blood pressure remains elevated, body tries to decrease this pressure by opening the collateral vessels that bypass the liver’s normal circulation (thus bypassing the resistance), examples of the collaterals include:

Esophageal varices

Gastric varices

Rectal varices

Periumbilical veins (caput medusa)

Splenic collaterals

Retroperitoneal collaterals

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Causes

Prehepatic: portal vein thrombosis, arteriovenous malformations or fistulas involving the portal vein

Intrahepatic: congenital hepatic fibrosis, schistosomiasis, liver cirrhosis, veno-occlusive disease

Post hepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome, inferior vena cava obstruction, constrictive pericarditis

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Clinical features

No symptoms until complications arise

Cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal hypertension and when patient have it, they present with jaundice, palmar erythema, spider nevi, gynecomastia, ascites, asterixis and hepatic encephalopathy

Patient might present with hematemesis or melena from bleeding varices

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Clinical features

Splenomegaly is reliable sign in the diagnosis of portal hypertension, if no splenomegaly think of other differential diagnosis

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Diagnosis

CBC to look for anemia from bleeding, thrombocytopenia from bleeding or liver failure

LFT, RFT looking for liver or renal failure

Coagulation profile to look for deficiencies in the coagulation factors from liver failure

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Diagnosis

Doppler US of the portal vein looking for stenosis or thrombosis

Abdominal US looking for liver cirrhosis, ascites and splenomegaly

Endoscopy looking for varices

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

Patient with ascites need paracentesis to look for the cause

Measurement of portal pressure often not required to make the diagnosis because the clinical features are enough

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Treat the cause: e.g. portal vein thrombosis treated with anticoagulation, liver cirrhosis treated with liver transplantation

Treat the complications: e.g. hematemesis treated with supportive measures (blood transfusions…) and endoscopic therapy

Empiric antibiotics for prophylaxis against SBP

Ascites treated with sodium restriction, diuretics and paracentesis

SOURCE SLIDE 14

SOURCE SLIDE 1

CURB-65 score

unsplash, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

CURB65 is a score used to evaluate the severity of pneumonia and help you to decide if you hospitalize the patient or not

Developed by the British thoracic society in 2002

SOURCE SLIDE 3

CURB-65

C: confusion, if pt confused gets one point

U: Blood Urea nitrogen greater than 19 mg/dL, gets one point

R: Respiratory rate of 30 or more gets one point

SOURCE SLIDE 4

CURB-65

B: Blood pressure: if systolic less than 90 or diastolic less than 60, patient gets one point

65: Age higher than 65 gets one point

You add all the points together and you get the score, If the score is equal or higher than 2 then hospitalize your patient

SOURCE SLIDE 5

If your pneumonia patient is hypoxemic (SpO2 < 92%) then please hospitalize without even considering the criteria

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Risk of death from pneumonia

Risk of death increase as the score increases

Score 0 = 0.7% risk of death

Score 1 = 3.2%

Score 2 = 13%

Score 3 = 17%

Score 4 = 41.5%

Score 5 = 57%

Primary Healing

Secondary Healing

vs

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Primary wound healing

Also called healing by primary intention

The wound edges are brought together closely and held in place using sutures

This method used for clean wounds and wounds with minimal tissue loss

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Primary wound healing

Wound looks good with minimal scar formed in this method

Take about 10 days to heal depending on the body part affected

Examples are surgical wounds

Nicola Davies (uploaded by Zureks), CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Secondary healing

Also called healing by secondary intension

Used for large wounds (cannot be sutured), wounds with a lot of tissue loss, contaminated wounds

Wound left open without surgical closure, granulation tissue (consists of blood vessels and connective tissue) forms and fill up the wound with time and fibrous tissue forms finally

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Secondary healing

Extensive scarring and ugly wound

Takes weeks to heal

Examples are injuries with a lot of contamination, injuries with a lot of tissue loss

Arria Belli, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Delayed primary closure

This method is done for contaminated wounds and wound with excessive tissue lost to heal by the primary healing method

You clean and debride the wound and you wait two days and then re debridement and cleaning again of the wound and primary tissue closure is done or skin grafting if there is a lot of tissue lost

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Primary healing Secondary healing
Small, clean wound with minimal tissue loss Larger, irregular edges, significant tissue loss
Minimal contamination Contaminated or infected
Heals in few weeks Heals in weeks to months
Minimal granulation tissue Granulation tissue fills the wound from bottom up
Minimal scarring, thin scar More noticeable, raised thick scar

SOURCE SLIDE 1

SIADH vs DI

William-Adolphe Bouguereau, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Phee, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Overview

SIADH and DI are both disorders affecting the ADH secretion

ADH hormone secreted from pituitary gland and work on the V2 receptor in the collecting duct to absorb more water from the duct into the circulation

SIADH is excessive release of ADH from the pituitary or other sources (such as tumors), this leads to more water being absorbed thus leading to dilutional hyponatremia

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Overview

Diabetes insipidus is deficiency or inadequacy of ADH secretion leading to decrease water absorption from collecting duct, thus leading to polyuria and polydipsia

DI on two types: nephrogenic (the V2 receptors doesn’t work), or central (the pituitary doesn’t secrete ADH)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Overview

Syndrome of inappropriate ADH: the inappropriate in SIADH, make students confused, thinking it could be increase or decrease in the secretion of the hormone, but in reality it is increase but it is variable increase that is why it is called inappropriate

Diabetes insipidus is a different disease than the diabetes mellitus, it is called diabetes because it shares some symptoms with the DM like polyuria and polydipsia, but otherwise it is quite different

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Next, The Key Differences Between the Two Conditions Will Be Explained:

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Causes

SIADH caused by:

Tumors secreting ADH such as lung cancer

Head injuries

Medications

Any disease affecting pituitary gland or hypothalamus

DI caused by:

Central caused by head trauma, tumors affecting pituitary or hypothalamus

Nephrogenic could be genetic or acquired due to kidney disorders or medications

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Presentation

SIADH present with nausea, vomiting, malaise, headache, lethargy and seizures from the cerebral edema caused by hyponatremia

Diabetes insipidus present with polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration and seizures

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Urine output

SIADH: urine output reduced and urine is concentrated because body is absorbing more water from the urine

DI: urine output is increased and urine is diluted because body losing more water

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Thirst

In SIADH, patients doesn’t feel thirsty as much as normal because they are retaining water

In DI, patients feel extremely thirsty and drink a lot of water because they are losing water

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Serum sodium levels

SIADH lead to dilutional hyponatremia (low sodium because of the excessive water in circulation)

DI: normal or high sodium levels

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Treatment

SIADH: treat the cause and restrict fluid intake to prevent further load on circulation

DI: treat according to the type and cause, and increase fluid intake

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Burkitt lymphoma

Facts

Classification

Pathophysiology

Microscopy

Immunohistochemistry

Treatment

Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Facts

It is one subtype of non Hodgkin's lymphomas, it affects the B cells

Named after Denis Burkitt, the Irish surgeon who first described it in 1958

Most common in developing countries and affect children

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

There are three variants of the disease:

Endemic variant

Sporadic variant

Immunodeficiency associated variant

SOURCE SLIDE 4

1. Endemic variant

Endemic variant almost always associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection

EPV causes infectious mononucleosis

Endemic variant expresses CD21 (also the same receptor affected by Epstein Barr virus, the virus gains entry to B cells through this receptor)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

1. Endemic variant

Endemic variant common in regions where malaria is endemic such as Africa and new guinea

Affects children 4-7 years , male to female ratio 2:1

Presents mostly with facial, mandibular masses, it also presents with abdominal masses or masses affecting nervous system

Mike Blyth, CC BY-SA 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

2. Sporadic variant

Common in America and Europe

Sporadic form also occur in children most of the times, male to female ratio is 4:1

Sporadic form mostly presents with abdominal masses in ileocecum and peritoneum, it also affects the bone marrow and nervous system

SOURCE SLIDE 7

3. Immunodeficiency associated variant

Associated with HIV infection, post transplant patients

Presents in adults 40-45 years, male to female ratio is 1:1

Affects GI tract, lymph nodes, bone marrow and nervous system

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Pathophysiology

Dysregulation of c-myc gene by some type of chromosomal translocation

C-myc is cell growth promotor

Translocation lead to overexpression of the gene

This lead to uncontrolled cell growth and tumor growth

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Microscopy

Tumor consist of cells that are similar in size and morphology with high proliferative and apoptotic activity

There is also scattered tangible body laden macrophages (containing apoptotic tumor cells) gives the tumor starry sky appearance on low power microscopy

Louis M. Staudt, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Immunohistochemistry

Express marker of B cells

CD19, CD20, CD22

Also expresses CD10 and BCL6

mantle cell and diffuse large b cell lymphomas also express CD19, CD20

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Treatment

Chemotherapy

GMALL-B-ALL/NHL2002 protocol,

the modified Magrath regimen (R-CODOX-M/IVAC)

COPADM

hyper-CVAD

Tumor lysis syndrome could occur in these patients due to fast response the chemotherapy

SOURCE SLIDE 12

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Spinal Cord Injury Classification According to ASIA

Sheldahl, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

DocSumomo, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Spinal cord injury classification

ASIA classification of spinal cord injury is the gold standard nowadays to classify these injuries

To classify spinal cord injury according to American spinal injury association, neurological examination has to be done looking for sensory or motor deficits

Motor examination is done using muscle power of the key muscles only looking for any motor deficits

Sensory examination is done using superficial modality (pinprick) and deep modality (touch) only looking for any deficits

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Key muscles

Table from slide 3
C5Elbow flexors
C6Wrist extensors
C7 Elbow extensors
C8 Finger flexors
T1 5th finger abductors
L2 Hip flexors
L3Knee extensors
L4 Ankle dorsiflexors
L5Big toe extensors
S1Ankle plantar flexors
SOURCE SLIDE 4

Neurological examination

Muscle power is graded out of 5 according to the MRC grading

0/5: no muscle movement

1/5: visible muscle movement but with no movement at the joint

2/5: movement at the joint but not against gravity

3/5: movement against gravity, but not against added resistance

4/5: movement against resistance, but less than normal

5/5: normal power

Sensory is graded out of 2 according to

0: absent sensation

1: altered

2: normal

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Classify by following these steps

Determine the sensory levels for right and left sides (each side graded independently), intact dermatome must be responding to pinprick and light touch sensation

Determine the motor levels for right and left sides (each side graded independently), motor level defined by the lowest key muscle (on the body) with grade 3 power and the muscles above this muscle are grade 5 power

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Classify by following these steps

Determine the neurological level of injury: NLI refers to the lowest segment with intact sensation and motor function (grade 3 muscle power), NLI is the lower level of the sensory and motor levels assigned in step 1 and 2

Determine if the injury is complete or incomplete: if patient can’t voluntarily contract anal sphincter and sensory exam of S4, S5 is 0 and deep anal pressure is negative then injury is complete, otherwise injury is incomplete

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Classify by following these steps

Now you can determine the injury grade according to ASIA impairment scale

SOURCE SLIDE 8

ASIA impairment scale (AIS)

Table from slide 8
Grade Description
A Complete: no sensory or motor at S4-5
BSensory incomplete: sensory is preserved below neurological level of injury including sensation at S4-5, but motor function is preserved only to three levels below the motor level on either side of the body
C Motor incomplete: motor is preserved at the S4-5 or the patient sensory is preserved at S4-5 with preservation of more than 3 motor levels below the level of injury (less than half key muscles below level of injury have muscle power equals to 3 or more)
D Motor incomplete: same as AIS C with more than half of the key muscles below level of injury have muscle power grade of 3 or more
ENormal

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Serum Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG)

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Subhaschandra Singh, Y. Sobita Devi, Shweta Bhalothia and Dr. Veeraraghavan Gunasekaran, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

SAAG

It is one of the investigations used to evaluate newly diagnosed or worsening ascites

It is used to distinguish the causes of ascites whether it is caused by portal hypertension or malignancy or other causes

Sample of the ascitic fluid is taken via paracentesis

Cancer Research UK, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

SAAG

And then the sample taken to laboratory to calculate albumin level and also sample of patient blood also taken for albumin level calculation

Then SAAG = serum albumin – ascites albumin

SOURCE SLIDE 4

SAAG

If SAAG > 1.1 g/dL

Means the albumin level in blood is much higher than the ascitic fluid

This means that the ascitic fluid is forming due to high pressure driving the fluid into the peritoneum (from the vessels into peritoneum)

This high pressure is caused by portal hypertension

Portal hypertension is caused by: liver cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd Chiari syndrome …

SOURCE SLIDE 5

SAAG

If SAAG < 1.1 g/dL

Means the albumin level in blood is little higher than the ascitic fluid

Here the problem is in the vessels, they are leaking the albumin and the fluid into the peritoneum

Causes: malignancy, infections, pancreatitis …

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Total ascitic protein

Total protein of the ascitic fluid is used with the SAAG to identify the cause of ascites

Same ascites sample taken for SAAG is used to calculate total protein

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Total ascitic protein

If total ascitic protein < 2.5 g/dL

Total ascitic protein is low

Mostly due to portal hypertension, other causes include nephrotic syndrome and tuberculosis peritonitis

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Total ascitic protein

If total ascitic protein > 2.5 g/dL

Total ascitic protein is high

Causes include: heart failure, malignancy

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Slide 9

Table from slide 9
SAAG
< 1.1 g/dL > 1.1 g/dL
Total protein < 2.5 g/dL Nephrotic syndrome Liver cirrhosis, Budd Chiari syndrome
> 2.5 g/dL Cancer, pancreatitis, infection Heart failure, veno occlusive disease

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Compartment syndrome

U.S. Navy photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Official Navy Page from United States of AmericaMC3 (AW) William Pittman/U.S. Navy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Contents

Definition

Pathophysiology

Causes

Clinical features

Treatment

Leg fasciotomy

Matt Writtle, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Definition

Compartment syndrome is muscle swelling within a fascial compartment resulting in increase intracompartmental pressure and tissue hypoperfusion

Muscle swell because of damage caused by trauma which lead to inflammation process

Mellowchillgpt, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Definition

If left untreated, ischemia and tissue necrosis occur and debridement procedures has to be done and limb amputation maybe needed

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pathophysiology

Muscle and soft tissue damage in arm or leg after trauma give rise to edema or inflammation => this will increase the pressure within one of the fascial compartments => reduced capillary flow => muscle ischemia => further edema => more pressure => more ischemia => after 6 hours necrosis of nerve and muscles within the compartment starts

Nerve capable of regeneration but muscle once infarcted is replaced by fibrous tissue

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Causes

Fractures

Blunt injuries

Burns

Hemorrhage into compartment, esp. patients taking anticoagulants

Reperfusion injury following a period of limb ischemia

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Causes

Emergency casting of a fracture using a tight cast

SOURCE SLIDE 8

High risk injuries

Fractures of the elbow

Forearm

Proximal third of the tibia

Multiple fractures of the hand or foot

Crush injuries

Circumferential burns

Operations (esp. internal fixation)

Infection

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Clinical features

Classic clinical features are the five Ps:

Pain

Pallor

Paresthesia

Paralysis

Pulselessness

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Clinical features

The earliest feature is severe pain and it maybe the only feature available, patient feel tightness of their limb and it is about to burst

The ischemia mostly occur in capillary level, so pulses may still be felt and the skin is not pale => not reliable for diagnosis

Paralysis (motor dysfunction) and paresthesia (sensory dysfunction) may occur and should be repeatedly checked => not reliable for diagnosis

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Clinical features

Pain on passive stretching of the muscles within the affected compartment because Ischemic muscle is highly sensitive to stretch, e.g. active extension of the toes lead to increased pain in the calf

Diagnoses is supported by measuring the intercompartment pressure, split pressure catheter is inserted into the compartment and pressure is measured close to the level of the fracture, differential pressure is the difference between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure, if less than 30 mmHg is indication for immediate compartment decompression

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Clinical features

The diagnosis is mainly clinical, pressure calculation is supportive, immediate open fasciotomy is done if there is high clinical suspicion even if the pressure difference more than 30 mmHg

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Treatment

Compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency

The threatened compartment should be decompressed

Casts, bandages and dressings must be removed

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Treatment

The limb should be flat (not elevated) , because elevation decrease blood reaching it thus aggravating muscle ischemia

Monitor differential compartment pressure through pressure catheter, if it falls below 30 mmHg then immediate open fasciotomy is performed

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Treatment

if the differential compartment pressure still higher than 30 and there is strong clinical indicator for compartment syndrome (severe pain, paralysis, paresthesia…), the limb should be examined every 30 minutes interval and if there is no improvement in the clinical signs for 2 hours then open fasciotomy should be done too

Sometimes pressure catheter not available, (most developing countries hospitals don’t have it), so diagnosis is even harder

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Treatment

Muscle die after about 6 hours, so you need to take action quickly

After fasciotomy, the wound should be left open and inspected 2 days later, if there is tissue necrosis then debridement is done and wounds sutured, if the tissues are healthy then sutured directly

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Fasciotomy of the leg

Fasciotomy is procedure by which you open the fascia that covers a group of muscles together (compartment) to relieve pressure

The leg is the most common area affected by compartment syndrome

Leg contains four compartments and all has to be opened to relieve the pressure

Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Fasciotomy of the leg

General anesthesia is used

Here will explain the double incision fasciotomy of the leg, there is another method using single incision fasciotomy of the leg and also there is decompression methods for the forearm, hand, foot …

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Fasciotomy of the leg

Posteromedial incision

The posterior superficial and deep compartments are accessed through medial longitudinal incision 3 cm behind the posterior border of the tibia

Avoid injuring saphenous vein and nerve by taking a slow dissecting approach

Make incisions along the length of the posterior superficial and deep compartments to release them

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Fasciotomy of the leg

Anterolateral incision

Anterior and lateral compartments are accessed through lateral incision placed halfway between the tibial crest and the line of the fibula

Avoid injuring the superficial peroneal nerve which has a variable course through the leg by using slow dissecting approach

The anterior and lateral compartments are released by opening the fascia and intermuscular septum

WascAsz4NLw.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Closed soft tissue injuries

Contusion

Hematoma

Swelling

Blister

Tenting

Degloving

SOURCE SLIDE 2

It is important to know the types of soft tissue injuries

To assess the severity of the injury sustained by the patient since every injury type is due to different severity of trauma

Gives an idea about the management

Knowing the types of injuries help you communicate your findings with your team members and seniors

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Contusions and hematomas

The most common closed soft tissue injuries you will see in your practice

Mechanism:

Fracture causes internal bleeding (at fracture site and in the skin) which gradually tracks to the skin and result in a bruise called contusion (contusion is the medical term for a bruise)

If blood collects at some place during this process , this blood collection is called hematoma

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Contusions and hematomas

Pattern of contusion gives you an idea about the fracture location and the severity of soft tissue injury associated with it (e.g. calcaneal fracture result in contusion on sole of the foot)

Contusion takes several hours to appear after injury (so you may not see it at time of presentation to emergency department) and take several days to reach its full extent

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Contusions and hematomas

Contusion stages:

Early stage: it start as reddish or purplish discoloration in the first 2 days with tenderness

Subacute stage: then turn to bluish or greenish color in the 5 days after as the body start to break down the blood

Healing stage: then transitions to yellowish or brownish as the body reabsorbs the broken down blood in the second week , and the size of the contusion decrease

Resolution stage: the bruise continue to fade and eventually disappears completely in the third week

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Contusions and hematomas

Now regarding hematomas, hematoma appears as a lump on the injured site

deep hematoma result in local swelling and tenderness, superficial hematoma may compromise skin viability (lead to skin necrosis) especially in skin areas that are thin and overlying a bone like pretibial region

Treatment: focus on treatment the fracture and the contusion or hematoma resolve by itself, if big hematoma then it might need to be drained or aspirated

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Jean van Kasteel, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Afrodriguezg, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Swelling

inflammatory response to the injury which causes local increase in vascular permeability => swelling of the tissue with increase temperature

Swollen area has reduction in capillary circulation and reduced capacity to heal

Operating on swollen skin will have higher risk of wound dehiscence

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Swelling

Treatment of swelling is with RICE: rest, ice (cooling), compression, elevation

When swelling resolves, skin takes on wrinkled appearance and regains elasticity and that is when surgery is safely performed

SOURCE SLIDE 12

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Blisters

Blisters are formed due to rapid development of swelling in some area over the body

Mechanism: The swelling cause an injury between the epidermis and dermis which lead those two layers to displace from each other and the space fills with serous fluid which is termed “clear fracture blister”, but if the underlying capillaries in the dermis are also injuries, the blister will fill with blood and termed “hemorrhagic blister”

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Blisters

Blisters are more famous in burned patients specifically second degree burns

Blisters resolve in two weeks after the injury

Treatment: Best if left undisturbed if possible, blister fluid is sterile but if deroofed then it get colonized with bacteria

If a surgical incision was done through a blister, then it takes longer for the skin to heal and carries higher risk of infection

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Cindy L. Budge, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

WillSmithPhoto, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Tenting

Skin pulled tightly over a prominent bone end, angulated fracture make prominent bone end that pulls the skin with it

Looks like a tent over the fracture area

Tented skin has impaired circulation with risk of necrosis and breakdown , this convert closed fracture to open fracture and increase chance of infection

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Tenting

Skin tenting is indication of urgent reduction of the fracture or the dislocation and maybe an indication of urgent surgery

Google: skin tenting injury

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Degloving

Mechanism: Result from significant shear forces causing separation of sub cut tissue from underlying fascial or osseous structures with collection of fat, blood and necrotic tissue

They most commonly affect the legs and are frequently associated with underlying fractures.

Common cause: soft tissue of a limb are crushed by wheels of a vehicle

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Degloving

Normal vascular supply arise directly from its underlying deep fascia, a degloving injury impairs the blood supply => skin necrosis after a while with infection and sepsis

It is unwise to make incisions through degloved skin because rate of wound dehiscence and infection are extremely high

Degloved skin is cool and can’t detect sensory input

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Degloving

Treatment: surgical exploration and excision of all non bleeding skin and fat and grafting or flapping the injuries after that

Google: degloving skin injuries

outline.heading: It is important to  know the types of soft tissue injuries
outline.summary: To assess the severity of the injury sustained by the patient since every injury type is due to different severity of trauma Gives an idea about the management Knowing the types of injuries help you communicate your findings with your team members and seniors

outline.heading: Contusions and hematomas
outline.summary: The most common closed soft tissue injuries you will see in your practice Mechanism: Fracture causes internal bleeding (at fracture site and in the skin) which gradually tracks to the skin and result in a bruise called contusion (contusion is the medical term for a bruise) If blood collects at some place during this process , this blood collection is called hematoma

outline.heading: Contusions and hematomas
outline.summary: Pattern of contusion gives you an idea about the fracture location and the severity of soft tissue injury associated with it (e.g. calcaneal fracture result in contusion on sole of the foot) Contusion takes several hours to appear after injury (so you may not see it at time of presentation to emergency department) and take several days to reach its full extent

outline.heading: Contusions and hematomas
outline.summary: Contusion stages: Early stage: it start as reddish or purplish discoloration in the first 2 days with tenderness Subacute stage: then turn to bluish or greenish color in the 5 days after as the body start to break down the blood Healing stage: then transitions to yellowish or brownish as the body reabsorbs the broken down blood in the second week , and the size of the contusion decrease Resolution stage: the bruise continue to fade and eventually disappears completely in the third week

outline.heading: Contusions and hematomas
outline.summary: Now regarding hematomas, hematoma appears as a lump on the injured site deep hematoma result in local swelling and tenderness, superficial hematoma may compromise skin viability (lead to skin necrosis)  especially in skin areas that are thin and overlying a bone like pretibial region Treatment: focus on treatment the fracture and the contusion or hematoma resolve by itself, if big hematoma then it might need to be drained or aspirated

Celecoxib

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Trade name

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Pill shape and colors

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of Action

Celecoxib is highly selective COX-2 inhibitor from the NSAIDs group.

COX-2 is expressed during inflammation and it is responsible for the pain and fever that comes with it

COX-1 is expressed normally and it has a lot of functions like the secretion of mucus that protect the stomach and the PG- mediated autoregulation of the renal system

Non selective NSAIDs inhibit both of them (COX-1 and COX-2) and that lead to side effects on the stomach and kidneys and other organs so that made the idea of creating a selective COX-2 NSAID comes and upon this Celecoxib was made

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Mechanism of Action

In practice there was fewer side effects regarding the GIT and renal systems but there was increase in cardiovascular events like myocardial infarctions and strokes which didn’t happen with the non selective NSAIDs

BUT why there was increase in the Cardiovascular events?

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Indications

Osteoarthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis

Juvenile Rheumatoid arthritis

Ankylosing spondylitis

Acute pain

Primary dysmenorrhea

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Cardiovascular thrombotic events

Gastrointestinal side effects

Hepatotoxicity

New onset or worsening of existing hypertension

Heart failure and edema

Renal toxicity

hyperkalemia

Anaphylactic reactions

Hematological toxicity

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Rockwood classification for AC joint injuries

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

6 grades classification system for acromioclavicular joint injuries

A modification for Allman and Tossy’s 3 grade system, the first and second grades are same in both models, while grade three in Allman and Tossy classification is subdivided into four grades in Rockwood classification

Rockwood classification takes into account

Acromioclavicular joint

Coracoclavicular ligament

Deltoid muscle

Trapezius muscle

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Normal Anatomy

The line between the inferior aspect of the clavicle and the inferior aspect of the acromion should be straight

It is okay if the superior aspect don’t match up

The joint space should be uniform

Normal Coracoclavicular distance is between 11- 13mm and there should be no greater than 5mm difference between right and left

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Grade 1

X ray: normal, the clavicle not elevated in respect to acromion

Acromioclavicular ligament: Incomplete injury

Coracoclavicular ligament: no injury

Joint capsule: no injury

Trapezius muscle: attached

Deltoid muscle: attached

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Grade 2

Clavicle elevated but not above superior border of acromion

Acromioclavicular ligament: complete injury

Coracoclavicular ligament: Incomplete injury

Joint capsule: complete injury

Trapezius muscle: minimal disruption of attachment

Deltoid muscle: minimal disruption of attachment

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 8

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Grade 3

Clavicle elevated above the superior border of acromion, the coracoclavicular distance is less than 25mm

Acromioclavicular ligament: complete injury

Coracoclavicular ligament: complete injury

Joint capsule: complete injury

Trapezius muscle: complete disruption of attachment

Deltoid muscle: complete disruption of attachment

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 10

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Grade 4

Result from posteriorly directed forces that make the clavicle penetrates the trapezius muscle, sometimes completely.

Acromioclavicular ligament: completely injured

Coracoclavicular ligament: completely injured

Joint capsule: completely injured

Trapezius muscle: complete disruption of attachment

Deltoid muscle: complete disruption of attachment

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 12

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Grade 5

Clavicle is markedly elevated and coracoclavicular distance is more than 25mm

Acromioclavicular ligament: completely injured

Coracoclavicular ligament: completely injured

Joint capsule: completely injured

Trapezius muscle: complete disruption of attachment

Deltoid muscle: complete disruption of attachment

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 14

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Grade 6

Inferior displacement of clavicle into the acromion or coracoid process.

Acromioclavicular ligament: completely injured

Coracoclavicular ligament: completely injured

Joint capsule: completely injured

Trapezius muscle: complete disruption of attachment

Deltoid muscle: complete disruption of attachment

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 16

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Airway foreign body

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Foreign body aspiration

Airway Foreign Body is when a foreign body (food or objects) enter the airway and either sit in the larynx or beyond in the trachea or bronchi

Airway foreign body is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among children especially older infants and toddlers (60% of all airway foreign body cases)

Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Epidemiology

Males are 1.7 more likely affected than females

In infants younger than 6 months, the cause is usually secondary to feeding by a well meaning sibling

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Epidemiology

Most common aspirated FB are food items (70%): ex. Nuts, seeds, bread and meat, hard candy, gum, bones, raw fruits and vegetables; common inorganic objects aspirated (30%): coins, latex balloons, pins, jewelry, magnets, pen caps, and toys

Globular, compressible or round objects such as grapes, meat and bread, grapes, nuts, balloons, marshmallows and candies can block the airway completely, so they are very dangerous

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Epidemiology

Unlike inorganic objects, aspirated vegetable commonly causes intense pneumonitis and subsequent pneumonia and suppurative bronchitis.

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pathophysiology

Young children are more at risk to aspirate a FB because they often use their mouths to explore their surroundings and they are generally more likely to be distracted, playing or ambulatory while eating

Young children are more vulnerable to chocking because they have smaller airway diameter than adults

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Clinical features

Clinical features are variable depending on the type, duration, and location of the FB

It ranges from asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress

The most serious complication is complete airway obstruction which manifest in the conscious child as sudden respiratory distress followed by inability to speak or cough

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Clinical features

FB Aspiration result in symptoms divided into three stages:

Initial event: paroxysms of coughing, choking, gagging and maybe airway obstruction occur immediately after aspiration of FB, sometimes the child expel the FB during this stage

Asymptomatic interval: the FB becomes lodged, reflexes are fatigued, and immediate symptoms subsides. Lack of symptoms in this stage is deceiving and lead to delayed and missed diagnosis

Complications: airway obstruction, erosions, pneumonia and atelectasis develop which will manifest as fever, cough, hemoptysis …

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Clinical features

A FB aspiration should be suspected if there is a history of sudden onset of coughing or choking and should be considered in all children with unilateral wheezing.

At presentation, many patients are in the asymptomatic interval

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Classifications

Laryngotracheal FB: patient present with stridor and hoarseness with a FB in the laryngotracheal area

Bronchial FB: patient present with unilateral wheezing and decreased breath sounds with a bronchial FB.

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Classifications

Wheeze may be present in 30% of laryngotracheal FB aspirations and stridor in up to 10% of bronchial aspirations.

80% of FBs are in the bronchi.

Patients with immediate onset of severe stridor and cardiac arrest usually have laryngotracheal aspirations.

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Diagnosis

Bronchoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and removal of the foreign body

History is the most important factor in determining the need for bronchoscopy, a positive history must never be ignored but a negative history can be misleading because FB aspiration can be missed and confused with more common causes of respiratory diseases because patients may have fever, wheezing, or rales

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Diagnosis

Child caregivers should be asked about nuts and seeds because they are the most common airway FBs

Examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx and lung sounds in important

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Diagnosis

Radiology also important, plain x rays are the first line, inspiratory PA chest is ordered first, expiratory or lateral decubitus films can assist in diagnosis

90% of FBs are radiolucent and not seen on x rays but secondary findings such as air trapping, asymmetric hyperinflation, obstructive emphysema, atelectasis, mediastinal shift and consolidation all important in identifying location of the FB

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Diagnosis

CT scan has no role in Airway foreign body due to radiation risk in pediatric population although it is highly sensitive and specific and able to detect radiolucent object

So if there is high index of suspicion despite negative or inconclusive imaging, bronchoscopy should be done

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Upper esophageal FBs

Upper esophageal FBs are usually radiopaque and can impinge on the posterior aspect of the trachea.

Patients may present with stridor, and typically have dysphagia.

Radiographically, flat FBs such as coins are usually oriented in the sagittal plane when located in the trachea and in the coronal plane when in the esophagus.

Samir, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Treatment

If FB aspiration or airway obstruction is clearly present, perform basic life support (BLS) procedures to relieve airway obstruction (back blows and abdominal thrusts)

If BLS maneuvers fail, perform direct laryngoscopy and extraction of the FB with Magill forceps. If the FB cannot be seen, orotracheal intubation with dislodgement of the FB distally may be lifesaving.

Dctrzl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Treatment

If an obstructive laryngotracheal FB cannot be removed or dislodged, an emergent surgical airway may be required.

Definitive treatment of partial airway obstruction usually requires rigid bronchoscopy in the operating room under general anesthesia by an otolaryngologist or pulmonologist

Complications of rigid bronchoscopy include bronchospasm, bleeding and airway edema

outline.summary: Bronchoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and removal of the foreign body History is the most important factor in determining the need for bronchoscopy, a positive history must never be ignored but a negative history can be misleading because FB aspiration can be missed and confused with more common causes of respiratory diseases because patients may have fever, wheezing, or rales

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Child caregivers should be asked about nuts and seeds because they are the most common airway FBs Examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx and lung sounds in important

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Radiology also important, plain x rays are the first line, inspiratory PA chest is ordered first, expiratory or lateral decubitus films can assist in diagnosis 90% of FBs are radiolucent and not seen on x rays but secondary findings such as air trapping, asymmetric hyperinflation, obstructive emphysema, atelectasis, mediastinal shift and consolidation all important in identifying location of the FB

outline.heading: Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Diagnosis
outline.summary: CT scan has no role in Airway foreign body due to radiation risk in pediatric population although it is highly sensitive and specific and able to detect radiolucent object So if there is high index of suspicion despite negative or inconclusive imaging, bronchoscopy should be done

outline.heading: Upper esophageal FBs
outline.summary: Upper esophageal FBs are usually radiopaque and can impinge on the posterior aspect of the trachea. Patients may present with stridor, and typically have dysphagia. Radiographically, flat FBs such as coins are usually oriented in the sagittal plane when located in the trachea and in the coronal plane when in the esophagus. Samir, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: If FB aspiration or airway obstruction is clearly present, perform basic life support (BLS) procedures to relieve airway obstruction (back blows and abdominal thrusts) If BLS maneuvers fail, perform direct laryngoscopy and extraction of the FB with Magill forceps. If the FB cannot be seen, orotracheal intubation with dislodgement of the FB distally may be lifesaving. Dctrzl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: If an obstructive laryngotracheal FB cannot be removed or dislodged, an emergent surgical airway may be required. Definitive treatment of partial airway obstruction usually requires rigid bronchoscopy in the operating room under general anesthesia by an otolaryngologist or pulmonologist Complications of rigid bronchoscopy include bronchospasm, bleeding and airway edema

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Scaphoid fractures

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Carpal fractures

Scaphoid fractures (75% of all carpal fractures)

Lunate

Triquetrum

Trapezium

Capitate

Hamate

BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Epidemiology

Scaphoid fractures account for 75% of all carpal fractures

Fractures of other carpal bones are all rare; they can be easily overlooked. Careful examination, X-rays inspection, especially after a significant traumatic mechanism, is important. If in still in doubt, CT or MRI are options.

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Epidemiology

A scaphoid fracture occur with a significant traumatic mechanisms, which would typically involve a sporting injury or high-energy fall. That is why it is more common in younger and active individuals.

Scaphoid fractures if missed, they can lead to morbidity as the risk of non-union can be high (14-50% if fracture is displaced)

If left untreated, arthritis, deformity and instability may develop within 5 years which leads to disability

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Scaphoid fractures MOI

Scaphoid bone lies in the line of loading between the thumb and forearm

So it can fracture in case of axial loading on the wrist in forced flexion or extension and compression; e.g. fall on the outstretched hand

Laboratories Elsevier via Wikimedia commons

Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Scaphoid fractures

Fractures occur on three anatomical locations on the scaphoid:

Distal tubercule

Waist: 65% of all scaphoid fractures

Proximal pole

Scaphoid blood supply arises from the dorsal distal pole via a branch from the radial artery and the superficial palmar arch so proximal pole gets its blood supply by retrograde flow; so it is considered to have a poor blood supply and less likely to heal than distal pole (high risk of avascular necrosis)

Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Clinical features

Symptoms

Patient present with wrist pain and they report some type of injury mechanism like falling on the outstretched hand, or getting hit by some type of object

InjuryMap, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Clinical features

Physical examination

Look

In scaphoid fractures, the wrist appearance looks deceptively normal; but if you look closely, you notice fullness in the anatomical snuffbox

An isolated scaphoid fracture will not usually cause any deformity, but deformity may be seen when associated with a dislocation of the carpus: for example, trans-scaphoid peri lunate fracture-dislocation.

Feel

There is tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox and there is pain on axial loading on the thumb, and pain on pushing the scaphoid tubercle backwards (more specific for scaphoid fractures)

SOURCE SLIDE 9

JonRichfield, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Clinical features

Physical examination

Move

In scaphoid fractures, there is limitation to wrist movements (more by pain than stiffness)

pain on passive ulnar deviation is highly specific to scaphoid fractures, conversely, lack of pain on ulnar deviation is highly indicative of absence of scaphoid fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Classification

Scaphoid fractures are classified according to the Herbert-Fischer classification (most commonly used classification)

Herbert classification is a 4 types classification system and it takes into consideration fracture stability and if it was acute/chronic

Herbert classification provides a guide to the management of scaphoid fractures

Herbert Type A and B are for acute scaphoid fractures while Type C and D for Chronic fractures

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Herbert classification

Type A: acute stable fractures

Type A1: Tuberosity fracture

Type A2: Undisplaced Waist fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Herbert classification

Type B: acute unstable fractures

Type B1: Oblique distal third fracture

Type B2: Displaced waist fracture

Type B3: Proximal third fractures

Type B4: Fracture dislocation

Type B5: Comminuted fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Herbert classification

Type C: Chronic

Type C: Delayed union

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Herbert classification

Type D: Chronic

Type D1: Fibrous non-union

Type D2: Sclerotic non-union

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Imaging

X-rays are the first line investigation modality for scaphoid fractures

Initially, four standard views are obtained:

PA with wrist in ulnar deviation (scaphoid view)

Lateral

Semi-pronated oblique

Semi-supinated oblique.

All must be carefully examined, often recent fracture only shows in the oblique views (other view are normal)

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Imaging

Look at the fracture line (transverse, or oblique)

Look at the location of the fracture line (waist, proximal pole or distal pole)

Look for displacement (translation, angulation or shortening)

If fracture line not visible, treat the clinical diagnosis and repeat x rays after 2 weeks (fracture line shows after a period of time due to bone resorption and movement)

15% of scaphoid fractures are not visible on initial x rays

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Imaging

MRI: highly sensitive for detecting scaphoid fractures and also very good in detecting soft tissue injuries such as scapholunate ligament injury; it is used initially if the x rays are normal and clinical examination highly suggest a fracture; but often not available in emergency departments

CT: This is also sensitive for detecting a fracture and is a suitable alternative to MRI. However, the risks associated with radiation must be considered and CT will not identify associated potentially significant soft tissue injuries around the carpus, such as a scapholunate ligament disruption.

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Slide 19

Mohamed Jarraya, Daichi Hayashi, Frank W. Roemer, Michel D. Crema, Luis Diaz, Jane Conlin, Monica D. Marra, Nabil Jomaah, and Ali Guermazi, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Emergency treatment

Scaphoid Fractures are managed by: reduce-hold-exercise

There is no role for closed reduction in displaced scaphoid fractures

So emergency treatment is all about holding (immobilization) of the fracture in most cases by a below elbow backslab or a wrist splint and patient is reviewed again after a week in the fracture clinic for assessment and to determine definitive treatment

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Emergency treatment

If a patient is suspected to have a fracture but the x rays are normal then patient is reviewed in the fracture clinic after 2 weeks to allow bone resorption and x rays is repeated (better fracture observation on x rays)

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type A1: tuberosity fractures

These are treated in a cast for 4-6 weeks

Non union is rare with these fractures => but if happens, it requires excision of a small fragment or grafting of larger fragment

Type A1: Tuberosity fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

These are treated either by casting or by percutanous fixation

Casting: 90% of waist fractures heal in a neutral below elbow POP cast (thumb doesn’t have to be included in the cast) for 6-8 weeks

Type A2: Undisplaced Waist fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

After that the cast is removed and wrist is examined clinically and radiologically by x rays, if wrist is painless and x rays is normal then treatment is complete; if still in doubt , CT scan is most reliable for confirming union

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

If tenderness on examination is present or fracture line still visible on x ray then cast reapplied for further 4 weeks

After 4 weeks, if wrist is painless and x ray is normal then cast is removed and treatment is complete, if tenderness is present or x rays showing signs of delayed healing (bone resporption and cavitation around the fracture) then bone grafting and internal fixation is indicated

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

Percutaneous fixation: it is considered in patients who want faster results (e.g. athletes) but impact and heavy load should still be avoided until fracture is fully healed

Percutaneous fixation is done by cannulated screws that are passed through mall incision in front of the scaphoid tubercle

SOURCE SLIDE 27

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type B fractures

Those also can be treated by casting but malunion and non union rates are higher

So it is better to reduce the fracture (closed if possible) and fix it with a compression screw => this will improve the union likelihood and reduce time of immobilization

SOURCE SLIDE 28

Herbert classification

Type B: acute unstable fractures

Type B1: Oblique distal third fracture

Type B2: Displaced waist fracture

Type B3: Proximal third fractures

Type B4: Fracture dislocation

Type B5: Comminuted fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 29

Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

This is due to either poor blood supply or displacement of these fractures;

in delayed union fracture line becomes more apparent and hard border develops (making it seem like an extra carpal bone);

in non union cavitation appears on sides of the fracture

Type C: Delayed union

SOURCE SLIDE 30

Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

In distal pole and waist fracture non union, distal fragment rotate forward and proximal fragment rotate backwards giving an appearance of a round scaphoid tubercle (ring sign) on the PA view and dorsally tilted proximal pole and lunate on lateral view (DISI)

Non union of proximal pole doesn’t lead to malalignment but it does lead to avascular necrosis

SOURCE SLIDE 31

Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

Sometimes patient is seen for the first time after an old wrist sprain; x ray shows non united fracture with sclerosed edges maybe several years old, In older patients with low demands or those asymptomatic; non union maybe left untreated if patient agrees after discussion

3-4 weeks of casting may suffice to make patient comfortable once again and no further treatment is required

SOURCE SLIDE 32

Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

In the acute stage of a scaphoid fracture, by 3 months it maybe obvious if the fracture will unite or not; surgery should be advised especially in young patients because it would reduce the chance for osteoarthritis

Surgical options include bone grafting and fixation with K wire or screws and this could be done by open or arthroscopic methods

SOURCE SLIDE 33

Complications

Nonunion

Avascular necrosis

Osteoarthritis

SOURCE SLIDE 34

Complications

Avascular necrosis

The proximal fragment in scaphoid fractures may undergo avascular necrosis especially in small proximal pole fractures which are far from the scaphoid blood supply

Although revascularization and union are theoretically possible but it is unpredictable and may take many years

SOURCE SLIDE 35

Complications

Avascular necrosis

small proximal pole fragments can be stabilized by a very small screw and if there is space, a bone graft from distal radius is inserted and healing is more possible if the graft is attached to an arterial pedicle or the fragment is grafted through arthroscope and stabilized with fine k wires

SOURCE SLIDE 36

Complications

Avascular necrosis

If this fails, the dead fragment can be excised but the wrist tends to collapse after this procedure and arthritis develops

A better option would be a proximal row carpectomy (to remove the entire proximal row of carpal bones) or a scaphoid excision and four corner fusion (remove scaphoid and fuse the capitate, hamate, triquetrum and lunate)

SOURCE SLIDE 37

SNAC (Scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse)

SNAC is an end stage condition due to vascular necrosis and often requires salvage surgery in the form of a proximal row carpectomy or a wrist fusion

SOURCE SLIDE 38

Complications

Osteoarthritis

Non union or avascular necrosis may lead to secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist

If the arthritis is localized to the distal pole, excising the radial styloid may help

SOURCE SLIDE 39

Complications

Osteoarthritis

As the arthritis progresses, changes appear in the scaphocapitate joint then in the capitate lunate joint; so stages of arthritis:

Stage 1 radioscaphoid arthritis

Stage 2 scaphocapitate arthritis

Stage 3 lunocapitate arthritis

The lunate radius joint is never affected, thus allowing salvage procedures either a proximal row carpectomy or four corner fusion

Carpal Injuries

Carpal injuries include

Simple self-limiting sprains of the joint capsule and interosseous ligaments (Dx of exclusion)

More serious unstable tears of the joint capsule and interosseous ligaments

Carpal bones fractures: scaphoid (most common), triquetrum …

Carpal dislocations: lunate and peri lunate dislocations …

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Normal anatomy: ligaments

Triangular fibrocartilage complex is a load bearing structure between the ulnar head, lunate and triquetrum , it act as a stabilizer of the ulnar side of the wrist

TFCC is composed of:

Triangular fibrocartilage disc

Extensor carpi ulnaris tendon sub sheath

Ulnotriquetral and ulnolunate ligaments

Ulnocarpal collateral ligament

Radioulnar ligament

Elatmani s, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

TFCC tear

TFCC can get injured in forced ulnar deviation in baseball players or when swinging a rachet

Risk factors for TFCC tear is positive ulnar variance (ulna is longer than radius so the articular surface of ulna is more distal than articular surface of radius) and that occur due to prior surgery or prior fracture

Iiibalesiii, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

TFCC tear

Patient present as ulnar sided wrist pain and maybe clicking or point tenderness between the pisiform and the ulnar head, ulnar deviation reproduces symptoms (TFCC compression test), applying a force across the ulna with the wrist in ulnar deviation reproduces symptoms (press test)

Injurymap, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

TFCC tear

Diagnosed by MRI and arthrography

Treatment is either conservative (rest, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections) or operative

Operative management indicated if conservative treatment failed or if there is DRUJ instability

Clinical features

Symptoms

Patient present with wrist pain and they report some type of injury mechanism like falling on the outstretched hand, or getting hit by some type of object

InjuryMap, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Clinical features

Physical examination

Look

Look for Swelling, contusions and lacerations

Deformity maybe seen (in dislocation)

Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture

Feel

Feel for tenderness over the forearm, wrist and hand

Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury, inquire about weakness, numbness, paresthesia and motor examination

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Clinical features

Physical examination

Tenderness should be carefully localized (blunt end of a pencil is useful for testing for point tenderness)

When the scapholunate ligament is injured => tenderness is present just beyond Lister’s tubercle

for lunate dislocation => in the middle of the wrist

for triquetral injuries => beyond the head of the ulna

for hamate fractures => at the base of the hypothenar eminence

for TFCC injuries => over the dorsum of the ulnocarpal joint.

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Slide 16

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Clinical features

Physical examination

Move

Movements are often limited (more by pain than by stiffness) and they may be accompanied by a palpable or an audible clunk.

If patient have a good range of active movement on their wrist joint then injury is most likely mild

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Imaging

X-rays are the first line investigation modality for carpal injuries

Initially, four standard views are obtained:

PA with wrist in ulnar deviation

Lateral

Semi-pronated oblique

Semi-supinated oblique.

An AP view with the ﬁst clenched is added when the space between the scaphoid and lunate is increased on initial x rays (scapholunate injury).

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Imaging

If the initial X-rays are ‘normal’, treat the clinical diagnosis and immobilize the wrist. 10–15% of scaphoid fractures are not visible on initial X-rays.

Early MRI is very helpful in detecting capsule, ligaments and tendon injuries and confirms fracture diagnosis but If MRI is not available, repeated X-rays are needed 2 weeks later (bone resorption and movement can make the fracture more apparent). If there is still doubt then x ray repeated after another 2 weeks

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Imaging

In the anteroposterior X-ray note the shape of the carpus, whether the individual bones are clearly outlined and whether there are any abnormally large gaps suggesting disruption of the ligaments.

The scaphoid may be fractured; or it may have lost its normal bean shape and look squat and foreshortened, sometimes with an inner circular density (the cortical ring sign) – features of an end-on view when the bone is hyperﬂexed because of damage to the restraining scapholunate ligament. The lunate is normally quadrilateral in shape but, if it is dislocated, it looks triangular.

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Slide 22

Mohamed Jarraya, Daichi Hayashi, Frank W. Roemer, Michel D. Crema, Luis Diaz, Jane Conlin, Monica D. Marra, Nabil Jomaah, and Ali Guermazi, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 23

Slide 23

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Slide 24

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Imaging

In the lateral X-ray the axes of the radius, lunate, capitate and third metacarpal are co-linear, and the scaphoid projects at an angle of about 45 degrees to this line. With traumatic instability the linked carpal segments collapse (like the buckled carriages of a derailed train). Two patterns are recognized: dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI), in which the lunate is torn from the scaphoid and tilted backwards; and volar intercalated segment instability (VISI), in which the lunate is torn from the triquetrum and turns towards the palm; the capitate shows a complementary dorsal tilt. There may be a ﬂake fracture off the back of a carpal bone (usually the triquetrum) that indicates avulsion of the dorsal radiocarpal ligament.

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Imaging

Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 27

Imaging

MRI can miss TFCC tears and interosseous ligament tears sometimes

Arthrography is used to look for these injuries

Bone scan will exclude injury if negative but it is not specific if positive

Arthroscopy is helpful in detecting scapholunate or lunotriquetral ligament injuries

SOURCE SLIDE 28

Management

‘Wrist sprain’ is a diagnosis of exclusion, when a more serious injury has been excluded with certainty, in serious injuries there is limitation to wrist movement.

Even with apparently trivial injuries, ligaments might be torn and patient may develop carpal instability later.

If the x-ray is normal and clinical picture highly suggest an injury, then immobilize the wrist and request further investigations to look for the injury

SOURCE SLIDE 29

Management

immobilization is done with below elbow backslab

SOURCE SLIDE 30

Slide 30

The aim is to treat as soon as possible if there is an injury, or to avoid an unnecessary period of immobilization and time from work. If these tests are not readily available, the patient should be re-examined repeatedly until the symptoms settle or a ﬁrm diagnosis is made.

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Fracture healing is a complex process that involves several stages: hematoma formation, inflammation, soft callus formation, hard callus formation and remodeling

Many factors affect fracture healing , including the diet

And here we will talk about the 10 Foods that delay fracture healing

SOURCE SLIDE 3

1. Alcohol

Alcohol interferes with fracture healing by inhibiting the proliferation and differentiation of osteoblasts

Osteoblasts are the cells responsible for formation of new bone

Alcohol also increase the production of inflammatory cytokines leading to prolongation of the inflammatory phase of the healing process

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

2. High Sugar Foods

Fast foods, deserts, sweets …

Foods high in sugar lead to high blood glucose levels which can cause inflammation and oxidative stress

These effects will prolong the inflammatory phase of the fracture healing process

formulatehealth, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

3. Excessive drinking of Caffeinated Beverages

Tea, coffee, soft drinks …

High levels of caffeine promote calcium excretion in urine and impairs calcium absorption in the intestines leading to Delay in fracture healing

Panamitsu, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

4. Foods high in Salt

High amount of salts promote the excretion of calcium through the kidney leading to delay of the fracture healing

Dubravko Sorić SoraZG on Flickr, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
