outline.summary: Emergency management Reduction Closed reduction Open reduction Holding reduction Continuous traction Cast splintage Functional bracing Internal fixation External fixation Exercise

outline.heading: Emergency Management
outline.summary: ATLS trauma protocol Take full history and examination of the injuries reduce – hold – exercise

outline.heading: Principles of treatment of closed fractures
outline.summary: Reduction: manipulation of the fragments to reach the normal anatomical position Holding the reduction (retaining reduction): holding the fragments together until they unite Exercise the joints proximal and distal and get the patient back to normal function

outline.heading: 1. Reduction
outline.summary: Reduction = returning the fracture fragments to their normal anatomical positions This procedure comes after stabilizing the patient Swelling of soft tissue in the first 12 hours after injury make reduction difficult

outline.heading: Reduction
outline.summary: During reduction, you should aim for adequate apposition and normal alignment of bone fragments The greater the contact surface area between fragments, the more likely healing is to occur

outline.heading: Reduction
outline.summary: Some overlap at the fracture surfaces is okay as long as the fracture is in location other than the articular surface Articular surface fractures should be reduced as near to perfection as possible because any irregularity might lead to abnormal load distribution and predispose to degenerative changes at the joint

outline.heading: Some situations in which reduction is unnecessary
outline.summary: When there is little or no displacement When displacement doesn’t matter initially (in clavicle fractures) When reduction is unlikely to succeed (e.g. in vertebral compression fractures)

outline.heading: Two types of reduction
outline.summary: Closed reduction Open reduction

outline.heading: Closed reduction
outline.summary: Analgesia, local anesthesia or general anesthesia might be used depending on the situation for pain and muscle relaxation Then reduction is done either through manipulation or through traction

outline.heading: Closed reduction
outline.summary: Manipulation done through these three steps The distal part of the limb is pulled in the line of the bone As the fragments disengage, they are repositioned by applying force that is opposite to the force caused the fracture Alignment is then adjusted in each plane

outline.heading: Closed reduction
outline.summary: Or done through traction which reduces fracture fragments through ligamentotaxis (ligament pulling) which is applicable to specific fractures Closed reduction is most effective when the periosteum and muscles on one side of the fracture remain intact (stable fracture), preventing over reduction and stabilize fracture after reduction

outline.heading: Closed reduction
outline.summary: Some fractures are difficult to reduce due to powerful muscle pull, so prolonged traction is needed Closed reduction is mostly adequate for all minimally displaced fractures

outline.heading: Closed reduction
outline.summary: Closed reduction is used for unstable fractures in emergency settings to be fixated at later times in theatre Closed reduction fails because either it is difficult to control fracture fragments or fracture fragments are stuck because soft tissue is interposed between them

outline.heading: Open reduction
outline.summary: Means operative opening of the fracture site and reduction under direct vision Indications When closed reduction fails When it is an articular fracture that can’t be reduced accurately when closed For avulsion fractures (because avulsed fragment is connected to a muscle that continuously pulls it away)

outline.heading: 2. Retaining reduction (Holding reduction)
outline.summary: The second step after reduction Previously called immobilization but the term not used anymore because it is rarely complete immobility, in most cases there is still little movements at fracture site and those are good for healing

outline.heading: Retaining reduction (Holding reduction)
outline.summary: So it means that you hold fracture in place until healing occurs You need a form of stabilization to the fracture site that hold it in place while the patient is able to exercise the joints proximal and distal to it

outline.heading: Retaining reduction (Holding reduction)
outline.summary: Holding reduction is achieved using various closed and open methods Closed methods Continuous traction Cast splintage Functional bracing Open methods Internal fixation External fixation

outline.heading: Retaining reduction
outline.summary: Closed Holding methods are more suitable for fractures with intact soft tissues and muscles because intact muscles and soft tissue act as support to the fracture with the holding method used Open holding methods used in fractures with severe soft tissue damage, e.g. unstable fractures, multiple fractures, fractures in non cooperative patient Next we will talk about the types of holding reduction methods

outline.heading: Continuous traction
outline.summary: Continuous traction is mostly used as a reduction method nowadays, and it is used as a holding method only as a bridging procedure to relieve pain until patient reaches operating room for open holding method to be applied Normally muscles attached proximal and distal to fracture site will pull the fragments towards each other and displace the fracture The idea behind traction is you counter the muscle pulling by pulling the limb the opposite side

outline.heading: Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Continuous traction
outline.summary: that is why traction is applied to the distal part of the limb to pull it away from the fracture site, thus countering the muscle pulling Of course once you are pulling the distal part , you need some stabilization to the patient body so it doesn’t all get pulled Traction is useful for shaft fractures (because they are highly affected by muscle pull), especially oblique and spiral fractures that are easily displaced by muscle contraction, it can also be used for acetabular fractures with femoral head subluxation or dislocation

outline.heading: Continuous traction
outline.summary: Traction cannot hold a fracture still, it can pull a long bone and hold it out to length but to maintain accurate reduction is difficult; that is why nowadays traction is used as bridging procedure to reduce the fracture and relieve pain until the operation is done to the patient for internal or external fixation of the fracture

outline.heading: Continuous traction
outline.summary: Traction includes three methods Traction by gravity: this applied to upper limb injuries only (mostly humeral shaft fractures) wrist sling (U-slab) is applied and it provides a continuous traction using the weight of the arm to pull it downward National Museum of  Health and Medicine, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Continuous traction
outline.summary: Skin traction: used for lower limbs mostly, allows a traction weight of no more than 4-5 kg Holland strapping or one way stretch Elastoplast are applied to shaved skin and held on with bandage and connected to a weight Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Continuous traction
outline.summary: Skeletal traction: a pin is inserted usually behind the tibial tuberosity and connected to weight for hip, thigh and knee injuries or through calcaneum for tibial fractures Bobjgalindo, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Complications of traction
outline.summary: Skin irritation Pressure sores Discomfort or pain Circulation compromise: check pulses after applying Nerve injury especially with skeletal traction (common perioneal nerve injury and foot drop) Pin site infection with skeletal traction

outline.heading: Cast splintage
outline.summary: Closed holding method The most common holding reduction Plaster of Paris is mostly used for casting in emergency department because it is versatile, easy to handle and strong but the downside that it is heavy

outline.heading: Cast splintage
outline.summary: Other materials like fiberglass or polypropylene are lighter and used for definitive casting but they are harder to handle Casting is used either to create a split cast (backslab) or full cast

outline.heading: Backslabs
outline.summary: Is a Split cast applied to one side of the injured limb to act as a splint Casting material used in slabs is several layers thick Doesn’t allow three point fixation thus provides less fracture support in comparison to full cast

outline.heading: Backslabs
outline.summary: Used in emergency settings only It allows swelling of the limb in comparison with full cast Easily applied and easily removed with a scissor only

outline.heading: Backslabs types
outline.summary: U-slab: provide continuous traction in humeral shaft fractures Above elbow slab: used for distal humerus fracture, elbow dislocations and forearm fracture Wrist slab: for distal radius and scaphoid fractures Volar hand slab: for metacarpal and phalangeal fractures

outline.heading: Backslabs types
outline.summary: Thumb spica: for base of thumb fracture and first metacarpophalangeal joint injury Above knee slab for tibial plateau fracture, tibial shaft fracture and knee dislocation Below knee slab for ankle fracture and foot injury

outline.heading: Full casts
outline.summary: Casting material in a full circle around the limb to provide support layers built up, one on the other, until the cast get the desired strength Full cast can be molded to shape allowing three point fixation and provide better fracture support than a backslab

outline.heading: Full casts
outline.summary: Full cast require more experience Harder to remove in the event of swelling and circulatory compromise, so if you expect the limb to swell then don’t apply it until swelling subside or apply with thick padding

outline.heading: Casting technique
outline.summary: After reduction of the fracture, preparation of the materials and equipment Then padding with cotton or synthetic materials applied to skin and bony prominences Application of plaster of Paris or any other casting material

outline.heading: Casting technique
outline.summary: Wait for it to dry and harden usually about 15- 30 minutes Follow up: watch for swelling if casting is done as emergency

outline.heading: Disadvantages of casting
outline.summary: Joints included in the cast can’t move and liable to stiffness Articular fractures need movement for the articular cartilage to heal but with casting articular fractures can’t move

outline.heading: Disadvantages of casting
outline.summary: Tight cast: cast maybe put tightly or become tight after swelling, patient complains of pain, check for vascular compromise => split the cast and ease it open through its length and through padding; if swelling is anticipated thick padding is used and plaster splitted before it sets Loose cast: after swelling subsided, cast become loose => should be replaced

outline.heading: Disadvantages of casting
outline.summary: Pressure sores: esp. bony prominences , patient complains of localized pain on the pressure spot => make a window through the cast and inspect the pain site Skin abrasions and laceration: it is a complication of removing the cast, esp. if electric saw is used

outline.heading: Functional bracing
outline.summary: Closed holding method Device used to stabilize the fracture, same as a cast but it is already made and has many variations depending on the bone that is broken More convenient than a cast Functional means patient can resume normal movements, there is also other types of braces like rehabilitative and prophylactic but functional is what we used in fractures

outline.heading: Functional bracing
outline.summary: Bracing is also referred to as orthosis Allow patient to adjust tightness of the device, remove it and wash it, and if used in lower limbs then allows walking better than a cast Used for stable injuries and after surgical stabilization of fractures Examples: moon boots, hinged braces, wrist splints and mallet splints

outline.heading: Mikael Granberg, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
outline.summary: Pagemaker787, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Bundesministerium für Gesundheit - German Federal Ministry for Health, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Internal fixation
outline.summary: Open holding method (surgical method) Internal meaning all the devices used to fixate and stabilize the fracture are inside, nothing is popping out of the skin In internal fixation, implants of various types used depending on the situation, they include: screws, plates, tension band wire, intramedullary nails

outline.heading: Indications of internal fixation:
outline.summary: Fractures that can’t be reduced by closed reduction, because once you use open reduction, it is obligatory to use open holding method which is either internal or external fixation Unstable fractures that are prone to displace after reduction Avulsion fractures

outline.heading: Indications of internal fixation:
outline.summary: Pathological fractures because bone healing is impaired Multiple fractures where early fixation reduce risk of general complications fractures in patient who present nursing difficulties (paraplegic, very elderly)

outline.heading: Screws
outline.summary: Device that convert rotational force into compressive one (to hold bone fragments together) Contain head and shaft, the head has a socket which can accommodate a screw driver; the shaft has a core and thread Separation distance between threads is called pitch which equals the distance the screw travels when turned 360 degrees Wouter Hagens, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Screws
outline.summary: Screw types according to shape: cortical screw has small diameter and pitch suitable for stabilizing dense cortical bone cancellous screw has a larger diameter and pitch which provide better grip in more porous cancellous bone Locking screws are used with locking plates and have threads in their heads Lag screws used to compress fracture fragments together Netha Hussain, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Jmarchn, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Plates
outline.summary: Device applied to the exterior of a bone to maintain alignment and reduction during bone healing, this device is held by screws Auxein, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Plates
outline.summary: Plates functions includes neutralization (protection) plate is used with a lag screw to control torsional forces between bone fragments Compression plate used to compress two bone fragments together and used for diaphyseal fractures Buttress plate is used to resist shear forces, especially in metaphyseal fractures Bridging plate bridges simple or multi fragmentary fractures to restore correct length, axis and rotation

outline.heading: Bluesharpkoenig, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Tension band wire
outline.summary: Metallic wire used in case the fracture fragments are too fragile to be fixed with plating Examples in olecranon fractures, medial malleolus, patella … Ard0 (Talk - Contribs), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Intramedullary nails
outline.summary: Long rod inserted in medullary bony canal (intramedullary) Standard of care for diaphyseal bone fractures of lower limb, mostly femoral shaft fractures Rotational forces resisted by adding interlocking screws to the nail Bullenwächter, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
Complications of internal fixation
outline.summary: Infection: iatrogenic because orthopedics implant increase the risk of infection, infection lead to chronic osteomyelitis Non union: when there is a gap between the fixed bones, or there is damage to the blood supply during the fixation process

outline.heading: Complications of internal fixation
outline.summary: Implant failure: if the device not capable of supporting the full load transferred through the limb Refracture: if the implants removed sooner than a year, safe removal should be after 18- 24 months

outline.heading: External fixation
outline.summary: Open holding method (surgical method) external meaning parts of the devices used to fixate and stabilize the fracture are popping out of the skin, using external fixator devices Types of external fixation include uniplanar, multiplanar, unilateral, bilateral and circular and this is achieved using the fixator device which held by pins and wires

outline.heading: The original uploader was Dekkanar at English Wikipedia., CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons
outline.summary: © Nevit Dilmen, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Indications of external fixation
outline.summary: Temporary stabilization of fractures in cases of severe soft tissue damage including open fractures to allow for redebridment Extensive contamination where internal fixation is risky Patients with severe multiple injuries (chest, abdomen, head) or with multiple fractures Fractures around joints where the soft tissue is swollen and internal fixation is risky Bone lengthening Infected fractures

outline.heading: Complications of external fixation
outline.summary: Damage to soft tissue structures: nerves, vessels, ligaments Non union: if there is gaps between fragments Pin track infection

outline.heading: Exercise
outline.summary: Exercise = restoring function of the injured limb and the patient as a whole Exercising lead to reduction of the edema, preserve joint movement, restore muscle power and guide patient back to normal activity The holding reduction method should allow patient to fully use of the affected limb immediately after the procedure but in practice that is not always the case

outline.heading: Exercise
outline.summary: Certain injuries require limiting function to avoid displacement during healing Movement restriction prolong hospital stay and lead to joint stiffness

outline.heading: Exercise
outline.summary: Patient encouraged to: Active exercise: helps pumping away edema fluid, stimulate circulation, prevents soft tissue adhesion and promotes fracture healing; if limb is encased in Plaster of Paris then static muscle contraction is taught to the patient, after removing the splint then joint mobilized; the unaffected joints should be exercised too Assisted movements: gentle assistance

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Management of Open Fractures

Emergency management

Cleaning of the wounds

Surgery

Wound debridement

Fracture stabilization

Soft tissue reconstruction

Bone defect reconstruction

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Management in Emergency department

ATLS trauma protocol

Take full history and examination of the injuries

Grade the fractures according to the Gustilo Anderson classification

Give antibiotic cover using IV antibiotics

Proceed to the steps in next slides

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Cleaning of the wounds and splinting

Initially no attempt should be made to remove anything other than gross contamination and then cover with simple sterile saline soaked dressing

Then the limb should be brought out to length and correct alignment and splinted or casted

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Surgery

Surgery consist of wound debridement and a form of fracture stabilization method

This is done either as emergency surgery (immediately after the injury) or urgent surgery ( in less than 24 hours after the injury)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Surgery

Indications of emergency surgery include

Gross contamination of the wound

Dysvascular limb requiring vascular repair

Compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy

All other open fractures should undergo debridement and fixation within 24 hours, the earlier the better, the expertise of the team is more important

SOURCE SLIDE 6

During surgery

Use of general anesthesia => better for muscle relaxation and patient comfort

Tourniquet is applied and inflated only to allow the identification of neurovascular structures and careful assessment of tissue integrity and then deflated to allow assessment of capacity of soft tissue and bone to bleed

SOURCE SLIDE 7

During surgery

Using tourniquet induces tissue ischemia in already badly injured limb so inflate only when necessary and deflate it back

Initial pre scrubbing of the limb is performed to remove gross contaminants

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Wound debridement

The wound edges are excised and the wound extended proximally and distally far enough for all traumatized tissue to be seen and assessed including the fractured bone ends, also it should take into account surgical exposure required for fracture stabilization and flapping or grafting procedures needed

Examination of the fracture surfaces cannot be adequately performed without extracting the bone from within the wound, the simplest method is to bend the limb in the same manner in which it was forced at the moment of injury

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Wound debridement

All contaminated and dead tissue should be excised including skin, fat, fascia, muscle and bone

Muscle viability is assessed according to the four Cs: color, contractility, consistency and capacity to bleed

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Wound debridement

Major peripheral nerves and vessels should be identified and protected

Soft tissues under the bone should also be examined and debrided carefully

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Wound debridement

Finally the wound is irrigated extensively with warmed normal saline (around 6 L) at low pressure to remove remaining contaminants

No benefit from pulsatile lavage (force contaminant deeper into tissue) , no benefit from adding antibiotics

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Fracture stabilization

Fracture stabilization is important in getting the bone to heal, reducing infection risk, assist recovery of the soft tissues and control pain

After wound debridement, patient repositioned on the table with traction, surgical team rescrub, limb should be reprepared and redraped, and new instruments should be used

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Fracture stabilization

Definitive fracture fixation is performed whenever possible depending if the debridement was adequate

but if there is extensive contamination and debridement wasn’t adequate (e.g. in blast injuries) , definitive fixation can’t be performed safely at the first procedure and temporary external fixation is required

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Wound closure

Primary wound closure done at the first procedure only if:

The patient has no significant comorbidities like DM, decrease immunity

The patient fully resuscitated

No gross contamination left in the wound

Debridement is complete and residual tissues are healthy

The fracture has been stabilized

The wound can be closed without tension

If the above criteria cannot be met and the patient need second procedure then the wound is left open and delayed primary closure is performed at the second procedure

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Wound closure

Interrupted sutures are preferred to continuous sutures: more stable, precise alignment, localized wound drainage and monitoring

Drains of no value

Low pressure vacuum dressing is applied to help minimize wound edge edema

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Repeated debridement (second procedure)

If there is doubt about the viability of the tissues, the wound left open and dressed for a second look within 48-72 hours

Dressing: best for these wounds are either a bead pouch consisting of a string of gentamicin beads under an adhesive dressing or a vacuum dressing

The patient then brought back to theatre after 48 hours for repeated assessment and debridement of the wound, several procedures maybe needed until debridement is complete

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Soft tissue reconstruction

Plastic surgeon task to reconstruct soft tissue

Tissue loss or wound edema may mean that the wound cannot be closed without tension, preventing either primary or delayed primary closure, and soft tissue coverage with a flap or graft is required

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Soft tissue reconstruction

Grafting or flapping should be performed as soon as possible and within 6 days after the injury

You should also know about the soft tissue reconstructive ladder to understand the available options for soft tissue coverage, you will study this more in plastic surgery rotation

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Soft tissue reconstructive ladder

Healing by secondary intention: the idea is that you leave the wound to heal by itself through granulation, no sutures no anything except for dressing, and that is only used for small residual skin defects

Primary tissue closure: primary closure only possible if two healthy viable skin edges can be brought together without tension, using sutures, glue, …

Grafting: skin graft can be applied to a healthy vascularized tissue such as muscle or fat but not directly to bone or tendon or metalwork

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Soft tissue reconstructive ladder

Local tissue transfer (local flap): this is needed to cover bone, tendon or metalwork. The flap may contain skin, fat, fascia, muscle or combination with its blood supply. Local flap are brought from area adjacent to the wound. Local flap maybe random (supplied by un named artery) or axial (supplied by named artery)

Regional tissue transfer (regional flap): flap from the nearby location as the wound

Free tissue transfer (free flap): flap from distant site

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Bone defect reconstruction

There might be residual defect in the bone after debridement

You can’t bone graft immediately after debridement to control infection, the bone graft require well vascularized tissue around it, it also require healed soft tissue around it and stable fracture => so for that you have to wait until grafting

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Bone defect reconstruction

So after debridement you either stabilize the fracture out to length with external or internal fixation and address the defect at a later procedure, the defect maybe filled with cement to maintain a gap to later fill it with bone graft

Or you shorten the limb acutely (so you stabilize it at shorter length by get the edges to be in direct contact to each other), either definitively in upper limbs or temporarily in lower limbs (you do later procedure for lengthening it again)

Acute skeletal shortening can decrease the effective size and complexity of soft tissue defect (so it is beneficial)

SOURCE SLIDE 23

In the ward

Limb is elevated and its circulation is carefully monitored

Antibiotics continued for 1 day after surgery if Gustilo grade 1 or for 3 days for other Gustilo grades

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Gustilo-Anderson Classification of Open Fractures

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Facts

Most commonly used system to classify open fractures

It was created by American orthopedic surgeons Ramon Gustilo, John Anderson and Thomas Williams in 1984

Classifies open fractures based on size of the wound, soft tissue damage and degree of contamination

Helps guiding treatment decisions and prognosis , also help in deciding the antibiotic cover used

The higher the grade of the injury , the higher the risk of infection and thus the more aggressive antibiotic regimen

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Grade 1

Wound length: Small wound less than 1 cm in length, punctured by a bone spike

The fracture caused by low energy injury mechanism

There is little soft tissue damage

Clean wound

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Grade 2

Wound length: Larger wound, more than 1 cm in length but less than 10 cm

Low to moderate energy injury mechanism

There is more soft tissue damage than type 1 but still minimal

Moderate contamination of the wound

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Grade 3

Wound length: even larger wound, more than 10 cm in length

High energy injury mechanism

Large laceration, extensive damage to skin and underlying soft tissue and maybe vascular compromise

Contamination is extensive

Furtherly classified into 3 types

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Grade 3 A

No extensive soft tissue loss or periosteal stripping => the fractured bone can be adequately covered by the available soft tissue

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Grade 3 B

Extensive periosteal stripping and tissue loss

The fracture cover not possible without the use of flaps

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Grade 3 C

Arterial injury that need to be repaired regardless of the amount of soft tissue damage

So any open fracture with any length if associated with arterial injury then considered type 3 C

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Antibiotic cover

Choice of antibiotic vary depending on local protocol

typically consist of either a cephalosporin antibiotic (e.g. cefuroxime 1.5g 3 times daily) or a penicillin antibiotic (e.g. co amoxiclav 1.2 g 3 times daily) but If patient has penicillin allergy then clindamycin (600mg four times daily)

This antibiotic is used as soon as possible when patient get to the hospital and continue to be used for 1 day after wound debridement if the injury was grade 1 and for 3 days after wound debridement if the injury was grade 2 and 3

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Antibiotic cover

At wound debridement add aminoglycoside antibiotic for all the grades (e.g. gentamicin 1.5 mg/kg three times daily)

If wound cover is not possible at debridement and to be delayed until grafting or the fracture is grade 3 b or c then add vancomycin or teicoplanin

Anti tetanus toxoid given with higher grades and depending on local protocol

SOURCE SLIDE 1

History and Examination of a patient presented with fracture

Public domain

Public domain

SOURCE SLIDE 2

General management

After you completed your primary and secondary surveys on your patient

Now you can focus on the fractures and start by inquiring a history then do an examination of the fracture sites

SOURCE SLIDE 3

History

History in trauma is the same as orthopedic history but there is some extra points that you should think of which explained here

History of presenting complaint

In fractures patient usually present with a history of trauma followed by pain, swelling and inability to use the injured limb but sometimes patient present with deformity which is very suggestive of fracture

Fracture not always at the site of trauma, it might be in different locations depending upon the size and direction of the applied force.

SOURCE SLIDE 4

History

Knowing mechanism of injury (how the fracture happened) is key in expecting the fractures locations and severity, so always ask for it.

Ask for the reason for the fall or the accident: mostly mechanical trip, some complain of chest pain or dyspnea or they aware they blacked out before falling (common causes: urinary or respiratory infections, postural hypotension, transient loss of consciousness, MI, PE)

If a fracture occurs with mild trauma, suspect a pathological lesion.

SOURCE SLIDE 5

History

If there was any pain before the fall at the affected region, suspect pathological fracture or stress fracture

Pain, bruising and swelling are common symptoms but they do not distinguish a fracture from a soft-tissue injury. Deformity is much more suggestive of a fracture or dislocation.

Consequences of the fall: head injury, how they got help,

SOURCE SLIDE 6

History

Systematic review

Cardiovascular: chest pain, syncope, palpitations, SOB

Respiratory: sputum, cough, hemoptysis, wheeze

Gastrointestinal: vomiting, abdominal pain, per rectum blood/mucus

Genitourinary: blood in urine, dysuria

Neurological: vertigo/dizziness, headache, limb weakness, paresthesia/sensory deficit

SOURCE SLIDE 7

History

Past medical history

Chronic disease (respiratory, cardiac, GI, ..)

PMH is important & Required before anesthesia

Social history

Occupation (physically demanding job => you have to consider management that make them handle their job), living situation (who supports them), smoking, drinking

SOURCE SLIDE 8

History

Drug history

Full drug history and allergies is important if the patient need surgery

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Examination

Examination in orthopedic trauma same as orthopedics in general but here we will explain some extra points to look for

In orthopedics we use the examination sequence: look , feel , move

Use a systematic approach to trauma patients:

Start with examining the obvious injuries.

Always test for vessel and nerve injuries.

Look for other injuries in the same region and in distant parts and examine them as well.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Examination

Cardiopulmonary, gastrointestinal and neurological examination should be also undertaken along with the musculoskeletal examination and injury specific examinations

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Look

Look equals inspection in internal medicine

Most importantly you need to look at the injured skin, if it is severely lacerated and bone communicates with the external environment then it is an open fracture and requires antibiotic cover and management accordingly ; but if the skin is intact then you assess if there is a fracture either by feeling the bone or by x ray examination

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Look

Swelling, bruising maybe obvious and they are not specific for fractures because it could be a fracture or just a soft tissue injury

Deformity is specific for fractures

Note also the extremity distal to the wound (color and posture) to have an idea of the damage occurred (vessel, nerve)

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Feel

Feel equals palpation in internal medicine

Tenderness: the injured bone is tender to pressure, there is direct pressure and indirect pressure that result in pain

Direct pressure is when you apply pressure near the fracture site, and the site of maximal tenderness is the fracture site

Indirect pressure: applying pressure at site away from fracture result in pain at fracture site (e.g. axial pressure on long bone will elicit pain at the fracture anywhere on the long bone, pinching the forearm bones at any site away from fracture result in pain at the fracture site)

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Feel

Sometimes you can feel the fracture edges and bony depressions when you palpate the long bones, but x ray examination is always superior

Some fractures would be missed if not speciﬁcally looked for (e.g. scaphoid fracture when feeling in the anatomical snuffbox)

You also feel for temperature of the extremity distal to the fracture and you feel the pulses if they intact or not

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Extra info

Some fractures are always associated with another fractures or ligament injuries so when you see one look for the other (e.g. an isolated fracture of the proximal ﬁbula associated with fracture or ligament injury of the ankle)

In high-energy injuries, always examine the spine and pelvis.

Vascular and peripheral nerve abnormalities should be tested for, both before and after treatment.

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Move

Crepitus and abnormal movement may be present when moving fractured bones but moving the injured bones is painful and x ray is available so use x rays

Movement is used mostly to assess the joints distal to the injury

We have fine crepitus and that is associated with osteoarthritis and we have coarse crepitus which is associated with fractures

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Differential diagnosis

Fracture

Ligament injury

Tendon injury

Muscle injury

Soft tissue injury

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Slide 18

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Management of Injured patient

Trauma systems

ATLS

Airway

Breathing

Circulation

Disability

Exposure

Trauma films

Orthopedic trauma management

Public domain

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Trauma systems

After the patient got injured, you need to do the critical procedures required for them to stay alive and then you manage their fractures and less critical injuries

There is systems for that including the ATLS developed by American college of surgeons and which we will discuss here but also there is other systems like PHTLS and ETC depending on your institution and what system they follow

SOURCE SLIDE 3

ATLS

ATLS contain three sections: primary survey, resuscitation and secondary survey

Primary survey is rapid assessment of patients ABCDE

Airway and cervical spine control

Breathing

Circulation and hemorrhage control

Disability

Exposure and environment

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Airway

Assessed for patency

If patient is talking or screaming then airway is patent at the moment

Noisy or absent breath sounds suggest compromised airway

Immediate interventions to airway such as head tilt and chin lift or jaw thrust in comatose patients, suctioning relief airway compromise in many patients and use of oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway maybe necessary => search it on YouTube

Sometimes the immediate interventions are enough but other times you need an advanced airway

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Head tilt / chin lift

Public domain

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Jaw thrust

Randhillon, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Public domain

ICUnurses, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Advanced airway

Types: orotracheal and nasotracheal intubation (non operative) , if failed then cricothyroidotomy and emergency tracheostomy needed (operative) => search it on YouTube

Indications of advanced airway

Apnea

Inability to protect airway (GCS <8)

Impending airway compromise in cases of inhalation injury, neck penetrating injuries (hematoma formation)

Extensive subcut air in the neck

Inability to maintain oxygenation

SOURCE SLIDE 9

bigomar2, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pöllö, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Cervical spine control

All patients with blunt trauma require cervical spine immobilization until injury excluded

Immobilization achieved by semi rigid cervical collar or placing sandbags on both sides of the head and the forehead taped across the bags

Soft collars are not effective

In penetrating neck wounds, cervical collars not recommended because they interfere with treatment

Search cervical collars on google and see what is the types and differences

SOURCE SLIDE 11

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Breathing

Second priority after the airway

All trauma patients should receive High flow oxygen and monitored by pulse oximetry

Watch for chest movement on examination

Rapid evaluation for life threatening chest injuries

Tension pneumothorax

Open pneumothorax

Massive hemothorax

Flail chest

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Circulation

Initially palpate pulses to check for CVS status

Palpable carotid pulse = systolic BP of 60 mmHg

Femoral pulse = 70

Radial pulse = 80

Blood pressure measurement gives you idea about the grade of hypovolemia if the patient is hypovolemic

Hypotension (systolic BP < 90) assume that it is caused by hemorrhage until proven otherwise

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Grades of hypovolemic shock

Table from slide 14
Clinical featureGrade IGrade IIGrade III Grade IV
Blood loss (mL)Up to 750750-15001500-2000≥2000
Blood loss (%)<1515-3030-40>40
Pulse rate (beats/min)<100100-120120-140>140
Blood pressure (mmHg)NormalNormalDecreasedDecreased
Pulse pressureNormal or increasedDecreasedDecreasedDecreased
Respiratory rate (breaths/min)14-2020-3030-40>35
Urine output (mL/hr)>3020-305-15Negligible
Mental statusSlightly anxiousMildly anxiousConfusedLethargic
SOURCE SLIDE 15

Circulation

Place two large bore IV cannula and blood should be drawn before starting resuscitation with fluids to prevent RBC cross linking and agglutination

Blood drawn for

Cross matching

Bedside hemoglobin level and trauma panel

Coagulation panel

ABG for base deficit

SOURCE SLIDE 16

IV Cannula

Saltanat ebli, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Table from slide 16
Cannula colorGauge Flow rate (ml/min)
Yellow 24G20
Blue 22G36
Pink20G60
Green18G90
Gray16G180
Orange14G240
SOURCE SLIDE 17

Circulation

Rapid evaluation for

Massive hemothorax

Cardiac tamponade

Massive hemoperitoneum

Mechanically unstable pelvic fractures with bleeding

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Hemorrhage control

Start with manual compression with a single gauze and a gloved hand

Bleeding of the extremities might be managed with tourniquets for the short term

Open fracture bleeding is controlled by reduction and stabilization with splints

Pelvis should be stabilized with a sheet or binder

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Fluid resuscitation

The best resuscitation is achieved with blood but that is not usually ready until later

So start with isotonic crystalloids typically Ringer’s lactate which is superior to normal saline (avoid hyperchloremic acidosis)

In massive transfusion give packed RBCs , platelets and fresh frozen plasma in ratio of 1:1:1

Aim for hypotensive resuscitation systolic pressure target of about 100 in bleeding patient (to protect the clot that has formed and thus decrease bleeding

Assess by monitoring vitals: pulse, BP, RR, SpO2, urine output

Also by monitoring labs: Hb, coagulation, lactate and base deficit

SOURCE SLIDE 20

The lethal triad

Lethal triad is 3 physiological abnormalities indicating inadequate resuscitation and increase risk of death

Coagulopathy PLT<120, INR>1.5: consumption of clotting factors (solved by using platelets and fresh frozen plasma early in the resuscitation)

Hypothermia <35C: exposure to cold and from fluid resuscitation and lead to impaired enzyme dependent pathways including clotting

Acidosis pH<7.25: maybe inadequate oxygenation (respiratory acidosis) or inadequate peripheral tissue hypoperfusion

SOURCE SLIDE 21

Disability

Neurologic evaluation include: level of consciousness (conscious, drowsy, confused, stuporous or comatose), pupil size and reactivity and motor function

Common causes of neurological deficits in trauma include: head injury, hypoxia, shock and alcohol or drugs intake

Assessment of disability by AVPU scale or GCS

AVPU: awake , responds to verbal, responds to pain, unresponsive

SOURCE SLIDE 22

Adult GCS

Table from slide 22
ScoreEye openingVerbal response Motor response
1None None None
2Open to pain Incomprehensible sounds (like moaning)Extensor posturing
3Open to voice Inappropriate words (random)Flexor posturing
4Open spontaneously Confused or disoriented Withdrawal in response to pain
5Oriented Localize pain
6Follows commands
SOURCE SLIDE 23

GCS interpretation

When GCS applied to head trauma patients

GCS 13-15= mild injury

GCS 9-12= moderate injury

GCS 3-8= severe injury

SOURCE SLIDE 24

Exposure & environment

All clothes of trauma patient are removed using scissors in order to make sure to examine all body parts from head to toe for trauma

Keep the body warm using blankets to prevent hypothermia

Hypothermia is used only in cases of severe brain injury

SOURCE SLIDE 25

Secondary survey

Head to toe examination

SAMPLE: signs and symptoms of the patient, allergies, medications, past medical history, last meal (when and what), event history

SOURCE SLIDE 26

Trauma films

Blunt trauma: lateral cervical spine x ray + erect AP chest + AP pelvis

Penetrating trauma: all of the above + x ray for the site of injury

eFAST

RUSH: rapid ultrasound for shock and hypotension

SOURCE SLIDE 27

Orthopedics trauma management

Recovery from orthopedic trauma is done by stabilizing the injuries

Early total care: definitive stabilization of all long bone fractures within 24 hours of injury if the patient is stable within that period

Damage control surgery: immediate surgery that is required to save life and limb when patient is unable to undergo early total care, other procedures delayed until patient’s condition improved ; DCS include stabilization of unstable fractures (pelvis, femur, vertebrae) also includes decontamination of open wounds, amputation and decompression of limb compartments

Patient should undergo as much of their surgery as is safe, as soon as they are physiologically able to cope with that surgery

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Displaced fracture

Displaced fracture: bone fragments not in its normal anatomical position

Because of:

The force applied to the bone

Muscle action on the fractured fragments

Gravity

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Fracture description

Important to learn how to describe fractures so you can communicate your findings with the other team members and with your seniors

First you mention the shape of the fracture: transverse, spiral, oblique, comminuted, segmental

Then you mention fracture location, you describe it according to the location on the bone (long bone: head, neck, shaft, condyle OR epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis)

Examples: fracture in the distal metaphysis of the femur OR fracture in the inferior third of the shaft of the femur

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Fracture description

Finally you mention displacement, you describe the displacement of distal fragment in relation with the proximal fragment

We have four patterns of displacement: translation (shift), angulation (tilt), rotation, shortening vs lengthening, depressed

And you mention the direction of the displacement (anterior, posterior, medial, latera)

If not displaced, you say without displacement

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Translation (shift)

Shift of fragments Sideways, backward or forward

Description of the example: transverse fracture in the mid shaft of tibia with lateral translation of the distal fragment

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Slide 6

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Angulation (tilt)

Bone fragments would be tilted in relation to each other (angle less/more than normal)

Description of the example: transverse midshaft tibial fracture with medial angulation of the distal fragment OR midshaft tibial fracture with the apex pointing laterally

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Slide 8

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Rotation

Fragment rotated around its longitudinal axis in relation to the other fragment

Sometimes can’t be detected on x ray so be attentive when doing physical exam

Description: transverse midshaft tibial fracture with rotation of the distal fragment

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Shortening

Overlapping of fragments due to muscle pull

Example description: transverse midshaft tibial fracture with shortening of the bone due to overlapping of the fragments

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Slide 11

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Lengthening

Bone fragments get further away from each other

Example description: transverse midshaft tibial fracture with lengthening of the bone

SOURCE SLIDE 13

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Fracture Healing Outcomes

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Outcomes of fracture healing

Union

Delayed union

Non union

Malunion

Refracturing

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Union

Complete healing of the fracture

Physical examination: Fracture site is painless on palpation and weight bearing

X rays shows bridging callus, the fracture line is replaced by bone

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Delayed union

Fracture healing takes twice as long as the expected time for a specific location

Physical examination: the fracture site has local swelling and movement or partial weight bearing is painful

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Non union

Bone fails to unite

Fracture healing doesn’t occur in less than 9 months since initial injury and no signs of healing in the final three months

Causes of non union

Mechanical instability

Impaired vascularity

Infection

Common sites: scaphoid bone, femoral neck, tibial shaft

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Non union

History of pain

Examination: tenderness over the fracture site

X ray: persistent fracture line seen

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Types of non union

Hypertrophic: abundant callus formation but there is radiolucent line at the non union line on x ray

Oligotrophic: little or no callus formation, radiolucent line on x ray too

Atrophic: no callus formation, osteopenia, sclerotic avascular bone segments

Infected: osteopenia, sclerotic avascular bone segments, segmental bone loss, clinical signs of infection

Synovial pseudoarthrosis (false joint) also could be (hypertrophic, oligotrophic, atrophic, infected)

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Slide 8

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Non union risk factors

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Non union risk factors

Old age

Poor nutrition

Drugs

Metabolic disease

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Malunion

Healing in non anatomical position

Partially compensated for by the remodeling of the bone

May lead to functional impairment or poor aesthetic

Causes:

Inaccurate reduction

Inadequate immobilization

Complications: osteoarthritis if there is intra articular malunion or joint instability

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Refracturing

Fixation materials should be removed within 18 months after fracture healing

If left in place for longer than that leads to cortical atrophy and high risk of refracturing

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Fracture healing

Requirements for fracture healing

Bone healing types

Secondary bone healing

Primary bone healing

Gap healing

Factors affecting fracture healing

Average healing times of fractures

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Requirements for fracture healing

Intact blood supply to the fractured fragments

Immobilization by cast, internal fixation or external fixation

Absence of infection

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Bone healing types

We have three types of bone healing

Secondary bone healing (indirect, spontaneous)

Primary bone healing (contact healing)

Gap healing

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Bone healing types

If there is small amount of tension (below 2%) on the fracture (the fracture ends held very stable) => primary bone healing occurs; such as when using plates and screws (type of internal fixation)

If the tension is between 2-10 % (there is a little movement between the fracture ends due to external forces) => secondary bone healing will occur such as when using a cast, intramedullary nail or external fixation

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Secondary bone healing (healing by callus)

Bone surfaces are placed close to each other but Not in direct contact in comparison with primary bone healing which occurs when there is direct contact between bone surfaces

Secondary bone healing process called endochondral ossification

Most common form of bone healing in long bones

Occurs in absence of rigid fixation

Advantages compared to primary bone healing

Mechanically stronger during healing

With increasing stress the callus grows stronger and stronger (according to Wolff’s law)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Secondary bone healing (healing by callus)

It is on five stages

Hematoma formation

Inflammation

Soft callus formation

Hard callus formation

Remodeling

SOURCE SLIDE 7

1. Hematoma formation

Bleeding occur from the bone and soft tissue at the fracture site

Leads to hematoma formation

SOURCE SLIDE 8

2. Inflammation

After the hematoma forms, inflammatory process start

Cytokines released

Inflammatory cells recruited (neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, t cells)

Osteoclasts formed to remove necrotic ends of bone fragments

Last until fibrous tissue, cartilage or bone formation begins (1-7 days) after fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 9

3. Soft callus formation

Callus is temporary bony material, cartilaginous material, fibrous connective tissue and woven bone that replaces the hematoma

Woven bone is bone tissue characterized by haphazard arrangement of collagen fibers and will be remodeled into cortical bone in the upcoming stages

Soft callus: soft bony material (collagen type 2= cartilage) so it is mainly formed by cartilage, secreted by mesenchymal stem cells that are gathered to injury site because of the inflammation process

SOURCE SLIDE 10

3. Soft callus formation

Soft callus forms After 2 weeks post fracture

The fragments can’t move freely now, they are stable in length but they can angulate

The stiffer the immobilization of the fracture the less amount of callus formed

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Mesenchymal stem cells

Mesenchymal stem cells are undifferentiated and they differentiate to osteoblasts and chondroblasts

Important source in fractures are periosteum, bone marrow and surrounding muscles

Gathered during the inflammation process

SOURCE SLIDE 12

4. Hard callus formation

Hard callus: hard bony material (woven bone which is type 1 collagen) so it is mainly bone material, secreted by osteoblasts and chondroblasts

starts after the formation of the soft callus and ends when the fragments are firmly united by 3-4 months post fracture

Forms in the periphery of the fracture and progressively moves centrally

SOURCE SLIDE 13

5. Remodeling

The woven bone is slowly replaced by lamellar bone

The medullary bone canal is continuous in this stage

Last from few months to several years post fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Primary bone healing (contact healing)

Bone ends are put in close contact

when fracture surfaces are in intimate contact (less than 0.1 mm distance) with absolute stability => osteoclasts will form cutting cones that traverse the fracture line => capillaries occupy the newly formed cavities with osteoblasts => form lamellar bone from osteons

The intermediate stages are skipped (no callus what so ever)

Primary bone healing process called cutting cone remodeling, haversian remodeling

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Gap healing

when there is small gaps between fracture surfaces (< 1mm) => gaps invaded by new capillaries and osteoblast cells that form => woven bone => remodeled to lamellar bone

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Factors affecting fracture healing

Age of the patient: healing is faster in children, the time to heal a fracture in children is half compared to adults

Type of bone: cancellous bones unite faster than cortical bones

Fracture pattern: spiral heals faster than > transverse > comminuted

Ischemic fracture ends (due to damage to the blood supply from trauma or from fixation) lead to slower healing or no healing at all

Soft tissue interposition between fracture ends prevent callus from bridging the fragments and lead to slower healing

SOURCE SLIDE 17

Factors affecting fracture healing

Reduction: good apposition of the fracture ends lead to faster healing

amount of movement at fracture site (movement lead to callus formation according)

Absolute stability and compression leads to primary bone healing

Relative stability leads to secondary bone healing

Excessive motion leads to delayed healing or non union

More factors will be discussed in the next lectures

SOURCE SLIDE 18

Average healing times of some fractures in adult patients

Upper limb

Clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna: 6-8 weeks

Wrist bones: 6-12 weeks

Hand/ fingers: 4-6 weeks

Lower limb

Hip, femur, tibia, fibula: 6- 12 weeks

Ankle bones: 6-8 weeks

Foot bones: 4-6 weeks

SOURCE SLIDE 19

Average healing times of fractures in pediatric patients

4-6 weeks in most fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 20

Types of fractures

SOURCE SLIDE 2

According to extent of fracture line

Complete fracture and incomplete fracture

Complete fracture: The bone split into two fragments or more

Incomplete fracture: incomplete split of the bone, periosteum remains continuous in part of the bone.

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Slide 3

SOURCE SLIDE 4

According to fracture displacement

Undisplaced fracture: bone fragments still aligned and in their normal place

Displaced fracture: bone fragments out of alignment and shifted from original position

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Slide 5

SOURCE SLIDE 6

According to fracture pattern

Linear fracture: could be transverse, short oblique, long oblique (spiral)

Comminuted fracture: more than 2 fracture fragments

Segmental fractures: fracture broken to segments, segments longer than fragment

Bone loss: part of the bone or all of the bone is lost

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Slide 7

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Slide 8

SOURCE SLIDE 9

According to relation with external environment

Closed fractures: overlying skin and soft tissue are intact

Open fracture: overlying skin and soft tissue are injured making bone exposed to the external environment

Internally open: sharp fractured bone pierces the skin to communicate with external environment

Externally open: object from outside causing laceration to skin and soft tissue causing bone to get exposed

SOURCE SLIDE 10

According to complexity of treatment

Simple fracture: fracture in two pieces, requires reduction and casting (easy to treat)

Complex fracture: fracture with multiple pieces (comminuted), requires surgery (harder to treat)

SOURCE SLIDE 11

According to force causing the fracture

High energy fracture: occur due to high impact force such as severe trauma, road traffic accidents and fall from height

Low energy fracture: occur due to low impact force such as ground level falls

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Bone Fractures Mechanisms

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Fracture mechanisms

Fractures that are caused by traumatic forces

Fractures caused due to stress (repetitive injury)

Fractures caused because of certain pathology in the fractured bone

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Traumatic forces types

Rotational force => Spiral fracture (long oblique fracture)

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Traumatic forces types

Compressing force on long axis of the bone => short oblique fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Traumatic forces types

Crushing force on long axis of the bone => comminuted fracture (multiple fragments)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Traumatic forces types

Bending force on the horizontal axis of the bone => fracture with a butterﬂy fragment or oblique fracture

Bone fragment looks like butterfly wing

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Traumatic forces types

Tension type of force => transverse fracture or avulse a small fragment of the bone at the point of ligament or tendon insertion.

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Stress fractures

Stress fracture is a small break in the bone that occur from repetitive injury or prolonged stress applied to the bone

Occur in weight bearing bones: tibia, fibula, femur

Mechanism: repetitive stress lead to bone resorption by osteoclasts happen faster than bone formation mediated by osteoblasts

Occur in people that do heavy exercise such as runners, dancers, gymnasts.

Also occur in nutritional deficiencies of calcium and vitamin D in elderly people

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Pathological fractures

Fractures that occur due to pathology in the fractured bone

Pathologies include: osteoporosis, osteogenesis imperfecta, bisphosphonate therapy, lytic bone lesions in metastasis or multiple myeloma

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Orthopedic Trauma definition

Orthopedic Trauma refers to injuries to bones, joints, ligaments, tendons caused by falls, motor vehicle accidents and sports.

Orthopedic Trauma includes medical and surgical management of those injuries.

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Fracture definition

Fracture is a break or crack in the continuity of the bone, Can occur in any part of any bone

Results in:

pain

swelling

deformity

instability

change in sensibility

loss of function

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Other definitions

Ligament is tissue connects bone with another bone while tendon connect muscle with a bone.

Dislocation is movement of a bone from its normal position in its joint, due to stretch or tear of the ligaments and other structures holding the joint.

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Other definitions

Subluxation is partial dislocation of a bone within its joint.

Sprain is ligamentous injury.

Strain is injury to a tendon or to a muscle.

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Bone types

Cortical bone

Compact, dense, strong

Found in the outer layer of the shafts of long bones, outer surface of flat bones such as skull, ribs and pelvis (80% of adult skeleton)

Slow turnover rate (slower healing)

Cancellous bone

Trabecular, spongy, weaker than cortical bone

Found in the ends of long bones and inner layer of their shafts and in the vertebral bodies, also found in inner layer of skull, ribs and pelvic bones (20% of adult skeleton)

High turnover rate (faster healing)

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

3 types classification system for odontoid process fractures

It takes into account the level of the fracture in relation to the odontoid process and the C2 vertebral body

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Type 1: fracture at the tip of the odontoid process

Type 2: fracture at the base of the odontoid process

Type 2a: comminuted fracture at the base of the odontoid process

Type 3: fracture at the body of the C2 vertebrae

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Type 1

Fracture location: at the tip of the odontoid process

Fracture type: simple avulsion fracture

Mechanism of injury: lateral force applied when head is extended

Rare

Stable

Treatment: immobilization until pain subsides

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Type 2

Fracture location: at the junction of the odontoid process and the body of the axis

Fracture type: simple

Mechanism of injury: hyperflexion => anterior displacement of the dens, hyperextension => posterior displacement

Most common

High non union rates

Unstable

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Treatment

Young patients with undisplaced fracture: traction followed by collar or halo vest

Elderly patients with undisplaced fracture: traction followed by collar, surgery has poor risk to benefit ratio

Patients with displaced fracture: Surgery by inserting anterior lag screw from C2 body into the dens

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 9

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Type 2a

Fracture location: at the base of the odontoid process

Fracture type: comminuted

Mechanism of injury: same as type 2

Even higher nonunion rates compared to type 2

Represent 5- 10% of type 2 fractures

Treatment: surgery (posterior C1- C2 fusion)

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 11

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Type 3

Fracture location: through the odontoid and into the lateral masses of the axis vertebrae

Fracture type: simple

Mechanism of injury: unclear

Relatively stable

Best prognosis for healing

Treatment

Undisplaced fractures: immobilization for 8- 12 weeks

Displaced fractures: reduction by traction then immobilization for 8- 12 weeks

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 13

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

Salter - Harris Classification of Pediatric Physeal Injuries

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

It is five grades system to describe physeal injuries

It is based on the fracture location in relation to the physis, metaphysis and epiphysis, fracture pattern, and prognosis

Those injuries occur in children and they involve the Physis (growth plate)

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Grade 1: Transverse fracture through the physis

Grade 2: Transverse through the physis and deviates to the metaphysis

Grade 3: Transverse through the physis and deviates to the epiphysis

Grade 4: fracture pass through the epiphysis, physis and metaphysis

Grade 5: Compression injury to the physis

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Grade 1

Fracture location: transverse through the hypertrophic or calcified zone of the plate

Growth plate state: not injured

Good prognosis

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Grade 2

Fracture location: transverse through the growth plate and it deviates away from the physis to split off a triangular metaphyseal fragment of bone

Growth plate state: not injured

Most common grade

Good prognosis

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 8

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Grade 3

Fracture location: transverse fracture through the physis and then deviates to the epiphysis

Growth plate state: injured

Intra articular

Poor prognosis

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Grade 4

Fracture location: fracture travels through the epiphysis, physis and metaphysis and it is liable to displacement which if happened result in asymmetrical growth

Growth plate state: injured

Intra articular

Poor prognosis

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 12

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Grade 5

Fracture location: longitudinal compression injury of the physis

Growth plate state: compression injury

Worst prognosis

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Danis and Weber Classification of Malleolar Fractures of The Ankle

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

It is three grades system to classify malleolar fractures of the ankle joint

it is based on the location of the fibular fracture (lateral malleolar fracture) in relation to the level of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and as a result we have grade A that is below the level of syndesmosis and grade B at the level of syndesmosis and grade C above level of syndesmosis.

Reminder: distal tibiofibular syndesmosis is formed by the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament and the interosseous tibiofibular ligament

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Grade A: below level of syndesmosis

A1: isolated

A2: with medial malleolus fracture

A3: with fracture of the posteromedial part of the tibia

Grade B: at level of syndesmosis

B1: isolated

B2: with medial malleolus fracture or deltoid ligament injury

B3: with B2 and fracture of the posteromedial part of the tibia

Grade C: above level of syndesmosis

C1: simple diaphyseal fracture of the fibula

C2: complex diaphyseal fracture of the fibula

C3: proximal fracture of the fibula

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Grade A

Fracture location: below level of syndesmosis

Mechanism of injury: supination- adduction

Transverse fracture

Tibiofibular syndesmosis: intact

Medial malleolus: occasionally fractured

Deltoid ligament: intact

Fracture stability: stable if medial malleolus intact

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 7

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Grade B

Fracture location: At the level of syndesmosis

Mechanism of injury: supination- external rotation and pronation abduction

Spiral or oblique fracture

Tibiofibular syndesmosis: intact or partially torn

Medial malleolus: could be fractured

Deltoid ligament: could be torn

Fracture stability: Variable

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 9

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Grade C

Fracture location: Above level of the syndesmosis

Mechanism of injury: pronation- external rotation

Tibiofibular syndesmosis: torn

Associated with medial malleolus fracture or deltoid ligament rupture

Fracture stability: unstable

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 11

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Schatzker Classification for Tibial Plateau Fractures

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

6 grades classification system for tibial plateau fractures

It combines fracture location, pattern, fracture energy and tibial plateau involved if it is lateral or medial or both to produce this system

Low energy vs high energy

Grade (I- III) low energy

Grade (IV- VI) high energy

Unicondylar vs bicondylar

Grade (I- IV) unicondylar

Grade (V and VI) bicondylar

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Grade I: split fracture of the lateral tibial plateau

Grade II: split- depression fracture of the lateral tibial plateau

Grade III: depression fracture of the lateral tibial plateau

Grade III A: lateral depression

Grade III B: central depression

Grade IV: split or depression fracture of the medial tibial plateau

Grade V: wedge shape pattern fracture involving both tibial plateaus

Grade VI: dissociation of the articular surface from the diaphysis + any other fracture

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Grade 1

Vertical split of the lateral condyle of the tibia in the sagittal plane

Most common in young people who have hard cancellous trabeculae and good bone density so the bone splits and doesn’t depress

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Grade 2

Split- depression fracture of the lateral tibial plateau

Most common grade

Associated with either greater energy than a Grade I or with poor bone quality

The lateral tibial plateau can’t stand the load of the lateral femoral condyle and that is why it sustains split- depression fracture

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 7

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Grade 3

Depression fracture of the lateral tibial plateau and it’s classified into two types: Grade III A with lateral depression while Grade III B with central depression of the lateral tibial plateau

Associated with poor bone quality and can be caused by very low energy mechanisms.

Most common in elderly

Joint stability is rarely affected but axial instability might occur with Grade III B

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 9

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Grade 4

Split or split- depression fracture in the medial plateau. The fracture pass lateral to the intercondylar eminence and goes back medially to separate the medial plateau from the tibia

Mechanism of injury: high energy Varus force with axial loading

Knee joint stability is extensively affected and they represent variant of knee dislocation

High risk for compartment syndrome and neurovascular injury

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 11

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Grade 5

Split or split- depression fracture involving both tibial plateaus. Intercondylar eminence is spared because of the cruciate ligament holding it

Total articular injury

Mechanism of injury is high energy force

unstable knee joint but it is more stable than Grade IV

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 13

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Grade 6

dissociation of the articular surface from the diaphysis + any other fracture

Mechanism of injury: high energy force, open fracture with extensive soft tissue injury and compartment syndrome is common with this grade

Unstable knee joint

High risk for compartment syndrome and neurovascular injury

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 15

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Evans-Jensen Classification of Intertrochanteric hip fractures

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Based on the stability of the fracture after close reduction and skeletal traction

Describes fracture patterns as stable or unstable, based on the integrity of the posteromedial bony cortex. Stable fractures have intact or minimally comminuted posteromedial cortex, while unstable fractures has greater comminution of the posteromedial cortex

Unstable fractures after reduction can be converted to stable if the posteromedial opposition can be achieved

Reverse oblique pattern was considered inheritably unstable fracture as distal femur has tendency to drift medially due to adductor pull

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Grade 1 (Stable)

A: two part non displaced fracture

B: two part displaced

Grade 2 (Non stable)

A: three part fracture with separate grater trochanter fragment

B: three part fracture with separate lesser trochanter fragment

Grade 3 (Non stable)

four part fracture

Non stable

Non stable

Pipkin classification of femoral head fractures

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

4 grade system that is used to classify femoral head fractures associated with posterior hip dislocations

Divides the Thompson-Epstein’s Grade 5 (femoral head fracture in association with posterior dislocation) of the hip into four subtypes

The classification based on the location of the femoral head fracture

These injuries occur after severe high impact trauma such as motor vehicle collisions

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Grade 1

Small fracture

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Mechanism of action

Rifaximin is a synthetic antimicrobial which is classified as a protein synthesis inhibitor

it work by inhibiting the bacterial ability to synthesize protein

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of action

Rifaximin has a broad spectrum activity against gram positive and gram negative aerobic and anaerobic bacteria and it also work on protozoal infections such Cryptosporidiosis and blastocytosis intestinal infections

Rifaximin is non absorbable so it works only on the GI tract

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved therapeutic uses:

Reduction in risk of hepatic encephalopathy recurrence in adults

Treatment of irritable bowel syndrome associated with diarrhea in adults

Treatment of travelers’ diarrhea caused by noninvasive strains of E coli in patients older than 12

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic uses

Off label therapeutic uses

In treatment of small intestine bacterial overgrowth, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, pouchitis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis , C. Difficile infection

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pharmacokinetics

it is available as an oral formula

It work locally on the GI tract and it is not absorbed into the blood

It is excreted in the feces

It is dosed between 200 mg three times a day to even 800 mg twice a day for a period between 2 to 12 weeks depending on the indication; and there is no dose adjustment in renal or liver disease and should be avoided in pregnancy (pregnancy category C)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Adverse effects

Those are limited to the GI tract due to minimal systemic absorption

they include: nausea, GI upset, fatigue , peripheral edema and muscle spasms

Long term use is associated with fungal or bacterial superinfections

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Lactulose

Lactulose is a non absorbable synthetic disaccharide made of galactose and fructose

Lactulose can’t be metabolized in the small intestine so it reaches the large intestine unchanged and that is where it get metabolized by the colonic bacteria to monosaccharides and then to fatty acids, hydrogen and methane

Yikrazuul, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of action

Monosaccharides in the colon act as an osmolyte that draws water out of the colon wall (osmotic effect) and it also lead to increased gas formation (methane) => more water and gas in the colon lead to laxative effect => reduction in transit time => treatment of constipation (it is classified as osmotic laxative)

By this mechanism, lactulose work to treat constipation and it is FDA approved for this indication

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Breakdown of lactulose to short chain fatty acids (e.g. lactic acid and acetic acid) lead to Reduction in PH which facilitates conversion of ammonia NH3 into ammonium NH4+ in the large intestine

Ammonium NH4+ would not diffuse to bloodstream as much as ammonia NH3 diffuses due to its charge; also it can’t cross BBB for the same reason

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

The acidic PH also work to destroy urease producing bacteria involved in the production of ammonia => less ammonia produced

Also, lactulose inhibit intestinal glutaminase activity which blocks the conversion of glutamate to glutamine and its metabolism to ammonia

By these 3 mechanisms, lactulose work to lower blood ammonia and treat hepatic encephalopathy and that is also an FDA approved therapeutic use for this medication

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved therapeutic uses

Prevention and treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, lactulose decreases blood ammonia levels by 25% to 50% and this improve patient mental state

Used as a third line in Management of chronic constipation (after lifestyle modifications and increasing fiber intake have failed)

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Therapeutic uses

Off label uses

Management of subacute clinical encephalopathy

Because of its ability to reduce intestinal transit time, lactulose can also reduce deoxycholic acid’s hypersaturation => leading to inhibition of cholesterol stone formation

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pharmacokinetics

Lactulose is available as syrup for oral administration and a rectal enema

Lactulose is poorly absorbed from GI tract and it work locally there

Less than 3% of the total dose is absorbed to the blood and excreted through urine

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Since lactulose doesn’t get absorbed into the blood, it produces side effects limited to the GI tract

The most significant side effect is diarrhea which is dose dependent and decreases in severity with dose reduction

Diarrhea may lead to electrolyte disturbances

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Adverse effects

It also may lead to increased bowel sounds, increased flatus, and sensation of bloating

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Notes

Lactulose is contraindicated in galactosemia patients requiring galactose free diet

Sorbitol is superior in treatment of constipation in elderly patients

Lactulose may lead to electrolyte imbalances due to its osmotic effect, electrolyte might require monitoring especially in elderly and critically ill patients

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Notes

Lactulose may induce lithium toxicity in psychiatry patients due to its ability to induce dehydration through its osmotic action leading to poor renal excretion of lithium
