SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Ondansetron (Zofran)

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Pharmacokinetics

Adverse effects

Drug-Drug interactions

Contraindications

Intropin, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of action

Ondansetron work by antagonizing the serotonin 5 HT3 receptors centrally and peripherally

Centrally it antagonizes the 5HT 3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (normally neurotransmitters like serotonin, toxins and other signals play a role in mediating nausea and vomiting by activating this zone); so by antagonizing serotonin 5HT 3 receptors there, ondansetron work to suppress nausea and vomiting

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Ondansetron also work peripherally by antagonizing the serotonin 5HT 3 receptors in the vagus nerve terminals; vagus nerve can sense nausea and vomiting triggers in the GI tract and delivering sensations to nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem (another region important in vomiting), so by blocking vagus nerve sensation, nausea and vomiting are suppressed

Most of ondansetron antiemetic effect is coming from the peripheral 5HT 3 receptor antagonism with a minor contribution coming from the central antagonism

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved therapeutic uses:

Prevention of chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting (first line)

Treatment of Radiation induced nausea and vomiting (first line)

Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (first line)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

Off label use:

Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy, According to ACOG, pyridoxine alone or combined with doxylamine is the preferred pharmacological therapy for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy but in refractory cases, ondansetron 4 mg orally every 8 hours maybe considered; ondansetron is pregnancy category B medication

Acute treatment of cyclic vomiting syndrome

For treatment of severe refractory diarrhea associated with neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid syndrome)

In treatment of nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis

In treatment of irritable bowel syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pharmacokinetics

Ondansetron is available as oral, IM, and IV formulations

Oral formula is rapidly absorbed from the GI tract, with 60% bioavailability

It is metabolized by CYP enzymes in the liver and excreted through kidney with a half life around 4 hours

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Adverse effects

Most commonly side effects include headaches, fatigue, dry mouth, malaise, diarrhea and constipation

Less common side effects include drowsiness, sedation, local injection site reactions and pruritus

Ondansetron may lead to a hepatocellular pattern of elevation in liver enzymes and rare cases of acute liver injury

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Ondansetron may lead to ECG changes such as QT interval prolongation => this may lead to torsade de pointes arrhythmias and other types of arrhythmias; IV administration has a higher risk for causing these effects; FDA does not recommend a single dose higher than 16 mg IV to prevent those effects

There is reported cases of bradycardia and asystole with this medication

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Adverse effects

Ondansetron impair gut motility to some degree that why there is reported cases of intestinal obstruction (rare)

It may also lead to SJS in some patients

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Drug- Drug interactions

Concurrent administration with pimozide with ondansetron should be avoided because both lead to QT interval prolongation, amiodarone and other torsadogenic drugs may do the same

Ondansetron may lead to serotonin syndrome if co administered with other serotonergic medications

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reactions to the drug

ondansetron is contraindicated in patients on apomorphine => this can lead to profound hypotension and loss of consciousness with ondansetron enhancing the hypotensive effect of apomorphine

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Monitoring

Electrolytes and ECG monitoring are suggested in patients treated with ondansetron who have high risk for arrhythmia; such as family history of prolonged QT interval, heart failure, electrolyte disturbance

bAt1Uc_SES0.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Metoclopramide

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Drug- Drug interactions

Contraindications

Intropin (Mark Oniffrey), CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of action

Metoclopramide work as antiemetic (anti nausea and vomiting) by antagonizing central Dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (which is part of the medulla oblongata of the brainstem) => this will inhibit nausea and vomiting triggered by most stimuli

At high doses, metoclopramide also antagonizes serotonin 5 HT3 receptors which also contribute to its antiemetic effect

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Metoclopramide also work as a prokinetic medication, prokinetic means drug that enhance motility of the upper GIT; Metoclopramide achieves that by:

It blocks the peripheral Dopamine D2 receptors => increase the amplitude and duration of esophageal contractions, this also increases the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter and relaxes the pyloric sphincter and duodenal bulb

increasing the muscarinic activation which also lead to increase GI motility

It also work as serotonin 5 HT4 receptor agonist which also lead to increase GI motility

metoclopramide prokinetic effect also contribute to its antiemetic effect

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved for:

Treatment of GERD in patients who fail to respond to life style modification and PPI

Treatment of nausea and vomiting in diabetic gastroparesis

IV metoclopramide is used in Treatment of nausea and vomiting in chemotherapy patients

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

It is used off label

Prophylactic prevention of nausea and vomiting in postoperative patients when nasogastric suctioning is contraindicated or unavailable

Treatment of nausea and vomiting and reduces headache intensity in acute migraines attacks in emergency settings

Treatment of nausea and vomiting in Hyperemesis gravidarum in pregnant patients, according to ACOG it is indicated for refractory cases because it can cross placenta and lead to methemoglobinemia and extrapyramidal signs in neonates

Treatment of nausea and vomiting in critically ill advanced liver disease patients

Treatment of Diamond-Blackfan anemia, metoclopramide hypothesized to stimulate erythropoiesis through induction of prolactin release in these patients

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pharmacokinetics

It is available as oral, rectal, intraperitoneal, nasal spray, IM and IV formulations, the last two options reserved for severe cases

Oral formulation is well absorbed with peak plasma concentrations reached after 1 to 2 hr. of oral administration

Half life is 4.5- 9 hr.

It is metabolized by CYP2D6, glucuronidation and sulfate conjugation and excreted through urine

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Adverse effects

Metoclopramide may lead to extrapyramidal side effects due to the central blocking of the dopamine D2 receptors; extrapyramidal symptoms include:

Tremor: shaking movements

Rigidity (hypertonia): resistance to passive movement

Dystonia: sustained muscle contractions (most common drug induced movement disorder)

Akathisia: inability to remain still

Dyskinesia: involuntary repetitive muscle movement, that occur with long term treatment; that is why metoclopramide advised to be used for less than 12 weeks

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Metoclopramide may lead to hyperprolactinemia which is also caused by the central dopamine D2 receptor blockade; hyperprolactinemia may present as gynecomastia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, impotence and hypogonadism

Metoclopramide may lead to neuroleptic malignant syndrome; which Present as autonomic disturbance in form of muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, high blood pressure, sweating and myoglobinemia; it is a serious complication with 20% mortality rate; to treat this, drug should be discontinued and dantrolene (help to relax muscles) is administered

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Adverse effects

In patients with G6PD deficiency or nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, metoclopramide can cause methemoglobinemia and sulfhemoglobinemia because metoclopramide increases oxidative stress

Metoclopramide can increase the serum aldosterone level leading to fluid retention and volume overload due to activation of RAAS by metoclopramide

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Adverse effects

Metoclopramide may lead to development of a purpuric rash not related to thrombocytopenia; it subsides once the drug is discontinued

Metoclopramide may lead to laxative effect in addition to its prokinetic effect leading to diarrhea (less common and occur mostly in children)

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Adverse effects

Metoclopramide may affect the mood and lead to psychiatric adverse effects because of its antagonist effect on 5 HT3 and agonist effect on 5 HT4 => agitation, irritability, abnormal behaviors, panic disorders, major depressive disorder and agoraphobia (rare)

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Drug- Drug interactions

Reduced efficacy of dopamine agonists e.g. bromocriptine and cabergoline since metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors

Concurrent administration of metoclopramide with antipsychotic drugs should be avoided because both lead to Dopamine receptors blockage and this would lead to additive effects and side effects (especially neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

Efficacy of metoclopramide is reduced if it is taken with anticholinergics or opioids because both slow gastric emptying

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Drug- Drug interactions

Oral metoclopramide increase serum aspirin levels due to increased absorption of aspirin (may lead to salicylate toxicity); same can happen with bupropion and cyclosporin ;; it also may decrease the absorption of some other medication e.g. digoxin

Metoclopramide shouldn’t be used with CYP2D6 inhibitors medications (e.g. fluoxetine) because this would inhibit metoclopramide metabolism => higher drug levels => higher risk for side effects

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Contraindications

Metoclopramide is contraindicated in patient with history of hypersensitivity reactions to the medication

It is contraindicated in suspected bowel obstruction or perforation, and in GI hemorrhage

It is also contraindicated in patients with clinical depression

It is contraindicated in patients with seizure disorders because it lower the seizure threshold

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Contraindications

It is contraindicated in Parkinson disease

It is contraindicated in patients with pheochromocytoma because it enhance the release of catecholamines and may lead to hypertensive crisis

US boxed warning: metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia (serious movement disorder), therefore avoid treatment for longer than 12 weeks

Misoprostol

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Pharmacokinetics

Adverse effects

Contraindications

Klaas `Z4us` van B. V, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of action

Misoprostol is a synthetic PG E1 analog

It work through direct stimulation of PG E1 receptor on the stomach parietal cell => inhibition of basal and nocturnal gastric acid secretion

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Misoprostol increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion and improves mucosal blood flow leading to faster healing of PUD

Misoprostol also binds to smooth muscle cells of the uterine lining leading to uterotonic effects, it also promote cervical ripening and dilation

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic uses

Misoprostol is FDA approved for prevention and treatment of NSAIDs induced PUD in patient taking NSAIDs and are at high risk for PUD (PPIs are preferred because they are better tolerated)

Misoprostol is used off label for short term treatment of active PUD caused by other factors; it is used for short term only because of the GI adverse effects and frequent dosing which is hard for patients to adhere to (200 mcg four times daily)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

A combination of misoprostol 200 mcg and mifepristone 200mg is FDA approved for medical abortions up to 70 days gestation; and misoprostol alone is indicated if mifepristone is unavailable

Misoprostol 800 mcg is used off label to terminate pregnancy in second trimester as monotherapy or combined with IM methotrexate

Misoprostol also used off label for expectant management of missed and incomplete abortions; and at much smaller doses for induction of labor 25 mcg and in treatment of postpartum hemorrhage 1000 mcg if other uterotonic meds not available

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Pharmacokinetics

Misoprostol is available as oral formulations, it is absorbed rapidly after administration, onset of action in 30 min and for 3 hours duration

Misoprostol is a prodrug, it is metabolized into active metabolite (misoprostol acid) and excreted as inactive metabolites in urine

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Adverse effects

Most common ADRs include diarrhea and abdominal pain secondary to exposure to misoprostol acid released during its metabolism

Fever and chills are also common and secondary to PG effect on the hypothalamus

Other common ADRs: nausea, vomiting, constipation, dyspepsia, headache, menstrual irregularities and breakthrough bleeding, lethargy, weakness and vertigo

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Less common ADRs: hypotension, sinus tachycardia, edema, MI (due to misoprostol induced vasospasm especially in patients with CVS disease), PE, anaphylactic reactions and thrombosis

If given to a pregnant woman: fetal bradycardia and death, uterine contractions and pain, vaginal bleeding, uterine rupture (highest risk if given beyond 8 weeks of gestation) , cervical lacerations and teratogenesis

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Contraindications

Contraindicated in pregnant women and women in child bearing age, if it has to be given then serum pregnancy test should be done and it has to be negative

Previous allergic reactions

SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Sucralfate

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Pharmacokinetics

Adverse effects

Drug-Drug interactions

Contraindications

Natalia Matallana, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Sucralfate

Sucralfate is anti ulcer drugs, it is an aluminum with the sucrose octa sulfate

Vaccinationist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Sucralfate doesn’t have a buffering or antisecretory effect against acid BUT it forms a protective coat and protects the gastric and duodenal mucosa from pepsin, HCl and bile salts

The protective coat is formed when the sucralfate binds to positively charged proteins in exudates

Natalia Matallana, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

Sucralfate also increase mucous production (by increasing prostaglandin production), also increase mucus viscosity, sulfation and aluminum and carbohydrate contents and prevent mucus breakdown by pepsin => leading to better mucosal protection from acid

Sucralfate increases prostaglandin production leading to higher bicarbonate production by the stomach and duodenum (bicarbonate work to neutralize the acid)

Sucralfate also increases the binding of epidermal growth and tissue growth factors to the tissues leading to angiogenesis and better tissue repair

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

It is FDA approved for treatment of duodenal ulcers, its efficacy for this use is comparable to the efficacy of H2 blockers

Off label uses include:

Gastric ulcers

Dyspepsia: same efficacy as H2 blockers

Epithelial wounds: used as a topical drug in treatment of ulcers (including oral ulcers in Behçet disease), inflammatory dermatitis, mucositis (including chemotherapy induced mucositis) and burn wounds

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Therapeutic uses

Off label uses also include:

Radiation proctitis by using sucralfate enema

prevention of ulceration in diversion colitis

Stress ulcer prophylaxis

GERD

Sucralfate is used in treatment of peptic ulcer disease not related to NSAIDs use; because NSAIDs lead to over secretion of acid which is best treated with antisecretory drugs (PPIs and H2 blockers)

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Pharmacokinetics

Sucralfate is available as oral, rectal and topical formulas

Only 5% is absorbed from the oral formula, onset of action after 1 hour of administration with up to 6 hours duration of action

It is broken down into aluminum and sucrose octa sulfate in the GI tract, it is not metabolized by the kidney or liver

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

The most common adverse effect is constipation which is seen in up to 10% of patients

Hyperglycemia is seen in diabetic patients using this med

Other adverse effects include: nausea and vomiting, flatulence, headache, dry mouth, pruritis, skin rash, formation of undigested and partially digested materials in the stomach, aluminum toxicity and hypophosphatemia

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Adverse effects

If this medication is administered IV by mistake, it may lead to fatal complications such as pulmonary emboli and cerebral edema

Use of this medication in patients with renal failure may lead to aluminum toxicity (use with caution)

Aluminum toxicity present with non specific symptoms such as proximal muscle weakness, bone pain, fractures and changes in mental state

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Drug interactions

Sucralfate if administered at the same time with the following medications, it decreases their concentrations:

Digoxin

Levothyroxine

Furosemide

Quinolones

Oral phosphate supplements

Warfarin

Antivirals

Bisphosphonates

Pheytoin

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Drug interactions

There has to be a 2 hour gap between administration of sucralfate and any of these medications

Antacids administered within 15 minutes of sucralfate can reduce its efficacy because sucralfate requires acidic environment to work

Multivitamins can increase its serum concentrations

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Contraindications

Absolute: documented hypersensitivity reactions

Relative: uncontrolled diabetes, impaired swallowing and end stage renal disease

Hu5-Bv_eVJU.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Pharmacokinetics

Adverse effects

W.carter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of Action

PPIs decrease acid secretion in the stomach by inhibiting the H/K ATPase (the proton pump) in the parietal cells

Meaning they inhibit the final step of acid secretion and that is why they have the highest efficacy in suppressing acid secretion

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Proton Pump Inhibitors

FDA approved PPIs include:

Omeprazole

Esomeprazole

Lansoprazole

Dexlansoprazole

Pantoprazole

Rabeprazole

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic Uses

PPIs are used as a first line for treatment of:

Peptic ulcer disease

Esophagitis

GERD

Prevention of NSAIDs induced PUD

Zollinger Ellison syndrome

In H. Pylori triple therapy

Off label uses include in patients on antiplatelet therapy before or after endoscopy procedure (high risk for bleeding)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pharmacokinetics

They are available as oral and IV formulations, and they are best administered before food intake

PPIs are prodrugs, they are activated after undergoing an acid catalyzed cleavage in the acidic secretory canaliculi of the parietal cells in the stomach

PPIs are metabolized by hepatic CYP2C19 enzyme, higher blood levels in patients from Asian ethnicities and in elderly patients

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Adverse effects

Common adverse effects include: headache, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue and dizziness

Infrequent adverse effects include: rash, constipation, anxiety, depression and myopathies

Rarely it may lead to hypomagnesemia, in this case magnesium level can’t be replenished by supplementation so PPIs has to be discontinued; hypomagnesemia present as tetany, seizure, muscle weakness, delirium and cardiac arrhythmias

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Adverse effects

Infection: acidic environment act as a chemical barrier against bacterial infections, PPIs suppress acid secretion leading to increased risk of C difficile infections, other enteric infections and CAP

Rebound acid secretion: prolonged acid suppression lead to increased levels of gastrin and histamine which when the PPIs are discontinued, they act to increase acid secretion to levels higher than before initiation of PPIs treatment

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Vit B12 deficiency with prolonged use: due to interference with IF secretion by the stomach (it needs acidic environment to be secreted)

Iron, calcium, magnesium deficiencies all due to lack of acid (because acid is important for breakdown of foods and release of micronutrients)

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Monitoring

On prolonged use, Magnesium level and vit B12 level have to be monitored

7VjKp18wQOo.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Histamine H2 Receptor Antagonists

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Pharmacokinetics

Adverse effects

Benjah-bmm27, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of Action

H2 receptor antagonists work by suppressing gastric acid secretion by competitively antagonizing the histamine H2 receptors located on gastric parietal cells

SOURCE SLIDE 3

H2 Blockers

FDA approved H2 blockers include:

Cimetidine

Famotidine

Nizatidine

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic uses

H2 blockers are FDA approved for:

Short term treatment of uncomplicated GERD

Gastric and duodenal ulcers (PPI is first line)

Mild to infrequent heartburn or indigestion

Off label uses include:

Stress ulcer prophylaxis (e.g. in trauma and burn patients) (PPI is first line)

Esophagitis and gastritis treatment (PPI is first line)

In GI hemorrhage treatment (PPI is first line)

Urticaria

H. Pylori eradication therapy (PPI is first line)

Heartburn during pregnancy (Antacids are first line)

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Pharmacokinetics

H2 blockers are available as oral fromulations and they have good absorption after oral administration

Onset of action start in about an hour after administration and duration of action is from 4- 10 hours

All of them have the same efficacy in decreasing gastric acid secretion

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Adverse effects

H2 Blockers are generally well tolerated

Adverse effects include:

Hypotension

Headache

Drowsiness

Fatigue

Abdominal pain

Constipation or diarrhea

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Adverse effects

Cimetidine and famotidine may lead to CNS side effects in patients older than 50, those include:

Delirium

Confusion

Hallucination

Slurred speech

Prolonged and high doses of cimetidine are linked with development of gynecomastia, reduced sperm count and impotence in men; galactorrhea in women; this is solved with drug discontinuation

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Tolerance and tachyphylaxis occur within 7 to 14 days of continued treatment

That is why intermittent or as needed use is preferred for these medications

Small bowel bacterial overgrowth or C. difficile infection can occur with these medications but it is rare

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Drug interactions

Cimetidine is a potent CYP P450 enzyme inhibitor, it raises the levels of medications that are metabolized by CYP, e.g. theophylline, SSRI and warfarin

SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Antacids

Types

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Interactions

Midnightcomm, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Types of antacids

Aluminum hydroxide

Calcium salts

Magnesium salts

Sodium bicarbonate

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Aluminum Hydroxide

Aluminum hydroxide work as antacids by neutralizing stomach acid and it also inhibit pepsin proteolytic activity leading to alleviation of heartburn, ulcer healing and pyloric spasm relief

In addition to its use as antacids; Aluminum hydroxide is also combined with sulfated polysaccharide sucrose octasulfate to form sucralfate (which help healing peptic ulcers by reducing pepsin and acid contact with the ulcer)

It is also used in treatment of hyperphosphatemia because of its ability to bind phosphate in the GI tract

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Calcium carbonate

Calcium carbonate work as antacids by neutralizing stomach acid, they also inhibit pepsin proteolytic activity and increase lower esophageal sphincter tone

The calcium released work also to increase esophageal peristalsis pushing the acid in the stomach and providing relief from the heartburn symptoms

Calcium salts also bind dietary phosphate and prevent its absorption

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

Antacids are over the counter meds and currently their use is restricted to relieving mild intermittent GERD (gives heartburn symptoms)

Previously antacids were the first line treatment for peptic ulcer disease, but when the PPIs got discovered, antacids stopped being used for PUD

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Adverse effects

Calcium carbonate may lead to:

Hypercalcemia

Abdominal pain

Anorexia

Acid rebound

Nausea and vomiting

Flatulence

Dry mouth

Headache

Hypophosphatemia

Milk alkali syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Milk alkali syndrome

Milk alkali syndrome is a triad of elevated calcium levels, metabolic alkalosis, and acute kidney injury

It is associated with consumption of large quantities of milk and calcium carbonate for peptic ulcer disease treatment especially in osteoporotic patients with CKD

If not treated, it may lead to AKI and metastatic calcification

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse effects

Antacids containing magnesium may cause diarrhea while antacids containing calcium or aluminum may cause constipation

Antacids overuse may lead to acid rebound

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Adverse effects

Aluminum is a heavy metal, its use in individuals with renal failure and infants is associated with increased risk of toxicity

Aluminum toxicity present as: osteopenia, microcytic anemia, neurotoxicity, osteomalacia, constipation, fecal impaction, nausea and vomiting, abdominal cramps, hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Drug interactions

Antacids impair the absorption of acidic drugs (e.g. digoxin, chlorpromazine and isoniazid) leading to reduction in their blood concentrations and failure of therapy

Antacids can increase the absorption of some drugs (e.g. pseudoephedrine and levodopa) leading to potential toxicity and adverse effects

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Drug interactions

Antacids containing magnesium slats can bind to drugs like tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics preventing their absorption

Sodium bicarbonate increase urine PH, which can alter renal elimination of some drugs; leading to inhibition of elimination of basic drugs and increase elimination of acidic drugs

outline.summary: Antacids impair the absorption of acidic drugs (e.g. digoxin, chlorpromazine and isoniazid) leading to reduction in their blood concentrations and failure of therapy Antacids can increase the absorption of some drugs (e.g. pseudoephedrine and levodopa) leading to potential toxicity and adverse effects

outline.heading: Drug interactions
outline.summary: Antacids containing magnesium slats can bind to drugs like tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics preventing their absorption Sodium bicarbonate increase urine PH, which can alter renal elimination of some drugs; leading to inhibition of elimination of basic drugs and increase elimination of acidic drugs

Mucoactive medications

Definition

Classification

Therapeutic uses

N-Acetylcysteine

Bromhexine

Guaifenesin

Carbocysteine

Patrick Pelletier, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Mucoactive medications are medications that aid in the clearance of mucus from the airways

http://www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Mucoactive drugs are classified into:

Mucolytics: reduce the viscosity of the mucus by breaking down the chemical bonds between molecules of the mucus; e.g. N acetylcysteine and bromhexine

Expectorants (secretolytics) increase volume of airway secretions making them easier to expel through coughing; e.g. guaifenesin

Mucokinetics: increase ciliary transport of mucus. E.g. bronchodilators and surfactant

Mucoregulators: suppress underlying mechanisms of mucus hypersecretion. E.g. Carbocysteine

Some of these medications work by multiple mechanisms

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Therapeutic uses

These medications are used in treatment of productive cough in respiratory diseases that are complicated by over secretion or higher viscosity of mucus such COPD, Asthma and cystic fibrosis

Mucoactive agents are used in treatment of productive cough while antitussives are used in treatment of dry cough

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Therapeutic uses

It is important to confirm the diagnosis before giving these medications; because most common cause for productive cough is infections and these medications may aggravate infections

Because the mucus layer entraps and clear bacteria and inhibit bacterial growth and biofilm formation . It also protect the airway from inhaled irritants and fluid loss

SOURCE SLIDE 6

N- Acetylcysteine

Acetylcysteine is a mucolytic, it has free sulfhydryl (-SH) groups that break disulfide bonds that connect the mucin oligomers in the mucus leading to reduction in mucus viscosity; it also has anti inflammatory and antioxidant properties

N acetylcysteine is FDA approved for treatment of abnormal viscid or inspissated mucous secretions in pneumonia, bronchitis, cystic fibrosis, postoperative pulmonary complications, tracheostomy patients…; it is also FDA approved for treatment of paracetamol toxicity

SOURCE SLIDE 7

N- Acetylcysteine

N acetyl cysteine is available as oral, IV and inhalational formulations

According to the American college of chest physicians; oral NAC is recommended for patients with moderate to severe COPD to prevent exacerbations

NAC adverse effects: GIT symptoms with oral NAC, anaphylactic reactions (e.g. bronchospasm) with IV NAC because it triggers histamine release; treat with anti histamine meds

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Bromhexine

Bromhexine acts on the mucus at the formative stages within the mucus secreting cells. It disrupts the structure of acid mucopolysaccharide fibers in mucoid sputum and produces a less viscous mucus which is easy to expel

Because bromhexine can disrupt the gastric mucosal barrier, it should be avoided in patients with peptic ulcer

Bromhexine also may lead to headache, vertigo, sweating and allergic reactions

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Guaifenesin

Guaifenesin act as an expectorant by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle tone and by irritating the respiratory tract leading to increasing the volume of fluid secreted in there => more fluid inside the mucus => mucus easier to expel

Guaifenesin available as capsules and syrup used in treatment of productive cough

Guaifenesin may lead to headache, drowsiness, diarrhea and insomnia

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Carbocysteine

Carbocysteine suppress underlying mechanisms of mucus hypersecretion and increases fluid volume inside the mucus

It is very effective and safe; it is used especially in Asthma and COPD

Carbocysteine may lead to allergic side effects

brQi0DrlKDI.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

In This Video

Cough suppressants

Definition

Classification

Mechanism of action

Dextromethorphan

Codeine

Benzonatate

Mos.ru, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Cough suppressants (Antitussives) are drugs that reduce the frequency or intensity of cough

They are used in patients who have dry cough

Mucolytics and expectorants is what is used in treatment of productive cough

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Classification

Central antitussives: e.g. Dextromethorphan and Codeine

Peripheral antitussives: e.g. Benzonatate, camphor, menthol, water steam inhalation

Dextromethorphan is what most commonly used out of all the antitussives

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

Cough is produced through stimulation of sensory receptors of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, which innervate the mucous membranes in the lower pharynx, larynx, trachea and smaller airways of the respiratory system

These sensory receptors transmit the signal to the cough center in the brain which triggers the cough reflex which result in contraction of vocal cords to close the glottis and contraction of the respiratory muscles => this result in sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure followed by relaxation of the vocal cords resulting in fast expulsion of air

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Mechanism of action

Centrally acting agents such as dextromethorphan and opioids work by inhibiting the cough center in the brain

Peripheral acting agents work by anesthetizing the sensory nerve endings in the throat, trachea and small airways

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Dextromethorphan

FDA approved over the counter cough suppressant that works centrally by inhibiting the cough center by unknown mechanism

Dextromethorphan is a synthetic analog of codeine but it does not have direct action on the opioid receptors, so it doesn’t produce the classic opioid CNS effects or side effects

Available as a syrup and liquid filled capsules

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Dextromethorphan

Dextromethorphan may lead to nausea and GIT discomfort, hallucinations and nystagmus and dizziness

In high doses it may lead to euphoria

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Codeine

Codeine is an opioid that is FDA approved for treatment of pain only; and its use as a cough suppressant is an off label use

Codeine work as an agonist on the opioid receptors and it inhibit the cough center

It is available as tablets taken orally

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Codeine

It has a lot of adverse effects same as with the other opioids; those include constipation, nausea, vomiting, sedation, euphoria, CNS depression (especially in children, that is why it has FDA warning not to be used for cough in patients < 12), urinary retention, bronchospasm, tremor, weakness …

For its use as a cough suppressants it is given in lower doses than those required for analgesia so it produces less side effects

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Benzonatate

It is peripherally acting cough suppressant; there is multiple studies that found that there is inadequate evidence to support effectiveness of safety of this medication in treatment of cough

It is thought to work by inhibiting the stretch receptors in the lungs leading to suppression of the cough reflex, it is structurally related to procaine

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Benzonatate

Benzonatate may lead to sleepiness, dizziness, headache, GIT discomfort, hallucinations and allergic reactions

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Video contents

Fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) drugs:

Physiological fibrinolysis

Fibrinolytic drugs

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Monitoring and toxicity

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Physiological Fibrinolysis

When a pathogenic fibrin clot is formed inside the human body, plasminogen gets in contact with this clot

Then Plasminogen becomes activated into plasmin by the help of tissue plasminogen activators (tPAs) released from the tissues around the clot

Plasmin causes the clot to dissolve

Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Physiological Fibrinolysis

These endogenous tissue plasminogen activators, bind selectively to the fibrin in the formed thrombus and avoid systemic activation of plasminogen

This process is slow, it takes several days to weeks until the clot fully dissolved

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Fibrinolytic Drugs

In some situations, like in acute MI, we need rapid plasminogen activation to dissolve the clots blocking the coronary arteries and improve blood flow to save the heart from dying

And that is when the fibrinolytic drugs came into use

Fibrinolytic drugs cause rapid activation of plasminogen to form plasmin and clot will dissolve in few minutes

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Fibrinolytic Drugs

BUT these medications activate both fibrin bound plasminogen and circulating plasminogen

This lead to dissolution of both pathogenic thrombi and protective hemostatic thrombi, leading to high risk of bleeding

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Fibrinolytic (Thrombolytic) Drugs

Streptokinase

Urokinase

Alteplase

Tenecteplase

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Streptokinase

Streptokinase is a protein that is isolated from streptococci bacteria, it works by converting plasminogen into plasmin indirectly

It works by binding to circulating plasminogen, to form a complex that convert additional plasminogen into active plasmin

It has lower efficacy compared to alteplase

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Streptokinase

It may cause allergy, fever and hypotension in some people

It is relatively cheap and it is the most widely used fibrinolytic med

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Urokinase

Urokinase is a protease that is formed normally inside the kidney to prevent clotting inside the kidney tubules, it is prepared as a recombinant for medical use

It has less incidence of allergy in comparison to streptokinase

It works on both fibrin bound plasminogen and circulating plasminogen leading to high risk of bleeding associated with its use

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Alteplase and Tenecteplase

Those are human tPAs obtained by recombinant DNA technology

Alteplase and Tenecteplase have a low affinity for circulating plasminogen in the plasma, but it rapidly activates plasminogen bound to fibrin in a thrombus or a hemostatic plug

Alteplase has a very short half life (30 minutes), that is why a portion is injected as bolus then the rest is given by continuous infusion; while Tenecteplase have long half life, this permits administration as a bolus IV injection rather than by continuous infusion

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Therapeutic uses of Fibrinolytics

Acute MI, ischemic stroke, massive PE, and arterial thrombosis

Before giving them, check for any contraindications that prevent giving them; so there would be no liability for bleeding

They are not used in DVT and most of the PE treatment due to the high bleeding risk

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Contraindications

Absolute

Recent intracranial hemorrhage (ICH)

Structural cerebral vascular lesion

Intracranial neoplasm

Ischemic stroke within three months

Possible aortic dissection

Active bleeding or bleeding diathesis (excluding menses)

Significant head injury or facial trauma within three months

Recent Intracranial or spinal surgery

Severe uncontrolled hypertension

For streptokinase, previous treatment within six months

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Contraindications

Relative

History of severe and poorly controlled hypertension

Severe hypertension at presentation (systolic blood pressure >180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >110mmHg)

Prolonged (>10 minutes) cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or major surgery within three weeks.

History of ischemic stroke.

Dementia

Internal bleeding within 2 to 4 weeks

Noncompressible vascular punctures

Pregnancy

Active peptic ulcer

Concurrent therapy of anticoagulants is associated with an elevated international normalized ratio (INR) higher than 1.7 or a prothrombin time (PT) longer than 15 seconds

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Adverse effects

Bleeding: risk is higher with streptokinase and urokinase

Streptokinase may lead to allergy, fever and hypotension

Alteplase may cause angioedema, especially if combined with ACE

Reperfusion arrhythmia if used in MI

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Monitoring

Patient receiving fibrinolytic therapy should undergo constant neurologic and cardiovascular evaluation and blood pressure every 15 minutes during treatment infusion and after for at least 2 hours

Then half hourly for 6 hours and hourly for 16 hours after injection

Treatment should stop when there is signs of neurologic deterioration or bleeding

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Treatment of bleeding

FFP or cryoprecipitate can help refurbish clotting factors

Antifibrinolytic drugs like aminocaproic acid or tranexamic acid can be used to reverse the fibrinolytics effects

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Video content

In this video, I will talk about the LMWH, topics that will be covered include:

Pharmacokinetics

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Monitoring

Adverse effects

Contraindications

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Intro

LMWH are classified as anticoagulant medications

Unfractionated heparin is a mixture of different molecular weight fractions (5000- 40000 Da) that can work on multiple coagulation factors and produce multiple side effects (e.g. thrombocytopenia)

LMWH is the fractions of heparin that works on factor X only, molecular weight of these fractions is less than 8000 Da; this lead to minimal effects on PLT and other clotting factors

Whispyhistory, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

LMWH examples

Dalteparin

Enoxaparin (Levonex, Clexan)

Frank C. Müller, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Pharmacokinetics

LMWH available as SC formulas

SC bioavailability is better than the unfractionated heparin (UFH binds to subcutaneous tissue more than LMWH)

Half life of LMWH is long enough to allow for once daily dosing while UFH half life is short, that’s why it is giving 3 times daily

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Mechanism of action

LMWH bind to antithrombin III and activate it to inhibit factor Xa

SteveKong3, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Therapeutic uses

Prophylaxis against DVT in medium and high risk groups

Treatment of venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

Used in the treatment of DVT, PE

Treatment of STEMI

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Therapeutic uses

Unstable angina

Prevention of clotting in extracorporeal circuits

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Monitoring

LMWH doesn’t require monitoring but if needed (in patients at extremes of weight or in renal dysfunction), it is by anti factor Xa assay

In comparison with the UFH, which need continuous monitoring with the APTT

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Adverse effects

Bleeding: risk for bleeding with LMWH is much less compared to the UFH

Thrombocytopenia: much less common in LMWH compared to UFH

Osteoporosis and spontaneous fractures especially on long term use

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Adverse effects

Hypersensitivity reactions

Hypoaldosteronism

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Antidote

Protamine sulfate work as an antidote but it is weaker in comparison with its work on UFH

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Contraindications

Trauma

Hemorrhagic disorders

Peptic ulcer disease

Recent cerebral hemorrhage

Severe hypertension

Recent surgery to the eye or the brain

History of heparin induced thrombocytopenia

In this video, I will compare the heparin against the warfarin, the topics of the comparison will include:

Source and chemistry

Pharmacokinetics

Mechanism of action

Pharmacological effects

Therapeutic uses

Monitoring of effects

Adverse effects

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Source and Chemistry

Table from slide 2
Heparin Warfarin
Natural sulfated polysaccharide present in mast cells

Carries negative charge

Commercial preparations are derived from bovine lung or porcine intestinal extracts and there is synthetic ones 		- Synthetic coumarin compound
SOURCE SLIDE 3

Pharmacokinetics

Table from slide 3
Heparin Warfarin
Absorption It can’t be absorbed by the GIT because it gets precipitated by the gastric HCL It can be absorbed and it is well absorbed with 100% bioavailability
Available formulas IV and SC Oral only
Distribution Cannot pass cross BBB or placenta Can cross both BBB and placenta
SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

Before we explain the mechanism of action for these medications, first we have to understand some vital points about the coagulation cascade:

SteveKong3, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Dr Graham Beards, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Mechanism of action

Unfractionated heparin works by activating the antithrombin III (natural clotting inhibitor available in plasma)

Antithrombin III work to inhibit several clotting factors especially factor X and factor II

SteveKong3, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Mechanism of action

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase enzyme in the liver leading to inhibition of the formation of the active form of vitamin K

This will lead to inhibition of the synthesis of vitamin K dependent clotting factors (X, IX, VII, and II)

The action of warfarin can be antagonized by vit K

SteveKong3, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Onset and duration of clinical effects

Table from slide 8
Heparin Warfarin
Rapid onset of action if given IV, and onset in 1-2 hours if given SC

It has short duration (2-4 hours) 		Delayed onset of action 24-72 hours after administration, this is the time needed for depletion of vit k and vit k dependent clotting factors

Long duration of action (2- 5 days), until the liver produce the depleted vit K and coagulation factors
SOURCE SLIDE 9

Pharmacological effects

Table from slide 9
Heparin Warfarin
Anticoagulation in vivo and in vitro

Stimulates lipoprotein lipase which lead to decrease serum triglycerides 		Anticoagulation in vivo only
SOURCE SLIDE 10

Therapeutic uses

Table from slide 10
Heparin Warfarin
Heparin is indicated for prevention and treatment of thrombotic events (to prevent thrombus propagation in established thrombosis) such as DVT, PE, AF, ACS; it can also be used to prevent coagulation during cardiac surgery, PCI, extracorporeal circulation and dialysis

Dosing is variable but it is common to start with a bolus dose of 80 units/Kg IV then maintained by 18 units/kg/h; Dosing in ACS and stroke is much lower because there is higher risk of bleeding 		Warfarin is indicated for prophylaxis and treatment (treatment means prevent thrombus propagation in established thrombosis) of DVT, PE, AF or cardiac valve replacement

Warfarin is also indicated in reduction in risk of death in recurrent MI, and thromboembolic events (e.g. stroke, systemic embolization) after MI

Given orally 2- 10 mg/day
SOURCE SLIDE 11

Monitoring of therapy

Table from slide 11
Heparin Warfarin
By activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)

APTT checked at baseline and then every 6 hours until 2 or more therapeutic values are obtained then it is checked every 24 hours

Dose titration is according to the APTT

Monitoring for adverse effects includes Hb, hematocrit (bleeding), PLT and vital signs 		By prothrombin time (PT) or international normalized ratio (INR)

INR is preferred over PT

INR value in patient without anticoagulation is 1

INR is monitored serially until the required therapeutic value is reached

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Adverse effects

Table from slide 12
Heparin Warfarin
Bleeding: very dangerous, e.g. intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleeding, intraocular bleeding, hemarthrosis…
bleeding could be treated with:
Immediate stopping of the medication
Fresh frozen plasma: to replace the clotting factors
Protamine sulfate: protamine carries a positive charge that bind to the heparin which have a negative charge to form a stable complex; 1 mg of protamine can bind to 100 U of heparin
Bleeding: very dangerous, e.g. intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleeding, intraocular bleeding, hemarthrosis…
bleeding could be treated with:
Immediate stopping of the medication
Fresh frozen plasma: to replace the clotting factors
Vitamin K: 10 mg slowly IV or IM to enhance synthesis of clotting factors
SOURCE SLIDE 13

Adverse effects

Table from slide 13
Heparin Warfarin
Heparin can’t be given IM but if it is given , it will lead to hematoma formation

Thrombocytopenia: there are 2 types of thrombocytopenia associated with heparin use, the first type is non immunogenic interaction with PLT that occur within the first 48-72 hours of initiation of heparin therapy, this is temporary drop in PLT and will recover once heparin is stopped; the second type is much more serious known as heparin induced thrombocytopenia and this is immune mediated reactions against PLT occur 5 days after heparin initiation and it can lead to thrombosis e.g. PE, DVT, stroke , MI… (HITT)
Warfarin may also lead to GI side effects like nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain

Hemorrhagic skin necrosis: when starting warfarin, biosynthesis of protein C is reduced leading to temporary procoagulant state. This can lead to hemorrhagic infarction of skin, breast, intestine and fatty tissue. Normally avoided by concurrent heparin administration

Purple toe syndrome: characterized by cholesterol microembolization that causes purple lesions to develop on the toes and sides of feet
SOURCE SLIDE 14

Adverse effects

Table from slide 14
Heparin Warfarin
Other heparin adverse effects include hyperkalemia, alopecia and osteoporosis (with long term use)
Teratogenicity: abnormal bone formation in early pregnancy (fetal warfarin syndrome)

CNS hemorrhage in the fetus if given in late pregnancy

Sudden withdrawal may lead to thrombotic catastrophes
SOURCE SLIDE 15

Anticoagulants contraindications

PLT count < 100 000

Active, uncontrollable bleeding except for DIC

Patient has a history of heparin induced thrombocytopenia can’t be given heparin

Routine monitoring tests can’t be performed for any reason

Threatened abortion, eclampsia or preeclampsia

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Intro

Wellbutrin (Bupropion) is atypical antidepressant medication that is used in the treatment of depression and in smoking cessation.

It works by blocking the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, leading to higher levels of these neurotransmitters available in the neurons synapse

In this video, I will explain the side effects of this medication

Ragesoss assumed (based on copyright claims)., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Cardiovascular side effects

Tachycardia and Higher blood pressure

Higher norepinephrine levels lead to activation of the sympathetic system (fight or flight response) leading to tachycardia and higher blood pressure

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Central nervous system

Insomnia: higher dopamine levels stimulate the brain leading to increase alertness and energy levels leading to insomnia

Headache: changes in neurotransmitter levels can affect brain chemistry leading to headache

Anxiety and agitation: higher levels of norepinephrine and dopamine may lead to anxiety and agitation

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

GIT side effects

Nausea and vomiting

That is because Increased norepinephrine levels also affects the enteric nervous system leading to nausea, vomiting

Also Elevated norepinephrine levels may stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brain leading to nausea and vomiting

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Respiratory side effects

Rhinitis

Pharyngitis

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Diaphoresis

Excessive sweating

Caused by increased body temperature caused by the elevations in norepinephrine levels

Egon Eagle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Dry mouth

Higher norepinephrine levels lead to activation of the sympathetic system (fight or flight response) leading to dry mouth

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Tremor (jitteriness)

Caused by sympathetic nervous system activation

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Weight loss

Higher dopamine levels lead to stimulant effect that can suppress the appetite leading to less food intake and weight loss

SOURCE SLIDE 10

Hepatotoxicity

Bupropion is metabolized in the liver and in some cases it may cause damage to the liver

Symptoms include yellow, skin and eye, itching, upper abdominal pain and dark urine

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Ophthalmologic

Higher risk of Triggering closed angle glaucoma attack

On the other hand, it mya decrease the risk of development of open angle glaucoma

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Seizures

Bupropion Lowers seizure threshold because it alters neurotransmitters concentrations in the brain

The effect is highly dose dependent

SOURCE SLIDE 13

Higher suicide risk

Worsening suicidal ideation especially in people younger than 25 years old

SOURCE SLIDE 14

Psychosis

Hallucinations and delusions

Because it increases the levels of dopamine in the brain

SOURCE SLIDE 15

Trigger mania or hypomania

Especially in patients with bipolar disorders

Chris martin, CC3.0 via Wikimedia commons

SOURCE SLIDE 16

Withdrawal syndrome

Occur where there is abrupt interruptions or sudden withdrawal of the medication

Symptoms include dizziness, insomnia, anxiety, agitation and irritability

fQ5OQIDBqgI.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Intro

Zoloft (Sertraline) is SSRI medication that is used in the treatment of depression, anxiety disorders and panic attacks

It works by blocking the reuptake of serotonin leading to increased serotonin levels in the neurons synapse

It is generally well tolerated by most patients, but sometimes may lead to side effects that will be explained here

Myling, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Random Side effects

Diarrhea

Nausea and abdominal pain

Dry mouth

Lightheadedness

Yawning

Insomnia

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Random Side effects

Dizziness

Excessive Sweating

Confusion

Tremor

Fatigue

Weight gain

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Emotional blunting

Reduced intensity of positive and negative emotions, apathy and decreased motivation

This is dose dependent

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Sexual side effects

Anorgasmia, decreased libido, genital numbness and sexual anhedonia in both genders, erectile dysfunction in males

Mechanism of by which Zoloft causes sexual side effects is not very well understood

Sexual side effects are managed with the use of medications such as sildenafil

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Increased Suicide risk

Higher risk of suicide especially during the first few months of the use of this medication especially in people younger than 25 years old

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Withdrawal syndrome

Occur where there is abrupt interruptions or sudden withdrawal of the medication

Symptoms include dizziness, insomnia, anxiety, agitation and irritability

This might occur even when missing a single dose

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Higher risk for Bipolar switch

This side effect occur in patients with bipolar disorder

Zoloft may precipitate the switch from depression in to hypomania or mania especially when used as monotherapy

the risk of switching is back to normal if Zoloft is taken with mood stabilizers

SOURCE SLIDE 9

Increased bleeding risk

Because it may inhibit platelet aggregation

SOURCE SLIDE 10

QT interval prolongation

QT interval prolongation: this is dose dependent and not that significant compared with other SSRI (citalopram)

SOURCE SLIDE 11

Serotonin syndrome

Caused by increased the serotonin levels

Occurs especially in case of combination of Zoloft with other drugs that elevate the serotonin levels like the TCA, triptans, tramadol, lithium, St John’s wort and tryptophan

Symptoms of serotonin syndrome include altered mental status, autonomic changes such as tachycardia and neuromuscular changes such as tremor, rigidity and myoclonus

SOURCE SLIDE 12

Induce SIADH

This occur especially in patients aged 65 and older

Lead to hyponatremia

This lead to symptoms like muscle pain, headache and disorientation

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Intro

Tofranil (Imipramine) is a tricyclic antidepressant that is used in treatment of depression and anxiety.

it works by blocking the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, it also blocks the muscarinic receptors leading to antimuscarinic effects, and it blocks the alpha 1 and 2 adrenergic and H1 receptors.

In this video, I will talk about the side effects of this medication

Jaroslav A. Polák, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 2

1. Antihistaminic side effects

Dizziness

Sedation

Confusion

Increased appetite and weight gain

http://www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 3

2. Antimuscarinic side effects

Blurred vision

Constipation

Tachycardia

Confusion

Dry mouth

Urinary retention

Cognitive impairment

Narrow angle glaucoma

Paralytic ileus

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

3. Cardiovascular effects

Imipramine effect on the CVS system are due to its blockade of adrenergic receptors and its blockade of the sodium channels in the heart (same as the quinidine medication), those effects include:

Orthostatic hypotension: blockade of alpha 1 adrenergic receptors lead to vasodilatation and reduced BP upon standing

Arrhythmias: caused by direct cardiac sodium channel blockade leading to conduction abnormalities

QT prolongation: due to blockade of cardiac potassium channels

SOURCE SLIDE 5

4. Psychiatric side effects

Mania and hypomania: due to increased levels of norepinephrine and serotonin can precipitate manic episodes

Agitation: due to increased serotonin and noradrenaline levels

Delirium: due to anticholinergic activity and possibly direct effects on the CNS

Chris martin, CC3.0 via Wikimedia commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

5. Tremors (jitteriness)

It is thought that tremors cause is related to serotonin and norepinephrine systems

SOURCE SLIDE 7

6. Mild elevation in liver enzymes

Because It is metabolized in the liver, and it might lead to liver damage and elevated liver enzymes

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 8

7. Sexual dysfunction

Include impaired arousal and orgasms

Caused by increased the serotonin levels

SOURCE SLIDE 9

8. Diaphoresis

Caused by noradrenergic receptor manipulation

Egon Eagle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 10

9. Hematological effects

Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and agranulocytosis

these effects are rare and it is thought that they are caused by some autoimmune mechanisms on the bone marrow precipitated by this medications

SOURCE SLIDE 11

10. Serotonin syndrome

Caused by increased the serotonin levels

Occurs in case of concurrent use with other drugs that elevate the serotonin levels like the SSRI, triptans, tramadol, lithium, St John’s wort and tryptophan

Symptoms of serotonin syndrome include altered metnal status, autonomic changes such as tachycardia and neuromuscular changes such as tremor, rigidity and myoclonus

SOURCE SLIDE 12

11. Seizures

Imipramine lowers the seizure threshold by altering the neurotransmitter levels and increases the neuronal excitability

This will increase the risk of seizures especially in susceptible people

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Intro

Adderall (Amphetamine) is a stimulant medication that is used in the treatment of ADHD, It works by increasing the amounts of dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin in the brain through variety of mechanisms

Adderall is generally well tolerated by most patients, but it sometimes may lead to side effects that will be mentioned here

Every person will have a different experience with the side effects

SOURCE SLIDE 2

1. Reduced appetite and weight loss

Higher levels of dopamine and norepinephrine will affect the hypothalamus leading to suppression of the hunger feeling

Reduced appetite lead to reduced caloric intake which ultimately lead to weight loss

In children, this may lead to slowing the growth velocity and ultimately it may lead to reduction in adult height by around 4 cm in children who consistently took the medication

SOURCE SLIDE 3

2. Increased heart rate and blood pressure

Higher levels of norepinephrine and dopamine lead to activation of the sympathetic nervous system

This will lead to activation of adrenergic receptors in the heart and blood vessels leading to elevated heart rate and blood pressure

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 4

3. Insomnia

Higher levels of dopamine and norepinephrine stimulate the CNS leading to wakefulness and inability to sleep

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 5

4. Headache

No good theory for why this happens

Jose Navarro, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 6

5. Dry mouth

Alpha adrenoceptors in the gums blood vessels get activated which lead to vasoconstriction in these blood vessels leading to less blood reaching the gums and less saliva production and dry mouth

SOURCE SLIDE 7

6. Anxiety

Increased CNS activity can induce the feeling of anxiety

SOURCE SLIDE 8

7. Vertigo

Altered levels of neurotransmitters can affect the vestibular system leading to vertigo

http://www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

SOURCE SLIDE 9

8. GIT side effects

Nausea and vomiting

That is because Increased norepinephrine levels also affects the enteric nervous system leading to nausea and vomiting

Also Elevated norepinephrine levels may stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brain leading to nausea and vomiting

SOURCE SLIDE 10

9. Sexual side effects

Those include erectile dysfunction, frequent and prolonged erections

Norepinephrine can affect the alpha adrenergic receptors in the genital region, which can affect blood flow and nerve signaling leading to sexual side effects

SOURCE SLIDE 11

10. Respiratory side effects

Amphetamine stimulates the medullary respiratory centers producing faster and deeper breaths

In normal therapeutic doses for ADHD , this effect is not noticeable but in higher doses it become obvious

SOURCE SLIDE 12

11. Urinary side effects

Activation of the alpha adrenergic receptors in the urinary bladder lead to contraction of the bladder sphincter leading to difficulty urinating

SOURCE SLIDE 13

12. Mood Swings

Higher levels of norepinephrine in certain brain regions lead to mood swings

Chris martin, CC3.0 via Wikimedia commons

SOURCE SLIDE 14

13. Tics and uncontrolled movements

Higher dopamine levels can affect the motor pathways in the brain

This may lead to development or exacerbation of motor tics

SOURCE SLIDE 15

14. Psychosis

Delusions and hallucinations

High levels of dopamine can lead to psychotic symptoms, this occur especially with higher doses of the medications

SOURCE SLIDE 16

15. Seizures

Adderall lowers the seizure threshold by altering the neurotransmitter levels and increases the neuronal excitability

This will increase the risk of seizures especially in susceptible people

SOURCE SLIDE 17

16. Cognitive effects

Long term overstimulation of the brain neurotransmitter systems may lead to cognitive deficits

SOURCE SLIDE 18

17. Dependency

Higher levels of dopamine in the brain produce a euphoric effect

Euphoric effect lead to psychological dependence and potential abuse

Euphoric effect require larger doses to be achieved

SOURCE SLIDE 19

18. Tolerance and withdrawal

Tolerance means with chronic use, higher doses of the medication are needed to achieve the same effect

Withdrawal means sudden withdrawal of the medication lead to withdrawal symptoms like fatigue, depression, sleep disturbances …

Strattera is metabolized in the liver and in rare cases it may cause damage to the liver

There might be an immune mediated component of the Strattera hepatotoxicity

Decreased libido in males and females, weak erections and difficulty ejaculating in males

Norepinephrine can affect the alpha adrenergic receptors in the genital region, which can affect blood flow and nerve signaling leading to sexual side effects

8. Allergic reactions

Ranges from mild rashes to severe angioedema

Higher levels of norepinephrine may suppress the appetite centers in the hypothalamus leading to anorexia and weight loss

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Clozapine is antipsychotic medication that is used in treatment of schizophrenia

It work by antagonizing serotonin receptors, dopamine receptors , it also antagonizes muscarinic receptors and alpha adrenergic receptors

Here we will talk about 3 most serious side effects of this medication

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Agranulocytosis

Agranulocytosis is severe decrease in granulocyte count in the blood, granulocytes are neutrophils, basophils and eosinophils which are white blood cells,

Granulocytes are related to immune system and fighting infections

Once there numbers decrease this lead to increase liability to infections , Symptoms include fever, rigors, sore throat, pneumonia , UTI and sepsis

It is caused by bone marrow suppression done by the clozapine , this occurs in 1% of people taking clozapine

Risk factors for developing agranulocytosis while taking clozapine include: old age, female gender, concurrent treatment with medications that lead to the same condition

Agranulocytosis maybe fatal

SOURCE SLIDE 4

GIT hypomotility

GIT hypomotility is decreased contractile forces or slower transit of the gi tract

This occur due to the antimuscarinic effects of the clozapine

This will lead to constipation, fecal impaction, paralytic ileus , bowel obstruction , acute megacolon, ischemia or necrosis

This is also might be fatal

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Myocarditis

Inflammation of the heart muscle , in 3 % of cases

Myocarditis symptoms include chest pain, fatigue, edema , arrhtymias SOB

Risk factors include rapid titration of the drug, concurrent use of SSRIs , illicit substance abuse

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Hypersalivation

Not a serious side effects

Most common , occur in 60% of patients, because clozapine is agonist in M4 which is highly expressed in salivary glands

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Clozapine also lead to weight gain and high blood sugar because of serotonin antagonism

It may lead to postural hypotension and palpitation due to blocking of alpha adrenergic receptors

Clozapine also lead to elevated temperature , sedation, and urinary retention due to its anticholinergic effects

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Statin are lipid lowering medications that are used in treatment of hyperlipidemia and atherosclerosis

Examples of these medications include atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin and fluvastatin

And here we will talk about what does these medications do to your body

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Administration

Statins are taken orally, they would go through the mouth , pharynx, esophagus, stomach and intestine where they got absorbed

After that they got distributed into the body tissues

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of action

After distribution statins work by

Statins work by inhibiting an enzyme called HMG CoA reductase =>this enzyme is involved in the production of cholesterol in the liver=> once this enzyme is inhibited, this lead to lowering the production of cholesterol

As a result there is lower total cholesterol, lower LDL concentrations (bad lipids) while increasing the HDL

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Metabolism

After that they got metabolized in the liver by CYP and after that they get excreted through urine and bile

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Side effects

Now statins are usually well tolerated but sometimes they may lead to side effects

Myopathy: damage to the muscles, manifest as muscle pain or weakness, treated by stopping the medication

Hepatotoxicity: elevation of liver enzymes with statin use is a possible side effect, this might lead to hepatocellular liver injury, manifest as weakness, fatigue, jaundice or dark colored urine

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Side effects

Diabetes mellitus, statin therapy also associated with increased risk of developing a new onset diabetes

Statin rarely associated with statin associated cognitive dysfunction

Acetaminophen is analgesic antipyretic used in treatment of mild to moderate pain and fever, it work by inhibiting the prostaglandin synthesis in the brain

Acetaminophen is well tolerated by most people

But some times it may lead to side effects which we will talk about here

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Liver damage

Acetaminophen is metabolized in the liver and it can be toxic to the liver when taken In high doses

Even in normal doses there is risk for hepatotoxicity

Liver damage may manifest as acute liver failure

Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, sweating, confusion, abdominal pain and yellowish discoloration of skin and eyes

SOURCE SLIDE 4

blood disorders

Anemia, leukopenia, neutropenia, pancytopenia

Symptoms of these conditions include unusual bleeding or bruising, fatigue and increased susceptibility to infections

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Electrolyte imbalances

Such as decreased serum bicarbonate, reduced concentrations of sodium and calcium, hyperammonemia, hyperchloremia, hyperuricemia , increase serum glucose and elevated levels of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Hypersensitivity reactions (Allergic reactions)

Skin rash , itching, swelling of the face, tongue or throat, trouble breathing

toxic epidermal necrolysis, SJ syndrome

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Other side effects

Abdominal pain

Nausea and vomiting

Increased risk for GIT bleeding

Increased risk for stroke and MI

Rarely may lead to drug induced lung injury

Rarely may lead to kidney impairment characterized by elevated urea and creatinine

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Amlodipine is antihypertensive medication that works by blocking all types of voltage gated Calcium channels in blood vessels to dilate these vessels and reduce blood pressure

Here we will talk about the 6 contraindications of amlodipine

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Hypersensitivity reactions (allergic reactions)

Patient with known Hypersensitivity to amlodipine

Allergic reactions include: Rash, itching, hives, swelling of the face, lips tongue or throat , SJS

This is an absolute contraindicated

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Unstable angina

Relative contraindication

Amlodipine cause reflex tachycardia which would be harmful to the heart in unstable angina leading to increase in myocardial oxygen demand and worsening ischemia

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Severe hypotension

Relative contraindication

Amlodipine further reduce blood pressure leading to vital organ hypoperfusion and syncope

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Cardiogenic shock

Relative contraindication

In cardiogenic shock , the heart can’t pump blood effectively and this is exacerbated by the vasodilatation caused by the amlodipine,

Because vasoditation means more blood flow required and more stress on the heart

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Severe aortic stenosis

The left ventricle is already exhausted from pumping blood through the stenosed aortic valve

Amlodipine causes vasodilatation (more blood flow required to be pumped through the stenosed valve leading to ventricular collapse and dysfunction

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Hepatic impairment

Relative contraindication

Metabolized by hepatic CYP enzyme system (CYP 3A4 ) , in hepatic impairment can’t be metabolized and will cause accumulation and toxicity

Can be solved by dose adjustment

itlm6w0M2W0.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Major locations of ion and water exchange in the nephron and action sites of diuretics

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Slide 2

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Slide 3

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Slide 2

Blood enters the nephron from the afferent arteriole to the glomerular tuft and then goes out to the efferent arteriole, the water that going to the bowman capsule is called GFR and normal value is about 125 ml/min,

If we multiply 125 to 60 to 24 we would get the total amount of filtrate per day which is about 180 l/d

The filtrate contains water, different organic compounds, ions except for proteins because the glomerular basement membrane won’t allow it to

And 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed again and that’s why our urine volume don’t exceed 1.5 liters per day

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Water is reabsorbed passively and it almost always moves with sodium (salt and water)

65% of filtraeted sodium is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule and of course same amount of water is reabsorbed too, proximal convoluted tubule also actively reabsorbs k, ca, mg, amino acids, organic compounds

Also in proximal convoluted tubule there is secretion of compounds like uric acid which reabsorbed again by the proximal convoluted tubule

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Tubular fluid moves after the proximal tubule into the descending part of henle

Then into the ascending part where the na is reabsorbed by 25% by NaKcc2 transporter and also the part where majority of ca and mg is reabsorbed

The ascending part of loop of henle is impermeable to water, so the descending part is going to absorb the 25% of water

Soo loop of henle absorbe 25% of sodium and water

The filtrate moves to the distal convoluted tubule

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Slide 5

By the proximal part of distal convoluted tubule 5-7 % of water and sodium are reabsorbed by na cl transporter and the rest of ca is reabsorbed there by the help of parathyroid hormone

By the distal part of distal convoluted tubule 2- 5% of sodium and water are reabsorbed there by the help of aldosterone in expense of potassium and hydrogen

And there rest of water is reabsorbed by ADH in collecting duct

SOURCE SLIDE 6

So diuretics are drugs that make kidney lose water but to make it do that, they have to make it lose sodium in the beginning

We have loop diuretics that work on nakcc2 in loop of henle and that lead to lose of na cl k and water and ca and mg and hydrogen ion

Thizides work on nacl transporter in distal convoluted tubule in lead to lose of na and cl and water

Potassium sparing diuretics work on aldosterone to lose na and h2o and conserve hydrogen and potassium

Y6Qf_lb3oKc.html:
SOURCE SLIDE 1

Alpha Blockers

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Definition

Drugs that competitively or irreversibly blocks the alpha receptors

Alpha receptors activation lead to smooth muscle contraction

Norepinephrine has higher affinity to alpha receptors compared to epinephrine

Alpha 1 receptors are Gq protein coupled located on the vessels walls, iris dilator muscle, prostate, urethral sphincter, pylorus, and anal sphincter and their activation lead to contraction of these smooth muscles

Alpha 2 receptors are Gi protein coupled and they located on the sympathetic post ganglionic pre synaptic nerve terminals and when activated they inhibit the release of norepinephrine to the presynaptic

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Mechanism of action

Blocks alpha adrenoceptors causes decrease in the sympathetic tone of the blood vessels

Decreased peripheral vascular resistance and decrease in blood pressure

Reflex tachycardia

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Phenoxybenzamine

Non selective inhibitor

Irreversible non competitive inhibition

Its effect last until the body synthesize new adrenoceptors which is about 24 hours

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Phenoxybenzamine

Therapeutic uses

Pheochromocytoma

Raynaud disease and frostbite

Adverse effects

Postural hypotension

Cardiac stimulation (more cardiac output and reflex tachycardia)

Nasal stuffiness

May inhibit ejaculation

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Phentolamine

Non selective

Competitive

Last for four hours after single injection

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Phentolamine

Uses

Pheochromocytoma

Treatment of hypertensive crisis due to abrupt withdrawal of clonidine, clonidine is alpha 2 agonist

To reverse local anesthesia in soft tissue sites; local anesthetics are often given with vasoconstrictors that slow their removal. Local phentolamine permits reversal at the end of the procedure

Adverse effects

Cardiac stimulation (more cardiac output and reflex tachycardia)

arrhythmias and anginal pain

SOURCE SLIDE 1

Proton Pump Inhibitors

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 2

Mechanism of Action

PPIs are prodrugs with enteric coating

They get absorbed in the intestine to blood

PPIs work on the parietal cells in the stomach

PPIs irreversibly inhibit gastric hydrogen potassium ATPase (H+/K+) ATPase Which is the final step of acid secretion in the stomach

that is why PPIs are the most effective at inhibiting gastric acid

PPIs have short half lives (around 1.5 hours) but acid inhibition lasts up to 24 hours because of irreversible inactivation of the proton pumps

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 4

6 PPI agents

Omeprazole

Esomeprazole

Lansoprazole

Dexlansoprazole

Rabeprazole

Pantoprazole

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 5

PPIs clinical uses

GERD, erosive esophagitis

Peptic ulcer disease

H pylori infection

NSAID-associated ulcers

GIT bleeding due to ulcer

Non ulcer dyspepsia

Gastrinoma and hypersecretory conditions

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Adverse Effects

Nausea, Diarrhea, Headache, GI disturbance

Decrease effectiveness of some drugs like clopidogrel when used with omeprazole and esomeprazole. Because they inhibit CYP2C19 which is involved in converting clopidogrel to its active metabolites

Increase risk of fractures

Decrease vitamin B12 absorption

Increase gastric cancer risk

YouTube: Mustafa Salahalden

SOURCE SLIDE 3

Uses of NSAIDs

Used in inflammation and for pain

May be used for mild antipyretic effect

Has been used to inhibit polyp formation in familial adenomatous polyposis

Long term use reduce the risk of colon cancer through unknown mechanism

SOURCE SLIDE 4

Mechanism of Action

NSAIDs have anti-inflammatory activity that is chiefly mediated by inhibition of prostaglandin biosynthesis

There is non selective NSAIDs and those work by inhibiting COX 1 and COX 2 and there is new agents which are selective for inhibiting COX 2 only

SOURCE SLIDE 5

Cyclooxygenase 1 and 2

COX 1 regulates normal cellular processes, such as gastric cytoprotection, vascular homeostasis, platelets aggregation, and reproductive and kidney functions

COX 2 expressed in tissues such as the brain , kidney and bone. It is expression at other sites is increased during states of chronic inflammation

Inhibition of COX 2 is thought to lead to the anti inflammatory and analgesic action of NSAIDs while inhibition of COX 1 leads to most of the side effects

SOURCE SLIDE 6

Selective NSAIDs

So they synthesized COX 2 selective NSAIDs which had the same efficacy to reduce pain and inflammation as it for the non selective NSAIDs and had improved GIT safety and reduced risk of bleeding

But these drugs had increased in incidence of edema, hypertension and possibly myocardial infarction which made their use limited

SOURCE SLIDE 7

Examples

Non selective

Aspirin

Diclofenac

Ibuprofen

Naproxen

Mefenamic acid

Indomethacin

Ketoprofen

Piroxicam

Selective

Celecoxib

Meloxicam

SOURCE SLIDE 8

Adverse Effects

Gastrointestinal

Increased risk of bleeding

Actions on the kidney

Cardiac effects

Drug interactions

Toxicity
